blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Derflow as a solution to the notoriously difficult problem of reasoning about correctness in distributed applications by introducing determinism into concurrent programming. The paper proposes a distributed single-assignment data store built on Riak Core, where variables are assigned once and never changed, ensuring that programs with the same inputs always produce the same outputs. Derflow supports streaming data via lists of dataflow variables and includes mechanisms for handling failures deterministically by restarting failed processes without altering outcomes. The blog post notes that while the model is easy to understand and provides strong guarantees, it remains unclear whether the restrictions imposed by determinism would feel limiting in real-world systems. The paper also situates Derflow within the broader context of Kahn Process Networks, which historically struggled to gain mainstream adoption despite their theoretical advantages.
paper_title: Derflow: Distributed Deterministic Dataflow programming for Erlang
paper_abstract: Erlang implements a message-passing execution model in which concurrent processes send each other messages asynchronously. This model is inherently non-deterministic: a process can receive messages sent by any process which knows its process identifier, leading to an exponential number of possible executions based on the number messages received. Concurrent programs in nondeterministic languages are notoriously hard to prove correct and have led to well-known disasters. Furthermore, Erlang natively provides distribution and process clustering. This enables processes to asynchronously communicate between different virtual machines across the network, which increases the potential non-determinism. We propose a new execution model for Erlang, “Deterministic Dataflow Programming”, based on a highly available, scalable single-assignment data store implemented on top of the riak core distributed systems framework. This execution model provides concurrent communication between Erlang processes, yet has no observable non-determinism. Given the same input values, a deterministic dataflow program will always return the same output values, or never return; liveness under failures is sacrificed to ensure safety. Our proposal provides a distributed deterministic dataflow solution that operates transparently over distributed Erlang, providing the ability to have highly-available, fault-tolerant, deterministic computations.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights 'Blazes' by Alvaro et al. (2014) as a novel approach to addressing the critical issue of distributed consistency in fault-tolerant systems. The paper introduces a dataflow-based model to analyze coordination requirements in distributed programs, determining the minimal coordination needed to avoid anomalies like run, instance, and divergent anomalies. Blazes leverages component annotations (e.g., Confluent, Order-Sensitive) and stream punctuations (sealing) to infer coordination strategies, generating code to enforce them. The key insight is that many systems can achieve consistency without costly global ordering, instead using efficient point-to-point communication (sealing) or replication. The blog emphasizes Blazes' potential to improve performance by eliminating over-cautious coordination, with throughput gains of up to 3x in larger clusters. Colyer also notes its complementarity to tools like TLA+ and its potential to guide data placement strategies.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights F1, Google's distributed SQL database designed to replace MySQL for the AdWords business. The paper stands out for its candid discussion of system design decisions and their implications for developers, emphasizing the importance of full ACID transactional consistency to avoid burdening developers with eventual consistency issues. Colyer praises F1's ability to achieve scalability, availability, consistency, and usability—goals often considered mutually exclusive—by building on Spanner and making trade-offs like higher CPU usage for developer-friendly features. Key insights include hierarchical schema design, Protocol Buffers integration, non-blocking schema changes, and a first-class change history mechanism. The paper also discusses the need for a new ORM approach tailored for distributed systems, avoiding common anti-patterns.
paper_title: F1: A Distributed SQL Database That Scales
paper_abstract: F1 is a distributed relational database system built at Google to support the AdWords business. F1 is a hybrid database that combines high availability, the scalability of NoSQL systems like Bigtable, and the consistency and usability of traditional SQL databases. F1 is built on Spanner, which provides synchronous cross-datacenter replication and strong consistency. Synchronous replication implies higher commit latency, but we mitigate that latency by using a hierarchical schema model with structured data types and through smart application design. F1 also includes a fully functional distributed SQL query engine and automatic change tracking and publishing.

figures.caption: The basic architecture of the F1 system, with servers in two datacenters.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Google's F1 database system's innovative approach to online, asynchronous schema changes as a key advancement for large-scale distributed SQL databases. The paper addresses the challenge of schema evolution in a massively distributed relational store without global synchronization, ensuring full data availability, minimal performance impact, and rapid development cycles. Colyer emphasizes the clever use of intermediate schema states—delete-only and write-only—to prevent data anomalies like orphan data or integrity violations during schema transitions. The formal modeling of the schema change process also helped uncover subtle bugs in production, demonstrating the value of formal methods in distributed systems. The solution's asynchronous nature and support for multiple schema versions simultaneously make it particularly noteworthy for systems requiring zero downtime and continuous evolution.
paper_title: Online, Asynchronous Schema Change in F1
paper_abstract: We introduce a protocol for schema evolution in a globally distributed database management system with shared data, stateless servers, and no global membership. Our protocol is asynchronous—it allows different servers in the database system to transition to a new schema at different times—and online—all servers can access and update all data during a schema change. We provide a formal model for determining the correctness of schema changes under these conditions, and we demonstrate that many common schema changes can cause anomalies and database corruption. We avoid these problems by replacing corruption-causing schema changes with a sequence of schema changes that is guaranteed to avoid corrupting the database so long as all servers are no more than one schema version behind at any time. Finally, we discuss a practical implementation of our protocol in F1, the database management system that stores data for Google AdWords.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights three key stories from Google's Spanner paper: 1) Google's experiences with MySQL and eventual consistency, noting how developer choices shaped system design—manual sharding was painful, eventual consistency was avoided where possible, and SQL-like interfaces remained popular. 2) The TrueTime API, which leverages accurate time intervals to simplify distributed system design by reifying clock uncertainty, enabling stronger time semantics with minimal overhead. 3) Spanner itself as a globally distributed database, addressing challenges like manual sharding, synchronous replication, and strong transactional semantics. Colyer emphasizes lessons learned from Google's internal experiments, such as the importance of avoiding manual sharding, the trade-offs of eventual consistency, the enduring value of SQL, and the simplification brought by transactions.
paper_title: Spanner: Google’s Globally-Distributed Database
paper_abstract: Spanner is Google’s scalable, multi-version, globallydistributed, and synchronously-replicated database. It is the first system to distribute data at global scale and support externally-consistent distributed transactions. This paper describes how Spanner is structured, its feature set, the rationale underlying various design decisions, and a novel time API that exposes clock uncertainty. This API and its implementation are critical to supporting external consistency and a variety of powerful features: nonblocking reads in the past, lock-free read-only transactions, and atomic schema changes, across all of Spanner.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this paper as a fascinating historical account of the Internet's early development, told directly by the key people involved. The paper traces the evolution from J.C.R. Licklider's 1962 'Galactic Network' concept to the ARPANET's first nodes in 1969, the introduction of email in 1972, and the eventual development of TCP/IP. Colyer notes the paper's emphasis on the technical milestones (like packet switching, ARPANET's first connections, and the shift from NCP to TCP/IP) as well as the social and organizational factors that drove adoption, such as the RFC process, Unix BSD integration, and the role of email. The key insight is how the Internet's open, decentralized architecture and collaborative development model enabled its rapid growth and eventual ubiquity.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Leslie Lamport's paper as a guide to modernizing mathematical proofs by introducing structure and rigor. Lamport argues that traditional prose-based proofs are error-prone and advocates for a structured approach that formalizes the roles of statements, uses clear naming, and employs hierarchical numbering to prevent scoping errors. The paper demonstrates this method by reworking a proof from Spivak's calculus textbook, revealing unstated assumptions and implications in the original. Lamport also introduces TLA+, a language designed for structured proofs in computer science, which he later adapted for mathematical contexts. The blog emphasizes that structured proofs make it easier to avoid errors, improve clarity, and can be adopted incrementally by mathematicians and computer scientists alike.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the Mirage project's approach to optimizing operating systems for cloud environments by introducing unikernels—library operating systems compiled into a single-purpose VM image. Adrian Colyer highlights the key insight that hypervisors provide a scalable virtual hardware abstraction, enabling library OSs to break up monolithic OS designs. The post emphasizes the benefits of Mirage's extreme specialization, including significant performance improvements, enhanced security, and drastically reduced binary sizes (e.g., a Mirage DNS server image of just 200KB compared to 400MB for BIND). The author notes the trade-offs, such as sacrificing backward compatibility and requiring OCaml for application development, but argues that the gains in security (via sealing and compile-time address space randomization) and performance justify the approach. Mirage's fast boot times (under 50ms) and competitive networking performance are also highlighted as notable achievements.
paper_title: Unikernels: Library Operating Systems for the Cloud
paper_abstract: Conﬁguration Files We present unikernels, a new approach to deploying cloud services via applications written in high-level source code. Unikernels are single-purpose appliances that are compile-time specialised into standalone kernels, and sealed against modification when deployed to a cloud platform. In return they offer significant reduction in image sizes, improved efficiency and security, and should reduce operational costs. Our Mirage prototype compiles OCaml code into unikernels that run on commodity clouds and offer an order of magnitude reduction in code size without significant performance penalty. The architecture combines static type-safety with a single address-space layout that can be made immutable via a hypervisor extension. Mirage contributes a suite of type-safe protocol libraries, and our results demonstrate that the hypervisor is a platform that overcomes the hardware compatibility issues that have made past library operating systems impractical to deploy in the real-world.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Irmin, an OCaml implementation of mergeable persistent data structures that brings Git-like version control to application data. The key insight is to leverage existing DVCS tools (clone, push, pull, branch, etc.) to manage mutable persistent data structures, enabling inspection, cloning, and reverting of states. Irmin uses Git's repository format and exposes DVCS operations as a library for OCaml applications, with bidirectional mapping to Git for tool compatibility. The paper explores merge mechanisms (CRDTs, data-structure-specific merges, or developer-defined) and delves into mergeable implementations of a queue and a rope (a binary tree-based string structure). The performance cost is noted as a factor of 5, and the blog appreciates the elegance of applying DVCS principles to application data. The mergeable queue and rope sections detail how conflicts are resolved and merged, with the rope's merge operation leveraging subtree comparisons and user-defined merge functions.
paper_title: Mergeable persistent data structures
paper_abstract: Irmin is an OCaml library to design purely functional data structures that can be persisted on disk and be merged and synchronized efficiently. In this paper, we focus on the merge aspect of the library and present two data structures built on top of Irmin: (i) queues and (ii) ropes that extend the corresponding purely functional data structures with a 3-way merge operation. We provide early theoretical and practical complexity results for these new data structures. Irmin is available as open-source code as part of the MirageOS project.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the critical importance of tail latency in large-scale distributed systems, a concept he terms 'tail-tolerance.' The blog post emphasizes how even small percentages of slow requests can disproportionately impact overall system performance, especially when requests fan out across many servers. For example, a system with 100 servers each having a 1% chance of a slow request can result in 63% of user requests experiencing delays. The post underscores that the slowest 5% of requests often account for half of the total 99th-percentile latency, making outliers a major performance bottleneck. Dean and Barroso argue that traditional fault-tolerance techniques are insufficient for addressing latency variability and propose seven design patterns to enhance tail tolerance, including hedged requests, tied requests, micro-partitioning, and canary requests. These techniques aim to mitigate the impact of slow outliers while maintaining system responsiveness.
paper_title: The Tail at Scale
paper_abstract: Low-latency message delivery is crucial for real-time systems. Data originating from a producer must be delivered to consumers, potentially distributed in clusters across metropolitan and continental boundaries. With the growing scale of computing, there can be several thousand consumers of the data. Such systems require a robust messaging system capable of transmitting messages containing data across clusters and efficiently delivering them to consumers. The system must offer guarantees like ordering and at-least-once delivery while avoiding overload on consumers, allowing them to consume messages at their own pace. This paper presents the design of Fast ACS (an abbreviation for Ads Copy Service), a file-based ordered message delivery system that leverages a combination of two-sided (intercluster) and one-sided (intra-cluster) communication primitives—namely, Remote Procedure Call and Remote Memory Access, respectively—to deliver messages. The system has been successfully deployed to dozens of production clusters and scales to accommodate several thousand consumers within each cluster, which amounts to Tbps-scale intra-cluster consumer traffic at peak. Notably, Fast ACS delivers messages to consumers across the globe within a few seconds or even sub-seconds (p99) based on the message volume and consumer scale, at a low resource cost.

figures.title: Kafka consumer-scaling experiment results
figures.caption: Results for Kafka consumer-scaling experiment. As consumers scaled, the consumer throughput went up to 14 Gbps, after which the performance degraded.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Alan Perlis' 1982 collection of epigrams on programming as a classic and timeless work. He notes that the paper consists of 120 concise, memorable statements that capture insights about programming, software engineering, and the nature of computing. Colyer shares ten of his favorite epigrams, praising their wit, wisdom, and relevance, and encourages readers to explore the full list. The blog post frames these epigrams as early examples of 'tweets' before the term existed, emphasizing their brevity and impact.

blog_summary: Mesa is Google's highly scalable, geo-replicated data warehousing system designed to handle petabytes of data, process millions of row updates per second, and serve billions of queries fetching trillions of rows daily. Adrian highlights Mesa's ability to provide consistent and repeatable query results at low latency, even during datacenter failures, as a key achievement. The paper emphasizes Mesa's versioning and delta-based aggregation mechanisms, which enable efficient updates and queries without locking, leveraging asynchronous processing and Paxos-based metadata replication. The system's decoupled update and query subsystems, along with its multi-level delta compaction policies, are noted as noteworthy design choices that contribute to its scalability and performance. Additionally, the blog underscores Mesa's robust data verification processes to handle transient hardware/software faults, a critical challenge at Google's scale.
paper_title: Mesa: Geo-Replicated, Near Real-Time, Scalable Data Warehousing
paper_abstract: Mesa is a highly scalable analytic data warehousing system that stores critical measurement data related to Google’s Internet advertising business. Mesa is designed to satisfy a complex and challenging set of user and systems requirements, including near real-time data ingestion and queryability, as well as high availability, reliability, fault tolerance, and scalability for large data and query volumes. Specifically, Mesa handles petabytes of data, processes millions of row updates per second, and serves billions of queries that fetch trillions of rows per day. Mesa is geo-replicated across multiple datacenters and provides consistent and repeatable query answers at low latency, even when an entire datacenter fails. This paper presents the Mesa system and reports the performance and scale that it achieves.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the paper 'Architecture of a Database System' by Hellerstein, Stonebraker, and Hamilton, highlighting it as an essential read for understanding database system architecture. The paper blends academic rigor with industrial experience, offering a guided tour through the main subsystems of a relational database management system (circa 2007), including process models, parallel architecture, storage systems, transaction systems, and query processors. Colyer praises the paper's wisdom, accessibility, and practical insights, noting its importance in preventing the repetition of historical mistakes in DBMS design. Key topics include process models (process-per-worker, thread-per-worker, process/thread pools), admission control for overload management, parallel architectures (shared-memory, shared-disk, shared-nothing), and the relational query processor's components (parser, rewriter, optimizer, executor). The paper also delves into storage management, emphasizing the DBMS's role in controlling data placement and I/O timing, and discusses the iterator model for query execution.
paper_title: Architecture of a Database System
paper_abstract: Database Management Systems (DBMSs) are a ubiquitous and critical component of modern computing, and the result of decades of research and development in both academia and industry. Historically, DBMSs were among the earliest multi-user server systems to be developed, and thus pioneered many systems design techniques for scalability and reliability now in use in many other contexts. While many of the algorithms and abstractions used by a DBMS are textbook material, there has been relatively sparse coverage in the literature of the systems design issues that make a DBMS work. This paper presents an architectural discussion of DBMS design principles, including process models, parallel architecture, storage system design, transaction system implementation, query processor and optimizer architectures, and typical shared components and utilities. Successful commercial and open-source systems are used as points of reference, particularly when multiple alternative designs have been adopted by diﬀerent groups.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes a 1993 paper by Lampson and Lomet that introduces optimizations to the classic Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol. The paper first explains the 'presumed nothing' (PrN) protocol, then discusses existing optimizations like 'presumed abort' (PrA) and 'presumed commit' (PrC), before proposing a new variant of PrC that reduces message and log write costs. The key insight is a trade-off: maintaining a small amount of state (the 'Initiated Set') indefinitely to avoid expensive logging during recovery. The paper argues this trade-off is worthwhile, as the state overhead is minimal (e.g., 1MB of crash-related information would take 6 years to accumulate at 1993 disk prices). The new PrC protocol avoids ACKs for committed transactions and reduces coordinator logging, making it more efficient than PrA for commit-heavy workloads.
paper_title: A new presumed commit optimisation for two phase commit
paper_abstract: l Two phase commit (ZPC) ia used to coordinate the commitment of trunsactiom in distributed systems. The presumed commit variant of 2PC wea even fewer messages, but its coordinator must do additional logging. We describe a new form of presumed commit that reduces the number of log writes while preserving the reduction in me.+ saged, bringing both these costs below those of presumed abort. The penalty for this is the need to retain a small amount of crash related information forever.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 1988 paper by David Clark as a foundational work that explains the underlying principles and design philosophy behind the Internet protocols, rather than just describing how they work. The paper traces the evolution of the Internet's architecture from high-level goals to implementation choices, emphasizing how the design was shaped by practical constraints and trade-offs. Clark argues that understanding the 'why' behind protocol decisions is crucial for appreciating their structure. The paper is particularly notable for introducing the concept of 'fate-sharing' as a guiding principle for reliability, which led to the datagram-based design of IP and the separation of TCP and IP into distinct layers. The author also underscores how the prioritization of goals (e.g., survivability over accountability) fundamentally influenced the architecture, reflecting the military context in which the Internet was initially developed.
paper_title: The Design Philosophy of the DARPA Internet Protocols
paper_abstract: The Internet protocol suite, TCP/IP, was first proposed fifteen years ago. It was developed by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), and has been used widely in military and commercial systems. While there have been papers and specifications that describe how the protocols work, it is sometimes difficult to deduce from these why the protocol is as it is. For example, the Internet protocol is based on a connectionless or datagram mode of service. The motivation for this has been greatly misunderstood. This paper attempts to capture some of the early reasoning which shaped the Internet protocols. The Internet architecture is still evolving. Sometimes a new extension challenges one of the design principles, but in any case an understanding of the history of the design provides a necessary context for current design extensions. The connectionless configuration of ISO protocols has also been colored by the history of the Internet suite, so an understanding of the Internet design philosophy may be helpful to those working with ISO. This paper catalogs one view of the original objectives of the Internet architecture, and discusses the relation between these goals and the important features of the protocols.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the MADlib Analytics Library as a pioneering effort to bridge scalable data platforms with advanced analytics in SQL databases. He emphasizes the shift from traditional data warehousing to predictive analytics, where data scientists use iterative, interactive processes and rich statistical models directly within a DBMS. The paper introduces the MAD acronym (Magnetic, Agile, Deep) to describe this new paradigm, where databases attract diverse data, support rapid iteration, and enable deep statistical modeling. Colyer notes MADlib's innovative use of user-defined aggregates (UDAs) and functions (UDFs) to implement algorithms like linear regression, logistic regression, and k-Means efficiently within a parallel DBMS. The paper also underscores the resurgence of SQL's role in analytics, contrasting it with Hadoop's evolution. Overall, the blog post positions MADlib as a critical tool for scalable analytics in SQL environments, connecting database research with practical market needs.
paper_title: The MADlib Analytics Library - MAD Skills, the SQL
paper_abstract: Research in enriching DBs with Machine Learning (ML) models is receiving increasingly greater attention. This paper experimentally analyzes the problem of empowering data systems with (and its users with access to) regression models (RMs). The paper offers a data system’s perspective, which unveils an interesting ‘impedance mismatch ′ problem: ML models aim to offer a high expected overall prediction accuracy, which essentially assumes that queries will target data using the same distributions of the data on which the models are trained. However, in data management it is widely recognized that query distributions do not necessarily follow data distributions. Queries using selection operators target specific data subspaces on which, even an overall highly-accurate model, may be weak. If such queried subspaces are popular, large numbers of queries will suffer. The paper will reveal, shed light, and quantify this ‘impedance mismatch ′ phenomenon. It will study in detail 8 real-life data sets and data from TPC-DS and experiment with various dimensionalities therein. It will employ new appropriate metrics, substantiating the problem across a wide variety of popular RMs, ranging from simple linear models to advanced, state-of-the-art, ensembles (which enjoy excellent generalization performance). It will put forth and study a new, query-centric, model that addresses this problem, improving per-query accuracy, while also offering excellent overall accuracy. Finally, it will study the effects of scale on the problem and its solutions.

blog_summary: Dremel is Google's interactive ad-hoc query system designed to run aggregate queries over trillions of rows in seconds, scaling to thousands of CPUs and petabytes of data. Inspired by web search's serving trees, Dremel pushes queries down a tree hierarchy, rewriting them at each level and aggregating results on the way back up. It uses a SQL-like language and a column-striped storage representation with a nested data model based on Google's Protocol Buffers. The paper highlights Dremel's innovative approach to handling nested data structures by splitting them into columns and reassembling them on demand using repetition and definition levels. The blog author emphasizes the system's scalability, efficiency, and the clever encoding scheme that enables fast record assembly and parsing. Key insights include Dremel's ability to achieve near-linear scalability, its complementary use with MapReduce, and its strategies for handling large-scale datasets, such as early query termination for acceptable accuracy.
paper_title: Dremel: Interactive Analysis of Web-Scale Datasets
paper_abstract: Dremel is a scalable, interactive ad-hoc query system for analysis of read-only nested data. By combining multi-level execution trees and columnar data layout, it is capable of running aggregation queries over trillion-row tables in seconds. The system scales to thousands of CPUs and petabytes of data, and has thousands of users at Google. In this paper, we describe the architecture and implementation of Dremel, and explain how it complements MapReduce-based computing. We present a novel columnar storage representation for nested records and discuss experiments on few-thousand node instances of the system.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights ZooKeeper as a foundational coordination service for distributed systems, designed to simplify complex coordination tasks like leader elections, group membership, and resource locking. Instead of implementing specific primitives, ZooKeeper provides a minimal API that allows developers to build their own coordination protocols on top of it. The paper emphasizes ZooKeeper's high throughput (tens to hundreds of thousands of transactions per second) under read-dominated workloads, achieved through a wait-free, non-blocking design where reads are processed locally while writes use an atomic broadcast protocol for linearizability. The blog also praises ZooKeeper's asynchronous API, which enables multiple outstanding operations, and its hierarchical node structure (znodes) with ephemeral and sequential nodes for tracking session state and ordering. Colyer notes the elegance of how simple primitives can be combined to implement complex coordination mechanisms, though he cautions about the subtleties in correctness proofs for such algorithms.
paper_title: ZooKeeper: Wait-free coordination for Internet-scale systems
paper_abstract: that implement mutually exclusive access to critical resources. One approach to coordination is to develop services for each of the different coordination needs. For example, Amazon Simple Queue Service [3] focuses specifically on queuing. Other services have been developed specifically for leader election [25] and configuration [27]. Services that implement more powerful primitives can be used to implement less powerful ones. For example, Chubby [6] is a locking service with strong synchronization guarantees. Locks can then be used to implement leader election, group membership, etc. When designing our coordination service, we moved away from implementing specific primitives on the server side, and instead we opted for exposing an API that enables application developers to implement their own primitives. Such a choice led to the implementation of a coordination kernel that enables new primitives without requiring changes to the service core. This approach enables multiple forms of coordination adapted to the requirements of applications, instead of constraining developers to a fixed set of primitives. When designing the API of ZooKeeper, we moved away from blocking primitives, such as locks. Blocking primitives for a coordination service can cause, among other problems, slow or faulty clients to impact negatively the performance of faster clients. The implementation of the service itself becomes more complicated if processing requests depends on responses and failure detection of other clients. Our system, Zookeeper, hence implements an API that manipulates simple waitfree data objects organized hierarchically as in file systems. In fact, the ZooKeeper API resembles the one of any other file system, and looking at just the API signatures, ZooKeeper seems to be Chubby without the lock methods, open, and close. Implementing wait-free data objects, however, differentiates ZooKeeper significantly from systems based on blocking primitives such as locks. Although the wai...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Eraser as a dynamic data race detector for multi-threaded programs, addressing the challenge of timing-dependent data races that are hard to debug. The paper introduces two main approaches for race detection: happens-before relationships and enforcing a consistent locking discipline. Eraser adopts the latter, arguing it is simpler, more efficient, and more thorough than happens-before-based methods. The core insight is the lockset algorithm, which dynamically infers and enforces a locking discipline by tracking candidate locks for shared variables. If a variable's candidate lock set becomes empty, a race is flagged. Colyer notes the algorithm's elegance and practical refinements for handling initialization, read-only variables, and read-write locks. He also mentions false alarms and limitations, such as memory reuse and private locks, and suggests potential extensions like deadlock detection.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Paul Baran's 1962 paper as a remarkably prescient work that laid the groundwork for modern distributed systems and networking. The paper explores the survivability of networks built from unreliable components under hostile conditions, such as missile attacks, and demonstrates that distributed networks exhibit superior resilience compared to centralized or decentralized designs. Baran introduces key concepts like redundancy levels, packet-switched networks, and 'hot-potato' routing, which foreshadow modern networking paradigms. The author particularly notes Baran's early vision of a shared digital data infrastructure and his insights into building reliable systems from unreliable elements, a challenge still relevant today. The paper also discusses adaptive routing strategies and Bayesian-like forgetting procedures for maintaining network performance under attack.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Dijkstra's 1960 paper as a foundational work that introduced the concept of the stack in programming language runtimes. The paper addresses the inefficiencies and limitations of fixed storage allocation for subroutines, which prevented recursive programming. Dijkstra proposes the stack as a solution, enabling dynamic memory management where subroutines can operate in the first free stack locations, supporting parameters, local variables, and intermediate results. The key insight is the stack's ability to maintain nested activation records, allowing recursive calls and proper state preservation. Colyer emphasizes the elegance and transformative impact of this idea, which underpins modern programming language implementations.
paper_title: Recursive Programming

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the Velox project as a critical missing piece in real-world analytics pipelines, addressing the overlooked challenge of deploying, serving, and managing trained machine learning models at scale. He notes that while much focus has been placed on model training, the practical deployment and lifecycle management of models—such as identifying when models need retraining or updating—are often handled in ad-hoc ways. Velox provides a low-latency, scalable interface for serving models as services, supporting incremental maintenance and performance monitoring. The paper's key insight is the division of the learning process into online and offline phases, enabling efficient personalization and low-latency predictions while supporting sophisticated models like deep neural networks. Colyer emphasizes Velox's practical contributions, such as caching, partitioning strategies, and contextual bandit algorithms for improving model recommendations.

Actions produce additional observations that, in turn, lead to further model training. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the WANalytics paper as addressing a critical challenge in geo-distributed data processing: the inefficiency of centralizing analytics in a world where data is inherently distributed and bandwidth between data centers is a scarce resource. The paper introduces a system that optimizes both data replication and distributed execution plans to minimize wide-area network (WAN) bandwidth usage. Key innovations include caching intermediate results and computing diffs to reduce cross-data center traffic, as well as a greedy heuristic optimizer that selects execution strategies and replication policies to minimize bandwidth while respecting data sovereignty constraints. The authors demonstrate a 257x reduction in WAN bandwidth on a Microsoft production workload, showcasing the practical impact of their approach. The paper argues that centralized analytics are unsustainable due to the mismatch between data growth and cross-data center bandwidth, as well as increasing data sovereignty regulations.
paper_title: WANalytics: analytics for a geo-distributed data intensive world
paper_abstract: Large organizations today operate data centers around the globe where massive amounts of data are produced and consumed by local users. Despite their geographically diverse origin, such data must be analyzed/mined as a whole. We call the problem of supporting rich DAGs of computation across geographically distributed data Wide-Area Big-Data (WABD). To the best of our knowledge, WABD is not supported by currently deployed systems nor sufficiently studied in literature; it is addressed today by continuously copying raw data to a central location for analysis. We observe from production workloads that WABD is important for large organizations, and that centralized solutions incur substantial cross-data center network costs. We argue that these trends will only worsen as the gap between data volumes and transoceanic bandwidth widens. Further, emerging concerns over data sovereignty and privacy may trigger government regulations that can threaten the very viability of centralized solutions. To address WABD we propose WANalytics, a system that pushes computation to edge data centers, automatically optimizing workflow execution plans and replicating data when needed. Our Hadoop-based prototype delivers 257× reduction in WAN bandwidth on a production workload from Microsoft. We round out our evaluation by also demonstrating substantial gains for three standard benchmarks: TPC-CH, Berkeley Big Data, and BigBench.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses 'Liquid', a new nearline data integration stack developed at LinkedIn to address the limitations of legacy MapReduce/(H)DFS models for handling high-volume append-only data. Adrian Colyer highlights Liquid's ability to support low-latency, incremental processing with resource isolation, contrasting it with traditional batch-oriented systems like MapReduce. The key insight is the need for a unified architecture that bridges online, nearline, and offline processing while avoiding the pitfalls of Lambda and Kappa architectures. Liquid achieves this through a two-layer design: a Kafka-based messaging layer for high-availability storage and rewindability, and a Samza-based processing layer for stateful stream processing with guaranteed service levels. The system's scalability, fault tolerance, and operational robustness are emphasized, along with its real-world use cases at LinkedIn.
paper_title: Liquid: Unifying Nearline and Offline Big Data Integration
paper_abstract: With more sophisticated data-parallel processing systems, the new bottleneck in data-intensive companies shifts from the back-end data systems to the data integration stack, which is responsible for the pre-processing of data for back-end applications. The use of back-end data systems with different access latencies and data integration requirements poses new challenges that current data integration stacks based on distributed file systems—proposed a decade ago for batch-oriented processing—cannot address. In this paper, we describe Liquid, a data integration stack that provides low latency data access to support near real-time in addition to batch applications. It supports incremental processing, and is cost-efficient and highly available. Liquid has two layers: a processing layer based on a stateful stream processing model, and a messaging layer with a highly-available publish/subscribe system. We report our experience of a Liquid deployment with backend data systems at LinkedIn, a data-intensive company with over 300 million users.

figures.title: Data integration with Liquid

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews Impala, Cloudera's open-source SQL engine designed for low-latency BI and analytic workloads on Hadoop. The paper highlights Impala's architecture, which consists of three services: the main Impala daemon (impalad) for query execution and orchestration, the Statestore for metadata publish-subscribe, and the Catalog service for metadata management. The blog notes Impala's lack of support for UPDATE or DELETE operations due to HDFS limitations, classifying its SQL support as 'CRAP' (Create, Read, and APpend). Key insights include Impala's use of LLVM-based JIT compilation for performance gains (up to 5.7x speedup) and its pipelined execution model to minimize memory consumption. The paper also discusses Impala's query optimization strategies, such as join reordering and data locality exploitation.
paper_title: Impala: A modern, open-source SQL engine for Hadoop
paper_abstract: Cloudera Impala is a modern, open-source MPP SQL engine architected from the ground up for the Hadoop data processing environment. Impala provides low latency and high concurrency for BI/analytic read-mostly queries on Hadoop, not delivered by batch frameworks such as Apache Hive. This paper presents Impala from a user’s perspective, gives an overview of its architecture and main components and briefly demonstrates its superior performance compared against other popular SQL-on-Hadoop systems.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Rajwar et al.'s keynote paper from CIDR'15, which argues that modern CPUs are increasingly incorporating specialized hardware primitives to accelerate common tasks, blurring the line between general-purpose and specialized processors. The paper traces the evolution of CPU specializations—such as floating-point, SIMD, synchronization, virtualization, and cryptographic support—and extrapolates performance trends to 2020. Colyer emphasizes the growing importance of performance-per-watt improvements, thread-level parallelism, and domain-specific optimizations like transactional memory and FPGA integration. The key insight is that CPUs are evolving toward hybrid designs where general-purpose cores coexist with specialized accelerators, enabling software to leverage hardware capabilities for significant performance gains.
paper_title: Specialized Evolution of the General Purpose CPU
paper_abstract: Commodity general-purpose CPUs remain the predominant computing platform for servers. However, these CPUs continuously evolve, incorporating increasingly specialized primitives to keep up with the evolving need of critical workloads. Specialization includes support for floating-point and vectors, compression, encryption, and synchronization and threading. These CPUs now have sufficient specialized support that the term general-purpose can often be misleading. Recent announcements such as a server product with an FPGA integrated with a CPU make the possibilities even more intriguing. This paper discusses the evolution of specialization in commodity general-purpose CPUs, trade-offs from an industrial perspective, and the opportunities for software going forward.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Jon Crowcroft's philosophical argument for improving privacy through mechanisms that also enhance system resilience. The paper contrasts the centralized cloud model, which monetizes personal data, with a decentralized peer-to-peer approach that leverages diversity and distribution to achieve both resilience and privacy. Crowcroft argues that decentralization can mitigate common mode failures and reduce attack surfaces, while Metcalfe's Law suggests that such systems can achieve greater value as they grow. The paper proposes advanced coding techniques (e.g., weaving data threads) to distribute and encrypt data, making it resilient to faults and attacks. Crowcroft acknowledges past failures of similar systems but suggests that modern hardware trends (e.g., smartphones with massive storage and compute) make this approach timely. He outlines a roadmap involving resilient coding, low-overhead payments, legal frameworks, decentralized differential privacy, and faster homomorphic encryption to realize this vision.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer introduces the concept of a 'Databox' as a personal data management system owned by individuals, designed to capture, index, store, and manage personal data while enabling controlled access to third parties. The paper highlights the need for fine-grained control over data sharing, including support for privacy-preserving techniques like differential privacy and homomorphic encryption. Colyer notes that while the Databox concept is promising, practical challenges remain, such as ensuring high availability, building trust, and simplifying user interaction. The blog post also explores potential business models, including monetization alternatives where users can choose between data access for free services or privacy with monetary payments. The authors argue that Databox could reduce exposure for organizations by letting users control their sensitive data, akin to third-party payment processors handling credit card data. The Nymote project at the University of Cambridge is mentioned as a related effort exploring lifelong control of personal data.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the foundational 'Volcano-style' query processing system introduced by Graefe in 1989, which encapsulates parallelism through a novel 'exchange operator.' The paper's key insight is that parallelism can be transparently added to query processing algorithms by inserting this single operator at any point in a query tree, without requiring modifications to existing operators. The exchange operator handles all parallelism issues, including process synchronization and dataflow translation, enabling three forms of parallelism: pipelined (vertical), bushy (inter-operator), and intra-operator (partitioned). Colyer emphasizes the elegance of this approach—operators remain unaware of parallelism, and the system scales from single-process to distributed execution with minimal overhead. The paper also demonstrates practical optimizations, such as a propagation tree for process forking and data-driven flow control to prevent producer-consumer imbalance.
paper_title: Encapsulation of parallelism in the volcano query processing system
paper_abstract: -To investigate the interactions of extensibility and parallelism in database query processing, we have developed a new dataflow query execution system called Volcano. The Volcano effort provides a rich environment for research and education in database systems design, heuristics for query optimization, parallel query execution, and resource allocation. Volcano uses a standard interface between algebra operators, allowing easy addition of new operators and operator implementations. Operations on individual items, e.g., predicates, are imported into the query processing operators using support functions. The semantics of support functions is not prescribed; any data type including complex objects and any operation can be realized. Thus, Volcano is extensible with new operators, algorithms, data types, and type-specific methods. Volcano includes two novel meta-operators. The choose-plan meta-operator supports dynamic query evaluation plans that allow delaying selected optimization decisions until run-time, e.g., for embedded queries with free variables. The exchange meta-operator supports intra-operator parallelism on partitioned datasets and both vertical and horizontal inter-operator parallelism, translating between demand-driven dataflow within processes and data-driven dataflow between processes. All operators, with the exception of the exchange operator, have been designed and implemented in a single-process environment, and parallelized using the exchange operator. Even operators not yet designed can be parallelized using this new operator if they use and provide the interator interface. Thus, the issues of data manipulation and parallelism have become orthogonal, making Volcano the first implemented query execution engine that effectively combines extensibility and parallelism. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes Stonebraker et al.'s 2014 paper, which critically examines the challenges of migrating enterprise database applications to the cloud. The authors argue that while stateless components adapt well to cloud environments, stateful database workloads (OLTP, OLAP, and NoSQL) face significant hurdles due to virtualization overheads. Key concerns include I/O virtualization (e.g., file system distribution, CPU virtualization) degrading performance by an order of magnitude, and incompatibilities with traditional DBMS replication strategies. The paper also highlights labor costs (80% of total expenses) as a motivator for cloud migration, despite technical obstacles. Colyer notes the paper's pessimistic tone but praises its insightful discussion of future hardware trends, particularly the shift toward many-core CPUs and non-volatile RAM, which could disrupt traditional DBMS architectures. The authors predict the rise of in-memory databases and the eventual obsolescence of block-structured systems.
paper_title: Enterprise Database Applications and the Cloud: A difficult road ahead
paper_abstract: Two decades ago, one of us co-authored a paper commenting on the previous 40 years of data modelling research and development [188]. That paper demonstrated that the relational model (RM) and SQL are the prevailing choice for database management systems (DBMSs), despite efforts to replace either them. Instead, SQL absorbed the best ideas from these alternative approaches. We revisit this issue and argue that this same evolution has continued since 2005. Once again there have been repeated efforts to replace either SQL or the RM. But the RM continues to be the dominant data model and SQL has been extended to capture the good ideas from others. As such, we expect more of the same in the future, namely the continued evolution of SQL and relational DBMSs (RDBMSs). We also discuss DBMS implementations and argue that the major advancements have been in the RM systems, primarily driven by changing hardware characteristics.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews Google's Chubby lock service, highlighting its role as a coarse-grained locking system that evolved into a primary name service and configuration repository within Google. The paper emphasizes Chubby's design principles: distributed consensus via Paxos for fault tolerance, consistent client-side caching to reduce server load, and a familiar file system interface. Colyer notes Chubby's scalability to tens of thousands of clients, its use in primary election for systems like GFS and Bigtable, and its role in replacing ad-hoc primary election mechanisms. The blog also discusses the unexpected popularity of Chubby as a name service, contrasting it with DNS due to DNS's high load under Google's workload. The design choices, such as advisory locks and explicit invalidation caching, are praised for simplifying debugging and administration while ensuring strong consistency guarantees.
paper_title: The Chubby lock service for loosely coupled distributed systems
paper_abstract: We describe our experiences with the Chubby lock service, which is intended to provide coarse-grained locking as well as reliable (though low-volume) storage for a loosely-coupled distributed system. Chubby provides an interface much like a distributed file system with advisory locks, but the design emphasis is on availability and reliability, as opposed to high performance. Many instances of the service have been used for over a year, with several of them each handling a few tens of thousands of clients concurrently. The paper describes the initial design and expected use, compares it with actual use, and explains how the design had to be modified to accommodate the differences.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 1984 paper by Halpern and Moses as a foundational work in distributed systems, emphasizing its deep insights into the role of knowledge and common knowledge in protocol design. The paper introduces a formal framework for reasoning about knowledge states in distributed systems, using examples like the muddy children puzzle and the two generals problem to illustrate subtle differences in group knowledge. Colyer notes that the paper's hierarchy of knowledge—from unknown to common knowledge—provides a powerful tool for understanding protocol limitations and correctness. A key insight is that common knowledge requires simultaneity, which is often unattainable in real-world systems with communication delays, leading to the introduction of weakened forms like epsilon-common knowledge and eventual common knowledge. The blog post underscores the paper's importance in simplifying protocol design and proving correctness, despite its complexity.
paper_title: Knowledge and Common Knowledge in a Distributed Environment
paper_venue: Proceedings of the Third ACM Symposium on Principles of Distributed Computing (PODC '84)
paper_abstract: Reasoning about knowledge seems to play a fundamental role in distributed systems. Indeed, such reasoning is a central part of the informal intuitive arguments used in the design of distributed protocols. Communication in a distributed system can be viewed as the act of transforming the system’s state of knowledge. This paper presents a general framework for formalizing and reasoning about knowledge in distributed sys- tems. We argue that states of knowledge of groups of processors are useful concepts for the design and analysis of distributed protocols. In particular, distributed knowledge corresponds to knowledge that is “distributed” among the members of the group, while common knowledge corresponds to a fact being “publicly known”. The relationship be- tween common knowledge and a variety of desirable actions in a distributed system is illustrated. Furthermore, it is shown that, formally speaking, in practical systems com- mon knowledge cannot be attained. A number of weaker variants of common knowledge that are attainable in many cases of interest are introduced and investigated. *This is a revised and expanded version of a paper with the same title that first appeared in the Proceedings of the 3rd ACM Conference on Principles of Distributed Computing, 1984. It is essentially identical to the version that appears in Journal of the ACM 37:3, 1990, pp. 549-587. The work of the second author was supported in part by DARPA contract N00039-82-C-0250.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Linda, a distributed programming language introduced by Gelernter in 1985, as a groundbreaking model of concurrent programming that is fully distributed in both space and time. Unlike traditional models like monitors or message passing, Linda's generative communication model allows tuples to exist independently in a 'tuple space' (TS) until explicitly withdrawn, enabling space and time uncoupling. This means processes can communicate without direct knowledge of each other, and tuples persist until removed, supporting distributed sharing and continuation-passing styles. The paper introduces core operations (out, in, read) and composed statements (sequence, and, or, star), demonstrating how structured naming and inverse structured naming enable flexible and expressive distributed programming patterns. Colyer emphasizes Linda's simplicity, expressiveness, and its influence on systems like JavaSpaces.
paper_title: Generative Communication in Linda
paper_abstract: Linda is a language for programming parallel applications whose most notable feature is a distributed shared memory called tuple space. While suitable for a wide variety of programs, one shortcoming of the language as commonly defined and implemented is a lack of support for writing programs that can tolerate failures in the underlying computing platform. This paper describes FT-Linda, a version of Linda that addresses this problem by providing two major enhancements that facilitate the writing of fault-tolerant applications: stable tuple spaces and atomic execution of tuple space operations. The former is a type of stable storage in which tuple values are guaranteed to persist across failures, while the latter allows collections of tuple operations to be executed in an all-or-nothing fashion despite failures and concurrency. The design of these enhancements is presented in detail and illustrated by examples drawn from both the Linda and fault-tolerance domains. An implementation of FT-Linda for a network of workstations is also described. The design is based on replicating the contents of stable tuple spaces to provide failure resilience and then updating the copies using atomic multicast. This strategy allows an efficient implementation in which only a single multicast message is needed for each atomic collection of tuple space operations.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the 2002 paper 'TAG: A Tiny Aggregation Service for ad-hoc Sensor Networks' as a remarkably prescient work that addresses the efficient processing of aggregate queries in wireless sensor networks. He emphasizes the paper's relevance to modern IoT applications and its innovative approach to minimizing communication and power consumption by computing aggregates in-network rather than centrally. The blog post praises the use of a declarative SQL-like query language for sensor networks, which enables independent planning and optimization, and demonstrates how TAG's tree-based routing and aggregate processing techniques can achieve order-of-magnitude improvements over naive broadcast schemes. Colyer also underscores the paper's broader significance, showcasing the database community's contributions to efficient data processing across diverse domains.
paper_title: TAG: A Tiny Aggregation Service for ad-hoc Sensor Networks
paper_venue: ACM SIGMOD International Conference on Management of Data (SIGMOD)
paper_abstract: We present the Tiny AGgregation (TAG) service for aggregation in low-power, distributed, wireless environments. TAG allows users to express simple, declarative queries and have them distributed and executed efficiently in networks of low-power, wireless sensors. We discuss various generic properties of aggregates, and show how those properties affect the performance of our in network approach. We include a performance study demonstrating the advantages of our approach over traditional centralized, out-of-network methods, and discuss a variety of optimizations for improving the performance and faulttolerance of the basic solution.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the paper's introduction of 'Broadcast Disks' as a novel push-based architecture to address asymmetric communication environments where downstream bandwidth far exceeds upstream capacity. The key insight is that servers can exploit their bandwidth advantage by broadcasting data to multiple clients, replacing traditional pull-based systems which are ill-suited for such scenarios. The paper explores constructing optimal broadcast schedules by prioritizing popular data items and managing client caches in this push-based model. Colyer notes the paper's practical relevance to scenarios like stock prices or weather updates, and its foundational ideas in data management for asymmetric networks. The authors also propose LIX, an extension to LRU caching, to adapt client-side caching strategies to the broadcast medium by accounting for broadcast frequency.
paper_title: Broadcast Disks: Data Management for Asymmetric Communication Environments

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Edelweiss as a groundbreaking approach to building distributed systems by automating storage reclamation through formal methods. The paper introduces a sublanguage of Bloom that eliminates mutation and deletion primitives, focusing instead on immutable state and Event Log Exchange (ELE) to preserve correctness while improving efficiency. Edelweiss automatically generates garbage collection logic, simplifying program design and making systems more declarative. The author praises the paper for its concise introduction to Bloom, demonstrating how Edelweiss can generate efficient implementations (e.g., a 19-line Edelweiss program for a distributed key-value store vs. a 13Kloc C++ implementation) while maintaining correctness. The refinement rules, like ARM (Avoiding Redundant Messages), showcase how Edelweiss optimizes programs without altering their semantics, making it a valuable tool for both practitioners and academics.
paper_title: Edelweiss: Automatic storage reclamation for distributed programming
paper_abstract: Event Log Exchange (ELE) is a common programming pattern based on immutable state and messaging. ELE sidesteps traditional challenges in distributed consistency, at the expense of introducing new challenges in designing space reclamation protocols to avoid consuming unbounded storage. We introduce Edelweiss, a sublanguage of Bloom that provides an ELE programming model, yet automatically reclaims space without programmer assistance. We describe techniques to analyze Edelweiss programs and automatically generate application-specific distributed space reclamation logic. We show how Edelweiss can be used to elegantly implement a variety of communication and distributed storage protocols; the storage reclamation code generated by Edelweiss effectively garbage-collects state and often matches hand-written protocols from the literature.

blog_summary: DroidSafe is a static analysis tool designed to detect sensitive information leaks in Android applications with remarkable accuracy. Unlike previous state-of-the-art tools, which detect less than 10% of malicious flows, DroidSafe identifies all 69 malicious information leaks in 24 real-world Android apps that were augmented by hostile Red Teams. The tool handles the complexity of the Android API (over 3,500 classes and 1.3 million lines of code) by developing an integrated model and analysis framework, including accurate stubs for native methods, event callbacks, and hidden runtime state. At its core, DroidSafe uses a Points-to Analysis (PTA) method with object sensitivity to track data flows, optimized to handle large applications within memory constraints. The analysis achieves high precision and recall, outperforming existing tools like FlowDroid+IccTA by a significant margin.
paper_title: Information-Flow Analysis of Android Applications in DroidSafe
paper_abstract: —We present DroidSafe, a static information flow analysis tool that reports potential leaks of sensitive information in Android applications. DroidSafe combines a comprehensive, accurate, and precise model of the Android runtime with static analysis design decisions that enable the DroidSafe analyses to scale to analyze this model. This combination is enabled by accurate analysis stubs, a technique that enables the effective analysis of code whose complete semantics lies outside the scope of Java, and by a combination of analyses that together can statically resolve communication targets identified by dynamically constructed values such as strings and class designators. Our experimental results demonstrate that 1) DroidSafe achieves unprecedented precision and accuracy for Android information flow analysis (as measured on a standard previously published set of benchmark applications) and 2) DroidSafe detects all malicious information flow leaks inserted into 24 real-world Android applications by three independent, hostile Red-Team organizations. The previous state-of-the art analysis, in contrast, detects less than 10% of these malicious flows. I. I NTRODUCTION Sensitive information leaks, as implemented by malicious or misused code (such as advertising libraries) in Android applications, constitute one of the most prominent security threats to the Android ecosystem [1, 2]. Android currently supports a coarse-grain information security model in which users grant applications the right to access sensitive information [3]. This model has been less than successful at eliminating information leaks [1], in part because many applications need to legitimately access sensitive information, but only for a specific limited purpose — for example, an application may legitimately need to access location information, but only with the right to send the information to authorized mapping servers. Motivated by this problem, researchers have developed a variety of systems that are de...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this NDSS '15 paper as an exciting demonstration of how homomorphic encryption can be practically applied to enable machine learning classification over encrypted data. The key achievement is enabling a classifier to process an input vector without revealing the input to the classifier or the classifier to the input, using composable cryptographic building blocks for operations like comparison, argmax, and dot product. The paper shows how these building blocks can be used to create privacy-preserving versions of hyperplane decisions, naive Bayes, decision trees, and AdaBoost classifiers. Colyer notes that the work is complementary to differential privacy, focusing on privacy during classification rather than training. The approach leverages efficient additively homomorphic cryptosystems (QR, Paillier, and a leveled FHE scheme) and combines them with garbled circuits for comparisons, demonstrating practical performance for real-world use cases like medical predictions or spam detection.
paper_title: Machine Learning Classification over Encrypted Data
paper_abstract: The ever growing use of machine learning (ML), motivated by the possibilities it brings to a large number of sectors, is increasingly raising questions because of the sensitive nature of the data that must be used and the lack of transparency on the way these data are collected, combined or shared. Therefore, a number of methods are being developed to reduce its impact on our privacy and make its use more acceptable, especially in areas such as healthcare where its potential is still largely under-exploited. This thesis explores different methods from the fields of cryptography and security, and applies them to machine learning in order to establish new confidentiality guarantees for the data used and the ML models. Our first contribution is the development of a technical foundation to facilitate experimentation of new approaches, through an open-source library named PySyft. We propose a modular architecture that allows one to pick the confidentiality blocks necessary for one’s study, or to develop and easily integrate new blocks. This library is reused in all the implementations proposed in this thesis. Our second contribution consists in highlighting the vulnerability of ML models by proposing an attack that exploits a trained model to reveal confidential attributes of an individual. This attack could, for example, subvert a model that recognizes a person’s sport from an image, to detect the person’s racial origins. We propose solutions to limit the impact of this attack. In a third step, we focus on some cryptographic protocols that allow us to perform computations on encrypted data. A first study proposes a functional encryption protocol that allows to make predictions using a small ML model over encrypted data and to only make the predictions public. A second study focuses on optimizing a functional secret sharing protocol, which allows an ML model to be trained or evaluated on data privately, i.e. without revealing either the model or the data to anyone. This ...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes the paper 'Bloom Cookies: Web search personalization without user tracking' by Mor et al. (2015), which explores the trade-off between privacy and personalization in web search. The paper critiques existing privacy-preserving techniques like profile generalization and noise addition, noting their limitations in balancing personalization quality and unlinkability. Generalization harms personalization significantly, while noise addition improves unlinkability but introduces high communication overhead. The authors propose a novel solution using Bloom filters (termed 'Bloom cookies') to obfuscate user profiles efficiently. By embedding fake bits into a Bloom filter of the exact profile, the approach introduces controlled noise that preserves personalization while ensuring unlinkability. Colyer highlights the elegance of this probabilistic data structure approach, emphasizing its efficiency, non-deterministic noise, and resistance to dictionary attacks.
paper_title: Bloom Cookies: Web search personalization without user tracking
paper_abstract: Using Machine Learning to Improve Internet Privacy Sebastian Zimmeck Internet privacy lacks transparency, choice, quantifiability, and accountability, especially, as the deployment of machine learning technologies becomes mainstream. However, these technologies can be both privacy-invasive as well as privacy-protective. This dissertation advances the thesis that machine learning can be used for purposes of improving Internet privacy. Starting with a case study that shows how the potential of a social network to learn ethnicity and gender of its users from geotags can be measured, various strands of machine learning technologies to further privacy are explored. While the quantification of privacy is the subject of well-known privacy metrics, such as k-anonymity or differential privacy, I discuss how some of those metrics can be leveraged in tandem with machine learning algorithms for purposes of quantifying the privacy-invasiveness of data collection practices. Further, I demonstrate how the current notice-and-choice paradigm can be realized by automated machine learning privacy policy analysis. The implemented system notifies users efficiently and accurately on applicable data practices. Further, by analyzing software data flows users are enabled to compare actual to purported data practices and regulators can enforce those at scale. The emerging cross-device tracking practices of ad networks, analytics companies, and others can be supplemented by machine learning technologies as well to notify users of privacy practices across devices and give them the choice they are entitled to by law. Ultimately, cross-device tracking is a harbinger of the emerging Internet of Things, in which I envision intelligent personal assistants that help users navigating through the increasing complexity of privacy notices and choices. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the Flash-Friendly File System (F2FS) from Samsung as a novel file system design optimized for NAND flash storage, addressing key limitations like erase-before-write requirements and sequential write constraints. He emphasizes F2FS's performance improvements (2-3x over EXT4) and its innovative features such as multi-head logging for hot/cold data separation, adaptive logging to mitigate fragmentation at high utilization, and roll-forward recovery for efficient fsync operations. The blog underscores the importance of tailoring file system designs to flash storage characteristics rather than relying on traditional HDD-oriented approaches.
paper_title: F2FS: A New File System for Flash Storage
paper_abstract: F2FS is a Linux file system designed to perform well on modern flash storage devices. The file system builds on append-only logging and its key design decisions were made with the characteristics of flash storage in mind. This paper describes the main design ideas, data structures, algorithms and the resulting performance of F2FS. Experimental results highlight the desirable performance of F2FS; on a state-of-the-art mobile system, it outperforms EXT4 under synthetic workloads by up to 3.1× (iozone) and 2× (SQLite). It reduces elapsed time of several realistic workloads by up to 40%. On a server system, F2FS is shown to perform better than EXT4 by up to 2.5× (SATA SSD) and 1.8× (PCIe SSD).

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the RIPQ paper, which explores advanced photo caching on flash storage for Facebook's infrastructure. Adrian Colyer highlights the paper's deep dive into flash memory characteristics, priority queue algorithms, and Facebook's caching strategies. The key insight is the challenge of optimizing caching algorithms for flash storage, which suffers from performance degradation due to small random writes and high write amplification. RIPQ introduces a restricted insertion priority queue (RIPQ) that approximates priority queue operations while minimizing flash wear and maintaining high hit ratios. The paper demonstrates that RIPQ can achieve similar performance to exact algorithms with a moderate memory footprint, making it suitable for large-scale systems like Facebook's photo-serving stack.
paper_title: RIPQ: Advanced Photo Caching on Flash for Facebook
paper_abstract: Facebook uses ﬂash devices extensively in its photocaching stack. The key design challenge for an efﬁcient photo cache on ﬂash at Facebook is its workload: many small random writes are generated by inserting cachemissed content, or updating cache-hit content for advanced caching algorithms. The Flash Translation Layer on ﬂash devices performs poorly with such a workload, lowering throughput and decreasing device lifespan. Existing coping strategies under-utilize the space on ﬂash devices, sacriﬁcing cache capacity, or are limited to simple caching algorithms like FIFO, sacriﬁcing hit ratios. We overcome these limitations with the novel Restricted Insertion Priority Queue (RIPQ) framework that supports advanced caching algorithms with large cache sizes, high throughput, and long device lifespan. RIPQ aggregates small random writes, co-locates similarly prioritized content, and lazily moves updated content to further reduce device overhead. We show that two families of advanced caching algorithms, Segmented-LRU and Greedy-Dual-Size-Frequency, can be easily implemented with RIPQ. Our evaluation on Facebook’s photo trace shows that these algorithms running on RIPQ increase hit ratios up to ~20% over the current FIFO system, incur low overhead, and achieve high throughput.

figures.caption: Facebook photo-serving stack. Requests are directed through two layers of caches. Each cache hashes objects to a flash equipped server.

blog_summary: The blog post introduces a mini-series on consensus protocols in distributed systems, highlighting the complexity and importance of understanding consensus algorithms. Adrian Colyer notes the extensive body of work in this space and aims to cover key papers over two weeks. The series includes foundational works like Lamport's Paxos papers, Viewstamped Replication, and more recent protocols like Raft and Zab. The author emphasizes the historical and technical significance of these papers, particularly their role in making consensus algorithms more accessible and practical for real-world systems. The series serves as a comprehensive exploration of the evolution and nuances of consensus protocols.
paper_title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)
paper_abstract: state space reduction (relative to Paxos, Raft reduces the degree of nondeterminism and the ways servers can be inconsistent with each other). A user study with 43 students at two universities shows that Raft is significantly easier to understand than Paxos: after learning both algorithms, 33 of these students were able to answer questions about Raft better than questions about Paxos. Raft is similar in many ways to existing consensus algorithms (most notably, Oki and Liskov’s Viewstamped Replication [29, 22]), but it has several novel features: • Strong leader: Raft uses a stronger form of leadership than other consensus algorithms. For example, log entries only flow from the leader to other servers. This simplifies the management of the replicated log and makes Raft easier to understand. • Leader election: Raft uses randomized timers to elect leaders. This adds only a small amount of mechanism to the heartbeats already required for any consensus algorithm, while resolving conflicts simply and rapidly. • Membership changes: Raft’s mechanism for changing the set of servers in the cluster uses a new joint consensus approach where the majorities of two different configurations overlap during transitions. This allows the cluster to continue operating normally during configuration changes. We believe that Raft is superior to Paxos and other consensus algorithms, both for educational purposes and as a foundation for implementation. It is simpler and more understandable than other algorithms; it is described completely enough to meet the needs of a practical system; it has several open-source implementations and is used by several companies; its safety properties have been formally specified and proven; and its efficiency is comparable to other algorithms. The remainder of the paper introduces the replicated state machine problem (Section 2), discusses the strengths and weaknesses of Paxos (Section 3), describes our general approach to understandability (Section 4), prese...
