blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes the 1988 paper by Oki and Liskov on Viewstamped Replication, a protocol for maintaining consistency in distributed systems through replication. The paper introduces the concept of 'views'—a group of cohorts with a designated primary—and 'viewstamps' (view ID + timestamp) to track state changes. The protocol ensures one-copy serializability by forcing state updates to a majority of cohorts before committing transactions. Colyer highlights the paper's theoretical rigor, noting that the authors proposed the method without a full implementation, yet it became foundational for later systems like Raft. The key insight is the use of view changes to handle failures while preserving consistency, leveraging the majority-quorum property to ensure state continuity across views. The paper also discusses client-server coordination for two-phase commit (2PC) and addresses message delivery challenges within the view framework.
paper_title: Viewstamped Replication: A New Primary Copy Method to Support Highly Available Distributed Systems
paper_abstract: One of the potential benefits of distributed systems is their use in providing highly-available services that are likely to be usable when needed. Availabilay is achieved through replication. By having inore than one copy of information, a service continues to be usable even when some copies are inaccessible, for example, because of a crash of the computer where a copy was stored. This paper presents a new replication algorithm that has desirable performance properties. Our approach is based on the primary copy technique. Computations run at a primary. which notifies its backups of what it has done. If the primary crashes, the backups are reorganized, and one of the backups becomes the new primary. Our method works in a general network with both node crashes and partitions. Replication causes little delay in user computations and little information is lost in a reorganization; we use a special kind of timestamp called a viewstamp to detect lost information. Our replication method assumes a model of computation in which a distributed program consists of modu/es, each of which resides at a single node of the network. Each module contains within it both data objects and code that manipulates the objects; modules can recover from crashes with some of their state intact. No other module can access the data objects of another module directly. instead, each module provides procedures that can b8 used to access its objects; modules communicate by means of remote pfoceduf8 calls. Modules that make calls (are called clients; the called module is a server.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the fascinating backstory of Lamport's 'Part-Time Parliament' paper, originally submitted in 1990 but initially dismissed due to its allegorical presentation. The paper introduces the Paxos algorithm, a foundational consensus protocol for fault-tolerant distributed systems, which later became central to many large-scale systems, including Google's infrastructure. Colyer appreciates the allegorical format, which makes the notoriously complex Paxos algorithm more accessible. The blog post summarizes the paper's core idea: a part-time parliament on the island of Paxos, where legislators (processes) and messengers (communication channels) face challenges akin to distributed systems, such as message delays, failures, and consistency. The paper describes a protocol for achieving consensus through ballots and quorums, ensuring consistency and progress under specific conditions.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Lamport's 'Paxos made simple' as a clear and accessible explanation of the Paxos consensus algorithm, which was previously considered difficult to understand due to its allegorical original presentation. The blog emphasizes that the core of the algorithm is surprisingly simple, relying on the fundamental property of majorities: if a majority of nodes agree on a value, no other majority can agree on a different value. Colyer breaks down the paper's structure, explaining the three roles (proposer, acceptor, learner) and the two-phase protocol (Prepare and Accept phases) that ensures consensus. He notes the paper's step-by-step derivation of the protocol and its practical implications for building fault-tolerant distributed systems, including the concept of multi-Paxos for implementing a distributed state machine.
paper_title: Paxos Made Simple
paper_abstract: The Paxos algorithm, when presented in plain English, is very simple. Contents

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the practical challenges of implementing Paxos in a production system, contrasting theoretical simplicity with real-world complexities. The paper from Google's Chubby team reveals that while Paxos can be described concisely, building a fault-tolerant, production-ready system requires addressing numerous engineering hurdles. Key insights include handling disk corruption, optimizing read performance via master leases, managing group membership changes, and maintaining log consistency through snapshots. The authors also discuss software engineering challenges like separating core algorithm logic from system code using a DSL, and the importance of rigorous testing with failure injection. The blog emphasizes the non-trivial gap between academic consensus protocols and their real-world deployment.
paper_title: Paxos Made Live - An Engineering Perspective
paper_abstract: We describe our experience in building a fault-tolerant data-base using the Paxos consensus algorithm. Despite the existing literature in the field, building such a database proved to be non-trivial. We describe selected algorithmic and engineering problems encountered, and the solutions we found for them. Our measurements indicate that we have built a competitive system.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this updated version of Viewstamped Replication (VR) as a significantly clearer and more practical explanation of the protocol compared to the original 1988 paper. The paper introduces several improvements, including support for reconfiguration (adding/removing group members), multiple optimizations, and a clean separation between the VR algorithm and the state-machine-based distributed system built on top. Colyer notes that VR differs from Paxos by being a replication protocol rather than a pure consensus protocol, and it avoids disk I/O during consensus operations. The paper describes four interlocking protocols (normal operation, view-change, recovery, and reconfiguration) and emphasizes VR's reliability guarantees under crash failures with a minimal replica group size of 2f+1. The blog post praises the protocol's simplicity and practicality, making it appealing for implementation.
paper_title: Viewstamped Replication Revisited
paper_abstract: change, e.g., to replace a faulty node with a different machine. A reconfiguration can also change the group size so that the number of failures the group can handle can increase or decrease. This paper presents an updated version of Viewstamped Replication, a replication technique that handles failures in which nodes crash. It describes how client requests are handled, how the group reorganizes when a replica fails, and how a failed replica is able to rejoin the group. The paper also describes a number of important optimizations and presents a protocol for handling reconfigurations that can change both the group membership and the number of failures the group is able to handle. 1 • The paper presents the protocol independently of any applications that use VR. The original papers explained the protocol as part of a database [11, 10] or file system [8], which made it difficult to separate the protocol from other details having to do with its use in an application.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the Zab protocol, which underpins ZooKeeper's atomic broadcast mechanism for primary-backup systems. Adrian Colyer highlights Zab's focus on replicating state changes rather than operations, with a critical observation that state changes are incremental and must be applied in order. The protocol is designed for high performance, enabling multiple outstanding transactions while maintaining FIFO ordering for operations from a single client. The author notes that while Zab argues Paxos cannot address this combination, Paxos (with a single distinguished proposer) might theoretically suffice under normal operation, but fails during leader failure scenarios where gaps in sequencing can occur. Zab's key innovation is the 'primary ordering' property, split into local and global orders, which ensures correct state transitions even during leader changes. The protocol operates in three phases: discovery, synchronization, and broadcast, with synchronization being crucial for maintaining primary order despite leader crashes. The paper also details process states (ELECTION, FOLLOWING, LEADING) and the leader oracle mechanism.

figures.title: Problem with Paxos under requirements
figures.caption: Figure 1 illustrates a problem we found with Paxos under our requirements. It shows a run with three distinct proposers that violates our requirement for the order of generated state changes. Proposer P1 executes Phase 1 for sequence numbers 27 and 28. It proposes values A and B for sequence numbers 27 and 28, respectively, in Phase 2 with ballot number 1. Both proposals are accepted only by acceptor A1. Proposer P2 executes Phase 1 against acceptors A2 and A3, and end up proposing C in Phase 2 to sequence number 27 with ballot number 2. Finally, proposer P3, executes Phase 1 and 2, and is able to have a quorum of acceptors choosing C for sequence number 27, B for sequence number 28, and D for 29.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a critical discrepancy between ZooKeeper's actual implementation and its published protocol (Zab) as described by Junqueira et al. The paper reveals that the Java-based implementation of ZooKeeper's atomic broadcast protocol, as of 2012, deviates significantly from the theoretical design, particularly in the leader election (Phase 0) and recovery phases. The implementation uses the Fast Leader Election (FLE) algorithm, which merges Phases 1 and 2 into a 'recovery phase' and optimizes state synchronization via SNAP, DIFF, or TRUNC messages. The author notes that these optimizations, while practical, introduce complexity and potential bugs, such as looping behavior between FLE and recovery phases or improper handling of TRUNC messages. Colyer emphasizes the broader lesson: distributed coordination systems like ZooKeeper are notoriously hard to implement correctly, and even minor deviations from the protocol can lead to subtle but critical failures. The paper serves as a cautionary tale about the gap between theory and practice in distributed systems.
paper_title: ZooKeeper's Atomic Broadcast Protocol: Theory and Practice
paper_abstract: Apache ZooKeeper is a distributed coordination service for cloud computing, providing essential synchronization and group services for other distributed applications. At its core lies an atomic broadcast protocol, which elects a leader, synchronizes the nodes, and performs broadcasts of updates from the leader. We study the design of this protocol, highlight promised properties, and analyze its official implementation by Apache. In particular, the default leader election protocol is studied in detail.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes a paper by van Renesse et al. that provides a unifying framework for understanding consensus protocols like Paxos, Viewstamped Replication (VR), and Zab using refinement theory. The paper constructs a 'family tree' of consensus protocols, showing how different algorithms can be derived from a common ancestor (Multi-Consensus) through a series of design decisions and refinements. The author highlights the paper's systematic approach to comparing protocols, noting that while Paxos uses active replication and VR/Zab use passive replication, these can be implemented on top of one another. The key insight is that the differences between these protocols are largely superficial, stemming from terminology and implementation choices rather than fundamental design differences. The paper also introduces Multi-Consensus-PO, a refinement that ensures prefix ordering, and provides guidance on when to use active vs. passive replication based on workload characteristics.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the Raft consensus algorithm, highlighting its primary goal of being understandable while providing a better foundation for building distributed systems compared to previous algorithms like Paxos. Adrian Colyer emphasizes Raft's structured approach, including strong leadership, randomized timers for leader election, and a joint consensus method for membership changes. The paper is praised for its readability and formal specification in TLA+, ensuring safety. The key insight is Raft's focus on clarity and practicality, making it easier to implement and reason about than alternatives like Paxos. The post also delves into Raft's leader election and log replication mechanisms, emphasizing how timing and consistency checks ensure system reliability.
paper_title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Edition)
paper_abstract: state space reduction (relative to Paxos, Raft reduces the degree of nondeterminism and the ways servers can be inconsistent with each other). A user study with 43 students at two universities shows that Raft is significantly easier to understand than Paxos: after learning both algorithms, 33 of these students were able to answer questions about Raft better than questions about Paxos. Raft is similar in many ways to existing consensus algorithms (most notably, Oki and Liskov’s Viewstamped Replication [29, 22]), but it has several novel features: • Strong leader: Raft uses a stronger form of leadership than other consensus algorithms. For example, log entries only flow from the leader to other servers. This simplifies the management of the replicated log and makes Raft easier to understand. • Leader election: Raft uses randomized timers to elect leaders. This adds only a small amount of mechanism to the heartbeats already required for any consensus algorithm, while resolving conflicts simply and rapidly. • Membership changes: Raft’s mechanism for changing the set of servers in the cluster uses a new joint consensus approach where the majorities of two different configurations overlap during transitions. This allows the cluster to continue operating normally during configuration changes. We believe that Raft is superior to Paxos and other consensus algorithms, both for educational purposes and as a foundation for implementation. It is simpler and more understandable than other algorithms; it is described completely enough to meet the needs of a practical system; it has several open-source implementations and is used by several companies; its safety properties have been formally specified and proven; and its efficiency is comparable to other algorithms. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer discusses the 'Raft Refloated' paper by Howard et al., which presents an independent implementation and rigorous evaluation of the Raft consensus protocol. The authors aim to assess Raft's claim of reducing cognitive complexity compared to alternatives like Paxos. They develop a production-quality Raft implementation in OCaml, complete with a distributed systems simulator and a formal model in Statecall Policy Language (SPL) to validate over 10,000 system traces. The paper highlights the challenges of building robust consensus systems, emphasizing the need for formal modeling, model checking, and careful instrumentation to avoid subtle bugs. The authors reproduce Raft's performance results and explore optimizations, demonstrating the value of simulation in uncovering rare but critical issues. While Raft's high-level concepts are found to be easier to understand than Paxos, the paper also reveals complexities in edge cases, such as livelocks, underscoring the difficulty of consensus protocol engineering.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights three major contributions in this paper: the introduction of the CALM principle for reasoning about distributed system behavior, a declarative language called Bloom designed to encourage CALM programming and leverage the inherent characteristics of distributed systems, and practical tools for developing software in this manner. The key insight is the CALM principle, which establishes a tight relationship between Consistency and Logical Monotonicity—monotonic programs guarantee eventual consistency under any interleaving of delivery and computation, while non-monotonic programs require coordination schemes that 'wait' for inputs to be complete. The paper argues that by building programs on logic-based languages like Bloom, developers can minimize coordination overhead (for better latency and availability) and use conservative tests for monotonicity to identify points where coordination may be necessary.
paper_title: Consistency Analysis in Bloom: a CALM and Collected Approach
paper_abstract: Distributed programming has become a topic of widespread interest, and many programmers now wrestle with tradeoffs between data consistency, availability and latency. Distributed transactions are often rejected as an undesirable tradeoff today, but in the absence of transactions there are few concrete principles or tools to help programmers design and verify the correctness of their applications. We address this situation with the CALM principle, which connects the idea of distributed consistency to program tests for logical monotonicity. We then introduce Bloom, a distributed programming language that is amenable to high-level consistency analysis and encourages order-insensitive programming. We present a prototype implementation of Bloom as a domain-specific language in Ruby. We also propose a program analysis technique that identifies points of order in Bloom programs: code locations where programmers may need to inject coordination logic to ensure consistency. We illustrate these ideas with two case studies: a simple key-value store and a distributed shopping cart service.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer analyzes the paper 'Consistency, Availability, and Convergence' (CAC) by Mahajan et al. (2014), which challenges the traditional CAP theorem by decoupling system model assumptions from properties like consistency, availability, and convergence. The paper argues that CAP mixes properties with system models and introduces convergence as a critical but often overlooked aspect. Colyer highlights the formal definitions of convergence (e.g., eventual consistency) and real-time causal consistency (RTC), emphasizing that RTC is the strongest consistency achievable in always-available, one-way convergent systems. The blog post delves into the nuances of these definitions, including the role of global time and the partial ordering of events in causal consistency. Part two introduces the COPS paper by Lloyd et al. (2011), which builds on causal+ consistency, a stronger variant of causal consistency, and demonstrates its practical implementation in a scalable key-value store.
paper_title: Consistency, Availability, and Convergence
paper_abstract: We examine the limits of consistency in fault-tolerant distributed storage systems. In particular, we identify fundamental tradeoffs among properties of consistency, availability, and convergence, and we close the gap between what is known to be impossible (i.e. CAP) and known systems that are highly-available but that provide weaker consistency such as causal. Specifically, in the asynchronous model with omission-failures and unreliable networks, we show the following tight bound: No consistency stronger than Real Time Causal Consistency (RTC) can be provided in an always-available, one-way convergent system and RTC can be provided in an always-available, one-way convergent system. In the asynchronous, Byzantine-failure model, we show that it is impossible to implement many of the recently introduced fork-based consistency semantics without sacrificing either availability or convergence; notably, proposed systems allow Byzantine nodes to permanently partition correct nodes from one another. To address this limitation, we introduce bounded fork join causal semantics that extends causal consistency to Byzantine environments while retaining availability and convergence. ∗ All correspondence should be addressed to: E-mail: princem@cs.utexas.edu; Address: Prince Mahajan, 1 University Station, #C0500, Austin, TX 78712-0233; Telephone: 512.366.0512

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the paper 'A comprehensive study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types' by Shapiro et al. (2011), highlighting CRDTs as a theoretically sound approach to eventual consistency in distributed systems. Adrian Colyer emphasizes that CRDTs avoid coordination overhead by ensuring operations either converge or commute, eliminating the need for consensus. The post explains the distinction between state-based and operation-based CRDTs, with examples like counters and sets, and notes the challenges in designing correct CRDTs, particularly around garbage collection and invariants like non-negativity. The paper is praised for providing a principled framework to address trade-offs between consistency, fault tolerance, and performance in distributed systems.
paper_title: A comprehensive study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types
paper_abstract: Eventual consistency aims to ensure that replicas of some mutable shared object converge without foreground synchronisation. Previous approaches to eventual consistency are ad-hoc and error-prone. We study a principled approach: to base the design of shared data types on some simple formal conditions that are sufficient to guarantee eventual consistency. We call these types Convergent or Commutative Replicated Data Types (CRDTs). This paper formalises asynchronous object replication, either state based or operation based, and provides a sufficient condition appropriate for each case. It describes several useful CRDTs, including container data types supporting both add and remove operations with clean semantics, and more complex types such as graphs, montonic DAGs, and sequences. It discusses some properties needed to implement non-trivial CRDTs. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this paper's focus on reducing coordination in distributed database systems to improve scalability and performance. The authors present a formal framework called invariant confluence (I-confluence) that determines when transactions can safely execute without coordination while maintaining application correctness. A key result is a system that scales linearly to 200 servers, processing 12.7M tps on the TPC-C benchmark—25x better than prior systems—without violating TPC-C invariants. The paper argues that minimizing coordination is crucial for high availability and performance, but unchecked coordination-free execution risks correctness. I-confluence provides a way to analyze invariants and transactions to identify when coordination can be avoided, offering a principled approach to designing scalable, correct distributed databases. Colyer notes that while the analysis is powerful, it relies on developers correctly specifying invariants and may require future language-level support for automation.
paper_title: Coordination Avoidance in Database Systems
paper_abstract: level correctness, or consistency.1 In canonical banking application examples, concurrent, coordination-free withdrawal operations can result in undesirable and “inconsistent” outcomes like negative account balances—application-level anomalies that the database should prevent. To ensure correct behavior, a database system must coordinate the execution of these operations that, if otherwise executed concurrently, could result in inconsistent application state. This tension between coordination and correctness is evidenced by the range of database concurrency control policies. In traditional database systems, serializable isolation provides concurrent operations (transactions) with the illusion of executing in some serial order [15]. As long as individual transactions maintain correct application state, serializability guarantees correctness [30]. However, each pair of concurrent operations (at least one of which is a write) can potentially compromise serializability and therefore will require coordination to execute [9, 21]. By isolating users at the level of reads and writes, serializability can be overly conservative and may in turn coordinate more than is strictly necessary for consistency [29, 39, 53, 58]. For example, hundreds of users can safely and simultaneously retweet Barack Obama on Twitter without observing a serial ordering of updates to the retweet counter. In contrast, a range of widely-deployed weaker models require less coordination to execute but surface read and write behavior that may in turn compromise consistency [2, 9, 22, 48]. With these alternative models, it is up to users to decide when weakened guarantees are acceptable for their applications [6], leading to confusion regarding (and substantial interest in) the relationship between consistency, scalability, and availability [1, 9, 12, 18, 21, 22, 28, 40]. In this paper, we address the central question inherent in this tradeoff: when is coordination strictly necessary to maintain applicatio...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer revisits 'Out of the Tar Pit' by Moseley & Marks, a foundational paper arguing that complexity is the root cause of most software system problems. The authors distinguish between essential complexity (inherent to the problem domain) and accidental complexity (introduced by implementation choices). They highlight state and control logic as the primary sources of accidental complexity, with state being particularly insidious due to its exponential impact on system behavior. The paper critiques object-oriented programming for its reliance on state and praises functional programming for its referential transparency, though acknowledges the challenges of managing state in real-world systems. The authors advocate for declarative programming and minimizing hidden mutable state to reduce complexity, positioning the paper as a manifesto for simpler, more maintainable software design.
paper_title: Out of the Tar Pit
paper_abstract: Complexity is the single major difficulty in the successful development of large-scale software systems. Following Brooks we distinguish accidental from essential difficulty, but disagree with his premise that most complexity remaining in contemporary systems is essential. We identify common causes of complexity and discuss general approaches which can be taken to eliminate them where they are accidental in nature. To make things more concrete we then give an outline for a potential complexity-minimizing approach based on functional programming and Codd’s relational model of data.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the Statecall Policy Language (SPL) as a practical approach to making model checking accessible to regular programmers, addressing the challenge of verifying distributed systems which are prone to subtle bugs. The paper introduces SPL as a language for specifying allowable sequences of program events, with a compiler that can translate models into multiple forms including PROMELA for static analysis with SPIN, graphical visualizations, and executable code in target languages like OCaml for runtime validation (safety monitoring). The blog emphasizes SPL's ability to model complex behaviors such as signal handlers and supports debugging through a real-time graphical view of automata. Colyer notes that despite the benefits, major protocol implementations like HTTP, SMTP, and DNS are rarely model-checked, leaving them vulnerable to serious security flaws. The key insight is combining static model checking with dynamic enforcement to catch both high-level protocol errors and low-level implementation bugs.
paper_title: Combining static model checking with dynamic enforcement using the Statecall Policy Language
paper_abstract: Internet protocols encapsulate a significant amount of state, making implementing the host software complex. In this paper, we define the Statecall Policy Language (SPL) which provides a usable middle ground between ad-hoc coding and formal reasoning. It enables programmers to embed automata in their code which can be statically modelchecked using SPIN and dynamically enforced. The performance overheads are minimal, and the automata also provide higher-level debugging capabilities. We also describe some practical uses of SPL by describing the automata used in an SSH server written entirely in OCaml/SPL. Constructing modern Internet servers is a difficult proposition, since the software must encapsulate a significant amount of state and deal with a variety of incoming packet types, complex configurations and versioning inconsistencies. Network applications are also expected to be liberal in interpreting received data packets and must reliably deal with timing and ordering issues arising from the “best-effort” nature of Internet data traffic. Due to this complexity, mechanical verification techniques are very useful to guarantee safety, security and reliability properties. One mature formal method used to verify properties about systems is model checking. Software modelchecking involves: (i ) creating an abstract model of a complex application; (ii ) validating this model against the application; and (iii ) checking safety properties against the abstract model. To non-experts, steps (i ) and (ii ) are often the most daunting. How does one decide which aspects of the application to include in the abstract model? How does one determine whether the abstraction inadvertently “hides” critical bugs? If a counter-example is found, how does one determine whether this is a genuine bug or just a modeling artifact? In this paper, we present the Statecall Policy Language (SPL) which simplifies the model specification and validation tasks with a view to making model checking more ...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights 'Building on Quicksand' by Helland & Campbell as a foundational paper that argues for a shift in database design towards embracing asynchrony and application-level semantics to achieve the ALPS properties (Availability, Latency, Partition tolerance, and Scalability). The paper critiques traditional log-shipping mechanisms in databases, where asynchronous replication introduces a window of inconsistency that can lead to lost work if the primary fails. The authors propose that business rules should be expressed at the application level to allow commutative operations to execute independently, enabling loose coupling and eventual consistency. They argue that storage-level abstractions (like reads and writes) are insufficient for this purpose and that application operations must be designed to tolerate out-of-order execution and occasional mistakes. The paper introduces the concept of 'ACID 2.0' (Associative, Commutative, Idempotent, Distributed) as a new consistency model that aligns with these principles, emphasizing tolerance for work happening in any order, anywhere in the system. The blog post underscores the importance of application-level semantics and the inevitability of probabilistic business rules in distributed systems.
paper_title: Building on Quicksand
paper_abstract: In this keynote I give a subjective but systematic overview of the landscape of distributed event-based systems, with an emphasis on two areas I have worked on over the last decade: large-scale stream processing with Apache Kafka and associated tools, and real-time collaboration software in the style of Google Docs. While these may seem at first glance to be very different topics, there are also important points of overlap. This paper lays out a taxonomy of event-based systems that shows where their commonalities and differences lie. It also highlights some of the key trade-offs that arise in the implementation of event-based systems, drawing both from distributed systems theory and from experience of their practical deployment. Finally, the paper outlines a number of open research problems in this field.

figures.title: A taxonomy of event-based systems
figures.caption: A flowchart categorizing event-based systems based on persistence, notification, ordering, windowed operations, and data models. The diagram includes examples like time-series databases, user interface events, stream processing, database replication, event sourcing, and CRDTs.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights SAMC (Semantic-aware model checking) as a significant advancement in distributed system verification, addressing a critical gap in existing distributed model checkers (dmck). While prior dmcks like MODIST and DIR effectively reduce state space using techniques such as dynamic partial order reduction (DPOR) and dynamic interface reduction, they struggle with failure scenarios—a major source of bugs in distributed systems. The author emphasizes that 50% of deep bugs in systems like ZooKeeper, Hadoop, and Cassandra involve complex reorderings of messages, crashes, and reboots, which existing tools often miss. SAMC solves this by incorporating application semantics and crash/reboot scenarios into its model checking, enabling it to uncover deep bugs up to three orders of magnitude faster than state-of-the-art techniques. The tool found 2 new bugs in recent versions of ZooKeeper and Hadoop and validated its approach by rediscovering 12 known deep bugs with minimal testing time. The key insight is that leveraging semantic awareness—beyond traditional reduction techniques—can drastically improve the efficiency and scalability of distributed model checking, making it practical for real-world systems.
paper_title: SAMC: Semantic-aware model checking for fast discovery of deep bugs in cloud systems
paper_abstract: † Surya University 52, 53]. The last five years have seen a rise of software model checkers targeted for distributed systems [22, 25, 43, 50, 51]; for brevity, we categorize such systems as dmck (distributed system model checker). Dmck works by exercising all possible sequences of events (e.g., different reorderings of messages), and hereby pushing the target system into corner-case situations and unearthing hard-to-find bugs. To address the state-space explosion problem, existing dmcks adopt advanced state reduction techniques such as dynamic partial order reduction (DPOR), making them mature and highly practical for checking large-scale systems [25, 51]. Despite these early successes, existing dmcks unfortunately fall short in addressing present reliability challenges of cloud systems. In particular, large-scale cloud systems are expected to be highly reliable in dealing with complex failures, not just one instance, but multiple of them. However, to the best of our knowledge, no existing dmcks can exercise multiple failures without exploding the state space. We elaborate this issue later; for now, we discuss complex failures in cloud environments. Cloud systems run on large clusters of unreliable commodity machines, an environment that produces a growing number and frequency of failures, including “surprising” failures [2, 26]. Therefore, it is common to see complex failure-induced bugs such as the one below. The last five years have seen a rise of implementationlevel distributed system model checkers (dmck) for verifying the reliability of real distributed systems. Existing dmcks however rarely exercise multiple failures due to the state-space explosion problem, and thus do not address present reliability challenges of cloud systems in dealing with complex failures. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the paper 'Lineage-driven Fault Injection' by Alvaro et al. (2015), presenting MOLLY, a system that takes a novel top-down approach to fault injection in distributed systems. Unlike traditional methods that blindly explore state spaces, MOLLY reasons backwards from successful outcomes to identify potential failure points, using data lineage to trace causes of correct results. The key insight is to leverage lineage to efficiently discover fault-tolerance bugs while providing completeness guarantees akin to formal methods. MOLLY transforms lineage conditions into CNF and uses SAT solvers to identify failure combinations that could falsify outcomes. The paper highlights MOLLY's effectiveness in quickly finding critical bugs in complex distributed systems and certifying correctness for given configurations, outperforming state-of-the-art fault injectors. The blog also emphasizes the interactive 'match' framework between programmers and MOLLY, illustrating how redundancy in space and time is crucial for fault tolerance.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the RAMP (Read Atomic Multiple Partition) transactions paper as a solution to the uncomfortable trade-off in distributed databases between performance and atomic visibility for multi-partition transactions. Traditional systems either sacrifice correctness for speed (e.g., NoSQL stores) or sacrifice scalability for consistency (e.g., slow global indexes). RAMP transactions, with three variants (RAMP-Fast, RAMP-Small, RAMP-Hybrid), demonstrate that atomic visibility can be achieved without significant performance degradation, scaling to over 7.1 million operations per second on 100 servers. The key insight is that reads and writes can proceed concurrently, with readers autonomously detecting and fetching missing in-flight writes using metadata, while writers use a two-phase atomic commitment protocol to ensure visibility. The paper also addresses critical issues like foreign key constraints, secondary indexing, and materialized view maintenance that break without atomic multi-partition isolation.
paper_title: Scalable Atomic Visibility with RAMP Transactions
paper_abstract: Databases can provide scalability by partitioning data across several servers. However, multi-partition, multi-operation transactional access is often expensive, employing coordination-intensive locking, validation, or scheduling mechanisms. Accordingly, many realworld systems avoid mechanisms that provide useful semantics for multi-partition operations. This leads to incorrect behavior for a large class of applications including secondary indexing, foreign key enforcement, and materialized view maintenance. In this work, we identify a new isolation model—Read Atomic (RA) isolation—that matches the requirements of these use cases by ensuring atomic visibility: either all or none of each transaction’s updates are observed by other transactions. We present algorithms for Read Atomic MultiPartition (RAMP) transactions that enforce atomic visibility while offering excellent scalability, guaranteed commit despite partial failures (via synchronization independence), and minimized communication between servers (via partition independence). These RAMP transactions correctly mediate atomic visibility of updates and provide readers with snapshot access to database state by using limited multi-versioning and by allowing clients to independently resolve non-atomic reads. We demonstrate that, in contrast with existing algorithms, RAMP transactions incur limited overhead—even under high contention—and scale linearly to 100 servers.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Sirius as an open-source end-to-end Intelligent Personal Assistant (IPA) system that integrates speech recognition, image recognition, and question-answering capabilities. The paper stands out for its comprehensive implementation, enabling research into IPA workloads without rebuilding the entire system from scratch. The blog emphasizes Sirius's multi-hardware support (CPUs, GPUs, Intel Phi, FPGAs) to evaluate architectural suitability for IPA workloads, and its extrapolation of results to future datacenter designs as natural interface queries grow. Key insights include the massive computational intensity of IPA queries (100x more than web search) and the identification of critical bottlenecks (e.g., ASR scoring, QA CRF, IMM feature extraction) that limit performance on general-purpose processors. The paper also introduces the Sirius Suite benchmark to compare acceleration across hardware platforms, revealing FPGAs as the most promising for bridging the scalability gap.
paper_title: Sirius: An Open End-to-End Voice and Vision Personal Assistant and its Implications for Future Warehouse Scale Computers

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Mojim, a system that provides replicated, reliable, and highly-available Non-Volatile Main Memory (NVMM) as an operating system service. The paper addresses the challenge of leveraging emerging byte-addressable NVMM technologies (like PCM and STTMs) which blur the line between memory and storage, offering DRAM-like performance with persistence. Mojim introduces novel system calls (msync and gmsync) to manage replication and synchronization between primary and mirror nodes over high-speed RDMA links (Infiniband), enabling trade-offs between reliability, availability, consistency, and cost. Notably, Mojim achieves a 40-45% latency reduction compared to unreplicated NVMM by offloading cache flushes to RDMA transfers. The paper also explores cost-effective configurations, such as using SSDs for mirror nodes or tiered backups over Ethernet. Colyer emphasizes how NVMM's performance characteristics necessitate rethinking traditional storage system designs, particularly replication protocols optimized for slower media.
paper_title: Mojim: A Reliable and Highly-Available Non-Volatile Memory System
paper_abstract: Next-generation non-volatile memories (NVMs) promise DRAM-like performance, persistence, and high density. They can attach directly to processors to form non-volatile main memory (NVMM) and offer the opportunity to build very low-latency storage systems. These high-performance storage systems would be especially useful in large-scale data center environments where reliability and availability are critical. However, providing reliability and availability to NVMM is challenging, since the latency of data replication can overwhelm the low latency that NVMM should provide. We propose Mojim, a system that provides the reliability and availability that large-scale storage systems require, while preserving the performance of NVMM. Mojim achieves these goals by using a two-tier architecture in which the primary tier contains a mirrored pair of nodes and the secondary tier contains one or more secondary backup nodes with weakly consistent copies of data. Mojim uses highlyoptimized replication protocols, software, and networking stacks to minimize replication costs and expose as much of NVMM’s performance as possible. We evaluate Mojim using raw DRAM as a proxy for NVMM and using an industrial NVMM emulation system. We find that Mojim provides replicated NVMM with similar or even better performance than un-replicated NVMM (reducing latency by 27% to 63% and delivering between 0.4 to 2.7× the throughput). We demonstrate that replacing MongoDB’s built-in replication system with Mojim improves MongoDB’s performance by 3.4 to 4×. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a paper that introduces cross-layer scheduling in cloud systems, coordinating application task placement with network route allocation via SDN to improve throughput. The approach demonstrates significant performance gains, with 26-34% throughput improvements for Hadoop and Storm in 30-node clusters, scaling further with larger clusters. The key insight is leveraging SDN to optimize both task placement and network routing iteratively, using simulated annealing to navigate the vast state space of possible configurations. The method integrates with existing schedulers like Hadoop's YARN and Storm's Nimbus, precomputing topology maps and dynamically adapting to network changes. Colyer notes the practical relevance of optimizing throughput for real-time analytics, though he observes that latency is often the more critical metric for user satisfaction.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the ApproxHadoop paper, which introduces techniques to reduce the computational cost of Hadoop jobs by trading a small amount of accuracy for significant performance gains. Adrian Colyer highlights that ApproxHadoop allows users to specify target error bounds and confidence levels, enabling jobs to process less data through input sampling, task dropping, or user-defined approximations. For example, tolerating a 1% error with 95% confidence can reduce job execution time by a factor of 32. The paper's key insight lies in using multi-stage sampling theory for aggregation tasks (e.g., sum, count) and extreme value theory for tasks involving extremes (e.g., min, max) to compute error bounds. The integration with Hadoop is seamless, requiring minimal code changes, and the framework dynamically adjusts sampling and dropping ratios based on runtime statistics.
paper_title: ApproxHadoop: Bringing Approximations to MapReduce Frameworks

blog_summary: The paper examines concurrent search data structures (CSDS) like linked lists, hash tables, skip lists, and binary search trees, evaluating how well they scale with multiple cores. Adrian Colyer highlights the authors' four derived principles for scalable concurrency, which emphasize minimizing stores, waiting, and retries in search and update operations to resemble sequential implementations. These principles, collectively termed 'asynchronized concurrency' (ASCY), are shown to improve existing algorithms and lead to the creation of new, highly scalable data structures. The evaluation across six diverse processors demonstrates that the best-performing CSDS algorithms closely match the performance of an idealized 'asynchronized' execution, with a new hash table (CLHT) outperforming the next best by 23%. The key insight is that memory access patterns resembling sequential execution—particularly minimizing cache-line transfers—are critical for portable scalability across hardware, workloads, and metrics like throughput, latency, and power consumption.
paper_title: Asynchronized Concurrency: The Secret to Scaling Concurrent Search Data Structures
paper_abstract: We introduce “asynchronized concurrency (ASCY),” a paradigm consisting of four complementary programming patterns. ASCY calls for the design of concurrent search data structures (CSDSs) to resemble that of their sequential counterparts. We argue that ASCY leads to implementations which are portably scalable: they scale across different types of hardware platforms, including single and multisocket ones, for various classes of workloads, such as readonly and read-write, and according to different performance metrics, including throughput, latency, and energy. We substantiate our thesis through the most exhaustive evaluation of CSDSs to date, involving 6 platforms, 22 state-of-the-art CSDS algorithms, 10 re-engineered state-of-the-art CSDS algorithms following the ASCY patterns, and 2 new CSDS algorithms designed with ASCY in mind. We observe up to 30% improvements in throughput in the re-engineered algorithms, while our new algorithms out-perform the state-ofthe-art alternatives.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights that the conventional wisdom about performance bottlenecks in big data analytics frameworks (network I/O, disk I/O, and straggler tasks) is often incorrect. Through a detailed study of Spark workloads using 'blocked task analysis,' the authors found that network optimization offers minimal median improvement (2%), disk I/O optimizations provide moderate gains (19%), and straggler task elimination yields 10% median improvement. Surprisingly, many workloads are CPU-bound due to deserialization and compression overheads, challenging the assumption that analytics tasks are I/O-bound. The paper emphasizes the importance of instrumentation and performance understandability in system design, noting that bottlenecks evolve with framework advancements. The authors provide open-source tools and benchmark traces to facilitate further research.
paper_title: Making Sense of Performance in Data Analytics Frameworks
paper_abstract: This paper makes two contributions towards a more comprehensive understanding of performance. First, we develop a methodology for analyzing end-to-end performance of data analytics frameworks; and second, we use our methodology to study performance of two SQL benchmarks and one production workload. Our results run counter to all three of the aforementioned mantras. The first contribution of this paper is blocked time analysis, a methodology for quantifying performance bottlenecks. Identifying bottlenecks is challenging for data analytics frameworks because of pervasive parallelism: jobs are composed of many parallel tasks, and each task uses pipelining to parallelize the use of network, disk, and CPU. One task may be bottlenecked on different resources at different points in execution, and at any given time, tasks for the same job may be bottlenecked on different resources. Blocked time analysis uses extensive white-box logging to measure how long each task spends blocked on a given resource. Taken alone, these per-task measurements allow us to understand straggler causes by correlating slow tasks with long blocked times. Taken together, the per-task measurements for a particular job allow us to simulate how long the job would have taken to complete if the disk or network were infinitely fast, which provides an upper bound on the benefit of optimizing network or disk performance. The second contribution of this paper is using blocked time analysis to understand Spark’s performance on two industry benchmarks and one production workload. In studying the applicability of the three aforementioned claims to these workloads, we find: There has been much research devoted to improving the performance of data analytics frameworks, but comparatively little effort has been spent systematically identifying the performance bottlenecks of these systems. In this paper, we develop blocked time analysis, a methodology for quantifying performance bottlenecks in distributed computatio...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a paper that extends declarative programming approaches to interactive data visualizations, addressing a key gap where interactions typically require imperative callbacks. The authors propose a declarative model for interactions like selections, panning, and zooming, inspired by Functional Reactive Programming (FRP). This approach treats event streams as first-class citizens, enabling automatic re-evaluation of dependent signals and simplifying complex state management. The paper introduces a CSS-inspired syntax for event stream selection and composition, scale inversion for visual transformations, and production rules for modifying visual representations. The authors demonstrate how their model can express interactions across all seven categories of user intent identified by Yi et al., and discuss trade-offs in terms of hidden dependencies and visibility. The work is positioned as a significant advancement in declarative design for interactive visualizations.
paper_title: Declarative Interaction Design for Data Visualization
paper_abstract: Declarative visualization grammars can accelerate development, facilitate retargeting across platforms, and allow language-level optimizations. However, existing declarative visualization languages are primarily concerned with visual encoding, and rely on imperative event handlers for interactive behaviors. In response, we introduce a model of declarative interaction design for data visualizations. Adopting methods from reactive programming, we model low-level events as composable data streams from which we form higher-level semantic signals. Signals feed predicates and scale inversions, which allow us to generalize interactive selections at the level of item geometry (pixels) into interactive queries over the data domain. Production rules then use these queries to manipulate the visualization’s appearance. To facilitate reuse and sharing, these constructs can be encapsulated as named interactors: standalone, purely declarative specifications of interaction techniques. We assess our model’s feasibility and expressivity by instantiating it with extensions to the Vega visualization grammar. Through a diverse range of examples, we demonstrate coverage over an established taxonomy of visualization interaction techniques. However, these languages provide little support for declarative design of interactions. Some tools [5, 6] offer a predefined palette of interaction techniques (brushing, zooming, etc.) that can be declaratively applied. However, these “interactor typologies” artificially restrict designers’ options and typically support customization of only a limited set of parameters. For custom interactions, designers must instead author imperative event handling callbacks. These callbacks undo the benefits of declarative design by exposing execution details, forcing users to manually maintain state [8] and coordinate interleavings — a complex and error-prone task colloquially referred to as “callback hell” [12]. In this paper, we introduce a model of declarative int...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the Chandy-Lamport algorithm as a foundational solution for capturing consistent global states in distributed systems without requiring a universal clock or disrupting ongoing computation. The paper demonstrates how to take a snapshot of both process states and channel states (message queues) to avoid inconsistencies like 'disappearing' or 'duplicated' messages (e.g., colored balls in the example). Colyer emphasizes the algorithm's elegance in using marker messages to logically partition time and ensure a consistent snapshot, while also noting its practical applications in detecting stable properties like deadlocks. The blog post includes a playful yet illustrative example to clarify the importance of capturing channel states alongside process states.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a startling security vulnerability in HbbTV (Hybrid Broadcast-Broadband Television), where the 'red button' standard enables virtually undetectable attacks by exploiting the auto-starting of web content when tuning to a TV channel. The blog emphasizes the broader implications of IoT security, noting how connecting physical and digital systems can create unforeseen attack vectors. Key insights include the emergent properties of composed systems, where security guarantees from individual components may not hold when combined, and the challenge of reasoning about such properties. The paper demonstrates how HbbTV applications can manipulate broadcast content, spoof origins, and perform malicious actions like DDoS, CSRF, or intranet attacks without user awareness.
paper_title: From the Aether to the Ethernet - Attacking the Internet using Broadcast Digital Television
paper_abstract: affects the physical world, our attack uses the physical broadcast network to attack the data network. In the attempt to bring modern broadband Internet features to traditional broadcast television, the Digital Video Broadcasting (DVB) consortium introduced a specification called Hybrid Broadcast-Broadband Television (HbbTV), which allows broadcast streams to include embedded HTML content which is rendered by the television. This system is already in very wide deployment in Europe, and has recently been adopted as part of the American digital television standard.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the Scalable Commutativity Rule by Clements et al. (2013), which posits that operations commuting in an API can be implemented in a conflict-free manner, thus improving scalability. The author emphasizes the importance of API design over implementation optimizations and introduces the COMMUTER tool, which identifies commutative operations and generates test cases to expose scalability issues. Colyer notes the practicality of exploiting conditional commutativity (SIM commutativity: State-dependent, Interface-based, and Monotonic) and the tool's ability to guide API design, as demonstrated in the redesign of 18 POSIX file-system calls and the creation of ScaleFS and RadixVM. The paper also provides guidelines for designing commutative interfaces and scalable implementations, offering actionable insights for system designers.
paper_title: The Scalable Commutativity Rule: Designing Scalable Software for Multicore Processors
paper_abstract: What fundamental opportunities for multicore scalability are latent in software interfaces, such as system call APIs? Can scalability opportunities be identified even before any implementation exists, simply by considering interface specifications? To answer these questions this dissertation introduces the scalable commutativity rule: Whenever interface operations commute, they can be implemented in a way that scales. This rule aids developers in building scalable multicore software starting with interface design and carrying on through implementation, testing, and evaluation. This dissertation formalizes the scalable commutativity rule and defines a novel form of commutativity named SIM commutativity that makes it possible to fruitfully apply the rule to complex and highly stateful software interfaces. To help developers apply the rule, this dissertation introduces an automated method embodied in a new tool named Commuter, which accepts high-level interface models, generates tests of operations that commute and hence could scale, and uses these tests to systematically evaluate the scalability of implementations. We apply Commuter to a model of 18 POSIX file and virtual memory system operations. Using the resulting 26,238 scalability tests, Commuter systematically pinpoints many problems in the Linux kernel that past work has observed to limit application scalability and identifies previously unknown bottlenecks that may be triggered by future hardware or workloads. Finally, this dissertation applies the scalable commutativity rule and Commuter to the design and implementation of a new POSIX-like operating system named sv6. sv6’s novel file and virtual memory system designs enable it to scale for 99% of the tests generated by Commuter. These results translate to linear scalability on an 80-core x86 machine for applications built on sv6’s commutative operations. Thesis Supervisor: M. Frans Kaashoek Title: Charles Piper Professor of Computer Science and Engineering Th...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the Musketeer paper's key insight: there is no universally 'best' big data processing system—performance varies widely depending on the workload, input data size, and system design. The paper's study of Hadoop, Spark, Naiad, PowerGraph, Metis, and GraphChi reveals that no single system outperforms all others across all scenarios. For 40-80% of MapReduce jobs, a single-machine system is more efficient than distributed frameworks. The blog emphasizes the importance of context in system selection, noting that factors like input size, data structure, computation type, and engineering decisions significantly impact performance. Gog et al. also critique the blind adoption of 'new shiny' systems without considering workload-specific needs. The analysis underscores the need for a more practical approach to data processing, which Musketeer aims to address by enabling workflows to be retargeted to optimal backends.
paper_title: Musketeer: all for one, one for all in data processing systems
paper_abstract: Many systems for the parallel processing of big data are available today. Yet, few users can tell by intuition which system, or combination of systems, is “best” for a given workflow. Porting workflows between systems is tedious. Hence, users become “locked in”, despite faster or more efficient systems being available. This is a direct consequence of the tight coupling between user-facing front-ends that express workflows (e.g., Hive, SparkSQL, Lindi, GraphLINQ) and the back-end execution engines that run them (e.g., MapReduce, Spark, PowerGraph, Naiad). We argue that the ways that workflows are defined should be decoupled from the manner in which they are executed. To explore this idea, we have built Musketeer, a workflow manager which can dynamically map front-end workflow descriptions to a broad range of back-end execution engines. Our prototype maps workflows expressed in four highlevel query languages to seven different popular data processing systems. Musketeer speeds up realistic workflows by up to 9× by targeting different execution engines, without requiring any manual effort. Its automatically generated back-end code comes within 5%–30% of the performance of hand-optimized implementations.

blog_summary: Musketeer addresses the challenge of portability in data processing workflows by introducing a DAG-based intermediate representation (IR) that decouples front-end frameworks from back-end execution systems. The system can analyze a given workflow and recommend the optimal system (or combination of systems) to run it on, even suggesting partial workflows be executed on different back-ends. This is significant because no single system excels across all workloads, and Musketeer's approach allows for automatic optimization and code generation tailored to the target system. The paper highlights Musketeer's ability to support both SQL-like and graph processing front-ends, perform optimizations at the IR level, and generate efficient back-end code through operator merging, idiom recognition, and type inference. The evaluation demonstrates that Musketeer can achieve performance comparable to hand-optimized code (within 30% overhead, often 5-20%) and significantly outperforms non-expert implementations. The key insight is the value of a unified IR and automatic system selection to simplify data processing workflows while maintaining high performance.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer analyzes a paper on scaling concurrent log-structured data stores (LSM-trees), highlighting that while LSM-trees were originally designed to mitigate slow disk I/O, in-memory contention becomes the bottleneck as systems scale to more cores. The paper proposes replacing the in-memory component of the LSM-tree with a concurrent hash map to improve scalability. The authors critique existing implementations like LevelDB and HyperLevelDB for their coarse-grained synchronization and single-threaded merge processes, which limit throughput in multi-core environments. Their solution, cLSM, demonstrates better performance and lower latency in production workloads by leveraging thread-safe in-memory structures and introducing atomic read-modify-write operations. The key insight is the simple yet effective idea of using an efficient concurrent in-memory data structure for the in-memory part of the LSM-tree, which significantly improves scalability without requiring complex partitioning schemes.
paper_title: Scaling Concurrent Log-Structured Data Stores
paper_abstract: 1. Log-structured data stores (LSM-DSs) are widely accepted as the state-of-the-art implementation of key-value stores. They replace random disk writes with sequential I/O, by accumulating large batches of updates in an in-memory data structure and merging it with the on-disk store in the background. While LSM-DS implementations proved to be highly successful at masking the I/O bottleneck, scaling them up on multicore CPUs remains a challenge. This is nontrivial due to their often rich APIs, as well as the need to coordinate the RAM access with the background I/O. We present cLSM, an algorithm for scalable concurrency in LSM-DS, which exploits multiprocessor-friendly data structures and non-blocking synchronization. cLSM supports a rich API, including consistent snapshot scans and general non-blocking read-modify-write operations. We implement cLSM based on the popular LevelDB keyvalue store, and evaluate it using intensive synthetic workloads as well as ones from production web-serving applications. Our algorithm outperforms state of the art LSMDS implementations, improving throughput by 1.5x to 2.5x. Moreover, cLSM demonstrates superior scalability with the number of cores (successfully exploiting twice as many cores as the competition). Over the last decade, key-value stores have become prevalent for real-time serving of Internet-scale data [16]. Gigantic stores managing billions of items serve Web search indexing [33], messaging [12], personalized media, and advertising [18]. A key-value store is essentially a persistent map with atomic get and put operations used to access data items identified by unique keys. Modern stores also support consistent snapshot scans and range queries for online analytics. In write-intensive environments, key-value stores are commonly implemented as Log-Structured Merge Data Stores (LSM-DSs) [2, 4, 8, 16, 18, 25, 36] (see Section 2). The main centerpiece behind such data stores is absorbing large batches of writes in a RAM data stru...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes a 2014 paper by Yu et al. that evaluates seven major concurrency control algorithms for OLTP DBMSs under extreme scaling (1024 cores). The study finds that none of the algorithms can defy the Universal Scalability Law, with performance degrading after an initial peak as cores increase. The paper explores pathological workloads (e.g., hotspot contention) and highlights the trade-offs between shared-nothing and shared-memory designs. Colyer notes that the work provides a comprehensive overview of concurrency control schemes, dividing them into two-phase locking (2PL) and timestamp ordering families, and discusses their scalability bottlenecks. The key insight is that no single algorithm scales perfectly for all workloads, emphasizing the need to optimize for typical OLTP characteristics (short-lived, repetitive transactions with small data access).
paper_title: Staring into the Abyss: An Evaluation of Concurrency Control with One Thousand Cores
paper_abstract: that instruction-level parallelism and single-threaded performance will give way to massive thread-level parallelism. As Moore’s law continues, the number of cores on a single chip is expected to keep growing exponentially. Soon we will have hundreds or perhaps a thousand cores on a single chip. The scalability of single-node, shared-memory DBMSs is even more important in the many-core era. But if the current DBMS technology does not adapt to this reality, all this computational power will be wasted on bottlenecks, and the extra cores will be rendered useless. In this paper, we take a peek at this dire future and examine what happens with transaction processing at one thousand cores. Rather than looking at all possible scalability challenges, we limit our scope to concurrency control. With hundreds of threads running in parallel, the complexity of coordinating competing accesses to data will become a major bottleneck to scalability, and will likely dwindle the gains from increased core counts. Thus, we seek to comprehensively study the scalability of OLTP DBMSs through one of their most important components. We implemented seven concurrency control algorithms in a main memory DBMS and used a high-performance, distributed CPU simulator to scale the system to 1000 cores. Implementing a system from scratch allows us to avoid any artificial bottlenecks in existing DBMSs and instead understand the more fundamental issues in the algorithms. Previous scalability studies used existing DBMSs [24, 26, 32], but many of the legacy components of these systems do not target many-core CPUs. To the best of our knowledge, there has not been an evaluation of multiple concurrency control algorithms on a single DBMS at such large scale. Our analysis shows that all algorithms fail to scale as the number of cores increases. In each case, we identify the primary bottlenecks that are independent of the DBMS implementation and argue that even state-of-the-art systems suffer from these limit...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the paper 'Putting Consistency Back into Eventual Consistency' by Balegas et al. (EuroSys 2015), which challenges the notion that weak eventual consistency is unavoidable in geo-replicated systems. The authors propose 'Explicit Consistency,' an alternative model where applications specify invariants (consistency rules) that the system must maintain, rather than relying on execution order constraints. The key insight is to use SMT solvers (Z3) to analyze these invariants and determine which operations can safely execute without coordination, while still enforcing application-level guarantees. The paper introduces two strategies for handling operations requiring coordination: invariant repair (post-facto correction of violations) and violation avoidance (proactive reservation mechanisms like multi-level locks and escrow reservations). The prototype, Indigo, demonstrates performance comparable to weak consistency for most operations while enforcing invariants, though it has limitations (e.g., single-object invariants). The violation avoidance strategy, based on a reservation system, is highlighted as particularly novel and interesting.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the paper 'Taming uncertainty in distributed systems with help from the network' by Leners et al. (2015), which introduces Albatross, a novel membership service that leverages SDN (Software-Defined Networking) to actively enforce network partitions. Adrian Colyer highlights several key benefits of Albatross: it detects failures faster than traditional timeout-based methods, provides definitive reports on process disconnections by blocking traffic from failed processes, and simplifies distributed algorithms by converting uncertainty about process liveness into certainty. The paper demonstrates that Albatross can enable simpler fault models, such as a unique leader selection mechanism for atomic broadcast, reducing complexity compared to majority-based agreement protocols like Zab. The author notes that this work represents a novel application of SDN beyond its original purpose of network management, potentially opening new avenues in distributed systems design.
paper_title: Taming Uncertainty in Distributed Systems with Help from the Network
paper_abstract: We introduce Express-Lane (X-Lane), a novel system for mitigating interference in data center infrastructure to improve the liveness of coordination services. X-Lane follows a novel design from the ground up to achieve interactions with ultralow latency in the single-digit microsecond range and jitter in the nanosecond range, while the remaining interaction is treated as usual. To show X-Lane’s applicability and genericity we implemented and evaluated two services atop it on commodity hardware in a production environment of SAP SE: a failure detector (X-FD) with detection time under 10 µs and a Raft implementation (X-Raft) with latencies under 20 µs. We further show the smooth integrability of X-Lane services by replacing the replication protocol of Redis with X-Raft, making it strongly consistent while improving latency 18× and write throughput 1.5×.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Blade, a distributed garbage collector designed to mitigate tail latency caused by garbage collection (GC) pauses in data centers. The key insight is a distributed systems approach where nodes collaborate with applications to temporarily offload work from a node about to perform GC, thereby hiding GC pauses. Blade integrates simply with runtimes via callback handlers, allowing nodes to signal GC needs and coordinate with load balancers or consensus leaders (e.g., in Raft-based systems like etcd) to schedule GC during low-traffic periods. The approach is notably effective with high-throughput stop-the-world GC algorithms, which are simple yet often avoided due to latency concerns. Experimental results show dramatic reductions in tail latency (e.g., from 164ms to 7ms in a HTTP service) and improved performance over GC-off baselines in some cases. The paper also contrasts GC schemes, arguing that Blade's coordination enables the use of simpler, higher-throughput stop-the-world collectors instead of complex concurrent or real-time alternatives.
paper_title: Blade: A Data Center Garbage Collector
paper_abstract: 1.0000 An increasing number of high-performance distributed systems are written in garbage collected languages. This removes a large class of harmful bugs from these systems. However, it also introduces high tail-latency do to garbage collection pause times. We address this problem through a new technique of garbage collection avoidance which we call B LADE. B LADE is an API between the collector and application developer that allows developers to leverage existing failure recovery mechanisms in distributed systems to coordinate collection and bound the latency impact. We describe B LADE and implement it for the Go programming language. We also investigate two different systems that utilize B LADE, a HTTP load-balancer and the Raft consensus algorithm. For the load-balancer, we eliminate any latency introduced by the garbage collector, for Raft, we bound the latency impact to a single network round-trip, (48 µs in our setup). In both cases, latency at the tail using B LADE is up to three orders of magnitude better. 1. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the significance of the Borg paper, noting that Borg has been running all of Google's workloads for over a decade and its learnings are foundational to Kubernetes. The blog post emphasizes Borg's role as a warehouse-scale computer OS, managing heterogeneous machines and tasks with high efficiency and scalability. Key insights include Borg's centralized architecture (using a Paxos-based Borgmaster), its focus on maximizing resource utilization (e.g., mixing production and non-production workloads), and its design choices like fine-grained resource requests and resource reclamation schemes. The post also discusses Borg from a user's perspective, detailing job submission, quota and priority systems, and the declarative configuration language BCL. The influence of Borg on Kubernetes is noted as a major takeaway.
paper_title: Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg
paper_venue: ACM European Conference on Computer Systems (EuroSys)
paper_abstract: Google’s Borg system is a cluster manager that runs hundreds of thousands of jobs, from many thousands of different applications, across a number of clusters each with up to tens of thousands of machines. It achieves high utilization by combining admission control, efficient task-packing, over-commitment, and machine sharing with process-level performance isolation. It supports high-availability applications with runtime features that minimize fault-recovery time, and scheduling policies that reduce the probability of correlated failures. Borg simplifies life for its users by offering a declarative job specification language, name service integration, real-time job monitoring, and tools to analyze and simulate system behavior. We present a summary of the Borg system architecture and features, important design decisions, a quantitative analysis of some of its policy decisions, and a qualitative examination of lessons learned from a decade of operational experience with it.
