blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Rodney Brooks' 1985 paper as a seminal work in robotics, drawing a parallel to David Parnas' influential paper on software modularity. The paper addresses the challenge of decomposing a mobile robot's control system into modules, emphasizing robustness, adaptability, and simplicity. Brooks introduces the concept of 'levels of competence'—informal specifications of desired robot behaviors—leading to a 'subsumption architecture' where layers of competence are added incrementally. Each layer operates independently, with higher layers able to suppress or modify the outputs of lower layers, enabling the robot to achieve higher levels of functionality without altering previously validated lower layers. The paper's key insight is that complex behavior can emerge from simple, layered systems interacting with a complex environment, and that robustness is achieved by isolating and debugging lower layers before adding higher ones. Colyer notes the paper's enduring relevance, particularly its principles on system decomposition and interface simplicity.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer introduces the SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) problem, a foundational challenge in robotics where a mobile robot must build a map of an unknown environment while simultaneously determining its own location within that map. The blog highlights the paper's historical overview of SLAM research and its explanation of the two main solution approaches: EKF-SLAM (using an extended Kalman filter) and FastSLAM (using a Rao-Blackwellized particle filter). Colyer emphasizes the key insight that correlations between landmark estimates improve monotonically as observations accumulate, ensuring that knowledge of relative landmark locations never diverges. The post also breaks down the probabilistic formulation of SLAM, including state transition and observation models, and discusses the practical challenges of translating this theory into executable algorithms. The paper is praised for its clear presentation of both historical context and technical depth.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the paper 'Monocular SLAM Supported Object Recognition' by Pillai & Leonard (2015), which addresses the challenge of object recognition in robotics by integrating SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) with object detection. Adrian Colyer highlights the key insight: robots observe objects from multiple viewpoints over time, and leveraging this temporal and spatial context can significantly improve object recognition robustness. The paper contrasts traditional object recognition methods (e.g., sliding-window templates, feature encoding like BoVW or VLAD) with a SLAM-aware approach that uses monocular SLAM (ORB-SLAM) to generate 'object seeds' and refine proposals across multiple views. The author praises the paper for its clear overview of related work and its practical demonstration of how integrating SLAM and object recognition can overcome limitations of per-frame methods. The blog also emphasizes the difficulty of basic tasks like object recognition in robotics, despite advances in AI and open-source tools.

figures.title: SLAM-aware object recognition system
figures.caption: The proposed SLAM-aware object recognition system is able to robustly localize and recognize several objects in the scene, aggregating detection evidence across multiple views. Annotations in white are provided for clarity and are actual predictions proposed by our system.

figures.title: SLAM-aware object recognition pipeline
figures.caption: Outline of the SLAM-aware object recognition pipeline. Given an input RGB image stream I, we first reconstruct the scene in a semi-dense fashion using an existing monocular visual-SLAM implementation (ORB-SLAM) with a semi-dense depth estimator, and subsequently extract relevant map M, keyframe K and pose information ξ. We perform multi-scale density-based segmentation on the reconstructed scene to obtain object proposals O that are consistent across multiple views. On each of the images in the input RGB image stream I, we compute Dense-SIFT (R128 ) + RGB (R3 ) and reduce it to Φ ∈ R80 via PCA. The features Φ are then used to efficiently encode each of the projected object proposals O (bounding boxes of proposals projected on to each of the images with known poses ξ) using VLAD with FLAIR, to obtain Ψ. The resulting feature vector Ψ is used to train and predict likelihood of target label/category p(xi | y) of the object contained in each of the object proposals. The likelihoods for each object o ∈ O are aggregated across each of the viewpoints ξ to obtain robust object category prediction.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a paper that introduces a novel approach to method naming in programming languages by allowing method parameters to follow a mini-grammar, enabling optional, repeated, or grouped parameters. This generalizes multi-part method names (like Smalltalk's 'between:and:') to define entire families of related method names within a single declaration. The key insight is that this blurs the line between APIs and domain-specific languages (DSLs), enabling more expressive and concise control structures, DSLs, and library initialization. Colyer emphasizes the practical benefits, such as reducing repetitive code (e.g., replacing nearly 2,000 lines of Grace code with a 9-line method) and improving error detection both statically and dynamically. The paper demonstrates the approach through examples in the Grace language, including control structures (e.g., 'if then else'), query DSLs (inspired by LINQ), and widget library initialization.
paper_title: From APIs to Languages: Generalising Method Names
paper_abstract: Method names with multiple separate parts are a feature of many dynamic languages derived from Smalltalk. Generalising the syntax of method names to allow parts to be repeated, optional, or alternatives, means a single definition can respond to a whole family of method requests. We show how generalising method names can support flexible APIs for domain-specific languages, complex initialisation tasks, and control structures defined in libraries. We describe how we have extended Grace to support generalised method names, and prove that such an extension can be integrated into a gradually-typed language while preserving type soundness.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a compelling idea from this OOPSLA 2015 paper: integrating runtime monitoring data from production deployments directly into developers' IDEs to create tighter feedback loops, a concept termed 'feedback-driven development' (FDD). The paper argues that operational data is often siloed in monitoring tools designed for operations teams, making it difficult for developers to act on it. The authors propose mapping this data onto source code artifacts (e.g., via abstract syntax trees) to annotate and inform development. A key insight is addressing the relevance of operational data over time, especially in continuous deployment environments, by using statistical changepoint analysis to determine when historical data is no longer applicable. The paper demonstrates the concept through three tools: Performance Spotter (IDE-integrated performance profiling), Performance Hat (Eclipse plugin for hotspot identification and loop execution time prediction), and a cost-of-changes visualizer to raise awareness of cloud application costs.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reflects on the 2015 State of DevOps Survey results, which revealed a 200x gap in lead times between the best and worst performers. He draws a parallel to Michael Kremer's 'O-Ring Theory of Economic Development' (1993), which explains how small drops in quality across a production process can lead to dramatic reductions in output. The theory posits that in systems where tasks are interdependent and quality cannot be substituted for quantity, even minor weaknesses can cause catastrophic failures. Colyer applies this model to DevOps, suggesting that small quality gaps in any stage of a pipeline (e.g., testing, deployment) can disproportionately harm overall performance, velocity, and quality. He highlights how high-performing organizations achieve both speed and quality, debunking the trade-off myth, and emphasizes the compounding benefits of incremental improvements in quality.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the challenges developers face with build systems, noting that a significant portion of development effort is spent maintaining build scripts that grow increasingly complex. The paper introduces Pluto, a build system by Erdweg et al., which is both sound (always produces correct output) and optimal (avoids unnecessary work). Pluto dynamically tracks dependencies during build execution, enabling fine-grained incremental rebuilding. Key innovations include dynamic dependency registration, custom timestamps for precise dependency tracking, automatic injection of builder implementation dependencies, and support for cyclic dependencies via custom cycle-breakers. The paper formalizes Pluto's dependency graph and proves the soundness and optimality of its rebuild algorithm. Case studies demonstrate Pluto's applicability to incremental compilation for languages like Stratego and SugarJ, simplifying their build processes by replacing custom dependency tracking with Pluto's general solution.
paper_title: A Sound and Optimal Incremental Build System with Dynamic Dependencies
paper_abstract: 1. Build systems are used in all but the smallest software projects to invoke the right build tools on the right files in the right order. A build system must be sound (after a build, generated files consistently reflect the latest source files) and efficient (recheck and rebuild as few build units as possible). Contemporary build systems provide limited efficiency because they lack support for expressing finegrained file dependencies. We present a build system called pluto that supports the definition of reusable, parameterized, interconnected builders. When run, a builder notifies the build system about dynamically required and produced files as well as about other builders whose results are needed. To support fine-grained file dependencies, we generalize the traditional notion of time stamps to allow builders to declare their actual requirements on a file’s content. pluto collects the requirements and products of a builder with their stamps in a build summary. This enables pluto to provides provably sound and optimal incremental rebuilding. To support dynamic dependencies, our rebuild algorithm interleaves dependency analysis and builder execution and enforces invariants on the dependency graph through a dynamic analysis. We have developed pluto as a Java API and used it to implement more than 25 builders. We describe our experience with migrating a larger Ant build script to pluto and compare the respective build times. Software developers struggle with build systems on a regular basis. Previous studies show that on average 12% of development effort is not spent on developing software but on maintaining build scripts [11]. Another study finds that build scripts in existing software projects continuously change and grow in complexity in sync with changes to the project’s source code [12]. These studies show that the development and maintenance of build scripts is an essential part of software development. As with any software artifact, build scripts are difficult...

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the paper 'Scrap Your Boilerplate with Object Algebras' by Zhang et al. (2015), which introduces the Shy framework to reduce boilerplate code in implementing visitor patterns for AST traversals using Object Algebras. The author highlights the Object Algebras design pattern as a solution to the 'Expression Problem'—enabling type-safe extension of data types and operations without recompilation. The Shy framework automates common traversals (queries and transformations) via annotations, reducing manual boilerplate. The post emphasizes the balance between static typing and flexibility, showing how Shy achieves modularity and extensibility in Java despite its rigid type system.
paper_title: Scrap Your Boilerplate with Object Algebras
paper_abstract: of thesis entitled “Disjoint Intersection Types: Theory and Practice” Submitted by Xuan Bi for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy at The University of Hong Kong in December 2018 Programs are hard to write. It was so 50 years ago at the time of the so-called software crisis; it still remains so nowadays. Over the years, we have learned—the hard way—that software should be constructed in a modular way, i.e., as a network of smaller and loosely connected modules. To facilitate writing modular code, researchers and software practitioners have developed new methodologies; new programming paradigms; stronger type systems; as well as better tooling support. Still, this is not enough to cope with today’s needs. Several reasons have been raised for the lack of satisfactory solutions, but one that is constantly pointed out is the inadequacy of existing programming languages for the construction of modular software. This thesis investigates disjoint intersection types, a variant of intersection types. Disjoint intersections types have great potential to serve as a foundation for powerful, flexible and yet type-safe and easy to reason OO languages, suitable for writing modular software. On the theoretical side, this thesis shows how to significantly increase the expressiveness of disjoint intersection types by adding support for nested composition, along with parametric polymorphism. Nested composition extends inheritance to work on a whole family of classes, enabling high degrees of modularity and code reuse. The combination with parametric polymorphism further improves the state-of-art encodings of extensible designs. However, the extension with nested composition and parametric polymorphism is challenging, for two different reasons. Firstly, the subtyping relation that supports these features is non-trivial. Secondly, the syntactic method used to prove coherence for previous calculi with disjoint intersection types is too inflexible. This thesis addresses the first problem b...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the 'Delta Debugging' technique introduced by Zeller et al. in 2002, which automates the process of isolating minimal failure-inducing inputs from larger failing test cases. The approach uses a binary-search-like algorithm to systematically strip away irrelevant parts of an input (e.g., characters in a C program or HTML) to produce a concise reproduction of a bug. Colyer emphasizes the elegance of the method, which requires no understanding of the input's syntax or semantics, as demonstrated by its ability to reduce a complex C program crashing gcc to a minimal 1-line snippet in seconds. The paper introduces two variants: ddmin for minimizing failing inputs and dd for isolating the specific change causing the failure. The algorithm's efficiency and generality are underscored, with guarantees of finding a 1-minimal test case and performance insights dependent on input structure knowledge.
paper_title: Simplifying and Isolating Failure-Inducing Input

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights that the original Delta Debugging (ddmin) approach can simplify inputs like C programs without understanding their syntax, but often produces unnatural or terse results. Hierarchical Delta Debugging (HDD) improves upon this by incorporating knowledge of the input's hierarchical structure (e.g., parse trees for programs, XML/HTML/JSON documents), ensuring that all tested subsets are syntactically valid. This approach is significantly more efficient—reducing test cases from 680 to 86 for a C program example—and produces more readable output. HDD works top-down, recursively minimizing failure-inducing configurations at each level of the parse tree using ddmin, and includes optimizations like HDD+ and HDD* to further refine results. The paper demonstrates HDD's practicality with a lightweight Python implementation for XML (150 lines) and argues that for systems dealing with hierarchical inputs, investing in a test-case minimizer is highly beneficial.
paper_title: Hierarchical Delta Debugging
paper_abstract: Inputs causing a program to fail are usually large and often contain information irrelevant to the failure. It thus helps debugging to simplify program inputs. The Delta Debugging algorithm is a general technique applicable to minimizing all failure-inducing inputs for more effective debugging. In this paper, we present HDD, a simple but effective algorithm that significantly speeds up Delta Debugging and increases its output quality on tree structured inputs such as XML. Instead of treating the inputs as one flat atomic list, we apply Delta Debugging to the very structure of the data. In particular, we apply the original Delta Debugging algorithm to each level of a program’s input, working from the coarsest to the finest levels. We are thus able to prune the large irrelevant portions of the input early. All the generated input configurations are syntactically valid, reducing the number of inconclusive configurations that need to be tested and accordingly the amount of time spent simplifying. We have implemented HDD and evaluated it on a number of real failure-inducing inputs from the GCC and Mozilla bugzilla databases. Our Hierarchical Delta Debugging algorithm produces simpler outputs and takes orders of magnitude fewer test cases than the original Delta Debugging algorithm. It is able to scale to inputs of considerable size that the original Delta Debugging algorithm cannot process in practice. We argue that HDD is an effective tool for automatic debugging of programs expecting structured inputs.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes Colin Scott et al.'s paper on minimizing faulty executions in distributed systems, highlighting the challenges of debugging complex distributed systems where bugs arise from concurrency, asynchrony, and partial failures. The paper introduces DEMi (Distributed Execution Minimizer), a framework that reduces large execution traces to their minimal necessary components to reproduce bugs, making debugging more efficient. DEMi combines delta debugging for external events, dynamic partial order reduction (DPOR) for internal events, and heuristics like message-fingerprint functions to prune irrelevant schedules. The tool was applied to Akka-raft and Apache Spark, reducing faulty execution traces by up to 97% and outperforming state-of-the-art blackbox minimization techniques. The key insight is that minimizing both external and internal events, along with message payloads, can significantly simplify bug reproduction while preserving fault-triggering properties.
paper_title: Minimizing Faulty Executions of Distributed Systems
paper_abstract: Reliability and availability are essential for cloud services to succeed. Unfortunetaly, building flawless cloud systems is hard due to latent distributed concurrency (DC) bugs. Distributed System Model Checking (dmck) helps developers to systematically and quickly expose DC bugs by testing the implementation code. However, one challenge exists for dmck: path explosion challenge. The state-of-the-art dmcks such as M O D IST, dBug, CrystallBall, and SAMC handle this challenge by implementing reduction algorithms. Although these dmcks have shown some early successes, we found that these dmcks are not scalable enough to handle deep DC bug scenarios. We present AMC, an automated, fast and scalable dmck that focuses on finding deep DC bugs. AMC implements four new path reduction algorithms that are generic and backed up by static analysis: state symmetry, disjoint-updates independence, parallel flips and no zero-crash-impact reordering. As a result, AMC outperforms existing dmcks reduction algorithms by one to two orders of magnitude. AMC is integrated with 5 real-world systems (a mix of open-sourced, production, and proprietary systems) and overall has successfully reproduced 9 bugs and found 7 new bugs. x CHAPTER 1

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights two papers: 'Fail at Scale' by Maurer (2015) and 'Controlling Queue Delay' by Nichols & Van Jacobsen (2012). In 'Fail at Scale,' Maurer discusses Facebook's strategies for maintaining reliability amid rapid changes, focusing on mitigating resource exhaustion through three techniques: CoDel (a variant of the controlled delay algorithm), Adaptive LIFO, and Concurrency Control. CoDel prevents standing queues by enforcing short timeouts, Adaptive LIFO prioritizes recent requests during high queueing periods, and Concurrency Control limits client-side resource monopolization. Nichols & Van Jacobsen's paper introduces CoDel as an 'Active Queue Management' (AQM) strategy to combat bufferbloat in network routers. The paper explains how standing queues in buffers cause excessive latency without improving throughput, a problem misclassified as congestion. CoDel addresses this by distinguishing between benign queues (absorbing bursts) and harmful standing queues, offering a 'no-knobs' solution that works across diverse scenarios.
paper_title: Controlling Queue Delay
paper_abstract: 1 Programmable packet scheduling enables scheduling algorithms to be programmed into the data plane without changing the hardware. Existing proposals either have no hardware implementations for switch ASICs or require multiple strict-priority queues. We present Admission-In First-Out (AIFO) queues, a new solution for programmable packet scheduling that uses only a single first-in first-out queue. AIFO is motivated by the confluence of two recent trends: shallow buffers in switches and fast-converging congestion control in end hosts, that together leads to a simple observation: the decisive factor in a flow’s completion time (FCT) in modern datacenter networks is often which packets are enqueued or dropped, not the ordering they leave the switch. The core idea of AIFO is to maintain a sliding window to track the ranks of recent packets and compute the relative rank of an arriving packet in the window for admission control. Theoretically, we prove that AIFO provides bounded performance to Push-In First-Out (PIFO). Empirically, we fully implement AIFO and evaluate AIFO with a range of real workloads, demonstrating AIFO closely approximates PIFO. Importantly, unlike PIFO, AIFO can run at line rate on existing hardware and use minimal switch resources—as few as a single queue. Packet scheduling is a central research topic in computer networking. Over the past several decades, a great many packet scheduling algorithms have been designed to provide different properties and optimize diverse objectives [6, 11, 23, 40, 41]. Unfortunately, most of these algorithms, despite many novel ideas among them, never have found their way to impact the real world. This is largely due to the high cost to design and deploy switch ASICs to implement them, since packet scheduling algorithms must run in the data plane at line rate in order to process every single packet. Programmable packet scheduling is a holy grail for packet scheduling as it enables scheduling algorithms to be programmed i...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Facebook's successful integration of the INFER static analyzer into their continuous delivery pipeline for mobile apps, demonstrating how formal verification can be adapted to fast-moving engineering environments. The blog emphasizes the challenges of merging formal verification with rapid development cycles, particularly in mobile platforms where bug fixes are harder to deploy. INFER, based on separation logic, addresses critical requirements like automation, scalability, precision, and speed, running asynchronously to provide feedback within 10 minutes. The paper also discusses the social challenges of gaining developer trust in verification tools and the need for more practical, compositional analysis techniques in industry. Key insights include the feasibility of inter-procedural analysis at scale and the importance of incremental analysis and caching for performance.
paper_title: Moving Fast with Software Verification
paper_abstract: This experience report describes a style of applying symbolic model checking developed over the course of four years at Amazon Web Services (AWS). Lessons learned are drawn from proving properties of numerous C-based systems, e.g., custom hypervisors, encryption code, boot loaders, and an IoT operating system. Using our methodology, we find that we can prove the correctness of industrial low-level C-based systems with reasonable effort and predictability. Furthermore, AWS developers are increasingly writing their own formal specifications. All proofs discussed in this paper are publicly available on GitHub.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the 1987 paper by Varghese and Lauck, which introduces efficient data structures for managing timers in systems with large numbers of outstanding requests. The blog post emphasizes the practical relevance of the paper, noting its use in modern systems like Apache Kafka's 'purgatory' data structure for tracking timeouts. Colyer explains the paper's exploration of seven different timer management schemes, ranging from simple unordered lists to hierarchical timing wheels, and their respective time complexities for operations like start, stop, and per-tick bookkeeping. The key insight is the introduction of hierarchical timing wheels (Scheme 7) and hashed timing wheels (Scheme 6) as optimal solutions for balancing memory usage and operational efficiency, particularly in systems requiring high scalability.
paper_title: Hashed and Hierarchical Timing Wheels: Data Structures for the Efficient Implementation of a Timer Facility
paper_venue: ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP)
paper_abstract: be detected by periodic checking (e.g. memory corruption) and such timers always expire. Other failures can be only be inferred by the lack of some positive action (e.g. message acknowledgment) within a specified period. If failures are infrequent these timers rarely expire. Conventional algorithms to implement an Operating System timer module take O(n) time to start or mainrain a timer, where n is the number of outstanding timers: this is expensive for large n. This paper begins by exploring the relationship between timer algorithms, time flow mechanisms used in discrete event simulations, and sorting techniques. Next a timer algorithm for small timer intervals is presented that is similar to the timing wheel technique used in logic sinmlators. By using a circular buffer or timing wheel, it takes O(1) time to start, stop, and maintain timers within the range of the wheel. Algorithms in which the notion of time or relative time is integral: Examples include algorithms that control the rate of production of some entity (process control, rate-based flow control in communications), scheduling algorithms, and algorithms to control packet lifetimes in computer networks. These timers almost always expire. Two extensions for larger values of the interval are described. In the first, the timer interval is hashed into a slot on the timing wheel. In the second, a hierarchy of timing wheels with different granularities is used to span a greater range of intervals. The performance of these two schemes and various implementation tradeoffs are discussed. 1 The performance of algorithms to implement a timer module becomes an issue when any of the following are true: • The algorithm is implemented by a processor that is interrupted each time a hardware clock ticks, and the interrupt overhead is substantial.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the GD-Wheel paper, which introduces a cost-aware replacement policy for key-value stores. Adrian Colyer highlights the paper's key insight: traditional LRU cache eviction policies are suboptimal when the cost of recomputing or re-fetching cached items varies significantly. The authors propose GD-Wheel, which combines the Greedy-Dual algorithm with Hierarchical Cost Wheels (a variation of Hierarchical Timing Wheels) to integrate both recency and recomputation cost into eviction decisions. The paper demonstrates that GD-Wheel, when integrated with memcached and evaluated using the Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark, significantly reduces recomputation costs and read access latencies compared to LRU. The blog also emphasizes the importance of literature search in solving problems and how ideas can be repurposed across different domains.
paper_title: GD-Wheel: A Cost-Aware Replacement Policy for Key-Value Stores
paper_abstract: Memory-based key-value stores, such as Memcached and Redis, are often used to speed up web applications. Specifically, they are used to cache the results of computations, such as database queries and dynamically generated web pages, so that a future request to the web application may not have to repeat the same computation. Currently, when memorybased key-value stores reach their capacity limits, they use replacement policies, like LRU and random, that are oblivious to differences among the cached results in their recomputation costs. However, this paper shows that if the costs of recomputing cached results vary significantly, as in the RUBiS and TPC-W benchmarks, then a cost-aware replacement policy will not only reduce the web application’s total recomputation cost but also reduce its average response time. To this end, this paper introduces GD-Wheel, which is an amortized constant-time implementation of the GreedyDual replacement algorithm that supports a limited range of costs. In effect, GD-Wheel integrates recency of access and cost of recomputation in an efficient manner. Moreover, this paper describes an implementation of GD-Wheel in Memcached, including the modifications to Memcached’s interface so that web applications can include cost information with each key-value pair, and a new cost-aware slab rebalancing policy for Memcached’s slab-based memory allocator. An evaluation of this implementation using the Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark shows that GD-Wheel, when compared to LRU, reduces the total recomputation cost by as much as 90%. blog_summary: The blog post introduces the FIT trade-off for distributed databases, which states that a system can have any two of Fairness, strong Isolation, and Throughput, but not all three. Adrian Colyer highlights that this challenges the common perception of an isolation-throughput trade-off by introducing fairness as a key variable. The paper argues that distributed coordination is unavoidable for distributed transactions, but systems can manage its cost by prioritizing or delaying transactions (fairness) rather than weakening isolation. The key insight is that strong isolation and high throughput are achievable if fairness is sacrificed, and vice versa. The post also clarifies the definitions of fairness, isolation, and the role of coordination in distributed transaction processing.
paper_title: FIT: A Distributed Database Performance Trade-off
paper_abstract: Designing distributed database systems is an inherently complex process, involving many choices and tradeoffs that must be considered. It is impossible to build a distributed database that has all the features that users intuitively desire. In this article, we discuss the three-way relationship between three such desirable features — fairness, isolation, and throughput (FIT) — and argue that only two out of the three of them can be achieved simultaneously.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a growing mismatch between efficient asynchronous machine learning algorithms and traditional distributed dataflow systems like Hadoop and Spark, which are optimized for coarse-grained, synchronous models. He notes that while asynchronous, lock-free implementations (e.g., HOGWILD!) can significantly speed up algorithms like stochastic gradient descent (SGD) by avoiding synchronization barriers, these approaches are not well-supported by commodity dataflow frameworks. The paper introduces an asynchronous communication mechanism called Asynchronous Sideways Information Passing (ASIP) that integrates into existing BSP-like dataflow systems with minimal changes. ASIP enables fine-grained, asynchronous communication between operators within the same stage, allowing algorithms like ASIP-SGD and ASIP-ADMM to bypass synchronous barriers and achieve better performance. The blog emphasizes the practicality of this approach, demonstrating that it can be implemented on top of Apache Spark with minor modifications while addressing challenges like fault tolerance and task scheduling.
paper_title: Asynchronous Complex Analytics in a Distributed Dataflow Architecture
paper_abstract: Scalable distributed dataflow systems have recently experienced widespread adoption, with commodity dataflow engines such as Hadoop and Spark, and even commodity SQL engines routinely supporting increasingly sophisticated analytics tasks (e.g., support vector machines, logistic regression, collaborative filtering). However, these systems’ synchronous (often Bulk Synchronous Parallel) dataflow execution model is at odds with an increasingly important trend in the machine learning community: the use of asynchrony via shared, mutable state (i.e., data races) in convex programming tasks, which has—in a single-node context—delivered noteworthy empirical performance gains and inspired new research into asynchronous algorithms. In this work, we attempt to bridge this gap by evaluating the use of lightweight, asynchronous state transfer within a commodity dataflow engine. Specifically, we investigate the use of asynchronous sideways information passing (ASIP) that presents single-stage parallel iterators with a Volcano-like intra-operator iterator that can be used for asynchronous information passing. We port two synchronous convex programming algorithms, stochastic gradient descent and the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), to use ASIPs. We evaluate an implementation of ASIPs within on Apache Spark that exhibits considerable speedups as well as a rich set of performance trade-offs in the use of these asynchronous algorithms.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a new data structure called CHAMP (Compressed Hash-Array Mapped Prefix-tree) for optimizing immutable collections in JVM-based languages like Scala and Clojure. CHAMP offers significant performance improvements over traditional Hash-Array Mapped Tries (HAMTs), with 1.3-6.7x faster iteration and 3-25.4x faster equality checking. The key insight is improving cache locality and reducing memory overhead by splitting the array into separate value and sub-node reference sections, using bitmaps for efficient indexing, and maintaining a compact canonical form even after deletions. The paper addresses inefficiencies in HAMTs when ported to the JVM due to memory indirection and lack of control over memory layout.
paper_title: Optimizing Hash-Array Mapped Tries for Fast and Lean Immutable JVM Collections
paper_abstract: 1. The data structures under-pinning collection API (e.g. lists, sets, maps) in the standard libraries of programming languages are used intensively in many applications. The standard libraries of recent Java Virtual Machine languages, such as Clojure or Scala, contain scalable and well-performing immutable collection data structures that are implemented as Hash-Array Mapped Tries (HAMTs). HAMTs already feature efficient lookup, insert, and delete operations, however due to their tree-based nature their memory footprints and the runtime performance of iteration and equality checking lag behind array-based counterparts. This particularly prohibits their application in programs which process larger data sets. In this paper, we propose changes to the HAMT design that increase the overall performance of immutable sets and maps. The resulting general purpose design increases cache locality and features a canonical representation. It outperforms Scala’s and Clojure’s data structure implementations in terms of memory footprint and runtime efficiency of iteration (1.3– 6.7 x) and equality checking (3–25.4 x). In this paper we reduce memory overhead and runtime performance overhead from the implementations of immutable collections on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). Collections under-pin many (if not most) applications in general purpose programming languages as well as domain specific languages that are compiled to the JVM. Optimizing collections implies optimizing many applications. Immutable collections are a specific area most relevant to functional/object-oriented programming such as practiced by Scala1 and Clojure2 programmers. With the advance of functional language constructs in Java 8 and functional APIs such as the stream processing API [6], immutable collections become more relevant to Java as well. Immutability for collections has a number of benefits: it implies referential transparency without giving up on sharing data [17]; it satisfies safety requirements for ...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes Szekeres et al.'s 2013 paper as a comprehensive 'Systematization of Knowledge' (SoK) on memory corruption attacks and defenses. The blog highlights the complexity of defending against these attacks, especially given space and time overhead constraints. The paper emphasizes that the best solution is using type-safe languages, but acknowledges the impracticality of rewriting existing C/C++ code. Colyer notes the paper's excellent conceptual framework, including a useful flow-chart summarizing attack models and exploit types. The blog underscores the non-trivial nature of defenses, with most approaches failing in practice due to performance overheads, compatibility issues, or incomplete protection. The key insight is the categorization of attacks (code corruption, control-flow hijacking, data-only attacks, information leaking) and defenses, providing a structured understanding of this persistent security challenge.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a groundbreaking attack technique described in Shacham's 2007 paper, which demonstrates that the widely deployed W⊕X defense against code corruption attacks is less effective than previously believed. The paper introduces new return-into-libc attack methods that allow arbitrary computation without any function calls, leveraging unintended instruction sequences in x86 code—particularly in the libc library. The key insight is that due to the dense and flexible nature of the x86 instruction set architecture (ISA), attackers can chain short, unintended instruction sequences (ending in a 'ret' instruction) to perform any desired task, effectively bypassing W⊕X protections. This technique, termed 'return-oriented programming,' repurposes existing code in a program's memory to execute malicious operations, making it resilient to defenses that remove specific functions from libraries or alter code generation. The paper catalogs numerous such sequences and demonstrates their Turing completeness, enabling full exploitation.
paper_title: The geometry of innocent flesh on the bone: Return-into-libc without function calls (on x86)
paper_venue: ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS'07)
paper_abstract: We present new techniques that allow a return-into-libc attack to be mounted on x86 executables that calls no functions at all. Our attack combines a large number of short instruction sequences to build gadgets that allow arbitrary computation. We show how to discover such instruction sequences by means of static analysis. We make use, in an essential way, of the properties of the x86 instruction set.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the alarming lack of security in modern automobile systems, drawing from a 2010 paper that analyzed a 2009 model year car. The author emphasizes the persistent vulnerabilities in automotive systems, noting that many cars on the road today (especially older models) likely share similar security flaws. The paper demonstrates how attackers can exploit physical access (e.g., via the OBD-II port) or wireless interfaces to compromise a car's internal networks. Colyer also critiques the poor software development practices in the automotive industry, citing examples like Toyota's 'Unintended Acceleration' lawsuit, which revealed critical flaws such as thousands of global variables, inadequate failsafes, and memory corruption risks. The key insight is that modern cars, despite their reliance on distributed computing systems, lack robust security measures to prevent digital attacks.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a critical security vulnerability in aftermarket telematic control units (TCUs) used in connected cars, which are loosely coupled and independently maintained devices. The paper demonstrates how these devices, often used for insurance telematics or fleet management, expose multiple attack vectors—both locally via USB and remotely through network interfaces or SMS. The authors uncover severe flaws, including hardcoded cryptographic keys across all devices, exposed administrative interfaces, and the ability to remotely update firmware without authentication or cryptographic signing. These weaknesses allow attackers to gain root access, inject malicious updates, or compromise the vehicle's CAN bus. The blog emphasizes the dangers of poor security practices like default keys, lack of update signing, and exposed services, while also demonstrating how such devices can be discovered and enumerated using tools like Shodan or sequential phone number patterns.

Since the TCUs were tightly coupled into their vehicles, they could be updated during scheduled vehicle service and mitigated through changes in the OEM-operated service. In this paper we have turned our attention to the thornier problem of aftermarket devices, which are typically purchased directly by consumers or through a third-party service offering (e.g., insurance or fleet management), are loosely coupled with the vehicle in which they are installed, and are maintained independent of normal automotive service channels. Most of such aftermarket devices take the form of small “dongles” that interface with automotive systems through the mandated On-Board Diagnostics port (OBDII in the US, EOBD in Europe, JOBD in Japan) typically located under the driver’s side dashboard. A series of standard protocols and schemas allow an OBD-II peer to access an array of low-level sensor information about the car’s operation (most of this is defined in SAE standards J1979, J2012, and J2178). In addition, it is common that the physical OBD-II port also provides access to the vehicle’s internal networks (typically one or more CAN buses) for monitoring additional, vehicle specific, information. In spite of the fact that most aftermarket TCUs are designed for monitoring only, CAN is a multi-master bus and thus any device with a CAN transceiver is able to send messages as well as receive. This presents a key security problem since as we, and others, have shown, transmit access to the CAN bus is frequently sufficient to obtain arbitrary control over all key vehicular systems (including throttle and brakes). Further, it is common that these devices, in addition to a microprocessor and a CAN transceiver, also provide a number of additional functionality including a GPS, accelerometers and, critically, external networking connectivity. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 1994 paper by Abadi and Needham as a foundational work on cryptographic protocol design, emphasizing how even experts often fail in creating secure protocols. The authors present 11 informal but practical principles to guide protocol design, arguing that these guidelines can simplify protocols and reduce common mistakes. The paper distinguishes between the role of formal methods in verifying correctness versus their inability to guide initial design. Key insights include the importance of clear message semantics (Principle 1), explicit trust assumptions (Principle 2 and 11), and careful use of cryptographic primitives like encryption and nonces. The blog post underscores that adherence to these principles could have prevented many published protocol failures.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 1997 paper as the foundational work that introduced Functional Reactive Programming (FRP). The authors, Elliott and Hudak, sought to simplify the creation of animations by moving away from tedious frame-by-frame construction and instead modeling animations as continuous behaviors over time. The key insight is elevating time-varying values (behaviors) and discrete events to first-class status in a programming model, enabling elegant, declarative specifications of animations. The paper introduces Fran, a Haskell-based system that composes behaviors and events through recursive data types and functions, demonstrating how concurrency, reactivity, and polymorphic media can be naturally expressed. Colyer emphasizes the clarity, composability, and semantic cleanliness of this modeling approach compared to imperative alternatives.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses a 2012 survey paper on reactive programming by Bainomugisha et al., which provides an overview and taxonomy of the field. Adrian Colyer highlights that reactive programming addresses challenges in event-driven applications by abstracting over time management, data dependencies, and computation flows, allowing programmers to focus on desired outcomes rather than control flow. The key insight is that reactive programming languages automatically propagate state changes across dependent computations, eliminating the need for manual updates. The post explains core concepts like behaviors (continuous time-varying values) and events (discrete value changes), and compares push-based vs. pull-based evaluation models, including their trade-offs like glitches and time/space leaks. The survey also categorizes reactive languages based on six properties, such as basic abstractions and evaluation models.
paper_title: A Survey on Reactive Programming
paper_abstract: ions to express time-varying values and automatically managing dependencies between such values. A number of approaches have been recently proposed embedded in various languages such as Haskell, Scheme, JavaScript, Java, .NET, etc. This survey describes and provides a taxonomy of existing reactive programming approaches along six axes: representation of time-varying values, evaluation model, lifting operations, multidirectionality, glitch avoidance, and support for distribution. From this taxonomy, we observe that there are still open challenges in the field of reactive programming. For instance, multidirectionality is supported only by a small number of languages, which do not automatically track dependencies between time-varying values. Similarly, glitch avoidance, which is subtle in reactive programs, cannot be ensured in distributed reactive programs using the current techniques. blog_summary: The blog post introduces Elm, a functional reactive programming (FRP) language designed for building responsive graphical user interfaces (GUIs), particularly for web applications. Adrian Colyer highlights Elm's use of FRP to model time-varying values (signals) in a purely functional and declarative way, which simplifies the creation of complex time-dependent relationships in GUIs. A key distinction in Elm is that signals change only in response to discrete events, unlike traditional FRP languages where signals change continuously. This design choice ensures that GUIs remain responsive even during long-running computations by allowing asynchronous processing. The post also discusses Elm's core abstractions, such as signals, lift (map), foldp, and async operations, and how they enable efficient and composable GUI development. The Featherweight Elm (FElm) formalism is mentioned as a stripped-down version of Elm used to explain its syntax and semantics.
paper_title: Asynchronous Functional Reactive Programming for GUIs
paper_abstract: Semantics of most FRP languages assume that signals change continuously. Thus, their implementations sample input signals as quickly as possible, and continually recompute the program with the latest values for the signals. In practice, however, many signals change discretely and infrequently, and so constant sampling leads to unnecessary recomputation. By contrast, Elm assumes that all signals are discrete, and uses this assumption to detect when a signal is unchanged, and in that case, avoid unnecessary recomputation. In Elm, signals change only when a discrete event occurs. An event occurs when a program input (such as the mouse position) changes. Events require recomputation of the program, as the result of the program may have changed. Previous FRP systems require that events are processed synchronously: one at a time in the exact order of occurrence. In general, synchronization is required to allow the programmer to reason about the behavior of the FRP system, and ensure correct functionality. However, processing an event may take significant time, resulting in delays to the entire FRP system. Pipelining event processing can help to reduce latency, but because the global order of events must be respected, an event cannot finish processing until all previous events have finished. In GUIs, this is unacceptable behavior: the user interface should remain responsive, even if a previous user action triggered a long-running computation. Graphical user interfaces (GUIs) mediate many of our interactions with computers. Functional Reactive Programming (FRP) is a promising approach to GUI design, providing high-level, declarative, compositional abstractions to describe user interactions and time-dependent computations. We present Elm, a practical FRP language focused on easy creation of responsive GUIs. Elm has two major features: simple declarative support for Asynchronous FRP; and purely functional graphical layout. Asynchronous FRP allows the programmer to specify whe...

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the paper 'We Have a DREAM: Distributed Reactive Programming with Consistency Guarantees' by Magara & Salvaneschi (2014), which addresses the challenge of distributing reactive programs while ensuring consistency. The authors highlight that most existing reactive programming solutions do not support distribution, and the paper introduces three propagation semantics—causal, glitch-free, and atomic—to handle consistency in distributed reactive applications. The blog author emphasizes the importance of these semantics, particularly in financial applications where glitches or inconsistent updates can lead to incorrect decisions, such as erroneous sell orders. The paper also explores the trade-offs between consistency guarantees and coordination overhead, demonstrating how different consistency models (e.g., causal, glitch-free, atomic) can impact application behavior. The DREAM system model is described, including its use of a dependency graph for reactive variables and the implementation details involving publish-subscribe over a distributed broker network.
paper_title: We Have a DREAM: Distributed Reactive Programming with Consistency Guarantees
paper_abstract: The reactive programming paradigm has been proposed to simplify the development of reactive systems. It relies on programming primitives to express dependencies between data items and on runtime/middleware support for automated propagation of changes. Despite this paradigm is receiving increasing attention, defining the precise semantics and the consistency guarantees for reactive programming in distributed environments is an open research problem. This paper targets such problem by studying the consistency guarantees for the propagation of changes in a distributed reactive system. In particular, it introduces three propagation semantics, namely causal, glitch free, and atomic, providing different trade-offs between costs and guarantees. Furthermore, it describes how these semantics are concretely implemented in a Distributed REActice Middleware (DREAM), which exploits a distributed event-based dispatching system to propagate changes. We compare the performance of DREAM in a wide range of scenarios. This allows us to study the overhead introduced by the different semantics in terms of network traffic and propagation delay and to assess the efficiency of DREAM in supporting distributed reactive systems.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights how Reactive Vega combines Event-driven Functional Reactive Programming (E-FRP) with dataflow and stream management techniques from the database community to enable declarative interactive visualizations. The key insight is a unified data model where input data, scene graph elements, and interaction events are all treated as first-class streaming data sources, enabling more expressive and efficient visualizations. The paper demonstrates how E-FRP's time-varying streams and signals can drive visual encodings, while leveraging streaming database techniques (e.g., Aurora, TelegraphCQ) for relational and hierarchical data. The architecture avoids glitches through a centralized scheduler that ensures topological order and prunes unnecessary computation, and supports dynamic graph restructuring for nested data.
paper_title: Reactive Vega: A Streaming Dataflow Architecture for Declarative Interactive Visualization
paper_abstract: —We present Reactive Vega, a system architecture that provides the first robust and comprehensive treatment of declarative visual and interaction design for data visualization. Starting from a single declarative specification, Reactive Vega constructs a dataflow graph in which input data, scene graph elements, and interaction events are all treated as first-class streaming data sources. To support expressive interactive visualizations that may involve time-varying scalar, relational, or hierarchical data, Reactive Vega’s dataflow graph can dynamically re-write itself at runtime by extending or pruning branches in a data-driven fashion. We discuss both compile- and run-time optimizations applied within Reactive Vega, and share the results of benchmark studies that indicate superior interactive performance to both D3 and the original, non-reactive Vega system. Index Terms—Information visualization, systems, toolkits, declarative specification, optimization, interaction, streaming data

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 1979 paper by Selinger et al. as a foundational work that introduced the concept of a query optimizer in the System R relational database management system. The paper demonstrates how a declarative query language (like SQL) can achieve performance comparable to procedural approaches, a key insight that revolutionized database systems. The author emphasizes the paper's systematic approach to access path selection, where the optimizer evaluates multiple execution strategies (e.g., index scans vs. full table scans) based on cost models incorporating I/O and CPU metrics. Colyer notes the paper's detailed cost estimation formulas and heuristics for selectivity factors, which remain influential in modern query optimizers. The four-phase SQL processing pipeline (parsing, optimization, code generation, execution) is also highlighted as a lasting architectural contribution.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 1975 paper by Gray et al. as a foundational work on database locking strategies, particularly focusing on the tradeoff between locking overhead and concurrency. The paper introduces a hierarchical locking mechanism where resources can be locked at different granularities (e.g., areas, files, records), with intention locks (IS, IX) enabling efficient access to subtrees. The author appreciates the paper's clarity and simplicity in explaining complex concepts without assuming prior knowledge. The blog emphasizes the introduction of six lock modes (NL, IS, IX, S, SIX, X) and their compatibility rules, as well as the protocol for requesting and releasing locks. The paper also generalizes the approach to acyclic DAGs, though the blog notes some complexity in this extension.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 1975 paper by Gray et al. as a foundational work introducing the concept of 'degrees of consistency' in database transactions. The paper defines four levels of consistency (0 through 3), which map closely to modern ANSI SQL isolation levels (e.g., Degree 1 = Read Uncommitted, Degree 2 = Read Committed, Degree 3 = Repeatable Reads). The author emphasizes the paper's insight into how transactions must manage locks to ensure consistency, particularly during concurrent execution. Colyer notes the paper's discussion of recoverability and the trade-offs between consistency and concurrency, including how lower degrees of consistency can still achieve higher levels in practice under certain conditions. The historical context and the paper's influence on later work, such as 'Coordination Avoidance in Database Systems,' are also highlighted.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 1987 paper as a critical examination of contradictory performance studies on concurrency control algorithms in database systems. The paper argues that the conflicting results from prior research stem from differing underlying assumptions about system resources, transaction behavior, and modeling choices, rather than inherent flaws in the algorithms themselves. Agrawal et al. build a comprehensive performance model that includes hardware resources, user behavior, and transaction workloads to systematically evaluate three concurrency control strategies: blocking, immediate-restart, and optimistic. The key insight is that the assumptions—such as infinite resources or the treatment of restarted transactions—dramatically influence performance outcomes, and by varying these assumptions, the authors reconcile seemingly contradictory prior findings. The paper underscores the importance of realistic resource modeling in performance evaluations.
paper_title: Concurrency Control Performance Modeling: Alternatives and Implications

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights ARIES (Algorithm for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics) as a foundational and canonical algorithm for implementing a 'No Force, Steal' write-ahead logging (WAL) based recovery manager in industrial-strength transaction processing systems. The paper is praised for its detailed approach to durability in database systems, where the log serves as the source of truth to ensure committed actions persist and uncommitted ones are undone. ARIES' key insight is its use of log sequence numbers (LSNs) to track page states, support for fine-granularity locking, and logical undo operations, enabling high concurrency and recovery efficiency. The algorithm's design—including compensation log records (CLRs), checkpointing, and policies like 'steal' and 'no-force'—allows databases to balance performance with robust recovery from failures, making it a de facto standard in commercial RDBMS systems.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the foundational work on transaction management in distributed database systems presented in Mohan et al.'s 1986 paper. The blog post focuses on the core Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol, which ensures atomicity in distributed transactions despite site or communication failures. Colyer emphasizes the protocol's two phases (prepare and commit), the roles of coordinator and subordinates, and the critical logging requirements to guarantee recovery and atomicity. He also notes the paper's emphasis on performance aspects, particularly logging and communication overhead in failure-free scenarios. The post sets the stage for discussing optimizations like Presumed Abort and Presumed Commit in subsequent entries.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer examines the Presumed Abort (PA) and Presumed Commit (PC) optimizations to the standard two-phase commit (2PC) protocol as described in Mohan et al.'s 1986 paper. The PA protocol optimizes abort scenarios by allowing the coordinator to 'forget' a transaction immediately after deciding to abort it, eliminating the need for forced log writes, ACKs from subordinates, or recording subordinate names. It also introduces READ VOTEs for read-only transactions, further reducing overhead. The PC protocol, designed for commit-heavy workloads, reverses the assumptions: it presumes commit in the no-information case but requires a 'collecting record' to be force-written before sending PREPARE messages to handle coordinator crashes safely. The post highlights the trade-offs between these protocols, showing how PA and PC reduce message and log overhead compared to 2PC, with PA generally performing better for read-heavy or mixed workloads, while PC can save messages in certain update scenarios. The key insight is that the choice of protocol can significantly impact performance based on transaction characteristics and failure scenarios.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this paper by Jim Gray and Leslie Lamport, which demonstrates that the classic two-phase commit (2PC) protocol is a special case of the consensus problem. The authors introduce Paxos Commit, a non-blocking transaction commit protocol that leverages the Paxos consensus algorithm to tolerate failures among coordinators. Unlike 2PC, which relies on a single coordinator and can block indefinitely upon failure, Paxos Commit uses multiple coordinators (2F+1) to ensure progress as long as a majority are operational. The paper provides TLA+ specifications for both 2PC and Paxos Commit, proving that Paxos Commit refines 2PC. Colyer praises the clarity of the formal specifications and the refinement proofs, noting that they provide a provably correct foundation for transaction commit protocols. The paper also formalizes the requirements for transaction commit, including safety properties (stability and consistency) and liveness properties (non-triviality and non-blocking).
paper_title: Consensus on Transaction Commit
paper_abstract: The distributed transaction commit problem requires reaching agreement on whether a transaction is committed or aborted. The classic Two-Phase Commit protocol blocks if the coordinator fails. Fault-tolerant consensus algorithms also reach agreement, but do not block whenever any majority of the processes are working. The Paxos Commit algorithm runs a Paxos consensus algorithm on the commit/abort decision of each participant to obtain a transaction commit protocol that uses 2F + 1 coordinators and makes progress if at least F +1 of them are working properly. Paxos Commit has the same stable-storage write delay, and can be implemented to have the same message delay in the fault-free case, as Two-Phase Commit, but it uses more messages. The classic Two-Phase Commit algorithm is obtained as the special F = 0 case of the Paxos Commit algorithm. Contents

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the key insight of this paper: by leveraging modern hardware trends—specifically RDMA-capable networks and non-volatile DRAM via distributed UPS—FaRM can achieve distributed transactions with strict serializability, high availability, and low latency without compromising on performance. The paper challenges traditional assumptions by demonstrating that in a world where network and storage I/O are no longer bottlenecks, CPU becomes the limiting factor, and FaRM's protocols are designed from first principles to optimize for CPU efficiency. Colyer emphasizes FaRM's novel transaction, replication, and recovery protocols, which use one-sided RDMA reads/writes to minimize CPU overhead, optimistic concurrency control, and precise membership mechanisms to handle failures in this unconventional setup. The result is staggering performance: a 90-machine FaRM cluster achieves 4.5 million TPC-C transactions per second with sub-2ms latency and 60ms recovery time.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes the ACM Queue article by Nanavati et al. (2016), highlighting the dramatic shift in system design assumptions due to the emergence of storage class memories (SCMs). The blog emphasizes that the traditional assumption—where CPUs are orders of magnitude faster than I/O devices—is being invalidated by SCMs like PCIe SSDs and NVDIMMs, which offer near-DRAM performance with persistence. Colyer notes that this 1,000x performance improvement over spinning disks forces a reevaluation of decades-old design choices, particularly around caching, data reduction, and I/O-centric scheduling. The article argues that simply replacing disks with SCMs won't yield proportional performance gains unless systems are rebalanced to fully utilize these devices, requiring horizontal scaling, contention-free scheduling, and workload-aware tiering. The key insight is that SCMs demand a fundamental rethinking of system architecture to avoid underutilization and inefficiency.
paper_title: Non-volatile Storage: Implications of the Datacenter's shifting center
paper_abstract: technologies and form factors [8, 10]. The second change is that both Linux [3, 1] and Microsoft [52, 48] have announced support for NVM in their respective kernels. Lastly, Intel has announced that there are new instructions coming in their next ISA update that are specifically for flushing data from CPU caches to NVM [69, 9]. All of these portend the soon arrival of NVM. But it is unclear at this point how to best leverage these new technologies in a DBMS. There are several aspects of NVM that make existing DBMS architectures inappropriate for them [33]. For example, disk-oriented DBMSs (e.g., Oracle RDBMS, IBM DB2, MySQL) are predicated on using block-oriented devices for durable storage that are slow at random access. As such, they maintain an in-memory cache for blocks of tuples and try to maximize the amount of sequential reads and writes to storage. In the case of memory-oriented DBMSs (e.g., VoltDB, MemSQL), they contain components for overcoming the volatility of DRAM. Such components may be unnecessary in a system with byte-addressable NVM with fast random access. The difference in the performance characteristics of volatile (DRAM) and non-volatile storage devices (HDD/SSDs) influences the design of database management systems (DBMSs). The key assumption has always been that the latter is much slower than the former. This affects all aspects of a DBMS’s runtime architecture. But the arrival of new non-volatile memory (NVM) storage that is almost as fast as DRAM with fine-grained read/writes invalidates these previous design choices. In this tutorial, we provide an outline on how to build a new DBMS given the changes to hardware landscape due to NVM. We survey recent developments in this area, and discuss the lessons learned from prior research on designing NVM database systems. We highlight a set of open research problems, and present ideas for solving some of them.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights RAMCloud as a groundbreaking distributed storage system that keeps all data in DRAM for ultra-low latency (5µs reads, 13.5µs durable writes) while ensuring durability via secondary storage. He notes the paper's comprehensive 5-year overview (2009-2014) and praises its design choices like kernel bypass, polling-based NIC communication, and single dispatch thread architecture to achieve sub-10µs latency goals. Colyer emphasizes RAMCloud's motivation: addressing the 3-5 order of magnitude latency gap between single-server and distributed systems, which hinders modern web applications. He also contrasts RAMCloud with RDMA-based systems like FaRM, noting RAMCloud's conclusion that RDMA's primary benefit is CPU offloading rather than latency reduction. The paper's vision of future applications (e.g., self-driving cars) requiring interactive-scale data access is highlighted as particularly noteworthy.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the 'rules-based programming' pattern developed by the RAMCloud team for writing Distributed, Concurrent, Fault-Tolerant (DCFT) modules. This approach uses (condition, action) pairs to handle the inherent non-determinism in DCFT systems, where traditional imperative programming fails due to concurrency, faults, and asynchronous events. The rules-based method proved highly effective in RAMCloud, enabling concise modules (30-100 lines), minimal overhead (200-300ns out of 13.5µs total write time), and even simplifying the Hadoop Map-Reduce job scheduler from 2,250 lines to just 117 lines. Colyer notes the approach's natural fit for formal specification (e.g., TLA+/PlusCal) and its ability to cleanly separate deterministic actions from non-deterministic events. The key insight is that DCFT problems are inherently non-monotonic, making rules-based programming a more intuitive and maintainable solution than traditional methods.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this paper as a concrete example of how non-volatile memory (NVM) and fast storage technologies (like NVMe) fundamentally alter traditional system design assumptions. The authors revisit the classic ARIES write-ahead logging (WAL) and recovery protocol, originally designed for spinning disks, and redesign it for NVM-based storage (MARS). Colyer emphasizes the paper's exploration of how performance characteristics of NVM (e.g., byte-addressability, in-place updates, and near-DRAM latency) eliminate the need for many ARIES optimizations like append-only logs, no-force policies, and steal policies. The key insight is that NVM enables simpler, more efficient transaction support by leveraging hardware capabilities such as editable atomic writes (EAW), which allow in-place updates and eliminate the need for undo logging. The paper demonstrates how storage-class memory can 'turn traditional system design assumptions on their head.'
paper_title: From ARIES to MARS: Transaction Support for Next-Generation Solid State Drives
paper_abstract: Transaction-based systems often rely on write-ahead logging (WAL) algorithms designed to maximize performance on disk-based storage. However, emerging fast, byte-addressable, non-volatile memory (NVM) technologies (e.g., phase-change memories, spin-transfer torque MRAMs, and the memristor) present very different performance characteristics, so blithely applying existing algorithms can lead to disappointing performance. This paper presents a novel storage primitive, called editable atomic writes (EAW), that enables sophisticated, highly-optimized WAL schemes in fast NVM-based storage systems. EAWs allow applications to safely access and modify log contents rather than treating the log as an append-only, write-only data structure, and we demonstrate that this can make implementating complex transactions simpler and more efficient. We use EAWs to build MARS, a WAL scheme that provides the same as features ARIES [26] (a widely-used WAL system for databases) but avoids making disk-centric implementation decisions. We have implemented EAWs and MARS in a nextgeneration SSD to demonstrate that the overhead of EAWs is minimal compared to normal writes, and that they provide large speedups for transactional updates to hash tables, B+trees, and large graphs. In addition, MARS outperforms ARIES by up to 3.7× while reducing software complexity. ∗Now working at Google Inc. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer discusses the paper 'Blurred Persistence: Efficient Transactions in Persistent Memory' which explores the challenges of managing transactions in persistent memory systems. The key issue is the shift from managing the relationship between volatile memory and disk to managing the relationship between the volatile CPU cache and persistent memory. The author highlights the performance overhead caused by frequent I/O halts required for storage consistency in persistent memory, as the CPU cache is hardware-controlled and tracking pages in software is cumbersome. The paper introduces two mechanisms, Execution in Log (XIL) and Volatile Checkpoint with Bulk Persistence (VCBP), to address these challenges. XIL allows transactions to execute in the log area and removes duplicated copies, while VCBP delays the persistence of committed transaction data and uses bulk persistence to improve cache efficiency. The blog post also mentions new hardware instructions like CLFLUSHOPT, CLWB, and PCOMMIT that can help with cache flushing and persistence, but the paper focuses on software solutions that work with existing hardware.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes key hardware trends in networking, memory, storage, and processing that are transforming data center design and distributed systems. He highlights the shift from 10GbE to 40GbE/100GbE/400GbE Ethernet, enabling ultra-low latency (down to ~2.4µs round-trip) with technologies like RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) and RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet), which can achieve ~1.4µs latency by bypassing the CPU. The blog also discusses NVRAM (Non-volatile RAM) technologies like 3D XPoint, which blur the lines between memory and storage, offering persistent memory with higher capacity and lower cost than DRAM. Storage advancements like NVMe and PCIe 4.0 further enhance performance, while new processing technologies such as FPGAs, hardware transactional memory (HTM), and persistent memory support are improving energy efficiency and reducing latency in data centers.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a curated reading list from Murat Demirbas' Distributed Systems Seminar for Spring 2016, featuring papers that are both high-quality and noteworthy. He expresses enthusiasm for the selection, noting that while he had read most of the papers, the ones he hadn't covered were particularly intriguing. The blog post introduces four key papers from the list, including 'The Design and Implementation of the Wave Transactional Filesystem,' 'Arabesque: A System for Distributed Graph Mining,' 'Petuum: A New Platform for Distributed Machine Learning on Big Data,' and 'Chimera: Large-scale classification using machine learning, rules, and crowdsourcing.' Additionally, it mentions 'Panopticon: A lock broker architecture for scalable transactions in the datacenter,' which won an IEEE Big Data 2015 Best Paper award, as a fitting conclusion to the series. The post serves as a guide to the seminar's reading list, emphasizing the importance of exploring these papers for insights into distributed systems, big data, and machine learning.
paper_title: The Design and Implementation of the Wave Transactional Filesystem
paper_abstract: current or non-sequential modifications to files. This obviates the need to worry about nuances in filesystem behavior, but fails to support use cases requiring concurrency or random-access writes. Flat Datacenter Storage [29] is eventually consistent and requires a network with full-bisection bandwidth, which can be cost prohibitive and is not possible in all environments. This paper introduces the Warp Transactional Filesystem (WTF), a new distributed filesystem that exposes transactional support with a new API that provides file slicing operations. A WTF transaction may span multiple files and is fully general; applications can include calls such as read, write, and seek within their transaction. This file slicing API enables applications to efficiently read, write, and rearrange files without rewriting the underlying data. For example, applications may concatenate multiple files without reading them; garbage collect and compress a database without writing the data; and even sort the contents of record-oriented files without rewriting the files’ contents. The key design decision that enables WTF’s advanced feature set is an architecture that represents filesystem data and metadata to ensure that filesystem-level transactions may be performed using, solely, transactional operations on metadata. Custom storage servers hold filesystem data and handle the bulk of I/O requests. These servers retain no information about the structure of the filesystem; instead, they treat all data as opaque, immutable, variable-length arrays of bytes, called slices. WTF stores references to these slices in HyperDex [17] alongside metadata that describes how to combine the slices to reconstruct files’ contents. This structure enables bookkeeping to be done entirely at the metadata level, within the scope of HyperDex transactions. blog_summary: The blog post discusses the Wave Transactional Filesystem (Wave FS), a distributed filesystem that introduces a transactional model spanning multiple files with reads, writes, and seeks. Adrian Colyer highlights Wave FS's novel file-slicing abstraction, which treats file data as immutable, arbitrarily-sized byte sequences (slices) stored separately from mutable metadata that tracks their arrangement. This design enables strong transactional guarantees and a richer API while maintaining performance comparable to HDFS. The paper demonstrates that a sample application using file slicing outperforms traditional approaches by a factor of four due to reduced I/O costs. The key insight is the separation of immutable data slices from mutable metadata, allowing filesystem-level transactions to be implemented via metadata transactions alone, leveraging HyperDex for atomic operations.
