blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a study from Li et al. that investigates the growing threat of malvertising—malicious activities exploiting web advertisements. The authors crawled 90,000 top websites and found over 1% had been compromised to deliver malicious content or fraudulent clicks, with large ad networks like DoubleClick infiltrated. The paper details how malvertising works, including a real-world campaign that infected high-traffic sites via a fake AV scam, using cloaking and evasion techniques to evade detection. The study categorizes malvertising attacks into drive-by-downloads, scams/phishing, and click-fraud, revealing that attackers exploit ad networks, redirectors, and compromised publishers. The authors propose detection methods based on identifying malicious nodes in ad-delivery paths, noting that malvertising paths are longer, involve unknown nodes, and use transient domains. Key insights include the rampancy of malvertising, the sophistication of attackers in evading detection, and the vulnerability of smaller ad networks.
paper_title: Knowing your enemy: understanding and detecting malicious web advertising
paper_abstract: 1. Online advertising drives the economy of the World Wide Web. Modern websites of any size and popularity include advertisements to monetize visits from their users. To this end, they assign an area of their web page to an advertising company (so called ad exchange) that will use it to display promotional content. By doing this, the website owner implicitly trusts that the advertising company will offer legitimate content and it will not put the site’s visitors at risk of falling victims of malware campaigns and other scams. In this paper, we perform the first large-scale study of the safety of the advertisements that are encountered by the users on the Web. In particular, we analyze to what extent users are exposed to malicious content through advertisements, and investigate what are the sources of this malicious content. Additionally, we show that some ad exchanges are more prone to serving malicious advertisements than others, probably due to their deficient filtering mechanisms. The observations that we make in this paper shed light on a little studied, yet important, aspect of advertisement networks, and can help both advertisement networks and website owners in securing their web pages and in keeping their visitors safe. The online advertising industry is constantly growing. A recent report showed that this industry generated a revenue of 42.8 billion dollars in 2013, which is 17% higher than what had been reported in the previous year [14]. In the World Wide Web, where most online services are free of charge, advertisements constitute the main revenue for website administrators, and it is very common to see promotional content alongside the actual information contained in such sites. Given the profitability of online advertising, many big players have entered the arena. Such players, known as ad exchanges, put in contact the advertisers, who want their content to be displayed, with the publishers, who want to show promotional content on their web pages, and ...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a concerning study by Xing et al. on malvertising via browser extensions, revealing that 56 out of 292 Chrome extensions surveyed inject malicious ads through 16 ad networks, affecting over 600,000 users. The paper identifies three ad injection practices: injecting ads relevant to search terms, overlaying ads on retailer pages, and aggressively inserting ads across most web pages. The authors built a tool called Expector to analyze 18,030 Chrome extensions, finding 292 ad-injecting extensions with a low false positive rate. The study found that ad-injecting extensions serve a higher fraction of malicious ads compared to natural ads, with some ad networks serving exclusively malicious content, likely due to collusion or ownership by miscreants. The paper also explores the mechanics of malvertising, including redirection chains to drive-by-download landing pages and malware hosting domains, and shows temporal correlations between users resolving ad network and malware domains. Notably, some extensions abuse privileges to hijack user interactions, leading to malware downloads.
paper_title: Understanding malvertising through ad-injecting browser extensions
paper_abstract: Keywords Malvertising is a malicious activity that leverages advertising to distribute various forms of malware. Because advertising is the key revenue generator for numerous Internet companies, large ad networks, such as Google, Yahoo and Microsoft, invest a lot of effort to mitigate malicious ads from their ad networks. This drives adversaries to look for alternative methods to deploy malvertising. In this paper, we show that browser extensions that use ads as their monetization strategy often facilitate the deployment of malvertising. Moreover, while some extensions simply serve ads from ad networks that support malvertising, other extensions maliciously alter the content of visited webpages to force users into installing malware. To measure the extent of these behaviors we developed Expector, a system that automatically inspects and identifies browser extensions that inject ads, and then classifies these ads as malicious or benign based on their landing pages. Using Expector, we automatically inspected over 18,000 Chrome browser extensions. We found 292 extensions that inject ads, and detected 56 extensions that participate in malvertising using 16 different ad networks and with a total user base of 602,417. Malvertising; Browser Extension; Adware

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the paper 'The landscape of domain name typosquatting: techniques and countermeasures' by Spaulding et al., which examines the growing threat of domain squatting. The paper categorizes typosquatting techniques, including traditional typo-based methods (e.g., missing dots, character substitutions) and advanced techniques like homograph attacks, bitsquatting, and soundsquatting. Colyer highlights the surprising effectiveness of bitsquatting, where hardware bit errors redirect traffic to malicious domains, and the alarming prevalence of typosquatting cross-site scripting (TXSS), which exploits developer typos in JavaScript library references. The paper also explores monetization strategies of typosquatters, such as ad parking, ransom demands, and affiliate fraud, and discusses countermeasures like defensive domain registration and legal actions under the Anti-cybersquatting Consumer Protection Act (ACPA).
paper_title: The landscape of domain name typosquatting: techniques and countermeasures
paper_abstract: —With more than 294 million registered domain names as of late 2015, the domain name ecosystem has evolved to become a cornerstone for the operation of the Internet. Domain names today serve everyone, from individuals for their online presence to big brands for their business operations. Such ecosystem that facilitated legitimate business and personal uses has also fostered “creative” cases of misuse, including phishing, spam, hit and traffic stealing, online scams, among others. As a first step towards this misuse, the registration of a legitimatelylooking domain is often required. For that, domain typosquatting provides a great avenue to cybercriminals to conduct their crimes. In this paper, we review the landscape of domain name typosquatting, highlighting models and advanced techniques for typosquatted domain names generation, models for their monetization, and the existing literature on countermeasures. We further highlight potential fruitful directions on technical countermeasures that are lacking in the literature.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Neumann's 2011 paper as a foundational work on optimizing query processing for modern hardware. The paper critiques the traditional iterator model used in query execution, which suffers from inefficiencies due to frequent virtual function calls, poor code locality, and excessive register evictions. Neumann proposes a push-based execution model that reverses the dataflow direction, pushing tuples through operators to minimize memory accesses and maximize data/code locality. This approach compiles query plans into tight, register-efficient code fragments that avoid materialization until necessary, leading to near-optimal performance. The generated code leverages LLVM for efficient assembly output, demonstrating significant speedups in query execution. The paper's insights have directly influenced modern systems like Apache Spark, which adopted similar techniques in its 2.0 release.
paper_title: Efficiently Compiling Efficient Query Plans for Modern Hardware
paper_abstract: In 2011 we showed how to use dynamic code generation to process queries in a data-centric manner. This execution model can produce compact and efficient code and was successfully used by both our own systems and systems of other groups. As the systems become used in practice, additional techniques were developed for shortcomings that did arrive, including low-latency compilation, multi-threading support, and others. This paper gives an overview of the evolution of our query engine within in the last ten years, and points out which problem have to be tackled to bring a compiling system into production usage. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights StreamScope as Microsoft's production streaming system, deployed on massive 20,000-server clusters processing tens of billions of events daily with complex computations. He emphasizes its strong guarantees for exactly-once processing (critical for accounting applications like fraud detection) and low latency requirements. The paper's key insight is the introduction of rStream and rVertex abstractions that decouple system components to achieve high scalability and fault tolerance, trading off some latency for robustness. Colyer particularly notes StreamScope's deterministic execution model, temporal semantics handling, and sophisticated recovery mechanisms as noteworthy contributions to large-scale stream processing systems.
paper_title: StreamScope: Continuous Reliable Distributed Processing of Big Data Streams
paper_abstract: S TREAM S COPE (or S TREAM S) is a reliable distributed stream computation engine that has been deployed in shared 20,000-server production clusters at Microsoft. S TREAM S provides a continuous temporal stream model that allows users to express complex stream processing logic naturally and declaratively. S TREAM S supports business-critical streaming applications that can process tens of billions (or tens of terabytes) of input events per day continuously with complex logic involving tens of temporal joins, aggregations, and sophisticated userdefined functions, while maintaining tens of terabytes inmemory computation states on thousands of machines. S TREAM S introduces two abstractions, rVertex and rStream, to manage the complexity in distributed stream computation systems. The abstractions allow efficient and flexible distributed execution and failure recovery, make it easy to reason about correctness even with failures, and facilitate the development, debugging, and deployment of complex multi-stage streaming applications.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the SocialHash framework from Facebook as a novel approach to optimizing distributed systems operations by exploiting structure in social network graphs. The key insight is that random distribution (e.g., consistent hashing) often leads to suboptimal performance, while structured partitioning can significantly improve metrics like cache hit rates and response times. At Facebook, SocialHash reduced cache miss rates by 25% and average response times by 50% after deployment. The framework decouples static optimization (grouping objects based on graph properties) from dynamic load balancing, using graph partitioning to co-locate related data and queries. The static assignment phase leverages Apache Giraph to partition the social graph into cohesive groups, while the dynamic phase adapts group-to-component assignments to maintain balance and stability.
paper_title: SocialHash: An assignment framework for optimizing distributed systems operations on social networks
paper_abstract: How objects are assigned to components in a distributed system can have a significant impact on performance and resource usage. Social Hash is a framework for producing, serving, and maintaining assignments of objects to components so as to optimize the operations of large social networks, such as Facebook’s Social Graph. The framework uses a two-level scheme to decouple compute-intensive optimization from relatively low-overhead dynamic adaptation. The optimization at the first level occurs on a slow timescale, and in our applications is based on graph partitioning in order to leverage the structure of the social network. The dynamic adaptation at the second level takes place frequently to adapt to changes in access patterns and infrastructure, with the goal of balancing component loads. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Social Hash with two real applications. The first assigns HTTP requests to individual compute clusters with the goal of minimizing the (memory-based) cache miss rate; Social Hash decreased the cache miss rate of production workloads by 25%. The second application assigns data records to storage subsystems with the goal of minimizing the number of storage subsystems that need to be accessed on multiget fetch requests; Social Hash cut the average response time in half on production workloads for one of the storage systems at Facebook.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights HCloud, a system for resource-efficient provisioning in shared cloud systems that balances performance and cost. The paper demonstrates that a hybrid approach combining reserved instances with on-demand provisioning, alongside a smart placement policy, can improve performance by 2.1x compared to using only on-demand instances and reduce costs by 46% compared to fully-reserved systems. A key insight is the importance of understanding application sensitivity to interference (noisy neighbors) and leveraging large instances to minimize external interference. The authors also introduce Quasar, a cluster manager that profiles jobs to estimate resource preferences and interference sensitivity, enabling better placement decisions. The study evaluates different provisioning strategies across static, low-variability, and high-variability workloads, showing that hybrid strategies outperform pure reserved or on-demand approaches in both performance and cost efficiency.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a groundbreaking paper from ASPLOS '16 that explores DNA as a medium for archival storage, emphasizing its extraordinary density (1 exabyte per mm³) and longevity (500+ year half-life). The authors build a functional DNA-based key-value store capable of random access, demonstrating its feasibility by encoding and retrieving a cat image from synthesized DNA. Colyer underscores the urgency of the work, noting that global data growth (projected to 16 zettabytes in 2017) outpaces storage capacity, and DNA offers a potential solution. The paper addresses critical challenges like error-prone synthesis/sequencing (1% per nucleotide) and slow random access by leveraging PCR amplification and robust encoding schemes (base-3, Huffman codes, and XOR-based redundancy akin to RAID 5). The system's architecture models DNA storage as a key-value store, using unique primers for random access and redundancy to tolerate errors.
paper_title: A DNA-Based Archival Storage System
paper_abstract: Demand for data storage is growing exponentially, but the capacity of existing storage media is not keeping up. Using DNA to archive data is an attractive possibility because it is extremely dense, with a raw limit of 1 exabyte/mm3 (109 GB/mm3 ), and long-lasting, with observed half-life of over 500 years. This paper presents an architecture for a DNA-based archival storage system. It is structured as a key-value store, and leverages common biochemical techniques to provide random access. We also propose a new encoding scheme that offers controllable redundancy, trading off reliability for density. We demonstrate feasibility, random access, and robustness of the proposed encoding with wet lab experiments involving 151 kB of synthesized DNA and a 42 kB randomaccess subset, and simulation experiments of larger sets calibrated to the wet lab experiments. Finally, we highlight trends in biotechnology that indicate the impending practicality of DNA storage for much larger datasets.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes a paper by Hammoudi et al. that investigates why record/replay tests for web applications frequently break. The authors conducted an extensive study across 300 versions of five open-source web apps, creating test suites and tracking 722 test breakages, later validating their findings with an additional 343 breakages in 153 versions of three more apps. They developed a taxonomy of five high-level causes for test breakages, with over 70% attributed to locator fragility—particularly attribute-based locators (e.g., element IDs or names) which account for over 50% of all breakages. The paper highlights that while attribute-based locators are the most fragile, they may still be among the most robust strategies in practice due to their common usage. The study provides actionable insights for practitioners to prioritize test repair efforts and build more resilient test suites.
paper_title: Why do Record/Replay Tests of Web Applications Break?
paper_abstract: Software engineers use record/replay tools to capture use case scenarios that can serve as regression tests for web applications. Such tests, however, can be brittle in the face of code changes. Thus, researchers have sought automated approaches for repairing broken record/replay tests. To date, such approaches have operated by directly analyzing differences between the releases of web applications. Often, however, intermediate versions or commits exist between releases, and these represent finer-grained sequences of changes by which new releases evolve. In this paper, we present WAT E RFALL, an incremental test repair approach that applies test repair techniques iteratively across a sequence of fine-grained versions of a web application. The results of an empirical study on seven web applications show that our approach is substantially more effective than a coarse-grained approach (209% overall), while maintaining an acceptable level of overhead.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a paper that presents a radical simplification in the design of static bug-finding tools. The authors argue that modern static checkers have become overly complex, making them hard to understand, scale, and maintain. In response, they propose a minimalist approach using 'micro-parsers' and 'micro-grammars' that focus only on the essential features needed for bug checking, ignoring the bulk of the programming language's complexity. The resulting checkers are orders of magnitude simpler (often under 40 lines of code) but remain highly effective, finding over 700 bugs in real-world systems, including bugs missed by commercial tools. The key insight is that by relaxing the requirement to fully parse a language, the system can achieve both simplicity and effectiveness. The paper also demonstrates the adaptability of the approach, showing how checkers can be easily ported to new languages with minimal effort.
paper_title: μchex: A Simple and Effective Approach to Static Checking
paper_abstract: Modern static bug finding tools are complex. They typically consist of hundreds of thousands of lines of code, and most of them are wedded to one language (or even one compiler). This complexity makes the systems hard to understand, hard to debug, and hard to retarget to new languages, thereby dramatically limiting their scope. This paper reduces the complexity of the checking system by addressing a fundamental assumption, the assumption that checkers must depend on a full-blown language specification and compiler front end. Instead, our program checkers are based on drastically incomplete language grammars (“micro-grammars”) that describe only portions of a language relevant to a checker. As a result, our implementation is tiny—roughly 2500 lines of code, about two orders of magnitude smaller than a typical system. We hope that this dramatic increase in simplicity will allow developers to use more checkers on more systems in more languages. We implement our approach in µchex, a language-agnostic framework for writing static bug checkers. We use it to build micro-grammar based checkers for six languages (C, the C preprocessor, C++, Java, JavaScript, and Dart) and find over 700 errors in real-world projects.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the extension of word vectors to sentences, paragraphs, and documents by Le and Mikolov, enabling distributed representations that outperform state-of-the-art methods in text classification and sentiment analysis tasks. He notes that traditional bag-of-words and bag-of-n-grams models lose semantic meaning and word order information, while paragraph vectors (PV) address these limitations by incorporating a 'memory' component (paragraph token) that captures context and topic. The blog describes two variants: PV-DM (Distributed Memory) and PV-DBOW (Distributed Bag of Words), with PV-DM performing better but their combination yielding the best results. Experimental results on sentiment analysis and paragraph classification tasks show significant improvements over prior methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of paragraph vectors in capturing semantic relationships without requiring parsing.
paper_title: Distributed Representations of Sentences and Documents
paper_abstract: Many machine learning algorithms require the input to be represented as a fixed-length feature vector. When it comes to texts, one of the most common fixed-length features is bag-of-words. Despite their popularity, bag-of-words features have two major weaknesses: they lose the ordering of the words and they also ignore semantics of the words. For example, “powerful,” “strong” and “Paris” are equally distant. In this paper, we propose Paragraph Vector, an unsupervised algorithm that learns fixed-length feature representations from variable-length pieces of texts, such as sentences, paragraphs, and documents. Our algorithm represents each document by a dense vector which is trained to predict words in the document. Its construction gives our algorithm the potential to overcome the weaknesses of bag-ofwords models. Empirical results show that Paragraph Vectors outperform bag-of-words models as well as other techniques for text representations. Finally, we achieve new state-of-the-art results on several text classification and sentiment analysis tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1. A framework for learning word vectors. Context of three words (“the,” “cat,” and “sat”) is used to predict the fourth word (“on”). The input words are mapped to columns of the matrix W to predict the output word.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this seminal work by Sutskever et al. as a breakthrough in machine translation using sequence-to-sequence learning with neural networks. The paper demonstrates how an LSTM-based model can encode an English sentence into a fixed-dimensional vector (8000 real numbers) and then decode it into a French translation, effectively mapping sequences to sequences. The author emphasizes the LSTM's ability to handle long-range dependencies and the surprising but effective technique of reversing the input sentence to reduce the minimal time lag between corresponding words in source and target languages. The paper also showcases the scalability of deep LSTMs (4 layers, 1000 cells each) and their superior performance over shallow models, achieving a BLEU score of 34.81 on the WMT'14 English-to-French task, outperforming traditional statistical machine translation systems. The qualitative evaluation further supports the model's ability to capture sentence meaning and word order invariance.
paper_title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
paper_abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are powerful models that have achieved excellent performance on difficult learning tasks. Although DNNs work well whenever large labeled training sets are available, they cannot be used to map sequences to sequences. In this paper, we present a general end-to-end approach to sequence learning that makes minimal assumptions on the sequence structure. Our method uses a multilayered Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) to map the input sequence to a vector of a fixed dimensionality, and then another deep LSTM to decode the target sequence from the vector. Our main result is that on an English to French translation task from the WMT-14 dataset, the translations produced by the LSTM achieve a BLEU score of 34.8 on the entire test set, where the LSTM’s BLEU score was penalized on out-of-vocabulary words. Additionally, the LSTM did not have difficulty on long sentences. For comparison, a phrase-based SMT system achieves a BLEU score of 33.3 on the same dataset. When we used the LSTM to rerank the 1000 hypotheses produced by the aforementioned SMT system, its BLEU score increases to 36.5, which is close to the previous state of the art. The LSTM also learned sensible phrase and sentence representations that are sensitive to word order and are relatively invariant to the active and the passive voice. Finally, we found that reversing the order of the words in all source sentences (but not target sentences) improved the LSTM’s performance markedly, because doing so introduced many short term dependencies between the source and the target sentence which made the optimization problem easier.

figures.title: Sequence to Sequence Model Architecture
figures.caption: Our model reads an input sentence “ABC” and produces “WXYZ” as the output sentence. The model stops making predictions after outputting the end-of-sentence token. Note that the LSTM reads the input sentence in reverse, because doing so introduces many short term dependencies in the data that make the optimization problem much easier.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Dai & Le's paper on semi-supervised sequence learning as a clever and significant contribution to the field of NLP and deep learning. The key insight is the use of a sequence-to-sequence autoencoder to pre-train an LSTM model in an unsupervised manner, which can then be fine-tuned for supervised tasks like document classification. By setting the target sequence identical to the input during unsupervised training, the model learns meaningful sentence representations without labeled data. Colyer emphasizes the practical benefits of this approach, such as improved training stability and the ability to leverage vast amounts of unlabeled data, which is far cheaper than labeled data. The SA-LSTM method achieves competitive or superior results across multiple benchmarks, including sentiment analysis and larger document classification tasks, demonstrating its generality and robustness. The paper stands out for its simplicity in method description, focusing heavily on evaluation and demonstrating the power of semi-supervised learning in deep learning models.
paper_title: Semi-Supervised Sequence Learning
paper_abstract: We present two approaches to use unlabeled data to improve Sequence Learning with recurrent networks. The first approach is to predict what comes next in a sequence, which is a language model in NLP. The second approach is to use a sequence autoencoder, which reads the input sequence into a vector and predicts the input sequence again. These two algorithms can be used as a “pretraining” algorithm for a later supervised sequence learning algorithm. In other words, the parameters obtained from the pretraining step can then be used as a starting point for other supervised training models. In our experiments, we find that long short term memory recurrent networks after pretrained with the two approaches become more stable to train and generalize better. With pretraining, we were able to achieve strong performance in many classification tasks, such as text classification with IMDB, DBpedia or image recognition in CIFAR-10.

figures.title: Sequence autoencoder architecture
figures.caption: Figure 1: The sequence autoencoder for the sequence “WXYZ”. The sequence autoencoder uses a recurrent network to read the input sequence in to the hidden state, which can then be used to reconstruct the original sequence.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews a study from ICSE 2016 that analyzes the impact of team size on productivity in open-source software projects. The paper challenges a previous finding (Sornette et al., 2014) that suggested open-source productivity increases super-linearly with team size, arguing instead that larger teams lead to decreased average productivity per developer. The authors validate the common assumption that team size negatively affects productivity due to duplication of efforts, coordination overhead, and reduced accountability. They analyze 580,000 commits from 58 top GitHub projects, measuring contributions using Levenshtein edit distance rather than raw commit counts. Key insights include the observation that most commits are minor, while a few large commits drive software evolution, and that mean developer productivity drops significantly as team size grows. The paper also highlights patterns in commit frequency and developer activity, such as peaks at 30-minute and daily intervals, and a sharp decline in mean commits per developer beyond 50 active contributors.
paper_title: From Aristotle to Ringelmann: A large-scale analysis of team productivity and coordination in open-source software projects
paper_abstract: 1 Massive data from software repositories and collaboration tools are widely used to study social aspects in software development. One question that several recent works have addressed is how a software project’s size and structure influence team productivity, a question famously considered in Brooks’ law. Recent studies using massive repository data suggest that developers in larger teams tend to be less productive than smaller teams. Despite using similar methods and data, other studies argue for a positive linear or even super-linear relationship between team size and productivity, thus contesting the view of software economics that software projects are diseconomies of scale. In our work, we study challenges that can explain the disagreement between recent studies of developer productivity in massive repository data. We further provide, to the best of our knowledge, the largest, curated corpus of GitHub projects tailored to investigate the influence of team size and collaboration patterns on individual and collective productivity. Our work contributes to the ongoing discussion on the choice of productivity metrics in the operationalisation of hypotheses about determinants of successful software projects. It further highlights general pitfalls in big data analysis and shows that the use of bigger data sets does not automatically lead to more reliable insights. Empirical research across disciplines is nowadays driven by the availability of big data and methods to process and analyse them efficiently. In empirical software engineering, massive data from software repositories and online collaboration tools are widely used to investigate social and human aspects in software development. This intersects with computational social science, which uses big data to test hypotheses about individual and collective human behaviour originally developed in sociology, social psychology, or organisational theory. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights BigDebug as a groundbreaking tool that brings real-time interactive debugging capabilities to Apache Spark, a popular Data-Intensive Scalable Computing (DISC) system. The paper addresses a critical gap in debugging DISC applications, which traditionally rely on post-mortem analysis or local testing with limited data samples, often failing to reproduce cloud-based failures. BigDebug introduces several innovative features, including breakpoints, watchpoints, latency monitoring, forward and backward tracing, crash monitoring, and a real-time fix-and-resume capability. The tool is notable for its low overhead (less than 24% for record-level tracing) and its ability to provide detailed crash culprits, stack traces, and provenance data. The key insight is enabling developers to debug DISC applications interactively and efficiently, reducing wasted computing cycles and improving productivity.
paper_title: BigDebug: Debugging primitives for interactive big data processing in Spark
paper_abstract: Developers use cloud computing platforms to process a large quantity of data in parallel when developing big data analytics. Debugging the massive parallel computations that run in today’s datacenters is time consuming and error-prone. To address this challenge, we design a set of interactive, real-time debugging primitives for big data processing in Apache Spark, the next generation data-intensive scalable cloud computing platform. This requires rethinking the notion of step-through debugging in a traditional debugger such as gdb, because pausing the entire computation across distributed worker nodes causes significant delay and naively inspecting millions of records using a watchpoint is too time consuming for an end user. First, B IG D EBUG’s simulated breakpoints and on-demand watchpoints allow users to selectively examine distributed, intermediate data on the cloud with little overhead. Second, a user can also pinpoint a crash-inducing record and selectively resume relevant sub-computations after a quick fix. Third, a user can determine the root causes of errors (or delays) at the level of individual records through a fine-grained data provenance capability. Our evaluation shows that B IG D EBUG scales to terabytes and its record-level tracing incurs less than 25% overhead on average. It determines crash culprits orders of magnitude more accurately and provides up to 100% time saving compared to the baseline replay debugger. The results show that B IG D EBUG supports debugging at interactive speeds with minimal performance impact.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a paper that explores the 'naturalness' of code—applying statistical language models (commonly used in NLP) to detect buggy code. The key insight is that buggy lines of code tend to have higher entropy (i.e., are less predictable or 'unnatural') compared to correct code. The authors analyze 8,296 bug fix commits across 10 open-source projects, showing that buggy lines are statistically more unnatural and that fixes reduce entropy. The technique, called NBF (Naturalness Bug Finder), can guide code reviews by prioritizing lines for inspection and complements static bug-finding tools like PMD and FindBugs. Combining NBF with static tools further improves defect detection performance by re-ranking warnings within priority categories.
paper_title: On the 'naturalness' of buggy code
paper_abstract: Real software, the kind working programmers produce by the kLOC to solve real-world problems, tends to be “natural”, like speech or natural language; it tends to be highly repetitive and predictable. Researchers have captured this naturalness of software through statistical models and used them to good effect in suggestion engines, porting tools, coding standards checkers, and idiom miners. This suggests that code that appears improbable, or surprising, to a good statistical language model is “unnatural” in some sense, and thus possibly suspicious. In this paper, we investigate this hypothesis. We consider a large corpus of bug fix commits (ca. 8,296), from 10 different Java projects, and we focus on its language statistics, evaluating the naturalness of buggy code and the corresponding fixes. We find that code with bugs tends to be more entropic (i.e. unnatural), becoming less so as bugs are fixed. Focusing on highly entropic lines is similar in cost-effectiveness to some wellknown static bug finders (PMD, FindBugs) and ordering warnings from these bug finders using an entropy measure improves the costeffectiveness of inspecting code implicated in warnings. This suggests that entropy may be a valid language-independent and simple way to complement the effectiveness of PMD or FindBugs, and that search-based bug-fixing methods may benefit from using entropy both for fault-localization and searching for fixes.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the paper 'Design Rule Spaces' by Xiao et al. as a significant contribution to understanding architectural debt in software systems. The work builds on Baldwin and Clark's concept of design rules—architectural interfaces that decouple systems into independent modules—by introducing 'design rule spaces' (DRSpaces) as a way to analyze software architecture at a higher level than individual code issues. The paper explores how error-prone files tend to cluster within specific DRSpaces, particularly those led by unstable or flawed design rules. Colyer notes that understanding these error-prone DRSpaces can help prioritize refactoring efforts for maximum impact, as a small number of such spaces often account for a large proportion of bugs in a project. The approach leverages design structure matrices (DSMs) and design rule hierarchies (DRHs) to reveal structural and evolutionary relationships in the codebase.
paper_title: Design Rule Spaces: A New Form of Architectural Insight
paper_abstract: —Over the past three decades software engineering researchers have produced a wide range of techniques and tools for understanding the architectures of large, complex systems. However, these have tended to be one-off research projects, and their idiosyncratic natures have hampered research collaboration, extension and combination of the tools, and technology transfer. The area of software architecture is rich with disjoint research and development infrastructures, and datasets that are either proprietary or captured in proprietary formats. This paper describes a concerted effort to reverse these trends. We have designed and implemented a flexible and extensible infrastructure (SAIN) with the goal of sharing, replicating, and advancing software architecture research. We have demonstrated that SAIN is capable of incorporating the constituent tools extracted from three independently developed, large, long-lived software architecture research environments. We discuss SAIN’s ambitious goals, the challenges we have faced in achieving those goals, the key decisions made in SAIN’s design and implementation, the lessons learned from our experience to date, and our ongoing and future work. Index Terms—architecture analysis, maintenance, interoperability, reproducibility, reusability

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a paper that introduces five architectural 'hotspot patterns' which are frequent root causes of high maintenance costs in software projects. These patterns—Unstable Interface, Implicit Cross-Module Dependency, Unhealthy Interface Inheritance Hierarchy, Cross-Module Cycle, and Cross-Package Cycle—are shown to significantly increase bug rates, change rates, and maintenance effort across both open-source and commercial projects. The paper formalizes these patterns, which are not covered by existing code smells or anti-patterns, and demonstrates their predictive power using historical data from ten projects. The study finds that files involved in these patterns are consistently more error-prone and require more maintenance effort, with Unstable Interface and Cross-Module Cycle having the greatest impact. The authors also developed a Hotspot Detector tool to automatically identify these issues, which was validated by a chief architect who confirmed the findings and planned refactoring efforts.
paper_title: Hotspot Patterns: The formal definition and automatic detection of architecture smells
paper_abstract: —Over the past three decades software engineering researchers have produced a wide range of techniques and tools for understanding the architectures of large, complex systems. However, these have tended to be one-off research projects, and their idiosyncratic natures have hampered research collaboration, extension and combination of the tools, and technology transfer. The area of software architecture is rich with disjoint research and development infrastructures, and datasets that are either proprietary or captured in proprietary formats. We discuss SAIN’s ambitious goals, the challenges we have faced in achieving those goals, the key decisions made in SAIN’s design and implementation, the lessons learned from our experience to date, and our ongoing and future work. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes Xiao et al.'s ICSE 2016 paper on identifying and quantifying architectural debt, highlighting its key contribution: moving beyond the metaphorical use of 'technical debt' by proposing a concrete model to quantify architectural debt as principal and interest, analogous to financial debt. The paper analyzes seven Apache projects, finding that 51-85% of maintenance effort is spent 'paying interest' on architectural debts, with non-trivial portions (20-61%) consumed by just five debts per project. The authors introduce a four-stage process using Design Rule Space analysis and History Coupling Probability (HCP) matrices to identify and track architectural debts over time, categorizing them into patterns like Hub, Anchor Submissive, Anchor Dominant, and Modularity Violation. They model debt growth using regression analysis, revealing that about half of debts accrue interest linearly, while others follow polynomial, logarithmic, or exponential trends. The paper demonstrates that modularity violations are the most common and costly form of architectural debt, consuming up to 82% of total effort in some projects.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Arrakis as a groundbreaking approach to data-center OS design, moving away from the traditional Unix model to a system where applications use protected software containers with direct hardware access via scalable library invocations. The paper removes the kernel from the I/O data path for nearly all operations while retaining OS protections, achieving significant performance gains: 2-5x latency improvement and 9x throughput improvement for Redis workloads. Colyer emphasizes that modern hardware trends, such as high-speed Ethernet and low-latency persistent memory, exacerbate kernel overheads, making Arrakis' approach increasingly attractive. The key insight is leveraging hardware virtualization (SR-IOV, IOMMU) to enable direct user-space I/O, eliminating kernel mediation, scheduling overheads, and data copying, thus bridging a 20-year-old idea (U-Net) with contemporary hardware capabilities.
paper_title: Arrakis: The Operating System is the Control Plane
paper_abstract: into user space [19, 22, 54]. Although commercially unsuccessful at the time, the virtualization market has now led hardware vendors to revive the idea [6, 38, 48], and also extend it to disks [52, 53]. This paper explores the OS implications of removing the kernel from the data path for nearly all I/O operations. We argue that doing this must provide applications with the same security model as traditional designs; it is easy to get good performance by extending the trusted computing base to include application code, e.g., by allowing applications unfiltered direct access to the network/disk. We demonstrate that operating system protection is not contradictory with high performance. For our prototype implementation, a client request to the Redis persistent NoSQL store has 2× better read latency, 5× better write latency, and 9× better write throughput compared to Linux. We make three specific contributions: Recent device hardware trends enable a new approach to the design of network server operating systems. In a traditional operating system, the kernel mediates access to device hardware by server applications, to enforce process isolation as well as network and disk security. We have designed and implemented a new operating system, Arrakis, that splits the traditional role of the kernel in two. Applications have direct access to virtualized I/O devices, allowing most I/O operations to skip the kernel entirely, while the kernel is re-engineered to provide network and disk protection without kernel mediation of every operation. We describe the hardware and software changes needed to take advantage of this new abstraction, and we illustrate its power by showing improvements of 2-5× in latency and 9× in throughput for a popular persistent NoSQL store relative to a well-tuned Linux implementation. 1 • We give an architecture for the division of labor between the device hardware, kernel, and runtime for direct network and disk I/O by unprivileged processes, and we show h...

figures.title: Packet processing workflow in Linux
figures.caption: Figure 1: Typical workflow for a UDP echo server application in Linux. The workflow shows the path of a packet through the kernel, including copying, scheduling, and kernel crossings, highlighting the overheads involved in traditional OS packet processing.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights IX as a novel operating system design that splits the OS into a control plane and data plane for networking, similar to Arrakis but with a focus on software-controlled network I/O policy enforcement. The paper addresses four key challenges in data center applications: microsecond tail latency, high packet rates under concurrent connections, application isolation, and resource efficiency. IX draws inspiration from middleboxes to achieve microsecond latency and high packet rates, introducing principles like separation of control/data planes, run-to-completion with adaptive batching, zero-copy API, and synchronization-free processing. The design leverages modern virtualization hardware for isolation and uses flow-consistent hashing to avoid synchronization overheads. The evaluation shows IX outperforming Linux and mTCP in throughput, scalability, and latency, achieving line rate on a 10GbE link with fewer cores.
paper_title: IX: A Protected Dataplane Operating System for High Throughput and Low Latency
paper_abstract: The conventional wisdom is that aggressive networking requirements, such as high packet rates for small messages and microsecond-scale tail latency, are best addressed outside the kernel, in a user-level networking stack. We present IX, a dataplane operating system that provides high I/O performance, while maintaining the key advantage of strong protection offered by existing kernels. IX uses hardware virtualization to separate management and scheduling functions of the kernel (control plane) from network processing (dataplane). The dataplane architecture builds upon a native, zero-copy API and optimizes for both bandwidth and latency by dedicating hardware threads and networking queues to dataplane instances, processing bounded batches of packets to completion, and by eliminating coherence traffic and multi-core synchronization. We demonstrate that IX outperforms Linux and state-of-the-art, user-space network stacks significantly in both throughput and end-to-end latency. Moreover, IX improves the throughput of a widely deployed, key-value store by up to 3.6× and reduces tail latency by more than 2×.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Haven as a groundbreaking system that introduces 'shielded execution' to protect the confidentiality and integrity of entire unmodified legacy applications running in an untrusted cloud environment. Unlike traditional sandboxing that protects the host from untrusted code, Haven flips the model by shielding applications from a potentially malicious cloud provider or host. The key innovation is leveraging Intel SGX's enclaves to create a secure execution environment where only inputs and outputs are visible, while intermediate states remain protected. Haven combines SGX with Drawbridge's picoprocess and LibOS to defend against 'Iago attacks' (where a malicious OS exploits assumptions of correct behavior) and provides secure persistent storage via encrypted virtual disks. The system's architecture ensures minimal trust in the host while maintaining efficient execution, with attestation mechanisms verifying the enclave's integrity to remote users.
paper_title: Shielding Applications from an Untrusted Cloud with Haven
paper_abstract: Today’s cloud computing infrastructure requires substantial trust. Cloud users rely on both the provider’s staff and its globally-distributed software/hardware platform not to expose any of their private data. We introduce the notion of shielded execution, which protects the confidentiality and integrity of a program and its data from the platform on which it runs (i.e., the cloud operator’s OS, VM and firmware). Our prototype, Haven, is the first system to achieve shielded execution of unmodified legacy applications, including SQL Server and Apache, on a commodity OS (Windows) and commodity hardware. Haven leverages the hardware protection of Intel SGX to defend against privileged code and physical attacks such as memory probes, but also addresses the dual challenges of executing unmodified legacy binaries and protecting them from a malicious host. This work motivated recent changes in the SGX specification.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights E2 as a framework designed to address the fragmentation in Network Function Virtualization (NFV) by providing a unified platform for managing common systems issues such as placement, elastic scaling, fault tolerance, and resource isolation. Inspired by data processing frameworks like Spark, E2 aims to let developers focus on writing network function logic while the platform handles underlying systems challenges. Colyer emphasizes E2's motivation in carrier networks' Central Offices (COs), where commodity hardware and a unified NFV approach could enable scalability, cost efficiency, and new business models. The paper argues for a software-centric alternative to monolithic hardware, with E2 acting as a bridge between high-level network policies and low-level packet processing. Key insights include E2's pipelet abstraction for traffic classes and DAG-based processing, its rich message abstractions for cross-NF communication, and its dynamic placement and scaling algorithms.
paper_title: E2: A Framework for NFV Applications
paper_abstract: boxes into virtualized software applications that can be run on commodity, general purpose processors. NFV has quickly gained signiﬁcant momentum with over 220 industry participants, multiple proof-of-concept prototypes, and a number of emerging product offerings [2, 9]. While this momentum is encouraging, a closer look “under the hood” reveals a less rosy picture: NFV products and prototypes tend to be merely virtualized software implementations of products that were previously offered as dedicated hardware appliances. Thus, NFV is currently replacing, on a one-to-one basis, monolithic hardware with monolithic software. While this is a valuable ﬁrst step – as it is expected to lower capital costs and deployment barriers – it fails to provide a coherent management solution for middleboxes. Each software middlebox still comes as a closed implementation bundled with a custom management solution that addresses issues such as overload detection, load balancing, elastic scaling, and fault-tolerance for that particular NF. This leads to two problems. First, the operator must cope with many NF-speciﬁc management systems. Second, NF developers must invent their own solutions to common but non-trivial problems such as dynamic scaling and fault tolerance; in the worst case this results in inadequate solutions (e.g., solutions that do not scale well) and in the best case results in vendors constantly reinventing the wheel. Inspired by the success of data analytic frameworks (e.g., MapReduce, Hadoop and Spark), we argue that NFV needs a framework, by which we mean a software environment for packet-processing applications that implements general techniques for common issues. Such issues include: placement (which NF runs where), elastic scaling (adapting the number of NF instances and balancing load across them), service composition, resource isolation, fault-tolerance, en- By moving network appliance functionality from proprietary hardware to software, Network Function Virtualiz...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the tension between the growing adoption of HTTPS and the need for middleboxes (e.g., caches, IDS, WAN optimizers) in enterprise networks. Traditional approaches like Split TLS are flawed because they break end-to-end security guarantees, leaving clients unaware of middlebox presence and granting them unrestricted access to decrypted data. The paper proposes mcTLS (Multi-Context TLS) as a principled solution, enabling explicit, secure middlebox integration into TLS sessions. mcTLS divides data into contexts (e.g., headers, body) with granular access controls (no access, read-only, read-write) for middleboxes, ensuring endpoints retain visibility and control. The protocol introduces encryption contexts and contributory keys to authenticate middleboxes and enforce minimal access permissions, upholding TLS security properties while adding middlebox transparency and accountability. Colyer emphasizes mcTLS's pragmatic approach to reconciling end-to-end encryption with real-world network functionality needs.
paper_title: Multi-Context TLS (mcTLS): Enabling secure in-network functionality in TLS
paper_abstract: 1. A significant fraction of Internet traffic is now encrypted and HTTPS will likely be the default in HTTP/2. However, Transport Layer Security (TLS), the standard protocol for encryption in the Internet, assumes that all functionality resides at the endpoints, making it impossible to use in-network services that optimize network resource usage, improve user experience, and protect clients and servers from security threats. Re-introducing in-network functionality into TLS sessions today is done through hacks, often weakening overall security. In this paper we introduce multi-context TLS (mcTLS), which extends TLS to support middleboxes. mcTLS breaks the current “all-or-nothing” security model by allowing endpoints and content providers to explicitly introduce middleboxes in secure end-to-end sessions while controlling which parts of the data they can read or write. We evaluate a prototype mcTLS implementation in both controlled and “live” experiments, showing that its benefits come at the cost of minimal overhead. More importantly, we show that mcTLS can be incrementally deployed and requires only small changes to client, server, and middlebox software. The increased personalization of Internet services and rising concern over users’ privacy on the Internet has led to a number of services (e.g., Facebook, Twitter, and Google) offering access solely over HTTPS. HTTPS currently accounts for a significant portion of all Internet traffic (40% in [26], and estimated to grow at 40% every 6 months [27]). Transport Layer Security (TLS), which underlies HTTPS, has become the standard for end-to-end encryption on the web because it ensures (i) entity authentication, (ii) data secrecy, and (iii) data integrity and authentication. Moreover, it will likely be the default transport protocol for HTTP/2. This is good news for privacy. However, TLS makes a fundamental assumption: all functionality must reside at the endpoints. In reality, Internet sessions are augmented by function...

figures.title: Examples of app-layer middleboxes and their permissions
figures.caption: Examples of app-layer middleboxes and the permissions they need for HTTP. No middlebox needs read/write access to all of the data.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the paper 'BlindBox: Deep packet inspection over encrypted traffic' by Sherry et al. from SIGCOMM 2015, which addresses the challenge of enabling deep packet inspection (DPI) for intrusion detection and prevention (IDS/IPS) on encrypted HTTPS traffic without violating end-to-end security. The paper introduces a novel approach called DPIEnc, a searchable encryption scheme, and a fast detection protocol that allows middleboxes to inspect encrypted traffic for attack patterns while preserving privacy. The system achieves inspection rates of up to 186Mbps per core, comparable to standard IDS implementations, though the initial HTTPS connection setup can be slow (up to 1.5 minutes for large rule sets). The paper proposes two privacy models: exact match privacy, where the middlebox only learns exact matches for attack keywords, and probable cause privacy, which allows decryption of traffic only if a match is found, enabling more detailed regular expression matching. The system architecture involves a rule generator, sender, receiver, and middlebox, with cryptographic protocols ensuring that the middlebox never learns the rules or private traffic data.
paper_title: BlindBox: Deep packet inspection over encrypted traffic
paper_abstract: Many network middleboxes perform deep packet inspection (DPI), a set of useful tasks which examine packet payloads. These tasks include intrusion detection (IDS), exfiltration detection, and parental filtering. However, a long-standing issue is that once packets are sent over HTTPS, middleboxes can no longer accomplish their tasks because the payloads are encrypted. Hence, one is faced with the choice of only one of two desirable properties: the functionality of middleboxes and the privacy of encryption. We propose BlindBox, the first system that simultaneously provides both of these properties. The approach of BlindBox is to perform the deep-packet inspection directly on the encrypted traffic. BlindBox realizes this approach through a new protocol and new encryption schemes. We demonstrate that BlindBox enables applications such as IDS, exfiltration detection and parental filtering, and supports real rulesets from both open-source and industrial DPI systems. We implemented BlindBox and showed that it is practical for settings with long-lived HTTPS connections. Moreover, its core encryption scheme is 3-6 orders of magnitude faster than existing relevant cryptographic schemes.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the BROP (Blind Return-Oriented Programming) attack, a novel technique that exploits stack buffer overflow vulnerabilities without prior knowledge of the target binary or source code. The author highlights how attackers can leverage the one-bit information of whether a server crashes or not to systematically probe and build a full attack, even against systems with modern defenses like NX (non-executable memory). The paper introduces a tool called Braille, an automated Ruby-based implementation of BROP, which can achieve remote code execution (e.g., a remote shell) in as little as a few minutes. The attack is particularly noteworthy for its ability to bypass ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization) and stack canaries, demonstrating that obscure software distributions offer little protection against such exploits. The key insight is that automated, blind exploitation is feasible and efficient, even without binary knowledge, making it a significant threat to system security.
paper_title: Hacking Blind
paper_venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P)
paper_abstract: 1 The widespread deployment of exploit mitigations such as CFI and shadow stacks are making code-reuse attacks increasingly difficult. This has forced adversaries to consider data-only attacks against which the venerable ASLR remains the primary deployed defense. Data-Space Randomization (DSR) techniques raise the bar against data-only attacks by making it harder for adversaries to inject malicious data flows into vulnerable applications. DSR works by masking memory load and store instructions. Masks are chosen (i) to not interfere with intended data flows and (ii) such that masking likely interferes with unintended flows introduced by malicious program inputs. In this paper, we show two new attacks that bypass all existing static DSR approaches; one that directly discloses memory and another using speculative execution. We then present CoDaRR, the first dynamic DSR scheme resilient to disclosure attacks. CoDaRR continuously rerandomizes the masks used in loads and stores, and re-masks all memory objects to remain transparent w.r.t. program execution. Our evaluation confirms that CoDaRR successfully thwarts these attacks with limited run-time overhead in standard benchmarks as well as real-world applications. Data-only attacks [14, 17, 26, 27] corrupt or leak program data without violating a control flow integrity (CFI) policy. Prior work showed that these attacks are powerful enough to escalate the program’s privileges, perform Turing-complete computation, or execute arbitrary system calls, all while bypassing code-reuse defenses such as CFI [14, 20, 22, 26, 27, 38]. To combat data-only attacks, defenders can either retrofit memory-safety techniques such as bounds checking into the program [46], rewrite the program in a safer programming language or language dialect [21, 29, 37], or apply exploit mitigations such as Data-Flow Integrity (DFI) [13], Write Integrity Testing (WIT) [2], or Data Space Randomization (DSR) [8, 11]. Historically, exploit mitigations have be...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights AI2 as a novel approach that combines human intelligence (HI) with artificial intelligence (AI) to improve cybersecurity threat detection. The system uses an ensemble of unsupervised learning models (PCA, Replicator Neural Networks, and copula functions) to identify suspicious events, which are then reviewed by human analysts. The human feedback is used to train a supervised model, creating a feedback loop that refines future detections. This hybrid approach significantly reduces false positives compared to pure unsupervised learning while detecting a higher percentage of attacks. The paper demonstrates that with a daily investigation budget of 200 events, AI2 detects 86.8% of attacks with a 4.4% false positive rate, outperforming unsupervised-only methods.
paper_title: AI2: Training a big data machine to defend
paper_venue: IEEE International Conference on Big Data Security

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the work of Spiegelman et al. on transactional data structure libraries (TDSL), which won a distinguished paper award at PLDI 2016. The paper addresses the challenge of adding transactional support to in-memory concurrent data structures without sacrificing performance, a problem that traditional software transactional memory (STM) and hardware transactions struggle with due to overhead and abort rates. The key insight is to leverage the semantics of specific data structures (e.g., maps, queues) to optimize transactional behavior, rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all approach. This approach is reminiscent of coordination avoidance in databases and avoids the overhead of STM by restricting the transactional alphabet to well-defined operations. The blog post also draws parallels to Redis and CRDTs, but emphasizes that TDSL is designed for in-process, traditional data structures. The paper demonstrates how transaction semantics can be integrated into data structures like skiplists and linked lists, with optimizations such as exploiting commutativity and using indices to reduce validation overhead.
paper_title: Transactional Data Structure Libraries
paper_abstract: 1 Transactional memory (TM) provides developers with a transaction primitive for concurrent code execution that transparently checks for concurrency conflicts. When such a conflict is detected, the system recovers by aborting and restarting the transaction. Although correct, this behavior wastes work and inhibits forward progress. In this paper, we present TardisTM, a software TM system that supports repairing concurrency conflicts while preserving unaffected computation. Our key insight is that existing conflict detection mechanisms can be extended to perform incremental transaction repair, when augmented with additional runtime information. To do so, we design a mechanism for localizing conflicts back to transactional program points, define the semantics for optional repair handler annotations, and extend the conflict detection algorithm to ensure all repairs are completed. To evaluate our system, we characterize the benefit of repair on a set of benchmark programs; we measure up to 2.95x speedup over mutual exclusion, and 93% abort reduction over a baseline software TM system that does not support repair. Transactional memory (TM) provides developers with firstclass transactional regions that guarantee atomicity, consistency, and isolation, avoiding the drawbacks of low-level concurrency control primitives [21]. These guarantees are ensured by the transactional runtime, which upon detecting a concurrency conflict, will abort, roll back, and restart a transaction. However, this behavior discards all work already performed within a transaction, which impedes forward progress and decreases performance. Transactions that are more likely to encounter conflicts, such as those that are high-contention or long-running, are particularly affected. Prior Work Helps But Still Aborts/Restarts: Prior work has developed various orthogonal strategies to mitigate this problem; namely, contention management, transaction scheduling, abort impact reduction, and conflict reduction.
