figures.title: Local validity threshold tracking
figures.caption: Each transaction tracks a local validity threshold, initialized to the global timestamp counter when the transaction starts. Read validation is performed only if a transactional read observes a newer timestamp or attempts to commit with a stale validity threshold.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews a 2015 survey paper by Serban et al. that catalogs datasets and techniques for building data-driven dialogue systems (chatbots). While the paper includes a comprehensive list of dialogue corpora across domains, it also provides a high-level survey of machine learning methods used in dialogue systems, focusing on corpus-based learning. Colyer highlights the distinction between goal-driven systems (e.g., travel assistants) and non-goal-driven systems (e.g., language learning tools), noting that most commercial chatbots fall into the former category. He emphasizes the importance of discriminative models and supervised learning in dialogue systems, as well as the challenges of generating natural responses, especially in multi-turn conversations. The blog post also discusses the differences between spoken and written dialogues, the role of external knowledge in chatbots, and the need for long-term interaction corpora to handle ambiguity and grounding in conversations.
paper_title: A survey of available corpora for building data-driven dialogue systems
paper_abstract: During the past decade, several areas of speech and language understanding have witnessed substantial breakthroughs from the use of data-driven models. In the area of dialogue systems, the trend is less obvious, and most practical systems are still built through significant engineering and expert knowledge. Nevertheless, several recent results suggest that data-driven approaches are feasible and quite promising. To facilitate research in this area, we have carried out a wide survey of publicly available datasets suitable for data-driven learning of dialogue systems. We discuss important characteristics of these datasets, how they can be used to learn diverse dialogue strategies, and their other potential uses. We also examine methods for transfer learning between datasets and the use of external knowledge. Finally, we discuss appropriate choice of evaluation metrics for the learning objective.

figures.title: Standard architecture for dialogue systems
figures.caption: The standard architecture for dialogue systems, shown in Figure 1, incorporates a Speech Recognizer, Language Interpreter, State Tracker, Response Generator, Natural Language Generator, and Speech Synthesizer.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this paper as an exploration of building a conversational bot using a purely data-driven approach with sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) learning. The key insight is that a neural model trained solely on conversational data—without domain-specific rules or feature engineering—can generate plausible and contextually appropriate responses. The paper demonstrates this with two datasets: an IT helpdesk troubleshooting corpus and OpenSubtitles movie dialogues. The model shows surprising capabilities like remembering facts, understanding context, and performing common-sense reasoning without explicit knowledge representation. However, Colyer notes limitations such as inconsistent personality, short and sometimes incorrect answers, and the inability to incorporate external knowledge or extract intent. The approach is praised for its simplicity and potential for generalization to unseen questions, though it remains far from practical for real-world chatbot services without additional logic.
paper_title: A Neural Conversational Model
paper_abstract: Conversational modeling is an important task in natural language understanding and machine intelligence. Although previous approaches exist, they are often restricted to specific domains (e.g., booking an airline ticket) and require handcrafted rules. In this paper, we present a simple approach for this task which uses the recently proposed sequence to sequence framework. Our model converses by predicting the next sentence given the previous sentence or sentences in a conversation. The strength of our model is that it can be trained end-to-end and thus requires much fewer hand-crafted rules. We find that this straightforward model can generate simple conversations given a large conversational training dataset. Our preliminary results suggest that, despite optimizing the wrong objective function, the model is able to converse well. It is able extract knowledge from both a domain specific dataset, and from a large, noisy, and general domain dataset of movie subtitles. On a domainspecific IT helpdesk dataset, the model can find a solution to a technical problem via conversations. On a noisy open-domain movie transcript dataset, the model can perform simple forms of common sense reasoning. As expected, we also find that the lack of consistency is a common failure mode of our model.

figures.title: Using the seq2seq framework for modeling conversations

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the CopyNet paper, which introduces a 'copying mechanism' to improve sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) models, making them more natural by mimicking human conversation where input subsequences are repeated in responses. The key insight is combining a generate mode (standard Seq2Seq) with a copy mode (selectively copying segments from the input) to handle out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words like entity names. CopyNet builds on Bahdanau et al.'s attention mechanism, which addresses the limitation of fixed-length encodings in long sentences by using a bi-directional RNN and adaptive attention over source sequences. The paper demonstrates CopyNet's effectiveness in synthetic tasks, text summarization (where it outperforms competitors), and dialogue systems, particularly in replicating critical input segments and generating coherent responses.
paper_title: Incorporating Copying Mechanism in Sequence to Sequence Learning
paper_abstract: arXiv:1603.06393v3 [cs.CL] 8 Jun 2016 We address an important problem in sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) learning referred to as copying, in which certain segments in the input sequence are selectively replicated in the output sequence. A similar phenomenon is observable in human language communication. For example, humans tend to repeat entity names or even long phrases in conversation. The challenge with regard to copying in Seq2Seq is that new machinery is needed to decide when to perform the operation. In this paper, we incorporate copying into neural networkbased Seq2Seq learning and propose a new model called C OPY N ET with encoderdecoder structure. C OPY N ET can nicely integrate the regular way of word generation in the decoder with the new copying mechanism which can choose subsequences in the input sequence and put them at proper places in the output sequence. Our empirical study on both synthetic data sets and real world data sets demonstrates the efficacy of C OPY N ET. For example, C OPY N ET can outperform regular RNN-based model with remarkable margins on text summarization tasks.

figures.title: Model overview of COPYNET
figures.caption: COPYNET is an encoder-decoder model with copying mechanism. The encoder is a bi-directional RNN that transforms the source sequence into hidden states (short-term memory M). The decoder generates the target sequence by either generating words from the vocabulary or copying segments from the input sequence.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the paper 'Building end-to-end dialogue systems using generative hierarchical neural network models' by Serban et al., presented at AAAI 2016. Adrian Colyer highlights the paper's approach to training dialogue systems end-to-end using hierarchical recurrent neural networks (RNNs), which model dialogues as sequences of utterances and tokens. The key insight is the use of a two-level hierarchy: one RNN for processing tokens within an utterance and another for tracking the sequence of utterances in the dialogue. The authors also emphasize the importance of bootstrapping the model with external data, such as pre-trained word embeddings from Google News and domain-specific corpora like the MovieTriples dataset, which significantly improves performance. The hierarchical architecture helps maintain context over long conversations and reduces computational steps between utterances, making training more stable. The post also notes the challenge of generic responses in dialogue systems and the potential of such models despite current limitations.
paper_title: Building end-to-end dialogue systems using generative hierarchical neural network models
paper_abstract: We investigate the task of building open domain, conversational dialogue systems based on large dialogue corpora using generative models. Generative models produce system responses that are autonomously generated word-by-word, opening up the possibility for realistic, flexible interactions. In support of this goal, we extend the recently proposed hierarchical recurrent encoder-decoder neural network to the dialogue domain, and demonstrate that this model is competitive with state-of-the-art neural language models and backoff n-gram models. We investigate the limitations of this and similar approaches, and show how its performance can be improved by bootstrapping the learning from a larger questionanswer pair corpus and from pretrained word embeddings.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 2011 paper by Collobert et al. as a foundational work in natural language processing (NLP) that demonstrates how neural networks can achieve state-of-the-art performance across multiple NLP tasks without relying on task-specific hand-engineered features or linguistic knowledge. The authors introduce SENNA, a neural network architecture that performs well on part-of-speech tagging, chunking, named-entity recognition, and semantic-role labeling, often matching or exceeding traditional systems while being significantly more efficient in terms of speed and memory usage. The key insight is that neural networks can learn effective intermediate representations from large unlabeled datasets, reducing the need for expert-designed features. Colyer notes that while the paper predates modern word embeddings like word2vec or GloVe, it anticipates their benefits by implicitly learning semantic similarities between words through backpropagation.
paper_title: Natural Language Processing (Almost) from Scratch
paper_abstract: We propose a unified neural network architecture and learning algorithm that can be applied to various natural language processing tasks including: part-of-speech tagging, chunking, named entity recognition, and semantic role labeling. This versatility is achieved by trying to avoid task-specific engineering and therefore disregarding a lot of prior knowledge. Instead of exploiting man-made input features carefully optimized for each task, our system learns internal representations on the basis of vast amounts of mostly unlabeled training data. This work is then used as a basis for building a freely available tagging system with good performance and minimal computational requirements. ar Xi arXiv:1103.0398v1 [cs.LG] 2 Mar 2011 Google, New York, NY.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this paper as a significant milestone in NLP, demonstrating that semantic role labeling (SRL) can be achieved end-to-end using deep learning without relying on traditional parsing features or expert-crafted linguistic knowledge. The authors from Baidu Research propose an 8-layer deep bi-directional LSTM (DB-LSTM) architecture that processes sentences word-by-word, incorporating features like predicate, argument, predicate-context, and region-mark. The model outperforms previous state-of-the-art systems that depended heavily on parsing results and feature engineering, achieving F1 scores of 81.07 and 81.27 on CoNLL-2005 and CoNLL-2012 benchmarks respectively. The key insight is that deep bidirectional LSTMs can learn semantic rules effectively without overfitting, even with limited training data, marking a shift toward end-to-end neural approaches in NLP tasks previously thought to require syntactic parsing.
paper_title: End-to-end learning of semantic role labeling using recurrent neural networks
paper_venue: International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (IJCNLP)
paper_abstract: Semantic role labeling (SRL) is one of the basic natural language processing (NLP) problems. To this date, most of the successful SRL systems were built on top of some form of parsing results (Koomen et al., 2005; Palmer et al., 2010; Pradhan et al., 2013), where pre-defined feature templates over the syntactic structure are used. The attempts of building an end-to-end SRL learning system without using parsing were less successful (Collobert et al., 2011). In this work, we propose to use deep bi-directional recurrent network as an end-to-end system for SRL. We take only original text information as input feature, without using any syntactic knowledge. The proposed algorithm for semantic role labeling was mainly evaluated on CoNLL-2005 shared task and achieved F1 score of 81.07. This result outperforms the previous state-of-the-art system from the combination of different parsing trees or models. We also obtained the same conclusion with F1 = 81.27 on CoNLL2012 shared task. As a result of simplicity, our model is also computationally efficient that the parsing speed is 6.7k tokens per second. Our analysis shows that our model is better at handling longer sentences than traditional models. And the latent variables of our model implicitly capture the syntactic structure of a sentence.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews a paper on Dialog State Tracking (DST), a critical component in spoken dialog systems and chatbots that determines user intent over multiple interactions. The blog highlights the shift from hand-crafted rules to machine-learned methods, which have proven superior in performance. Colyer explains the core concepts of DST, including 'slots' (informable and requestable) and the challenges of modeling uncertainty in dialog states. He contrasts generative approaches (Bayesian dynamic networks) with discriminative models (static classifiers and sequence models like RNNs/LSTMs), noting the latter's dominance in modern systems. Key insights include the use of delexicalization for generalization and the benefits of word-based DST that bypasses traditional Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) models. The paper is praised for its comprehensive references and practical techniques.
paper_title: Machine learning for dialog state tracking: a review
paper_abstract: Spoken dialog systems help users achieve a task using natural language. Noisy speech recognition and ambiguity in natural language motivate statistical approaches that model distributions over the user’s goal at every step in the dialog. The task of tracking these distributions, termed Dialog State Tracking, is therefore an essential component of any spoken dialog system. In recent years, the Dialog State Tracking Challenges have provided a common testbed and evaluation framework for this task, as well as labeled dialog data. As a result, a variety of machine-learned methods have been successfully applied to Dialog State Tracking. This paper reviews the machine-learning techniques that have been adapted to Dialog State Tracking, and gives an overview of published evaluations. Discriminative machine-learned methods outperform generative and rule-based methods, the previous state-of-the-art.

figures.title: Example dialog from DSTC 2 restaurant information domain
figures.caption: Example dialog from the DSTC 2 restaurant information domain, annotated with Dialog State labels. The left column shows the actual system action a and user action u. The second column shows example SLU M-best hypotheses and their scores. In the DSTC2 data, up to 10 SLU M-best hypotheses are given. Turn 2 demonstrates an addition to the goal constraints. In turn 3, the goal constraint for the area slot changes, and the search method changes from by constraints to by alternatives. The last turn demonstrates a non-empty set of requested slots.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses a paper on multi-domain dialog state tracking (DST) using recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to address the challenge of bootstrapping chatbot systems in new domains with limited data. Adrian Colyer highlights the key insight: transferring knowledge from out-of-domain data can significantly improve model performance, especially when in-domain data is scarce. The approach leverages delexicalised features (generic slot-value placeholders) to generalize across domains, enabling the model to learn dialog dynamics that apply to unseen slots or values. The paper demonstrates that out-of-domain pre-training outperforms even similar-domain data, and combining this with slot-specific specialization further enhances accuracy. The experiments show that models pre-trained on diverse domains achieve better joint goal accuracy, even when fine-tuned with in-domain data.
paper_title: Multi-domain dialog state tracking using recurrent neural networks
paper_venue: Proceedings of the 2015 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
paper_abstract: Dialog state tracking is a key component of many modern dialog systems, most of which are designed with a single, welldefined domain in mind. This paper shows that dialog data drawn from different dialog domains can be used to train a general belief tracking model which can operate across all of these domains, exhibiting superior performance to each of the domainspecific models. We propose a training procedure which uses out-of-domain data to initialise belief tracking models for entirely new domains. This procedure leads to improvements in belief tracking performance regardless of the amount of in-domain data available for training the model.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews a 2015 position paper by Ward and De Vault that outlines ten key challenges for highly-interactive dialog systems, with a focus on spoken dialog. The authors categorize these challenges into three main areas: improving power and robustness, reducing development costs, and deepening understanding. Colyer highlights the compelling argument for 'superhuman' dialog systems, which could surpass human performance by leveraging real-time sensing, advanced planning, and cognitive advantages. He also notes the importance of modeling multifunctional behaviors (e.g., backchanneling) and integrating learned and designed behaviors. The paper emphasizes the need for continuous dialog state tracking, compositional behavior specifications, and better evaluation methods. Colyer underscores the disconnect between dialog systems research and social science findings, advocating for more comprehensible models and interdisciplinary collaboration.
paper_title: Ten challenges in highly-interactive dialog systems
paper_abstract: Systems capable of highly-interactive dialog have recently been developed in several domains. This paper considers how to build on these successes to make systems more robust, easier to develop, more adaptable, and more scientifically significant.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Facebook's 'Realtime Data Processing at Facebook' paper as a comprehensive overview of their systems for handling real-time workloads, emphasizing five key design decisions. The blog underscores the growing importance of near real-time systems and the critical role of ease-of-use in system design, noting that industry systems often prioritize usability over purely performance or correctness metrics. Colyer appreciates Facebook's explicit focus on ease-of-use in their design, covering aspects like application development, testing, debugging, deployment, and monitoring. He also speculates on a potential convergence between data processing platforms and application architectures, given their similarities in structure and event-driven styles. The paper details a diverse set of real-time systems at Facebook, each tailored to specific use cases, and explains how their design decisions address qualities like performance, fault-tolerance, scalability, and correctness.
paper_title: Realtime Data Processing at Facebook
paper_abstract: Realtime data processing powers many use cases at Facebook, including realtime reporting of the aggregated, anonymized voice of Facebook users, analytics for mobile applications, and insights for Facebook page administrators. Many companies have developed their own systems; we have a realtime data processing ecosystem at Facebook that handles hundreds of Gigabytes per second across hundreds of data pipelines. Many decisions must be made while designing a realtime stream processing system. In this paper, we identify five important design decisions that affect their ease of use, performance, fault tolerance, scalability, and correctness. We compare the alternative choices for each decision and contrast what we built at Facebook to other published systems. Our main decision was targeting seconds of latency, not milliseconds. Seconds is fast enough for all of the use cases we support and it allows us to use a persistent message bus for data transport. This data transport mechanism then paved the way for fault tolerance, scalability, and multiple options for correctness in our stream processing systems Puma, Swift, and Stylus. We then illustrate how our decisions and systems satisfy our requirements for multiple use cases at Facebook. Finally, we reflect on the lessons we learned as we built and operated these systems.

figures.caption: An overview of the systems involved in realtime data processing: from logging in mobile and web products on the left, through Scribe and realtime stream processors in the middle, to data stores for analysis on the right.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Google's Goods (Google Dataset Search) as a compelling alternative to centralized Enterprise Data Management (the 'data cathedral') by embracing a decentralized 'data bazaar' approach. Goods autonomously crawls and catalogs datasets across Google (indexing over 26 billion datasets), extracting metadata from diverse sources (datasets, logs, source code) to provide a unified view. The system tracks dataset provenance, monitors changes, and offers searchable profile pages with schema, usage, and access snippets. Colyer praises its post-hoc organization model, which avoids the friction of centralized control while enabling engineers to discover and manage datasets efficiently. The paper details the technical challenges of scale (e.g., crawling 26B+ datasets) and solutions like importance-based crawling and dataset clustering to reduce cognitive and computational overhead.
paper_title: Goods: Organizing Google's Datasets
paper_abstract: Enterprises increasingly rely on structured datasets to run their businesses. These datasets take a variety of forms, such as structured files, databases, spreadsheets, or even services that provide access to the data. The datasets often reside in different storage systems, may vary in their formats, may change every day. In this paper, we present Goods, a project to rethink how we organize structured datasets at scale, in a setting where teams use diverse and often idiosyncratic ways to produce the datasets and where there is no centralized system for storing and querying them. Goods extracts metadata ranging from salient information about each dataset (owners, timestamps, schema) to relationships among datasets, such as similarity and provenance. It then exposes this metadata through services that allow engineers to find datasets within the company, to monitor datasets, to annotate them in order to enable others to use their datasets, and to analyze relationships between them. We discuss the technical challenges that we had to overcome in order to crawl and infer the metadata for billions of datasets, to maintain the consistency of our metadata catalog at scale, and to expose the metadata to users. We believe that many of the lessons that we learned are applicable to building large-scale enterprise-level datamanagement systems in general.

figures.title: Overview of Google Dataset Search (Goods)
figures.caption: Overview of Google Dataset Search (Goods). The figure shows the Goods dataset catalog that collects metadata about datasets from various storage systems as well as other sources. We also infer metadata by processing additional sources such as logs and information about dataset owners and their projects, by analyzing content of the datasets, and by collecting input from the Goods users. We use the information in the catalog to build tools for search, monitoring, and visualizing flow of data.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Ambry, LinkedIn's scalable geo-distributed object store, as a robust solution for handling the massive scale of modern social networks. The paper emphasizes Ambry's ability to efficiently manage read-heavy workloads (over 95% of traffic) for immutable blobs, ranging from small files to large media objects, with high throughput (up to 88% of network bandwidth) and low latency (under 50ms for 1MB blobs). Key design choices include a multi-master architecture with configurable consistency levels (similar to Cassandra), asynchronous replication across datacenters, and a partitioning scheme that decouples logical and physical data placement to enable transparent rebalancing. The system also employs load balancing techniques to mitigate hotspots, achieving significant reductions in request rate and disk usage imbalance (6-10x and 9-10x, respectively). The blog praises Ambry's production readiness, having operated across four datacenters for over two years, and its innovative approaches to handling large blobs via chunking and append-only logs.
paper_title: Ambry: LinkedIn's scalable geo-distributed object store
paper_abstract: The infrastructure beneath a worldwide social network has to continually serve billions of variable-sized media objects such as photos, videos, and audio clips. These objects must be stored and served with low latency and high throughput by a system that is geo-distributed, highly scalable, and load-balanced. Existing file systems and object stores face several challenges when serving such large objects. We present Ambry, a production-quality system for storing large immutable data (called blobs). Ambry is designed in a decentralized way and leverages techniques such as logical blob grouping, asynchronous replication, rebalancing mechanisms, zero-cost failure detection, and OS caching. Ambry has been running in LinkedIn’s production environment for the past 2 years, serving up to 10K requests per second across more than 400 million users. Our experimental evaluation reveals that Ambry offers high efficiency (utilizing up to 88% of the network bandwidth), low latency (less than 50 ms latency for a 1 MB object), and load balancing (improving imbalance of request rate among disks by 8x-10x).

figures.title: Ambry system architecture
figures.caption: The overall architecture of Ambry is shown in Figure 1. The system is composed of three main components: Frontends that receive and route requests, Datanodes that store the actual data, and Cluster Managers that maintain the state of the cluster.

blog_summary: DBSherlock is a performance diagnostic tool designed to help database administrators (DBAs) diagnose performance anomalies in transactional databases. The tool addresses the challenge of interpreting vast amounts of statistical data, which can be overwhelming even for highly skilled DBAs. DBSherlock compares regions of interest (anomalies) with normal behavior by analyzing historical statistics to identify likely causes of performance issues. It provides two types of outputs: concise predicates describing system configurations or workload characteristics linked to the anomaly, and high-level diagnoses based on causal models. The tool learns from user feedback, refining its causal models over time to improve future diagnoses. The approach emphasizes explaining anomalies rather than detecting them, leveraging predicate generation, domain knowledge pruning, and causal modeling layers. The system integrates with DBSeer, an open-source database administration suite, to collect and visualize performance statistics at one-second intervals, enabling real-time analysis.
paper_title: DBSherlock: A Performance Diagnostic Tool for Transactional Databases
paper_abstract: Bohan Zhang Peking University ggordon@cs.cmu.edu bohan@pku.edu.cn many configuration knobs [22, 47, 36]. Part of what makes DBMSs so enigmatic is that their performance and scalability are highly dependent on their configurations. Further exacerbating this problem is that the default configurations of these knobs are notoriously bad. As an example, the default MySQL configuration in 2016 assumes that it is deployed on a machine that only has 160 MB of RAM [1]. Given this, many organizations resort to hiring expensive experts to configure the system’s knobs for the expected workload. But as databases and applications grow in both size and complexity, optimizing a DBMS to meet the needs of an application has surpassed the abilities of humans [11]. This is because the correct configuration of a DBMS is highly dependent on a number of factors that are beyond what humans can reason about. Previous attempts at automatic DBMS configuration tools have certain deficiencies that make them inadequate for general purpose database applications. Many of these tuning tools were created by vendors, and thus they only support that particular company’s DBMS [22, 33, 37]. The small number of tuning tools that do support multiple DBMSs still require manual steps, such as having the DBA (1) deploy a second copy of the database [24], (2) map dependencies between knobs [49], or (3) guide the training process [58]. All of these tools also examine each DBMS deployment independently and thus are unable to apply knowledge gained from previous tuning efforts. This is inefficient because each tuning effort can take a long time and use a lot of resources. In this paper, we present a technique to reuse training data gathered from previous sessions to tune new DBMS deployments. blog_summary: The blog post discusses a paper that challenges the traditional approach to viral marketing, which assumes targeting a few influential individuals maximizes reach. Instead, the authors propose focusing on the 'spheres of influence' of each node in a network, which represents the typical cascade of nodes reached from a source, along with a measure of stability. The key insight is to compute the typical cascade using the Jaccard median of sampled cascades, which is shown to outperform the standard greedy algorithm for influence maximization when the number of seeds grows. The paper introduces efficient algorithms for computing typical cascades by leveraging strongly connected components (SCCs) and provides theoretical guarantees on the sample size needed for accurate approximations. The approach is demonstrated to achieve better expected spread compared to the standard method, attributed to its ability to discriminate among nodes more effectively before reaching saturation.
paper_title: Spheres of influence for more effective viral marketing
paper_abstract: 1. What is the set of nodes of a social network that, under a probabilistic contagion model, would get infected if a given node s gets infected? We call this set the sphere of influence of s. Due to the stochastic nature of the contagion model we need to define a notion of “expected” or “typical” cascade: this is a set of nodes which is the closest to all the possible cascades starting from s. We thus formalize the Typical Cascade problem which requires, for a given source node s, to find the set of nodes minimizing the expected Jaccard distance to all the possible cascades from s. The expected cost of a typical cascade also provides us a measure of the stability of cascade propagation, i.e., how much random cascades from a source node s deviate from the “typical” cascade. In this sense source nodes with lower expected costs are more reliable. We show that, while computing the quality of a candidate solution is #P-hard, a method based on (1) sampling random cascades and (2) computing their Jaccard Median, can obtain a multiplicative approximation with just O(1) samples. We then devise an index that allows to efficiently compute the sphere of influence for any node in the network. Finally, we propose to approach the influence maximization problem as an instance of set cover on the spheres of influence. Through exhaustive evaluation using real-world networks and different methods of assigning the influence probability to each edge, we show that our approach outperforms in quality the theoretically optimal greedy algorithm. The phenomenon of influence-driven cascades in social networks has received tremendous attention in the last years thanks to its applications, among which the most appealing is viral marketing. The idea of viral marketing is to exploit a pre-existing social network in order to increase brand awareness or to achieve other marketing objectives (such as product sales) through self-replicating viral processes, analogous to the spread of viruses. blog_summary: The blog post discusses the 'skyline operator' in database systems, which is crucial for multi-criteria decision-making applications. Adrian Colyer explains that the skyline operator returns objects that are not dominated by any other object in all dimensions. For example, in a hotels dataset with price and distance attributes, a hotel is in the skyline if no other hotel is both cheaper and closer to the beach. The paper introduces the Branch-and-Bound Skyline (BBS) algorithm, which efficiently computes the skyline using R-trees and nearest-neighbor search techniques. BBS is praised for its progressiveness, fairness, and I/O optimality, ensuring it only visits relevant nodes and avoids false hits or misses. The post also highlights incremental maintenance of skylines and variations like constrained skyline queries.
paper_title: Progressive skyline computation in database systems
paper_abstract: The skyline of a d-dimensional dataset contains the points that are not dominated by any other point on all dimensions. Skyline computation has recently received considerable attention in the database community, especially for progressive methods that can quickly return the initial results without reading the entire database. All the existing algorithms, however, have some serious shortcomings which limit their applicability in practice. In this paper we develop BBS (branch-andbound skyline), an algorithm based on nearest neighbor search, which is I/O optimal, i.e., it performs a single access only to those nodes that may contain skyline points. BBS is simple to implement and supports all types of progressive processing (e.g., user preferences, arbitrary dimensionality etc). Furthermore, we propose several interesting variations of skyline computation, and show how BBS can be applied for their efficient processing. To appear in ACM-TODS, special issue on best of SIGMOD/PODS 2003 Long version of [PTFS03]

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the Sharing-aware Outlier Processing (SOP) algorithm by Cao et al., which addresses the challenge of handling large-scale outlier detection queries over high-volume data streams. Traditional methods struggle with scalability when processing hundreds or thousands of concurrent outlier queries with varying parameters. SOP introduces a novel approach by leveraging a single skyband query—a generalization of skyline queries—to efficiently determine outlier status for all queries simultaneously. The key insight is that a skyband query can provide minimal yet sufficient evidence to evaluate whether a data point is an outlier across all queries in the workload. This method significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art techniques (e.g., LEAP or MCOD) by reducing CPU usage by three orders of magnitude and scaling to workloads with thousands of queries. The algorithm also introduces K-SKY, an optimized skyband query processing technique that efficiently handles sliding window semantics, further improving performance.
paper_title: Sharing-aware Outlier Analytics over High-volume Data Streams
paper_abstract: Users Real-time outlier detection from a data stream has become increasingly important in the current hyperconnected world. This paper focuses on an important yet unaddressed challenge in continuous outlier detection—the multiplicity and dynamicity of queries. This challenge arises from various contexts of outliers evolving over time, but the state-of-the-art algorithms cannot handle the challenge effectively, as they can only process a fixed set of outlier detection queries for each data point separately. In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm, abbreviated as MDUAL, based on a new idea called duality-based unified processing. The underlying rationale is to exploit the duality of data and queries so that a group of similar data points are processed together by a group of similar queries incrementally. Two main techniques embodying the idea, data-query grouping and prioritized group processing, are employed. Comprehensive experiments showed that MDUAL runs 216 to 221 times faster while consuming 11 to 13 times less memory than the state-of-the-art algorithms through its efficient and effective handling of the multiplicity–dynamicity challenge. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a SIGMOD 2016 paper that tackles the problem of efficiently handling range threshold queries (RTS) over data streams, where the goal is to detect when a cumulative weight of events within a specified range reaches a threshold. The blog notes that naive approaches scale quadratically with the number of queries, making them computationally infeasible at scale. The authors propose a novel algorithm called Distributed Tracking (DT), which breaks this quadratic barrier with a polylogarithmic time complexity. The key insight is drawing a surprising connection between RTS and the distributed tracking problem, where a coordinator monitors counters across participants. The paper then adapts this distributed tracking solution to the RTS problem through a binary search tree structure and efficient heap-based query management, enabling real-time triggers at scale.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the paper 'Time-adaptive sketches (Ada Sketches) for Summarizing Data Streams' by Shrivastava et al., presented at SIGMOD 2016. Adrian Colyer highlights the challenge of extracting meaningful information from data streams where patterns change over time (volatility), focusing on the heavy hitters problem with a twist: prioritizing recent trends. The key insight is the introduction of time-adaptive sketches, which generalize traditional sketching algorithms like Count-Min Sketches (CMS) by weighting recent data more heavily. Instead of incrementing counters uniformly, the algorithm uses a monotone function f(t) to inflate recent counts, with experiments showing good results for both linear and exponential functions. The paper provides theoretical guarantees, compares prior approaches, and demonstrates superior accuracy and runtime performance over the Hokusai algorithm on real-world datasets.
paper_title: Time-adaptive sketches (Ada Sketches) for Summarizing Data Streams
paper_abstract: 1 Burst is a common pattern in data streams which is characterized by a sudden increase in terms of arrival rate followed by a sudden decrease. Burst detection has attracted extensive attention from the research community. In this paper, we propose a novel sketch, namely BurstSketch, to detect bursts accurately in real time. BurstSketch first uses the technique Running Track to select potential burst items efficiently, and then monitors the potential burst items and capture the key features of burst pattern by a technique called Snapshotting. Experimental results show that our sketch achieves a 1.75 times higher recall rate than the strawman solution.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer revisits David Parnas' 1971 classic paper, highlighting its enduring relevance to modern software development, particularly in the context of microservices and cloud-native architectures. The paper argues that the effectiveness of modularization depends critically on the criteria used to divide a system into modules. Parnas defines modules as work assignment units rather than subprograms, and outlines three key benefits: reduced development time, improved flexibility, and better comprehensibility. The paper illustrates these ideas through a case study of a KWIC index generator, comparing two decompositions—one based on workflow steps and another based on information hiding. The latter approach, which encapsulates design decisions likely to change, proves superior in isolating changes, simplifying interfaces, and improving comprehensibility, though it may introduce performance overhead. Colyer emphasizes that modern developers should pay more attention to the criteria for module boundaries, as these choices profoundly impact agility, development time, and system understanding.
paper_title: On the criteria to be used in decomposing systems into modules
paper_abstract: This paper discusses modularization as a mechanism for improving the flexibility and comprehensibility of a system while allowing the shortening of its development time. tion 11 The effectiveness of a "modulariza is dependent upon the criteria used in dividing the system into modules. Two system design problems are presented, and for each, both a conventional and unconventional decomposition are described. It is shown that the unconventional decompositions have distinct advantages for the goals outlined. tions are discussed. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Fred Brooks' seminal 1987 essay 'No Silver Bullet' as a timeless and quotable exploration of why software engineering remains inherently difficult despite technological advances. The post emphasizes Brooks' distinction between 'essential difficulties' (inherent to software's nature) and 'accidental difficulties' (self-imposed challenges). Brooks argues that complexity, conformity, changeability, and invisibility are fundamental properties of software that cannot be abstracted away. The blog underscores Brooks' key insight: there is no 'silver bullet' solution to dramatically reduce software costs, as the essence of software development revolves around conceptual constructs that are abstract and non-linear. Colyer praises the essay's readability and its enduring relevance, noting that Brooks' recommendations—reuse, incremental development, and investing in developers—still resonate today.
paper_title: No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accident in Software Engineering
paper_abstract: 1 All software construction involves essential tasks, the fashioning of the complex conceptual structures that compose the abstract software entity, and accidental tasks, the representation of these abstract entities in programming languages and the mapping of these onto machine languages within space and speed constraints. Most of the big past gains in software productivity have come from removing artificial barriers that have made the accidental tasks inordinately hard, such as severe hardware constraints, awkward programming languages, lack of machine time. How much of what software engineers now do is still devoted to the accidental, as opposed to the essential? Unless it is more than 9/10 of all effort, shrinking all the accidental activities to zero time will not give an order of magnitude improvement. Therefore it appears that the time has come to address the essential parts of the software task, those concerned with fashioning abstract conceptual structures of great complexity. I suggest: • Exploiting the mass market to avoid constructing what can be bought. • Using rapid prototyping as part of a planned iteration in establishing software requirements. • Growing software organically, adding more and more function to systems as they are run, used, and tested. • Identifying and developing the great conceptual designers of the rising generation.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews Tony Hoare's 1981 ACM Turing Award lecture, which serves as a powerful critique of overambitious software design and committee-driven language standardization. The paper emphasizes the pursuit of simplicity as the key to reliability, contrasting two approaches to software design: making systems so simple that deficiencies are obvious, or so complex that deficiencies are hidden. Hoare shares personal experiences from his work on ALGOL, PL/I, and Ada, highlighting the dangers of committee-based design and the importance of static type checking and safety-first principles. He argues that reliability cannot be achieved without simplicity, and that overambition often leads to failure despite the best intentions of intelligent programmers. The lecture also recounts the invention of QuickSort and the axiomatic approach to programming, offering timeless lessons on humility and the limits of ambition in software engineering.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reflects on Donald Knuth's 1974 Turing Award acceptance lecture, 'Computer Programming as an Art,' which argues that programming is both an art and a science. Knuth emphasizes the aesthetic and creative aspects of programming, advocating for 'beautiful programs' that are correct, maintainable, readable, and efficient. He critiques the overemphasis on premature optimization and highlights the importance of tools that make programming a pleasure rather than a chore. The blog post underscores Knuth's view that programming can be a source of intellectual and emotional satisfaction when approached with creativity and skill.
paper_title: Computer Programming as an Art

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Ken Thompson's 1984 Turing Award Lecture as a masterclass in subtle, insidious security vulnerabilities. The paper builds from self-reproducing programs (quines) to show how a compiler can be subverted to inject trojan horses into other programs, including itself. Thompson demonstrates a 'double-blind' attack where a malicious compiler inserts a backdoor into the login command while also embedding a self-replicating mechanism to reinstall the backdoor in future compiler versions. The brilliance lies in the attack leaving no trace in source code—only the compiled binary carries the infection. Colyer emphasizes the paper's shocking 'oh *!$&#' moment, where the realization hits that trusting any part of the software stack (even the compiler) is perilous. The moral is stark: you cannot trust code you didn't create entirely yourself, and the attack surface extends to any program-handling tool (assemblers, loaders, microcode).

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights James Hamilton's 2007 LISA paper as a foundational resource for building cloud-native applications, packed with timeless wisdom on designing and deploying operations-friendly services. The paper emphasizes three core tenets: expecting failures, prioritizing simplicity to avoid complexity-driven problems, and automating everything to reduce human error. Hamilton argues that 80% of operations issues originate in design and development, not operations, and advocates for proactive system design that embeds operational efficiency. The paper is structured into ten detailed sub-sections covering best practices in application design, automation, dependency management, testing, hardware selection, monitoring, and customer communication. Colyer particularly praises Hamilton's forward-thinking insights, such as treating failure testing like security threat modeling, the economic case for single-version services, and the counterintuitive approach to staging environments versus limited production testing. The paper's practical advice, though nearly two decades old, remains highly relevant and has influenced modern cloud-native practices.
paper_title: On designing and deploying internet-scale services
paper_abstract: The system-to-administrator ratio is commonly used as a rough metric to understand administrative costs in high-scale services. With smaller, less automated services this ratio can be as low as 2:1, whereas on industry leading, highly automated services, we’ve seen ratios as high as 2,500:1. Within Microsoft services, Autopilot [1] is often cited as the magic behind the success of the Windows Live Search team in achieving high system-to-administrator ratios. While auto-administration is important, the most important factor is actually the service itself. Is the service efficient to automate? Is it what we refer to more generally as operations-friendly? Services that are operationsfriendly require little human intervention, and both detect and recover from all but the most obscure failures without administrative intervention. This paper summarizes the best practices accumulated over many years in scaling some of the largest services at MSN and Windows Live.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Pat Helland's 2005 paper as a foundational work on understanding data management in service-oriented architectures (modernly referred to as microservices). The key insight is the stark contrast between 'data on the inside' (private, transactional data within a service) and 'data on the outside' (shared, immutable data exchanged between services). Helland draws an analogy to Einstein's relativity, where each service operates in its own 'now' while external data represents a 'past' or 'future' state. The paper argues that traditional ACID transactions and mutable data models break down across service boundaries, necessitating immutable, versioned identifiers for external data. Colyer emphasizes the paper's enduring relevance, noting its prescient observations about the challenges of distributed systems and the need for careful data modeling in microservices architectures.
paper_title: Data on the Outside vs. Data on the Inside
paper_abstract: Recently, a lot of interest has been shown in SOA (Service Oriented Architectures). In these systems, there are multiple services each with its own code and data, and ability to operate independently of its partners. In particular, atomic transactions with two-phase commit do not occur across multiple services because this necessitates holding locks while another service decides the outcome of the transaction. This paper proposes there are a number of seminal differences between data inside a service and data sent into the space outside of the service boundary. We then consider objects, SQL, and XML as different representations of data. Each of these models has strengths and weaknesses when applied to the inside and outside of the service boundary. The paper concludes that the strength of each of these models in one area is derived from essential characteristics underlying its weakness in the other area.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes John Hughes' influential 1990 paper 'Why Functional Programming Matters,' which argues for the superiority of functional programming (FP) by highlighting its modularity benefits. Hughes critiques the common arguments for FP (e.g., immutability, lack of side effects) as too negative and unconvincing to outsiders. Instead, he posits that FP's true power lies in its ability to enable modular design through two key mechanisms: higher-order functions and lazy evaluation. These 'glues' allow programmers to compose small, reusable modules into larger systems, improving productivity and maintainability. Hughes contrasts this with the limitations of imperative programming, where modularity is constrained by traditional control structures. The paper is praised for its eloquent prose and compelling examples, particularly in demonstrating how higher-order functions like `foldr` can abstract common patterns, while lazy evaluation enables modularization of infinite or large datasets.
paper_title: Why Functional Programming Matters
paper_abstract: As software becomes more and more complex, it is more and more important to structure it well. Well-structured software is easy to write and to debug, and provides a collection of modules that can be reused to reduce future programming costs. In this paper we show that two features of functional languages in particular, higher-order functions and lazy evaluation, can contribute significantly to modularity. As examples, we manipulate lists and trees, program several numerical algorithms, and implement the alpha-beta heuristic (an algorithm from Artificial Intelligence used in game-playing programs). We conclude that since modularity is the key to successful programming, functional programming offers important advantages for software development.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Richard Gabriel's 1990 paper 'Lisp: Good News, Bad News, How to Win Big,' which introduces the 'Worse is Better' philosophy and contrasts it with the 'Right Thing' approach. The blog focuses on Section 2.1, where Gabriel describes two opposing software design philosophies: the MIT/Stanford 'Right Thing' school, which prioritizes simplicity, correctness, consistency, and completeness, and the 'New Jersey' approach (e.g., C and Unix), which favors simplicity of implementation over interface simplicity, correctness over absolute correctness, pragmatic inconsistency over complexity, and simplicity over completeness. Colyer notes that while the 'Right Thing' aims for near-perfection, it often results in overly complex systems that take too long to develop. In contrast, 'Worse is Better' software spreads quickly due to its simplicity and portability, conditioning users to accept imperfections before gradually improving toward 90% correctness. Colyer reflects on the trade-offs between these approaches and questions whether the marketplace's preference for the 'Worse is Better' model sacrifices long-term quality.
paper_title: Lisp: Good News, Bad News, How to Win Big
paper_abstract: Lisp has done quite well over the last ten years: becoming nearly standardized, forming the basis of a commercial sector, achieving excellent performance, having good environments, able to deliver applications. Yet the Lisp community has failed to do as well as it could have. In this paper I look at the successes, the failures, and what to do next. The Lisp world is in great shape: Ten years ago there was no standard Lisp; the most standard Lisp was InterLisp, which ran on PDP-10’s and Xerox Lisp machines (some said it ran on Vaxes, but I think they exaggerated); the second most standard Lisp was MacLisp, which ran only on PDP-10’s, but under the three most popular operating systems for that machine; the third most standard Lisp was Portable Standard Lisp, which ran on many machines, but very few people wanted to use it; the fourth most standard Lisp was Zetalisp, which ran on two varieties of Lisp machine; and the fifth most standard Lisp was Scheme, which ran on a few different kinds of machine, but very few people wanted to use it. By today’s standards, each of these had poor or just barely acceptable performance, nonexistent or just barely satisfactory environments, nonexistent or poor integration with other languages and software, poor portability, poor acceptance, and poor commercial prospects. Today there is Common Lisp (CL), which runs on all major machines, all major operating systems, and virtually in every country. Common Lisp is about to be standardized by ANSI, has good performance, is surrounded with good environments, and has good integration with other languages and software. But, as a business, Lisp is considered to be in ill health. There are persistent and sometimes true rumors about the abandonment of Lisp as a vehicle for delivery of practical applications. To some extent the problem is one of perception—there are simply better Lisp delivery solutions than are generally believed to exist and to a disturbing extent the problem is one of unplaced ...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Butler Lampson's 1983 paper 'Hints for Computer System Design' as a timeless guide to fundamental challenges in system design, despite its age. The paper offers practical advice on balancing simplicity, consistency, correctness, and completeness in system design, with a strong focus on interface design. Lampson emphasizes that interfaces should be simple, complete, and implementable, avoiding overgeneralization while ensuring predictable performance. Key insights include prioritizing fast, basic operations over cumbersome higher-level abstractions, using information hiding judiciously, and addressing normal and worst-case scenarios separately. The paper also covers implementation strategies like divide-and-conquer, resource allocation, fault tolerance, and performance optimization, all framed as actionable 'hints' backed by real-world examples.
paper_title: Hints for Computer System Design
paper_abstract: Studying the design and implementation of a number of computer has led to some general hints for system design. They are described here and illustrated by many examples, ranging from hardware such as the Alto and the Dorado to application programs such as Bravo and Star.

figures.title: Summary of the slogans
figures.caption: Figure 1 organizes the slogans along two axes: Why it helps in making a good system (functionality, speed, or fault-tolerance) and Where in the system design it helps (ensuring completeness, choosing interfaces, or devising implementations). Fat lines connect repetitions of the same slogan, and thin lines connect related slogans.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this Google paper as a landmark shift toward deep learning for large-scale recommendation systems, marking a 'changing of the guard' in the field. The blog emphasizes the YouTube recommendation system's two-stage architecture: a candidate generation model that narrows down millions of videos to a few hundred candidates, followed by a ranking model that scores these candidates using hundreds of features. Key insights include the system's scale (training on hundreds of billions of examples with one billion parameters), the challenges of freshness (prioritizing new content without sacrificing relevance) and noise (using watch time over click-through rate to avoid clickbait). The paper also details the use of embeddings for videos and users, inspired by language models, and the importance of temporal patterns in user behavior. Despite deep learning's promise to reduce feature engineering, the authors note significant manual effort remains in transforming raw data for the models.
paper_title: Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations
paper_abstract: YouTube represents one of the largest scale and most sophisticated industrial recommendation systems in existence. In this paper, we describe the system at a high level and focus on the dramatic performance improvements brought by deep learning. The paper is split according to the classic two-stage information retrieval dichotomy: first, we detail a deep candidate generation model and then describe a separate deep ranking model. We also provide practical lessons and insights derived from designing, iterating and maintaining a massive recommendation system with enormous userfacing impact.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights AlphaGo's groundbreaking approach to mastering the game of Go, a challenge long considered the pinnacle of AI due to its vast search space and complex position evaluation. The paper introduces a novel combination of deep neural networks and Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), using policy networks to reduce search breadth and value networks to reduce search depth. Colyer emphasizes the three-stage training pipeline: supervised learning from human expert moves, reinforcement learning through self-play, and value network training to predict game outcomes. The system's success—beating the European Go champion 5-0—demonstrates the power of combining deep learning with traditional search algorithms, offering a blueprint for tackling other complex decision-making tasks in AI.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes his talk at the Operability.io conference, highlighting key insights from computer science research papers that relate to operability in modern systems. He emphasizes that operability should be integrated into system design from the outset, not bolted on later, citing James Hamilton's 2007 LISA paper 'On designing and deploying internet-scale services' as a foundational work. The talk also explores techniques for understanding distributed systems, such as Google's Dapper for distributed tracing and Facebook's Mystery Machine, which leverages logs to infer system behavior and performance bottlenecks. Colyer underscores the importance of automation, simplicity, and graceful failure handling in operable systems.
paper_title: On designing and deploying internet-scale services
paper_abstract: The 2008 LADIS workshop on Large Scale Distributed Systems brought together leaders from the commercial cloud computing community with researchers working on a variety of topics in distributed computing. The dialog yielded some surprises: some hot research topics seem to be of limited near-term importance to the cloud builders, while some of their practical challenges seem to pose new questions to us as systems researchers. This brief note summarizes our impressions. Workshop Background LADIS is an annual workshop focusing on the state of the art in distributed systems. The workshops are by invitation, with the organizing committee setting the agenda. In 2008, the committee included ourselves, Eliezer Dekel, Paul Dantzig, Danny Dolev, and Mike Spreitzer. The workshop website, at http://www.cs.cornell.edu/projects/ladis2008/, includes the detailed agenda, white papers, and slide sets [23]; proceedings are available electronically from the ACM Portal web site [22]. LADIS 2008 Topic The 2008 LADIS topic was Cloud Computing, and more specifically: •

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this KDD 2016 paper by Ribeiro et al. as addressing a critical challenge in machine learning: understanding why classifiers make certain predictions and whether those predictions are trustworthy. The authors introduce LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), an algorithm that explains individual predictions by approximating the model's behavior locally with an interpretable surrogate model. They also propose SP-LIME, a method to build global trust in a model by selecting representative explanations. The paper demonstrates that human users, even without machine learning expertise, can use these explanations to identify flawed models (e.g., ones relying on spurious features like email headers) and improve them by removing irrelevant features. Experiments show that humans can correctly identify the better model 89% of the time and iteratively refine classifiers to generalize better to real-world data. The key insight is that local, interpretable explanations can provide meaningful insights into model behavior without requiring global model transparency.
paper_title: Why Should I Trust You?: Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier
paper_abstract: Despite widespread adoption, machine learning models remain mostly black boxes. Understanding the reasons behind predictions is, however, quite important in assessing trust, which is fundamental if one plans to take action based on a prediction, or when choosing whether to deploy a new model. Such understanding also provides insights into the model, which can be used to transform an untrustworthy model or prediction into a trustworthy one. In this work, we propose LIME, a novel explanation technique that explains the predictions of any classifier in an interpretable and faithful manner, by learning an interpretable model locally around the prediction. We also propose a method to explain models by presenting representative individual predictions and their explanations in a non-redundant way, framing the task as a submodular optimization problem. We demonstrate the flexibility of these methods by explaining different models for text (e.g. random forests) and image classification (e.g. neural networks). We show the utility of explanations via novel experiments, both simulated and with human subjects, on various scenarios that require trust: deciding if one should trust a prediction, choosing between models, improving an untrustworthy classifier, and identifying why a classifier should not be trusted.

figures.title: Explaining individual predictions
figures.caption: Explaining individual predictions. A model predicts that a patient has the flu, and LIME highlights the symptoms in the patient’s history that led to the prediction. Sneeze and headache are portrayed as contributing to the “flu” prediction, whilesneeze “no fatigue” is evidence against it. With these, a doctor can make an informed decision about whether to trust the model’s prediction.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the Texture Networks paper as a breakthrough that enables fast, memory-efficient texture synthesis and image stylization, which powers apps like Prisma. The paper contrasts with Gatys et al.'s earlier approach, which required 10 seconds and 1.1GB of memory per image, while Ulyanov et al.'s method achieves similar quality in just 20ms and 170MB. The key insight is replacing Gatys' iterative optimization with a feed-forward neural network trained per texture/style, enabling real-time generation. Colyer notes the potential for applying this to video processing and praises the broader applicability of feed-forward networks for complex data generation tasks.
paper_title: Texture Networks: Feed-forward synthesis of textures and stylized images
paper_abstract: Gatys et al. recently demonstrated that deep networks can generate beautiful textures and stylized images from a single texture example. However, their methods requires a slow and memoryconsuming optimization process. We propose here an alternative approach that moves the computational burden to a learning stage. Given a single example of a texture, our approach trains compact feed-forward convolutional networks to generate multiple samples of the same texture of arbitrary size and to transfer artistic style from a given image to any other image. The resulting networks are remarkably light-weight and can generate textures of quality comparable to Gatys et al., but hundreds of times faster. More generally, our approach highlights the power and flexibility of generative feed-forward models trained with complex and expressive loss functions.

figures.title: Comparison of texture synthesis methods
figures.caption: Texture networks proposed in this work are feed-forward architectures capable of learning to synthesize complex textures based on a single training example. The perceptual quality of the feed-forwardly generated textures is similar to the results of the closely related method suggested in (Gatys et al., 2015a), which use slow optimization process.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights GraphTau as an innovative solution for processing time-evolving graphs in real-time, addressing a critical gap in existing systems. The paper introduces a framework built on GraphX (Spark's graph processing library) that treats dynamic graphs as a series of consistent snapshots, enabling iterative graph algorithms to run efficiently on evolving data. Colyer emphasizes GraphTau's ability to handle real-time updates, combine graph-structured data with unstructured/tabular data, and support windowed analytics—capabilities lacking in specialized systems. The key insight is the convergence of stream processing and graph processing, with two computational models (pause-shift-resume and online rectification) tailored to different algorithm classes. The blog also praises GraphTau's fault tolerance, scalability, and programming interface, which simplifies complex graph-stream operations.
paper_title: GraphTau: A System for Time-Evolving Graph Processing at Scale
paper_abstract: Time-evolving graph-structured big data arises naturally in many application domains such as social networks and communication networks. However, existing graph processing systems lack support for efficient computations on dynamic graphs. In this paper, we represent most computations on time evolving graphs into (1) a stream of consistent and resilient graph snapshots, and (2) a small set of operators that manipulate such streams of snapshots. We then introduce GraphTau, a time-evolving graph processing framework built on top of Apache Spark, a widely used distributed dataflow system. GraphTau quickly builds fault-tolerant graph snapshots as each small batch of new data arrives. GraphTau achieves high performance and fault tolerant graph stream processing via a number of optimizations. These optimizations range from incremental and differential computation spanning multiple graphs over time to techniques for efficiently allowing fine-grained graph updates using immutable data structures. GraphTau also unifies data streaming and graph streaming processing. Our preliminary evaluations on two representative datasets show promising results. Besides performance benefit, GraphTau API relieves programmers from handling graph snapshot generation, windowing operators and sophisticated differential computation mechanisms.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a significant but simple observation by Howard et al. that revisits quorum intersection in Paxos, a foundational consensus algorithm. The key insight is that Paxos's requirement for majority quorums in both phases is overly conservative; instead, it only needs to ensure intersection between phase one (leader election) and phase two (value agreement) quorums. This relaxation allows for improved fault tolerance and throughput by enabling flexible trade-offs between quorum sizes in different phases. The paper introduces Flexible Paxos (FPaxos), which generalizes quorum requirements and demonstrates practical benefits through majority, simple, and grid quorum systems. Colyer emphasizes the elegance of the idea and its potential to break the traditional trade-off between resilience and performance in consensus systems.
paper_title: Flexible Paxos: Quorum intersection revisited
paper_abstract: Distributed consensus is integral to modern distributed systems. The widely adopted Paxos algorithm uses two phases, each requiring majority agreement, to reliably reach consensus. In this paper, we demonstrate that Paxos, which lies at the foundation of many production systems, is conservative. Specifically, we observe that each of the phases of Paxos may use non-intersecting quorums. Majority quorums are not necessary as intersection is required only across phases. Using this weakening of the requirements made in the original formulation, we propose Flexible Paxos, which generalizes over the Paxos algorithm to provide flexible quorums. We show that Flexible Paxos is safe, efficient and easy to utilize in existing distributed systems. We conclude by discussing the wide reaching implications of this result. Examples include improved availability from reducing the size of second phase quorums by one when the number of acceptors is even and utilizing small disjoint phase-2 quorums to speed up the steady-state.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer introduces the second edition of the 'Research for Practice' series from ACM Queue, focusing on two critical areas: distributed consensus and non-volatile memory (NVM). For distributed consensus, he highlights papers that explore the practical challenges and complexities of implementing consensus systems, including 'Paxos made live,' 'The Chubby lock service,' and 'In search of an understandable consensus algorithm.' Colyer also adds his own picks like 'Viewstamped Replication Revisited,' 'Raft Refloated,' and 'Flexible Paxos,' emphasizing the need for more accessible and understandable consensus algorithms. The second topic, NVM's implications for database management systems (DBMS), is introduced by Joy Arulraj and Andrew Pavlo. They argue that NVM fundamentally changes the traditional memory-storage dichotomy in DBMSs, requiring novel architectures and protocols. The selected papers, such as 'From ARIES to MARS,' 'Let's talk about storage and recovery methods for non-volatile memory database systems,' and 'Write-limited sorts and joins for persistent memory,' explore how existing DBMS designs must adapt to leverage NVM's unique properties, particularly its read/write cost imbalance and limited write endurance.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this SIGMOD 2015 paper as a crucial analysis of how non-volatile memory (NVM) impacts database storage systems and recovery methods. The authors implement three traditional DBMS storage engines (in-place updates, copy-on-write, and log-structured) and evaluate their performance on NVM hardware, then propose NVM-aware variants optimized for NVM's byte-addressability and persistence. The key insight is that traditional DBMS engines, designed for slow block storage, are suboptimal for NVM's low-latency, byte-addressable nature. The NVM-aware engines achieve up to 5.5x higher throughput and reduce write operations by up to 2x compared to their traditional counterparts. The paper demonstrates that rearchitecting storage algorithms to exploit NVM's unique properties can yield significant performance and efficiency gains.
paper_title: Let's talk about storage and recovery methods for non-volatile memory database systems
paper_abstract: The advent of non-volatile memory (NVM) will fundamentally change the dichotomy between memory and durable storage in database management systems (DBMSs). These new NVM devices are almost as fast as DRAM, but all writes to it are potentially persistent even after power loss. Existing DBMSs are unable to take full advantage of this technology because their internal architectures are predicated on the assumption that memory is volatile. With NVM, many of the components of legacy DBMSs are unnecessary and will degrade the performance of data intensive applications. To better understand these issues, we implemented three engines in a modular DBMS testbed that are based on different storage management architectures: (1) in-place updates, (2) copy-on-write updates, and (3) log-structured updates. We then present NVMaware variants of these architectures that leverage the persistence and byte-addressability properties of NVM in their storage and recovery methods. Our experimental evaluation on an NVM hardware emulator shows that these engines achieve up to 5.5× higher throughput than their traditional counterparts while reducing the amount of wear due to write operations by up to 2×. We also demonstrate that our NVM-aware recovery protocols allow these engines to recover almost instantaneously after the DBMS restarts.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a paper that explores optimizing database storage algorithms for Non-Volatile Memory (NVM), focusing on the asymmetry between read and write operations. The key insight is that writes are significantly slower than reads in NVM (e.g., 150ns vs. 10ns), making it crucial to design algorithms that minimize writes to improve performance and reduce wear. The paper introduces write-limited sorting and join algorithms that trade reads for writes, such as segment sort (a hybrid of external mergesort and selection sort) and lazy sorting (which defers writes until the cost of recomputation exceeds the write cost). For joins, the paper proposes partitioned and lazy hash joins that adjust the write intensity based on the read/write ratio of the medium. The evaluation shows that blocked memory, where persistent collections are implemented as linked lists of memory blocks, performs best for these algorithms.
paper_title: Write-limited sorts and joins for persistent memory
paper_abstract: main memory L1 cache To mitigate the impact of the widening gap between the memory needs of CPUs and what standard memory technology can deliver, system architects have introduced a new class of memory technology termed persistent memory. Persistent memory is byteaddressable, but exhibits asymmetric I / O: writes are typically one order of magnitude more expensive than reads. Byte addressability combined with I / O asymmetry render the performance profile of persistent memory unique. Thus, it becomes imperative to find new ways to seamlessly incorporate it into database systems. We do so in the context of query processing. We focus on the fundamental operations of sort and join processing. We introduce the notion of write-limited algorithms that effectively minimize the I / O cost. We give a high-level API that enables the system to dynamically optimize the workflow of the algorithms; or, alternatively, allows the developer to tune the write profile of the algorithms. We present four different techniques to incorporate persistent memory into the database processing stack in light of this API. We have implemented and extensively evaluated all our proposals. Our results show that the algorithms deliver on their promise of I / O-minimality and tunable performance. We showcase the merits and deficiencies of each implementation technique, thus taking a solid first step towards incorporating persistent memory into query processing. 1. 21 LL cache 23 25 27 DRAM persistent memory 29 211 high-performance disk flash 213 215 217 HDD 219 221 223 Figure 1: Typical access latency in processor cycles on a 4GHz processor (figure adapted from [22]) The need for persistent memory is practical. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer introduces Naor & Wool's 1998 paper on quorum systems, highlighting its role as the foundation for the 'fundamental theorem of quorum intersection' referenced in later work like Flexible Paxos. The paper provides theoretical tools for analyzing quorum systems, including definitions, load/capacity/availability metrics, and proofs of optimality. Colyer emphasizes the paper's key insight: the load of a quorum system (minimal load on its busiest element) directly determines its capacity (1/load(S)), forming a critical trade-off with availability. The authors also present novel quorum systems with optimal or near-optimal load and high availability, including the 'Paths' system, which achieves O(1/√n) load and exponential failure resilience. Colyer admires the theoretical rigor but notes the practical complexity of the Paths system's construction.
