blog_summary: The blog post discusses Cyclades, a system designed to speed up machine learning on a single NUMA node by enabling conflict-free asynchronous processing. Unlike other systems that rely on asynchronous processing but may deviate from serial execution, Cyclades guarantees serial equivalence, meaning it produces the same results as a serial implementation. This is achieved through a clever graph partitioning strategy that allocates connected-component subgraphs to different cores, eliminating the need for cross-core coordination. The system works for a wide range of stochastic update-based algorithms, including logistic regression, stochastic gradient descent, and matrix factorization. The core insight is the use of a sampling technique based on a combinatorics result by Krivelevich, which ensures that the conflict graph can be partitioned into small connected components, allowing efficient parallel processing without conflicts. The evaluation shows Cyclades achieves up to 5x speedup over HogWild! and maintains correctness without requiring convergence guarantees for the parallel algorithm.
paper_title: CYCLADES: Conflict-free Asynchronous Machine Learning
paper_abstract: We present C YCLADES, a general framework for parallelizing stochastic optimization algorithms in a shared memory setting. C YCLADES is asynchronous during shared model updates, and requires no memory locking mechanisms, similar to H OGWILD !-type algorithms. Unlike H OGWILD !, C YCLADES introduces no conflicts during the parallel execution, and offers a black-box analysis for provable speedups across a large family of algorithms. Due to its inherent conflict-free nature and cache locality, our multi-core implementation of C YCLADES consistently outperforms H OGWILD !-type algorithms on sufficiently sparse datasets, leading to up to 40% speedup gains compared to the H OGWILD ! implementation of SGD, and up to 5× gains over asynchronous implementations of variance reduction algorithms.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews a paper that explores why deep learning works so well by drawing connections between machine learning and the laws of physics. The authors argue that the success of deep learning stems from fundamental properties of the real world that make many machine learning tasks tractable. They introduce the concept of a 'combinatorial swindle,' where physics allows us to replace exponential complexity with polynomial complexity, making learning feasible even with relatively small neural networks. The paper highlights how Hamiltonians—used in physics to quantify energy—can be approximated efficiently by neural networks, especially when they exhibit sparsity, symmetry, and low-order polynomial forms. The authors also explain why depth in neural networks is beneficial, attributing it to the hierarchical structure of real-world data and processes, which can be modeled as Markov chains. This hierarchical structure further reduces the complexity of learning tasks.

figures.title: Neural networks can approximate probability distributions
figures.caption: Neural networks can approximate probability distributions. Given many samples of random vectors y and x, both classification and prediction involve viewing x as a stochastic function of y and attempting to estimate the probability distributions for y given x and x given y, respectively. In contrast, unsupervised learning attempts to approximate the joint probability distribution of y and x without making any assumptions about causality. In all three cases, the neural network searches for patterns in the data that can be used to better model the probability distribution. A word of caution: we are following the machine learning convention where y refers to the model parameters and x refers to the data, although thinking of y as causing x may suggest the opposite convention.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a key insight from this OSDI 2014 paper: most catastrophic failures in distributed data-intensive systems stem from simple, often trivial mistakes in error handling. The authors analyzed 198 production failures across five systems (Cassandra, HBase, HDFS, MapReduce, Redis) and found that 92% of catastrophic failures (48 total) were caused by incorrect handling of non-fatal errors explicitly signaled in software. Notably, a third of these were due to trivial mistakes like ignoring errors, leaving 'TODO' comments in error handlers, or catching overly broad exceptions. The paper introduces Aspirator, a static checker that could have prevented 33% of catastrophic failures in the studied systems. The blog also emphasizes that most failures are easy to reproduce (77% via unit tests, 98% on ≤3 nodes) and that their triggering events are typically logged (84%), suggesting deterministic replay is feasible.
paper_title: Simple testing can prevent most critical failures: an analysis of production failures in distributed data-intensive systems
paper_abstract: raises the questions of why these systems still experience failures and what can be done to increase their resiliency. To help answer these questions, we studied 198 randomly sampled, user-reported failures of five dataintensive distributed systems that were designed to tolerate component failures and are widely used in production environments. The specific systems we considered were Cassandra, HBase, Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS), Hadoop MapReduce, and Redis. Our goal is to better understand the specific failure manifestation sequences that occurred in these systems in order to identify opportunities for improving their availability and resiliency. Specifically, we want to better understand how one or multiple errors1 evolve into component failures and how some of them eventually evolve into service-wide catastrophic failures. Individual elements of the failure sequence have previously been studied in isolation, including root causes categorizations [33, 52, 50, 56], different types of causes including misconfiguraitons [43, 66, 49], bugs [12, 41, 42, 51] hardware faults [62], and the failure symptoms [33, 56], and many of these studies have made significant impact in that they led to tools capable of identifying many bugs (e.g., [16, 39]). However, the entire manifestation sequence connecting them is far less well-understood. For each failure considered, we carefully studied the failure report, the discussion between users and developers, the logs and the code, and we manually reproduced 73 of the failures to better understand the specific manifestations that occurred. Overall, we found that the error manifestation sequences tend to be relatively complex: more often than not, they require an unusual sequence of multiple events with specific input parameters from a large space to lead the system to a failure. This is perhaps not surprising considering that these systems have undergone thorough testing using unit tests, random error injections [18], and stat...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights DeepDive, a system from Stanford that sits at the intersection of distributed systems, database systems, machine learning, and stream processing. The paper focuses on incremental knowledge base construction (KBC) from semi-structured and unstructured data ("dark data"), aiming to extract high-quality structured data with high precision and recall. DeepDive has been used to build dozens of KBC systems and won competitions. The author emphasizes the system's iterative development process and its incremental techniques for grounding and inference, which improved performance by two orders of magnitude in real scenarios while maintaining high quality. The blog post also provides a detailed overview of the KBC pipeline, including ingestion, extraction, supervised learning, and inference using factor graphs and Gibbs sampling.
paper_title: Incremental Knowledge Base Construction Using DeepDive
paper_abstract: complex relationships. Typically, quality is assessed using two complementary measures: precision (how often a claimed tuple is correct) and recall (of the possible tuples to extract, how many are actually extracted). These systems can ingest massive numbers of documents–far outstripping the document counts of even well-funded human curation efforts. Industrially, KBC systems are constructed by skilled engineers in a months-long (or longer) process–not a oneshot algorithmic task. Arguably, the most important question in such systems is how to best use skilled engineers’ time to rapidly improve data quality. In its full generality, this question spans a number of areas in computer science, including programming languages, systems, and HCI. We focus on a narrower question, with the axiom that the more rapid the programmer moves through the KBC construction loop, the more quickly she obtains high-quality data. This paper presents DeepDive, our open-source engine for knowledge base construction.1 DeepDive’s language and execution model are similar to other KBC systems: DeepDive uses a high-level declarative language [11, 28, 30]. From a database perspective, DeepDive’s language is based on SQL. From a machine learning perspective, DeepDive’s language is based on Markov Logic [13, 30]: DeepDive’s language inherits Markov Logic Networks’ (MLN’s) formal semantics.2 Moreover, it uses a standard execution model for such systems [11, 28, 30] in which programs go through two main phases: grounding, in which one evaluates a sequence of SQL queries to produce a data structure called a factor graph that describes a set of random variables and how they are correlated. Essentially, every tuple in the database or result of a query is a random variable (node) in this factor graph. The inference phase takes the factor graph from grounding and performs statistical inference using standard techniques, e.g., Gibbs sampling [42, 44]. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the groundbreaking work from Google DeepMind on asynchronous methods for deep reinforcement learning, particularly the A3C (Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic) algorithm. The blog post emphasizes the remarkable scalability and performance of A3C, which achieves superlinear speedups in training time (24x with 16 threads) and outperforms prior GPU-based systems like DQN while using only CPUs. The key insight is replacing experience replay—a memory-intensive and computationally expensive technique—with parallel instances of the game, each exploring different parts of the environment using diverse exploration policies. This parallelism not only stabilizes training but also enables on-policy methods like actor-critic, leading to faster convergence and superior results across Atari games, TORCS simulations, physics-based tasks, and 3D maze environments. Colyer praises the elegance of leveraging parallelism to fundamentally rethink the approach to reinforcement learning.
paper_title: Asynchronous Methods for Deep Reinforcement Learning
paper_abstract: We propose a conceptually simple and lightweight framework for deep reinforcement learning that uses asynchronous gradient descent for optimization of deep neural network controllers. We present asynchronous variants of four standard reinforcement learning algorithms and show that parallel actor-learners have a stabilizing effect on training allowing all four methods to successfully train neural network controllers. The best performing method, an asynchronous variant of actor-critic, surpasses the current state-of-the-art on the Atari domain while training for half the time on a single multi-core CPU instead of a GPU. Furthermore, we show that asynchronous actor-critic succeeds on a wide variety of continuous motor control problems as well as on a new task of navigating random 3D mazes using a visual input.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the paper 'Progressive Neural Networks' by Rusu et al. (2016), which introduces a novel neural network architecture designed to enable transfer learning across multiple tasks without catastrophic forgetting. Unlike traditional fine-tuning methods that overwrite prior knowledge, progressive networks maintain a pool of pre-trained models and add new columns (networks) for each new task. These columns are connected laterally to previous columns, allowing the reuse of learned features while avoiding interference with prior knowledge. The author highlights the key benefits of this approach: incorporating prior knowledge at each layer, reusing computations, and immunity to catastrophic forgetting. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of progressive networks through experiments on Atari games, showing improved performance and positive transfer compared to baseline methods, including fine-tuning. However, the approach has limitations, such as the growth in parameters with additional tasks, which the authors suggest could be addressed through pruning or compression techniques.
paper_title: Progressive Neural Networks
paper_abstract: Learning to solve complex sequences of tasks—while both leveraging transfer and avoiding catastrophic forgetting—remains a key obstacle to achieving human-level intelligence. The progressive networks approach represents a step forward in this direction: they are immune to forgetting and can leverage prior knowledge via lateral connections to previously learned features. We evaluate this architecture extensively on a wide variety of reinforcement learning tasks (Atari and 3D maze games), and show that it outperforms common baselines based on pretraining and finetuning. Using a novel sensitivity measure, we demonstrate that transfer occurs at both low-level sensory and high-level control layers of the learned policy.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this paper as a compelling exploration of combining symbolic reasoning with deep learning, particularly in reinforcement learning. He emphasizes the intuitive appeal of learning representations and then performing higher-order reasoning on them, comparing it to how humans learn and form rules. The key insight is that such a hybrid system could be more data-efficient, interpretable, and capable of transfer learning compared to purely neural approaches. The paper proposes a prototype system that outperforms conventional deep reinforcement learning on a stochastic game variant by acquiring human-comprehensible symbolic rules. Colyer notes that this approach could bridge decades of AI research, addressing issues like brittleness, opacity, and the need for large training sets in modern DRL systems.
paper_title: Towards deep symbolic reinforcement learning
paper_abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) brings the power of deep neural networks to bear on the generic task of trial-and-error learning, and its effectiveness has been convincingly demonstrated on tasks such as Atari video games and the game of Go. However, contemporary DRL systems inherit a number of shortcomings from the current generation of deep learning techniques. For example, they require very large datasets to work effectively, entailing that they are slow to learn even when such datasets are available. Moreover, they lack the ability to reason on an abstract level, which makes it difficult to implement high-level cognitive functions such as transfer learning, analogical reasoning, and hypothesis-based reasoning. Finally, their operation is largely opaque to humans, rendering them unsuitable for domains in which verifiability is important. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end reinforcement learning architecture comprising a neural back end and a symbolic front end with the potential to overcome each of these shortcomings. As proof-ofconcept, we present a preliminary implementation of the architecture and apply it to several variants of a simple video game. We show that the resulting system – though just a prototype – learns effectively, and, by acquiring a set of symbolic rules that are easily comprehensible to humans, dramatically outperforms a conventional, fully neural DRL system on a stochastic variant of the game.

figures.title: The proposed reinforcement learning architecture
figures.caption: The proposed reinforcement learning architecture. The neural back end learns to map raw sensor data into a symbolic representation, which is used by the symbolic front end to learn an effective policy.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Dijkstra's classic 1968 paper 'Go to statement considered harmful' as a timeless reminder of the importance of program clarity and understandability. The core argument is that the gap between static program text and dynamic runtime behavior must be minimized to avoid confusion and errors. Dijkstra contends that humans are better at understanding static relationships than dynamic processes, so programs should be structured to make this correspondence as trivial as possible. The paper critiques the unrestricted use of 'goto' statements, which complicate the ability to describe and reason about program execution flow. Dijkstra emphasizes that the program's runtime process is the true subject of the programmer's activity, and that poor program structure can lead to unmanageable complexity. The post underscores the paper's enduring relevance in programming language design and software engineering.
paper_title: Go to statement considered harmful

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Wirth's 1971 paper as a foundational work emphasizing the importance of program design methodology over mere language syntax mastery. The paper introduces the concept of stepwise refinement, demonstrating how to gradually develop a program from a high-level sketch to a concrete implementation by decomposing tasks and data representations in parallel. The author illustrates this with a detailed worked example solving the eight-queens problem, showing how initial brute-force approaches can be systematically refined through backtracking and optimization. Colyer notes the paper's emphasis on deferring design decisions (particularly data representation) until necessary, aligning with Parnas' later principles of information hiding. While acknowledging the paper's use of Algol 60 may feel dated to modern readers, he praises the underlying thinking process as valuable for teaching systematic program development and design decision-making.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews David Parnas' 1971 paper on information distribution in system design, drawing parallels to modern microservices architecture. Parnas argues that inadvertent coupling between modules (or microservices) arises from uncontrolled information sharing, particularly internal implementation details. He emphasizes that exposing such details harms system modularity and maintainability, as programmers inevitably exploit available information, even when it leads to poor design decisions. Parnas advocates for strict control over information distribution, suggesting that only interface specifications (not internal details) should be shared. He also discusses the trade-offs in early system partitioning, noting that time pressures often lead to suboptimal modular boundaries. The paper highlights how early design decisions, especially those based on transient requirements, become harder to change as the system evolves. Parnas' key insight is that information control is critical to preserving system structure and enabling future modifications.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 1972 paper as foundational for introducing hierarchical program structures, with a key insight being that architectural layers should mirror conceptual layers in programming. The paper argues for hierarchical decomposition of complex systems to match human cognitive limits, where higher-level concepts are built upon lower-level ones. Colyer particularly notes the paper's early introduction of class inheritance-like mechanisms ('prefix' mechanism) and the idea of program concatenation as a primitive form of inheritance. The author also emphasizes the paper's discussion of coroutines as a fundamental modeling tool alongside classes, and the concept of building 'pyramids' of abstraction layers to bridge the gap between problem domains and programming languages.
paper_title: Hierarchical program structures
paper_abstract: Object-oriented programming is inextricably bound up with the pioneering work of Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard on the design of the Simula language, which started at the Norwegian Computing Center in the Spring of 1961. However, object orientation, as we think of it today — fifty years later — is the result of a complex interplay of ideas, constraints and people. Dahl and Nygaard would certainly recognize it as their progeny, but might also be amazed at how much it has grown up. This article is based on a lecture given on 22nd August 2011, on the occasion of the scientific opening of the Ole-Johan Dahl Hus at the University of Oslo. It looks at the foundational ideas from Simula that stand behind object-orientation, how those ideas have evolved to become the dominant programming paradigm, and what they have to offer as we approach the challenges of the next fifty years of informatics.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews Morris Jr.'s 1973 paper on protection mechanisms in programming languages, highlighting its foundational ideas on module isolation and security. The paper explores various mechanisms like procedures as objects, local objects, memory protection, type-based protections, seals, trademarks, and access keys to ensure program modules are protected and can be reasoned about independently. Colyer notes that while some ideas (like functions as first-class citizens) are now commonplace, others (such as type tags and seals) offer unique insights into dynamic typing and lightweight authentication. The paper's key insight is the importance of encapsulation and controlled access to objects, with modern parallels in systems like Pony's capability-based security and cryptographic constructs like signatures and encryption keys.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the monumental impact of Barbara Liskov and Stephen Zilles' 1974 paper on abstract data types (ADTs), which laid the foundation for modern object-oriented programming. The blog emphasizes how the paper introduced core OOP concepts like strong typing, generic types, and encapsulation—features that remain central to programming languages today. Colyer notes the paper's foresight in advocating for programming with abstractions, deferring implementation details, and promoting modular design through operation clusters (precursors to classes). The key insight is the power of ADTs to enable 'general-purpose indefinitely-high-level languages' by allowing programmers to extend languages with user-defined abstractions while hiding irrelevant implementation details. The paper also underscores the importance of separating logical and physical program structures, trusting compilers to optimize efficiency without sacrificing design clarity.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Barbara Liskov's 1972 paper as a foundational work on designing reliable software systems. The blog emphasizes that traditional debugging approaches are insufficient for achieving reliability, and instead advocates for a design methodology that tames complexity through modularity and abstraction. Liskov argues that good system design requires dividing the system into hierarchical partitions (modules) based on levels of abstraction, where each partition owns exclusive resources and connections between partitions are strictly controlled. The paper introduces key principles for modularization, such as limiting information flow, encapsulating change-prone areas, and ensuring partitions support a single abstraction. The design process is iterative, involving the identification of abstractions, analysis of their utility, and structured programming to validate the design. The blog underscores Liskov's insight that the design process itself, rather than post-hoc testing, is critical to building reliable systems.
paper_title: A Design Methodology for Reliable Software Systems
paper_abstract: The idea of a data abstraction has had a significant impact on the development of programming languages and on programming methodology. CLU was the first implemented programming language to provide direct linguistic support for data abstraction. This paper provides a history of data abstraction and CLU. CLU contains a number of other interesting and influential features, including its exception handling mechanism, its iterators, and its parameterized types.1

blog_summary: The blog post discusses a paper that analyzes Git's conceptual design, highlighting its usability issues as stemming from deep-rooted problems in its underlying concepts rather than just surface-level command syntax. The authors argue that Git's complexity arises from a lack of conceptual integrity, violating principles like orthogonality, propriety, generality, and consistency. They introduce 'gitless,' a reworked tool based on a simpler conceptual model, to demonstrate how addressing these conceptual flaws can improve usability. The paper builds a concept-relationship diagram for Git, revealing its intricate state and role distinctions (e.g., staged vs. working files), which often lead to confusion. The authors critique Git's staging area, branch-switching conflicts, and other features as violations of good conceptual design, suggesting that a more fundamental rethinking of user-facing concepts is necessary.
paper_title: What's wrong with Git? A conceptual design analysis
paper_abstract: of identifying underlying concepts, and of separating them from their realization in code. Doing so enables conceptual design to be pursued independently of implementation decisions; in short, the most basic form of “what” before “how.” Nevertheless, most research to date has focused narrowly on the question of how to represent concepts – as database semantic models, formal specifications, ontologies, and so on. Much less attention has been paid to the concepts themselves: how they are chosen, and the role they play in design. Sometimes the conceptual basis of a software product is built by analogy to the real world; an online store, for example, has concepts such as “shopping cart,” “item” and “order.” But often the connection to the real world is tenuous and concepts make sense only in the designer’s invented world. Git is an example of this, with concepts such as “tracked file,” “staging area” and “local repository” that have no a priori meaning. The best software designers already know how important it is to discover or invent the right concepts, and that rough edges in these concepts and their relationships will lead to rough edges in the delivered product. Back in 1975, in The Mythical Man Month [13], Fred Brooks described conceptual integrity as “the most important consideration in system design” and twenty years later in the afterword of a new edition [14] wrote “I am more convinced than ever. Conceptual integrity is central to product quality.” Despite this, there have been few attempts to study the design of concepts and their impact in software. It is commonly asserted that the success of a software development project, and the usability of the final product, depend on the quality of the concepts that underlie its design. Yet this hypothesis has not been systematically explored by researchers, and conceptual design has not played the central role in the research and teaching of software engineering that one might expect. As part of a new research project ...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes the OOPSLA '16 paper 'Purposes, concepts, misfits, and a redesign of Git' by De Rosso and Jackson, which critically examines Git's conceptual model and its impact on user confusion. The authors introduce a framework for conceptual design, emphasizing the relationship between a system's purposes (user goals) and its concepts (design elements). They identify operational misfits in Git—scenarios where Git's behavior fails to meet user needs—and analyze 2400 Stack Overflow questions and a small user study (11 participants) to validate their findings. While the authors' analysis of Git's difficulties and their conceptual framework is compelling, Colyer notes that the user study's small sample size limits quantitative conclusions. The paper also highlights a polarization in reactions: experts defend Git's complexity, while casual users find it frustratingly opaque. The authors propose a redesign based on a simpler conceptual model but acknowledge that rigorous evidence of its superiority remains lacking.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights AttackTagger, a factor-graph-based framework for preemptive intrusion detection that identifies malicious users before system misuse occurs. The paper's key insight is reasoning about attack stages collectively rather than per-event, leveraging factor graphs to model dependencies between user states, events, and profiles. The author praises the approach for its early detection capabilities (74% of attacks detected before misuse) and its ability to uncover previously unknown malicious users. The use of Gibbs sampling for real-time inference and the simplicity of factor graphs over other graphical models are also noted as noteworthy contributions.
paper_title: Preemptive Intrusion Detection: Theoretical Framework and Real-World Measurements
paper_abstract: This paper presents a Factor Graph based framework called AttackTagger for highly accurate and preemptive detection of attacks, i.e., before the system misuse. We use security logs on real incidents that occurred over a six-year period at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) to evaluate AttackTagger. Our data consist of security incidents that led to compromise of the target system, i.e., the attacks in the incidents were only identified after the fact by security analysts. AttackTagger detected 74 percent of attacks, and the majority them were detected before the system misuse. Finally, AttackTagger uncovered six hidden attacks that were not detected by intrusion detection systems during the incidents or by security analysts in post-incident forensic analysis.

blog_summary: Replex, a best paper award winner at USENIX 2016, tackles the challenge of building scalable, highly available key-value stores that also support efficient queries by non-primary keys. Traditional NoSQL databases scale by partitioning data based on a single primary key, but this makes secondary index queries inefficient as they require querying all partitions. Maintaining secondary indices with distributed transactions for data integrity further degrades performance. Replex innovates by combining replicas and indices into 'replexes'—each replex serves as both a replica and an index, sorted differently. This dual role reduces overhead, as secondary indices come at minimal cost. The paper introduces a novel replication scheme using chain replication to ensure consistency across replexes, where operations are validated by consensus before replication. Hybrid replexes further optimize recovery and query performance under failures by sharing failure tolerance across multiple replexes, reducing storage and network overhead. Experimental results show Replex outperforms state-of-the-art systems like HyperDex and Cassandra by up to 10×.
paper_title: Replex: A scalable, highly available multi-index data store
paper_abstract: made scaling NoSQL datastores easy: by using the key to divide the data into partitions or “shards”, the datastore could be efﬁciently mapped onto multiple nodes. Unfortunately, this model is inconvenient for programmers, who often still need to query data by a value other than the primary key. The need for scalable, high-performance datastores has led to the development of NoSQL databases, which achieve scalability by partitioning data over a single key. However, programmers often need to query data with other keys, which data stores provide by either querying every partition, eliminating the beneﬁts of partitioning, or replicating additional indexes, wasting the beneﬁts of data replication. In this paper, we show there is no need to compromise scalability for functionality. We present Replex, a datastore that enables efﬁcient querying on multiple keys by rethinking data placement during replication. Traditionally, a data store is ﬁrst globally partitioned, then each partition is replicated identically to multiple nodes. Instead, Replex relies on a novel replication unit, termed replex, which partitions a full copy of the data based on its unique key. Replexes eliminate any additional overhead to maintaining indices, at the cost of increasing recovery complexity. To address this issue, we also introduce hybrid replexes, which enable a rich design space for trading off steady-state performance with faster recovery. We build, parameterize, and evaluate Replex on multiple dimensions and ﬁnd that Replex surpasses the steady-state and failure recovery performance of HyperDex, a state-of-the-art multi-key data store. 1 Several NoSQL datastores[1, 3, 14, 9, 15, 7] have emerged that can support queries on multiple keys through the use of secondary indexes. Many of these datastores simply query all partitions to search for an entry which matches a secondary key. In this approach, performance quickly degrades as the number of partitions increases, defeating the reason for pa...

blog_summary: The blog post highlights a Bayesian approach to graphical record linkage and de-duplication, addressing the challenge of matching records across multiple datasets without unique identifiers. Adrian Colyer emphasizes the paper's value in solving a high-impact problem, particularly in privacy-preserving data integration where datasets may lack common keys or have distorted fields. The author notes the paper's elegance in introducing a flexible linkage structure that can work with various models, demonstrating its potential even with a simple Bayesian model. The core insight is the use of a hybrid MCMC algorithm (SMERED) to efficiently explore linkage structures, handling noise and distortions in data while preserving transitivity in record matching. The method's ability to link records based on probabilistic fields (e.g., gender, birth year) and its application to real-world datasets like NLTCS are also highlighted.
paper_title: A Bayesian approach to graphical record linkage and de-duplication
paper_abstract: We propose an unsupervised approach for linking records across arbitrarily many files, while simultaneously detecting duplicate records within files. Our key innovation involves the representation of the pattern of links between records as a bipartite graph, in which records are directly linked to latent true individuals, and only indirectly linked to other records. This flexible representation of the linkage structure naturally allows us to estimate the attributes of the unique observable people in the population, calculate transitive linkage probabilities across records (and represent this visually), and propagate the uncertainty of record linkage into later analyses. Our method makes it particularly easy to integrate record linkage with post-processing procedures such as logistic regression, capture-recapture, etc. Our linkage structure lends itself to an efficient, linear-time, hybrid Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm, which overcomes many obstacles encountered by previously record linkage approaches, despite the high-dimensional parameter space. We illustrate our method using longitudinal data from the National Long Term Care Survey and with data from the Italian Survey on Household and Wealth, where we assess the accuracy of our method and show it to be better in terms of error rates and empirical scalability than other approaches in the literature.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Parnas' 1979 paper as a seminal work on designing software systems for extensibility and maintainability. The blog emphasizes the importance of conscious design decisions regarding flexibility and generality, noting that poor structuring often leads to situations where minimal changes require extensive rewrites or prevent early releases. Colyer underscores Parnas' key insights: the dangers of excessive information distribution, chain-like component structures, and combining multiple functions into single components. The post also praises Parnas' four-step approach to better system design, including identifying minimal subsets, using information hiding, designing software machine extensions, and carefully structuring the 'uses' hierarchy to avoid cycles and interdependencies. The discussion ties modern system design challenges to Parnas' timeless principles, making it highly relevant for contemporary software engineers.

blog_summary: The blog post highlights MemC3, a system that improves Memcached through two key innovations: an optimized cuckoo hashing algorithm (optimistic cuckoo hashing) and a CLOCK-based eviction policy. The author emphasizes the elegance of the hashing scheme, which introduces tags to reduce key comparisons and enable efficient concurrent access with minimal overhead. The paper demonstrates significant performance gains—up to 30% memory reduction and 3x higher queries per second—on read-heavy workloads with small objects, typical of Facebook's use case. The evaluation section is praised for its thorough breakdown of contributions, though the blog focuses more on the algorithmic insights. The concurrent access support is particularly noteworthy, as it achieves high space efficiency (>90% occupancy) while enabling multi-reader, single-writer operations through clever use of version counters and shared locks.
paper_title: MemC3: Compact and Concurrent MemCache with Dumber Caching and Smarter Hashing
paper_abstract: Standard Memcached, at its core, uses a typical hash table design, with linked-list-based chaining to handle collisions. Its cache replacement algorithm is strict LRU, also based on linked lists. This design relies on locking to ensure consistency among multiple threads, and leads to poor scalability on multi-core CPUs [11]. This paper presents MemC3 (Memcached with CLOCK and Concurrent Cuckoo Hashing), a complete redesign of the Memcached internals. This re-design is informed by and takes advantage of several observations. First, architectural features can hide memory access latencies and provide performance improvements. In particular, our new hash table design exploits CPU cache locality to minimize the number of memory fetches required to complete any given operation; and it exploits instruction-level and memory-level parallelism to overlap those fetches when they cannot be avoided. Second, MemC3’s design also leverages workload characteristics. Many Memcached workloads are predominately reads, with few writes. This observation means that we can replace Memcached’s exclusive, global locking with an optimistic locking scheme targeted at the common case. Furthermore, many important Memcached workloads target very small objects, so per-object overheads have a significant impact on memory efficiency. For example, Memcached’s strict LRU cache replacement requires significant metadata—often more space than the object itself occupies; in MemC3, we instead use a compact CLOCK-based approximation. The specific contributions of this paper include: This paper presents a set of architecturally and workloadinspired algorithmic and engineering improvements to the popular Memcached system that substantially improve both its memory efficiency and throughput. These techniques—optimistic cuckoo hashing, a compact LRU-approximating eviction algorithm based upon CLOCK, and comprehensive implementation of optimistic locking—enable the resulting system to use 30% less memory for smal...

blog_summary: The blog post discusses a paper from EuroSys 2014 that extends optimistic cuckoo hashing to support multiple writers and achieve higher throughput. The authors initially aimed to leverage Intel Haswell's hardware transactional memory (HTM), but found that algorithmic and data structure optimizations were more impactful. The paper introduces a design that minimizes critical sections, reduces cuckoo path lengths via breadth-first search, increases set-associativity, and employs fine-grained locking. The result is a hash table achieving ~40M inserts/second on a 16-core machine, outperforming Intel's Thread Building Blocks by 2.5x while using less memory. The author highlights the paper's focus on algorithmic engineering over hardware-specific optimizations, emphasizing the importance of good concurrent design principles.
paper_title: Algorithmic improvements for fast concurrent cuckoo hashing
paper_abstract: —Cuckoo hashing is widely used for its worst-case constant lookup performance even at very high load. However at high load, collision resolution will involve lots of probes on item relocation and may still fail in the end. To address the problem, we propose an efficient Cuckoo hashing scheme called Multi-copy Cuckoo or McCuckoo. Different from the blind kick-outs of standard Cuckoo hashing during a collision, we can foresee which way to successfully kick items by using multiple copies. Furthermore, with the knowledge of how many copies each item has in the table, we can identify impossible buckets and skip them during a lookup. In order to avoid expensive rehashing during insertion failures, McCuckoo also supports more efficient stash strategy that minimizes stash checking. McCuckoo uses simple logic and simple data structure, so it is suitable for both software and hardware implementation on platforms where intensive access to the slow and bandwidth limited off-chip external memory is the main bottleneck. Keywords—Cuckoo Hashing, Hashing algorithm, Multi-copy I. INTRODUCTION Hash tables [1] are basic data structures that are widely used in various fields such as database, networking, storage, security, etc. When working at low load, hash collisions rarely happen; but when load increases, collisions will happen frequently. Traditional solutions such as chaining methods and linear probing [2] need extra time and resource to resolve the collisions, affecting both insertion and lookup and losing the favorable performance bound. Unlike traditional hash structures that only provide one candidate location for each item, Cuckoo hashing [3] uses d hash functions to provide multiple candidate buckets for each item to choose so as to reduce collision. Most importantly, existing items can be “kicked out” and relocated to another candidate bucket if necessary to make room in search of an overall arrangement for all items to settle down in their own buckets. This flexibility pro...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 2015 VLDB paper from the Databricks team, which examines the transition of Apache Spark from a research project to a widely-adopted commercial system. The paper focuses on three key challenges: improving the programming model's usability, enhancing performance and scalability, and increasing runtime visibility for troubleshooting. The authors found the original functional API difficult for non-developers and even experienced users, leading to inefficiencies like the groupByKey vs. reduceByKey performance pitfall. They addressed this by introducing higher-level APIs (like DataFrames) that compile to optimized relational plans, achieving 2-5x speedups through runtime code generation and algebraic optimizations. The paper also details memory management improvements to handle compressed datasets and large clusters, networking optimizations using Netty, and a new Tungsten project for runtime code generation. Finally, it discusses the importance of runtime visibility tools to debug distributed programs, noting that performance issues often stem from data skew or memory inefficiencies.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the importance of formal methods in security analysis, demonstrating their value through a comprehensive formal security analysis of OAuth 2.0 by Fett et al. The paper presents the first extensive formal model of OAuth 2.0 in a web context, identifying four previously unknown vulnerabilities in the widely deployed protocol. These vulnerabilities—307 redirect attack, IdP mix-up attack, state leak attack, and naïve RP session integrity attack—were confirmed by the OAuth and OpenID Connect working groups, who also adopted fixes for at least one of the attacks. The authors propose simple fixes and prove that, with these alterations, OAuth can provide strong guarantees for authorization, authentication, and session integrity. The blog post emphasizes the rigor of the approach, built on the FKS web model and Dolev-Yao style formalism, and notes the practical implications of the findings for real-world OAuth deployments.
paper_title: Comprehensive Formal Security Analysis of OAuth 2.0

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Bertrand Meyer's 1985 paper as a classic defense of formal specification in software engineering. The post emphasizes that while natural language is ideal for broad communication, software specifications require rigorous formalism to avoid ambiguities and uncover hidden issues. Meyer argues that formal specifications not only improve the clarity of natural language descriptions but also help identify questions and ambiguities that informal approaches might miss. The paper uses a toy problem (originally from Naur, later critiqued by Goodenough and Gerhart) to illustrate the 'seven sins' of informal specifications—noise, remorse, silence, contradiction, overspecification, ambiguity, forward references, and wishful thinking—showing how formal methods can mitigate these pitfalls. Colyer praises Meyer's structured approach and the balance between formal and informal specifications, noting that the latter remains essential for readability and stakeholder comprehension.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a concerning side-channel attack where smartphones can be used to reconstruct objects being fabricated on factory floors, including CNC mills and 3D printers. The attack leverages phone sensors (audio and magnetometer) to capture machine sounds and movements, enabling the reconstruction of high-value intellectual property (IP) such as product designs. The paper demonstrates that even a simple phone call to an employee near the machine can facilitate the attack. The authors use signal processing and machine learning to analyze audio signatures, comparing them against a pre-recorded reference library of machine sounds at different angles. Domain constraints (e.g., layer-by-layer printing in 3D printers) and human assistance help refine the reconstruction. The study shows that even complex shapes (e.g., airplanes, stars, guns) can be reconstructed with reasonable accuracy, underscoring the vulnerability of manufacturing processes to espionage.
paper_title: Leave your phone at the door: side channels that reveal factory floor secrets
paper_abstract: Keystroke privacy is critical on mobile devices, as typed content often includes passwords and sensitive personal data. This paper revisits cross-app keystroke inference and shows that software sandboxing cannot prevent keystroke leakage at the physical layer because co-resident apps inevitably share the same hardware. Our insight is twofold. (1) Keystroke-induced vibrations propagate through the touchscreen and internal components and are captured by zeropermission motion sensors, preserving spatial traits tied to key positions. (2) Typing habits enable cross-app generalization, as users typically rely on the same virtual keyboard layout across apps, causing identical letters to yield similar vibration patterns. Based on these properties, we propose CaMi, a practical cross-app keystroke inference attack. CaMi learns letter-level vibration signatures using labeled samples in any commonly used app and then covertly collects motion sensor data to infer keystrokes typed in a target app. We implement CaMi on smartphones and tablets, and extensive experiments show high inference accuracy across devices. We also discuss potential software-level defenses.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights WindTalker, a novel side-channel attack that exploits channel state information (CSI) from WiFi signals to infer mobile phone passwords. The attack leverages the unique interference in multi-path signals caused by finger motions during PIN entry, enabling password recovery without physical access to the victim's device. Colyer notes the ingenuity of the approach while expressing concern about the broader implications for security, given that the attack piggybacks on existing WiFi connections and requires minimal victim interaction. The paper demonstrates how CSI data, combined with signal processing techniques like PCA and DTW, can effectively extract and classify keystroke patterns, achieving high recovery rates even with minimal training data. The case study on Alipay PINs underscores the practical feasibility of the attack in real-world scenarios.
paper_title: WindTalker: Inferring Your Mobile Phone Password via WiFi Signals
paper_abstract: 1. In this study, we present WindTalker, a novel and practical keystroke inference framework that allows an attacker to infer the sensitive keystrokes on a mobile device through WiFi-based side-channel information. WindTalker is motivated from the observation that keystrokes on mobile devices will lead to diﬀerent hand coverage and the ﬁnger motions, which will introduce a unique interference to the multi-path signals and can be reﬂected by the channel state information (CSI). The adversary can exploit the strong correlation between the CSI ﬂuctuation and the keystrokes to infer the user’s number input. WindTalker presents a novel approach to collect the target’s CSI data by deploying a public WiFi hotspot. Compared with the previous keystroke inference approach, WindTalker neither deploys external devices close to the target device nor compromises the target device. Instead, it utilizes the public WiFi to collect user’s CSI data, which is easy-to-deploy and diﬃcult-to-detect. In addition, it jointly analyzes the traﬃc and the CSI to launch the keystroke inference only for the sensitive period where password entering occurs. WindTalker can be launched without the requirement of visually seeing the smart phone user’s input process, backside motion, or installing any malware on the tablet. We implemented Windtalker on several mobile phones and performed a detailed case study to evaluate the practicality of the password inference towards Alipay, the largest mobile payment platform in the world. The evaluation results show that the attacker can recover the key with a high successful rate. Smartphones and tablets are commonly used for performing privacy sensitive transactions of banking, payment, and social applications. Unlike stationary devices connecting to a secure network and sitting in a physically-secure space, these mobile devices are often carried by a mobile user and connected to a dynamic network environment where attackers can physically approach the target u...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a novel and dangerous attack on the Control Area Network (CAN) protocol used in modern vehicles, called the 'bus-off attack'. Unlike prior attacks, this method doesn't require reverse engineering vehicle-specific CAN messages, works universally across all vehicles, and bypasses MAC-based protections and state-of-the-art intrusion detection systems (IDS). The attack exploits CAN's built-in error-handling mechanisms, particularly the transmit error counter (TEC), to force a targeted ECU into a 'bus-off' state where it is permanently disabled. The author emphasizes the attack's ease of deployment, its potential safety implications for drivers, and the urgency to develop countermeasures, noting that even future security-enhanced in-vehicle networks may remain vulnerable. The paper argues for concerted efforts from academia and industry to address this flaw.
paper_title: Stealing Cars: Secure CAN Message Specification using CAN Message Reverse Engineering
paper_abstract: 1 Modern Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) are equipped with an increasing number of Electronic Control Units (ECUs), many of which produce large amounts of data. Data is exchanged between ECUs via an in-vehicle network, with the Controller Area Network (CAN) bus being the de facto standard in contemporary vehicles. Furthermore, CAVs have not only physical interfaces but also increased data connectivity to the Internet via their Telematic Control Units (TCUs), enabling remote access via mobile devices. It is also possible to tap into, and read/write data from/to the CAN bus, as data transmitted on the CAN bus is not encrypted. This naturally generates concerns about automotive cybersecurity. One commonality among most vehicular security attacks reported to date is that they ultimately require write access to the CAN bus. In order to cause targeted and intentional changes in vehicle behavior, malicious CAN injection attacks require knowledge of the CAN message format. However, since this format is proprietary to OEMs and can differ even among different models of a single make of vehicle, one must manually reverse-engineer the CAN message format of each vehicle they target — a time-consuming and tedious process that does not scale. To mitigate this difficulty, we develop LibreCAN, which can translate most CAN messages with minimal effort. Our extensive evaluation on multiple vehicles demonstrates LibreCAN’s efficiency in terms of accuracy, coverage, required manual effort and scalability to any vehicle. Nearly all functions inside a modern vehicle, even in more traditionally mechanical domains like the powertrain, are controlled electronically. Moreover, purely electronic systems have become more prevalent as the number of sensors present in a vehicle has increased, particularly given the rise of Advanced Driver Assistance (ADAS) systems. All of these systems are controlled by Electronic Control Units (ECUs), embedded microprocessors that interface between a gi...

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the paper 'Acing the IOC game: toward automatic discovery and analysis of open-source cyber threat intelligence' by Liao et al., presented at CCS 2016. The author, Adrian Colyer, highlights iACE, a system that automatically extracts Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) from security blogs and converts them into OpenIOC schema-based reports for use in detection and prevention systems. The paper is notable for its practical approach to cyber threat intelligence (CTI), demonstrating how semi-structured information in blog posts can be systematically analyzed to extract actionable security data. The authors analyzed over 71,000 articles, extracting over 900K IOCs, and derived new insights into attacks over the last 13 years. The blog emphasizes the scalability challenges in CTI and the novel end-to-end pipeline of iACE, which integrates existing tools and techniques to efficiently process and extract IOCs with high precision.
paper_title: Acing the IOC game: toward automatic discovery and analysis of open-source cyber threat intelligence
paper_abstract: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) is being used to search for indicators of attacks that might have compromised an enterprise network for a long time without being discovered. To have a more effective analysis, CTI open standards have incorporated descriptive relationships showing how the indicators or observables are related to each other. However, these relationships are either completely overlooked in information gathering or not used for threat hunting. In this paper, we propose a system, called Poirot, which uses these correlations to uncover the steps of a successful attack campaign. We use kernel audits as a reliable source that covers all causal relations and information flows among system entities and model threat hunting as an inexact graph pattern matching problem. Our technical approach is based on a novel similarity metric which assesses an alignment between a query graph constructed out of CTI correlations and a provenance graph constructed out of kernel audit log records. We evaluate Poirot on publicly released real-world incident reports as well as reports of an adversarial engagement designed by DARPA, including ten distinct attack campaigns against different OS platforms such as Linux, FreeBSD, and Windows. Our evaluation results show that Poirot is capable of searching inside graphs containing millions of nodes and pinpoint the attacks in a few minutes, and the results serve to illustrate that CTI correlations could be used as robust and reliable artifacts for threat hunting.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this paper as an insightful analysis of BoPETs (Build-On-Property-revealing-EncrypTion) systems, which aim to enable cloud services to operate on encrypted data while preserving privacy. The paper critiques the current state of BoPETs, using the Mylar system (built on Meteor.js) as a case study to demonstrate both their potential and limitations. Key takeaways include the dangers of assuming security against snapshot passive adversaries when deploying systems against active adversaries, the exposure of metadata even in seemingly secure systems, and the need for realistic threat models and formal cryptographic definitions. The paper also provides practical lessons from porting real-world applications to BoPETs, revealing the subtle and critical decisions required in access control and encryption strategies. The authors emphasize that security proofs must be carefully contextualized, as real-world deployments often violate implicit assumptions.
paper_title: Breaking Web Applications Built on Top of Encrypted Data
paper_abstract: We develop a systematic approach for analyzing client-server applications that aim to hide sensitive user data from untrusted servers. We then apply it to Mylar, a framework that uses multi-key searchable encryption (MKSE) to build Web applications on top of encrypted data. We demonstrate that (1) the Popa-Zeldovich model for MKSE does not imply security against either passive or active attacks; (2) Mylar-based Web applications reveal users’ data and queries to passive and active adversarial servers; and (3) Mylar is generically insecure against active attacks due to system design flaws. Our results show that the problem of securing client-server applications against actively malicious servers is challenging and still unsolved. We conclude with general lessons for the designers of systems that rely on property-preserving or searchable encryption to protect data from untrusted servers.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a groundbreaking paper that establishes fundamental limits on what can be achieved with encrypted databases in the cloud. The authors examine what data can be recovered by observing encrypted queries and their responses, focusing on 'access leakage' (which records are accessed) and 'volume leakage' (how much data is returned). They demonstrate reconstruction attacks that can recover secret attributes of every database record if either type of leakage occurs—a condition that applies to every known outsourced database system. The attacks operate under a weak adversarial model, requiring only the ability to observe queries over time without prior knowledge of the data or queries. While the attacks may require observing a large number of queries for high-entropy data (e.g., social security numbers), they are feasible for lower-entropy attributes like those in medical datasets. The paper argues that secure outsourced databases must avoid static, non-storage-inflating designs and fixed communication overhead to mitigate these vulnerabilities.
paper_title: Generic Attacks on Secure Outsourced Databases
paper_abstract: With the rise of remote cloud services and the consequent rise in data breaches, there is an increased need for the secure outsourcing of data. The problem of enabling query processing over encrypted data without decryption is a challenging one, and approaches ranging from software to hardware solutions have been proposed. In this work, we take a closer look at a class of solutions that are efficient and deployable in the near-term future and that employ the use of light weight symmetric key primitives. In exchange for this added efficiency, these schemes leak certain information about the underlying data and queries. We explore the limitations of what a passive server-side adversary can learn from this information leakage, and present practical constructions that minimize leakage while supporting complex queries. In the first two parts of this work, we present the first attacks on schemes that support range queries over multi-attribute (or multi-dimensional) data. We describe the information theoretic limitation of reconstruction attacks in two settings and show that, in both cases, there can be an exponential number of distinct databases that produce equivalent leakage. We present a full database reconstruction attack that reconstructs the database when all queries are observed. We then relax these assumptions, and present an order reconstruction attack and an approximate database reconstruction attack that require only a strict subset of the possible range queries to succeed. In the third part of this work, we shift our focus to schemes that support shortest path queries on graph-structured data. We initiate our study by describing a query recovery attack on a graph encryption scheme, which we call the GKT scheme (Ghosh et al. AsiaCCS 2021). We then present a modified version of the GKT scheme with reduced leakage at the expensive of interactive queries and increased storage overhead. Our proposed scheme uses data-structure techniques to decompose the graph into ...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a critical but often overlooked issue in software security: vulnerabilities introduced when migrating 32-bit codebases to 64-bit platforms. The paper by Wressnegger et al. demonstrates that code secure on 32-bit systems can become vulnerable on 64-bit systems due to subtle changes in integer handling. The authors conduct a thorough empirical analysis of 200 GitHub projects and Debian packages, revealing widespread integer truncations and signedness issues—many of which are not inherently vulnerabilities but indicate developer unawareness of 64-bit migration pitfalls. Notably, they also uncover real vulnerabilities in high-profile projects like Google’s Chromium, the GNU C Library, the Linux Kernel, and Boost C++ Libraries. The key insight is that 64-bit migration introduces new truncations, overflows, and signedness issues that are platform-dependent and often hard to detect, making this a widespread and technically challenging problem for developers and auditors.
paper_title: Twice the bits, twice the trouble: vulnerabilities induced by migrating to 64-bit platforms
paper_abstract: Protecting Smart Devices from the Bottom-up by Aravind K Machiry Modern systems are mainly composed of IoT devices and Smartphones. Most of these devices use ARM processors, which, along with flexible licensing, have new security architecture features, such as ARM TrustZone, that enables execution of a secure application in an untrusted environment. Furthermore, with well-supported, extensible, open-source embedded operating systems like Android allows the manufactures to quickly customize their operating system with device drivers, thus reducing the time-to-market. Unfortunately, the proliferation of device vendors and race to the market has resulted in poor quality device drivers containing critical security vulnerabilities. Furthermore, the patches for these vulnerabilities get merged into the end-products with a significant delay resulting in the Patch Gap, which causes privacy and security of billions of users to be at risk. In this dissertation, I will show how the new architecture features can lead to security issues by introducing new attack vectors. Second, I will show that the existing techniques are inadequate to find the security issues in Linux kernel drivers and how, with certain well-defined optimizations, we can precisely find security issues. Third, I will present my solution to the problem of Patch Gap by showing a principled approach to automatically port patches to vendor product repositories. Finally, I will present our on-going work to automatically port C to Checked C, which provides a low overhead, backward-compatible, and memory-safe C alternative that could be used on resource-constrained modern systems to prevent security vulnerabilities. ix Through this work, I presented effective ways to find, fix, propagate, and prevent vulnerabilities in modern system software, thus improving modern systems security. x Contents Curriculum Vitae vi Abstract ix

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the HoneyBadgerBFT paper as a groundbreaking work in Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) protocols, particularly in the context of cryptocurrencies and blockchain systems. The paper addresses the limitations of traditional BFT systems, which rely on weak synchrony assumptions (e.g., timeouts) that can fail under adversarial network conditions. HoneyBadgerBFT is presented as the first BFT atomic broadcast protocol to achieve optimal asymptotic efficiency in asynchronous settings, refuting the notion that such protocols are impractical. The author emphasizes its relevance to blockchain applications, where robustness and censorship resistance are critical, even at the expense of performance. The paper also introduces clever batching strategies and threshold encryption to improve throughput and fairness, making it a significant contribution to both distributed systems theory and real-world cryptocurrency deployments.
paper_title: The Honey Badger of BFT Protocols
paper_abstract: The surprising success of cryptocurrencies has led to a surge of interest in deploying large scale, highly robust, Byzantine fault tolerant (BFT) protocols for mission-critical applications, such as financial transactions. Although the conventional wisdom is to build atop a (weakly) synchronous protocol such as PBFT (or a variation thereof), such protocols rely critically on network timing assumptions, and only guarantee liveness when the network behaves as expected. We argue these protocols are ill-suited for this deployment scenario. We present an alternative, HoneyBadgerBFT, the first practical asynchronous BFT protocol, which guarantees liveness without making any timing assumptions. We base our solution on a novel atomic broadcast protocol that achieves optimal asymptotic efficiency. We present an implementation and experimental results to show our system can achieve throughput of tens of thousands of transactions per second, and scales to over a hundred nodes on a wide area network. We even conduct BFT experiments over Tor, without needing to tune any parameters. Unlike the alternatives, HoneyBadgerBFT simply does not care about the underlying network.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the Stanford University One Hundred Year Study of Artificial Intelligence (AI100) report, which assesses AI's current state and projected societal impact by 2030. The report, while not a technical research paper, provides a broad, accessible overview of AI trends and applications across domains like transportation, healthcare, and education. Colyer highlights the report's balanced perspective, noting that while AI will drive significant societal and economic changes, it is unlikely to pose an imminent existential threat. He also points out the report's focus on practical advancements rather than visionary breakthroughs, emphasizing that societal impact often lags behind technological innovation. Key areas of AI research discussed include large-scale machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, robotics, computer vision, and natural language processing. The report also explores emerging topics like algorithmic game theory, neuromorphic computing, and human-aware systems, suggesting a future where AI systems are designed to better understand and interact with humans.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a groundbreaking achievement in the paper: for the first time, a system has surpassed human performance in conversational telephone speech recognition (CTS), a notoriously difficult task due to spontaneous, informal speech with disfluencies. The Microsoft team measured human error rates (5.9% for Switchboard and 11.3% for CallHome datasets) using their internal transcription pipeline and matched these rates with their ASR system. The key insight is the systematic combination of LSTMs for acoustic and language modeling, CNNs for acoustic modeling, and advanced techniques like speaker-adaptive modeling (i-vectors), lattice-free MMI training, and model fusion (ResNet + VGG). The paper also demonstrates significant engineering optimizations, including parallelized training with 1-bit SGD in Microsoft's CNTK toolkit, reducing training time from months to weeks. Colyer emphasizes the rapid assembly of powerful AI building blocks into effective systems, foreshadowing broader applications of deep learning in speech recognition and beyond.
paper_title: Achieving Human Parity in Conversational Speech Recognition
paper_abstract: Conversational speech recognition has served as a flagship speech recognition task since the release of the Switchboard corpus in the 1990s. In this paper, we measure the human error rate on the widely used NIST 2000 test set, and find that our latest automated system has reached human parity. The error rate of professional transcribers is 5.9% for the Switchboard portion of the data, in which newly acquainted pairs of people discuss an assigned topic, and 11.3% for the CallHome portion where friends and family members have open-ended conversations. In both cases, our automated system establishes a new state of the art, and edges past the human benchmark, achieving error rates of 5.8% and 11.0%, respectively. The key to our system’s performance is the use of various convolutional and LSTM acoustic model architectures, combined with a novel spatial smoothing method and lattice-free MMI acoustic training, multiple recurrent neural network language modeling approaches, and a systematic use of system combination.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this paper as a significant step toward AI agents playing complex 3D first-person shooter (FPS) games, which are far more challenging than traditional Atari-style games due to partial observability, navigation, and combat tasks. The authors, Lample and Chaplot, develop an AI agent for deathmatch scenarios in the VizDoom environment using a Deep Recurrent Q-Network (DRQN) architecture. They address the limitations of a single DRQN by splitting the task into two modular networks: one for navigation (handling movement in the environment) and another for action (combat and item collection). This modular approach improves training efficiency and mitigates issues like 'camper behavior' seen in single-network models. The paper also introduces a novel training augmentation by providing additional binary game feature indicators (e.g., enemy presence) during training, which boosts enemy detection accuracy to 90% and enables the agent to outperform built-in bots and even human players in certain scenarios. The key insight is the combination of modular neural networks and game feature augmentation to handle the complexity of FPS environments.
paper_title: Playing FPS Games with Deep Reinforcement Learning
paper_abstract: Advances in deep reinforcement learning have allowed autonomous agents to perform well on Atari games, often outperforming humans, using only raw pixels to make their decisions. However, most of these games take place in 2D environments that are fully observable to the agent. In this paper, we present the first architecture to tackle 3D environments in first-person shooter games, that involve partially observable states. Typically, deep reinforcement learning methods only utilize visual input for training. We present a method to augment these models to exploit game feature information such as the presence of enemies or items, during the training phase. Our model is trained to simultaneously learn these features along with minimizing a Q-learning objective, which is shown to dramatically improve the training speed and performance of our agent. Our architecture is also modularized to allow different models to be independently trained for different phases of the game. We show that the proposed architecture substantially outperforms built-in AI agents of the game as well as average humans in deathmatch scenarios.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Google's Smart Reply system for email, which generates automated response suggestions used in 10% of mobile replies. The paper illustrates the gap between research and production-scale machine learning systems, emphasizing the practical challenges of deploying such a system. Key concerns include ensuring high-quality responses, maintaining diversity in suggestions, meeting latency constraints, and protecting user privacy by avoiding raw data inspection. The system processes emails through preprocessing, smart triggering (to filter unsuitable messages), and a sequence-to-sequence LSTM model to generate response candidates. A trie-based beam search efficiently ranks responses, while a diversity component ensures varied suggestions. The blog praises the paper for its transparency about real-world deployment challenges and solutions.
paper_title: Smart Reply: Automated response suggestion for email
paper_abstract: In this paper we propose and investigate a novel end-to-end method for automatically generating short email responses, called Smart Reply. It generates semantically diverse suggestions that can be used as complete email responses with just one tap on mobile. The system is currently used in Inbox by Gmail and is responsible for assisting with 10% of all mobile responses. It is designed to work at very high throughput and process hundreds of millions of messages daily. The system exploits state-of-the-art, large-scale deep learning. We describe the architecture of the system as well as the challenges that we faced while building it, like response diversity and scalability. We also introduce a new method for semantic clustering of user-generated content that requires only a modest amount of explicitly labeled data. An initial study covering several million email-reply pairs showed that ∼25% of replies have 20 tokens or less. Thus we raised the following question: can we assist users with composing these short messages? More specifically, would it be possible to suggest brief responses when appropriate, just one tap away?
