blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews a 2016 paper demonstrating the Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM) neural network model's capabilities in continuous online sequence learning. The paper highlights HTM's strengths in handling real-time streaming data, including its ability to learn in a single pass without buffering, make higher-order predictions across multiple time steps, handle multiple simultaneous predictions, and exhibit robustness to sensor noise and fault tolerance. Notably, HTM achieves comparable accuracy to state-of-the-art algorithms like LSTMs without requiring task-specific hyperparameter tuning. The blog post emphasizes HTM's unique properties, such as sparse distributed representations (SDRs) and local learning rules, which contribute to its performance and adaptability. The paper also explores HTM's application to predicting New York City taxi passenger demand, further validating its practical utility.
paper_title: Continuous online sequence learning with an unsupervised neural network model
paper_abstract: The ability to recognize and predict temporal sequences of sensory inputs is vital for survival in natural environments. Based on many known properties of cortical neurons, hierarchical temporal memory (HTM) sequence memory is recently proposed as a theoretical framework for sequence learning in the cortex. In this paper, we analyze properties of HTM sequence memory and apply it to sequence learning and prediction problems with streaming data. We show the model is able to continuously learn a large number of variable-order temporal sequences using an unsupervised Hebbian-like learning rule. The sparse temporal codes formed by the model can robustly handle branching temporal sequences by maintaining multiple predictions until there is sufficient disambiguating evidence. We compare the HTM sequence memory with other sequence learning algorithms, including statistical methods: autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA), feedforward neural networks: online sequential extreme learning machine (ELM), and recurrent neural networks: long short-term memory (LSTM) and echo-state networks (ESN), on sequence prediction problems with both artificial and real-world data. The HTM model achieves comparable accuracy to other state-of-the-art algorithms. The model also exhibits properties that are critical for sequence learning, including continuous online learning, the ability to handle multiple predictions and branching sequences with high order statistics, robustness to sensor noise and fault tolerance, and good performance without task-specific hyperparameters tuning. Therefore the HTM sequence memory not only advances our understanding of how the brain may solve the sequence learning problem, but is also applicable to a wide range of real-world problems such as discrete and continuous sequence prediction, anomaly detection, and sequence classification. Can machine learning algorithms gain any insight from cortical algorithms? The current state-of-the-art statistical and ma...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes a paper by Hawkins et al. that explores the structural and functional role of the six layers in the neocortex, focusing on how pairs of layers learn predictive models of static objects as sensory input changes due to movement. The paper proposes that each cortical column contains a location signal (an allocentric reference frame) that helps neurons compute predicted new locations based on movement and object orientation. The authors hypothesize that grid cells in the entorhinal cortex, which perform similar spatial transformations, inspired the neocortex's layered structure. Colyer highlights the elegance of the two-layer input-output circuit motif (e.g., layers 4 and 2/3) as a fundamental building block of cortical processing. The paper then introduces a multi-layer model inspired by this biology, demonstrating how two layers of pyramidal neurons in a column can disambiguate objects like cubes and wedges through repeated sensory input. The model, built using HTM neurons, shows robustness to noise and scales well in terms of representational capacity.
paper_title: Why does the neocortex have layers and columns?
paper_abstract: Neocortical regions are organized into columns and layers. Connections between layers run mostly perpendicular to the surface suggesting a columnar functional organization. Some layers have long-range lateral connections suggesting interactions between columns. Similar patterns of connectivity exist in all regions but their exact role remains a mystery. In this paper, we propose a network model composed of columns and layers that performs robust object learning and recognition. Columns integrate their changing inputs over time to learn complete models of observed objects. Lateral connections across columns allow the network to more rapidly infer objects based on the partial knowledge of adjacent columns. Because columns integrate input over time and space, the network learns models of complex objects that extend well beyond the receptive field of individual cells. Our network model introduces a new feature to cortical columns. We propose that a representation of location is calculated within the subgranular layers of each column. The representation of location is relative to the object being sensed. Pairing sensory features with locations is a requirement for modeling objects and therefore must occur somewhere in the neocortex. We propose it occurs in every column in every region. Our network model contains two layers and one or more columns. Simulations show that small single-column networks can learn to recognize hundreds of complex multi-dimensional objects. Given the ubiquity of columnar and laminar connectivity patterns throughout the neocortex, we propose that columns and regions have more powerful recognition and modeling capabilities than previously assumed. Lacking a theory of why the neocortex is organized in columns and layers, almost all artificial neural networks, such as those used in deep learning (LeCun et al., 2015) and spiking neural networks (Maass, 1997), do not include these features, introducing the possibility they may be missing key functiona...

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the QUIC transport protocol, developed by Google to improve HTTPS performance. Adrian Colyer highlights three key aspects: the motivations behind QUIC (Why), its design and features (What), and its real-world deployment and evolution (How). QUIC addresses latency issues in web applications by combining the cryptographic and transport handshakes into a single round trip, enabling 0-RTT connections for repeat visits. It avoids head-of-line blocking through stream multiplexing, improves loss recovery with packet-level sequence numbers, and enhances security by encrypting transport headers. The protocol is built on UDP to bypass kernel dependencies and middlebox ossification. Google's iterative, Internet-scale experimentation with QUIC in Chrome, YouTube, and Google Search demonstrated measurable latency reductions and fewer playback interruptions, though at the cost of higher CPU usage compared to TCP/TLS.
paper_title: The QUIC transport protocol: design and Internet-scale deployment
paper_abstract: We present our experience with QUIC, an encrypted, multiplexed, and low-latency transport protocol designed from the ground up to improve transport performance for HTTPS traffic and to enable rapid deployment and continued evolution of transport mechanisms. QUIC has been globally deployed at Google on thousands of servers and is used to serve traffic to a range of clients including a widely-used web browser (Chrome) and a popular mobile video streaming app (YouTube). We estimate that 7% of Internet traffic is now QUIC. We describe our motivations for developing a new transport, the principles that guided our design, the Internet-scale process that we used to perform iterative experiments on QUIC, performance improvements seen by our various services, and our experience deploying QUIC globally. We also share lessons about transport design and the Internet ecosystem that we learned from our deployment. Figure 1: QUIC in the traditional HTTPS stack. TCP (Figure 1). We developed QUIC as a user-space transport with UDP as a substrate. Building QUIC in user-space facilitated its deployment as part of various applications and enabled iterative changes to occur at application update timescales. The use of UDP allows QUIC packets to traverse middleboxes. QUIC is an encrypted transport: packets are authenticated and encrypted, preventing modification and limiting ossification of the protocol by middleboxes. QUIC uses a cryptographic handshake that minimizes handshake latency for most connections by using known server credentials on repeat connections and by removing redundant handshake-overhead at multiple layers in the network stack. QUIC eliminates head-of-line blocking delays by using a lightweight data-structuring abstraction, streams, which are multiplexed within a single connection so that loss of a single packet blocks only streams with data in that packet. On the server-side, our experience comes from deploying QUIC at Google’s front-end servers, which collectively ha...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights an innovative pedagogical approach from Stanford's Advanced Topics in Networking class, where students reproduce results from networking research papers as part of a three-week project. The blog post emphasizes the educational value of this method, noting that students gain deep understanding of papers and key insights through hands-on experimentation. Colyer praises the project's dual benefits: teaching engineering rigor and critical thinking while fostering contributions to the networking community. The process involves selecting papers, using emulators like Mininet or Mahimahi, contacting original authors, recreating experiments, and publishing results on a public blog with peer validation. The approach is shown to break down barriers between students and the research community, with students gaining confidence, practical skills, and even inspiration for their own work.
paper_title: Learning networking by reproducing research results
paper_abstract: our experience, students who experience “building their own Internet” gain a thorough knowledge of how the Internet works, how to read and implement RFCs, and how to build network systems. For a more advanced graduate class in networking, it is less obvious what the most appropriate programming assignments are. Should students build more advanced pieces of the Internet—such as firewalls, load-balancers, and new transport layers? This has the advantage of giving them more experience building network systems, but lacks a research ingenuity component where they can dream up and test their own ideas. And so it is more common in graduate studies for students to do a more creative open-ended project of their own design, perhaps using a simulator, testbed or analytical tools. In our earlier experience with CS244, we opted for the second style, and had students create openended projects of their own design. But we kept finding the projects to be lacking—mostly because it is hard to build a meaningful networking system or a persuasive prototype in such a short time. Often, students picked projects that turned out to be too ambitious, and on an incomplete prototype it was hard to collect meaningful experimental results. As a result, the projects tended to be incremental, and the educational experience of the students seemed to be too susceptible to their choice of project. After all, it is hard enough to build a realistic, interesting, and functioning networking system in a matter of weeks; it is harder still to devise a novel one from scratch and then get it to work. And so instead, for the past five years, we have experimented with a completely di↵erent style of project. Since 2012, students taking CS244 work in pairs on a three week project in which they attempt to reproduce experimental results from published research in prominent networking conferences like SIGCOMM and NSDI. For example, students might reproduce the main experimental results in the Hedera [4], DCTCP [5],...

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the paper 'Occupy the cloud: distributed computing for the 99%' by Jonas et al., which won the best vision paper award at SoCC'17. The authors argue that serverless computing with stateless functions could serve as a simple, elastic, and user-friendly platform for distributed data processing, challenging traditional complex frameworks like Spark or Hadoop. The key insight is that despite the overhead of serializing and deserializing data, the performance degradation is negligible for many workloads, making serverless architectures a viable alternative. The paper highlights that casual users (the '99%') prefer minimal setup and deployment complexity, and serverless models align well with this need. The PyWren prototype, built on AWS Lambda, demonstrates how simple map operations can be executed efficiently using remote storage (S3) and a single shared Lambda function. The authors show that even complex abstractions like MapReduce, BSP, and parameter servers can be implemented on top of this model, though with some limitations due to Lambda's constraints.
paper_title: Occupy the cloud: distributed computing for the 99%
paper_abstract: framework. Yet even at UC Berkeley, we have found via informal surveys that the majority of machine learning graduate students have never written a cluster computing job due to complexity of setting up cloud platforms. In this paper we argue that a serverless execution model with stateless functions can enable radically-simpler, fundamentally elastic, and more user-friendly distributed data processing systems. In this model, we have one simple primitive: users submit functions that are executed in a remote container; the functions are stateless as all the state for the function, including input, output is accessed from shared remote storage. Surprisingly, we find that the performance degradation from using such an approach is negligible for many workloads and thus, our simple primitive is in fact general enough to implement a number of higherlevel data processing abstractions, including MapReduce and parameter servers. Recently cloud providers (e.g., AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions) and open source projects (e.g., OpenLambda [16], OpenWhisk [30]) have developed infrastructure to run event-driven, stateless functions as microservices. In this model, a function is deployed once and is invoked repeatedly whenever new inputs arrive and elastically scales with input size. Our key insight is that we can dynamically inject code into these functions, which combined with remote storage, allows us to build a data processing system that inherits the elasticity of the serverless model while addressing the simplicity for end users. We describe a prototype system, PyWren1 , developed in Python with AWS Lambda. By employing only stateless functions, PyWren helps users avoid the significant developer and management overhead that has until now been a necessary prerequisite. The complexity of state management can instead be captured by a global scheduler and fast remote storage. With PyWren, we seek to understand the trade-offs of using stateless functions for large scale data ana...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this paper as a clever method for generating datasets that maintain identical statistical properties while producing visually distinct graphs. The authors, Matejka and Fitzmaurice, demonstrate how simulated annealing can iteratively perturb an initial dataset to achieve target shapes—such as the Datasaurus or Simpson’s paradox examples—without altering key summary statistics. Colyer draws an analogy to adversarial inputs in deep learning, emphasizing how the same statistical outcomes can arise from fundamentally different underlying causes. The paper also explores practical applications like dataset anonymization and showcases the technique’s flexibility across dimensions (1D, 2D, etc.). The core insight is that small, controlled perturbations to data points can systematically reshape visualizations while preserving statistical fidelity, offering a powerful tool for data exploration and privacy-preserving transformations.
paper_title: Same stats, different graphs: generating datasets with varied appearance and identical statistics through simulated annealing
paper_abstract: While summary statistics are used consistently to report data results, their limitations (and the importance of visualizing data) are well known. Yet, current methods that aim to approximate shapes to match some desired summary statistics are quite complex and can fail the approximation for complex shapes. We present a simple linear transformation LT that performs the same approximation more effectively and efficiently. We show that this method works well for complicated shapes and large datasets, visually outperforms almost all baseline algorithms for most shapes, while being significantly faster and simpler. We also present an iterative approach that improves the method LT in case of extreme statistical values.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights DeepXplore as a groundbreaking approach to systematically test deep learning systems for bugs and corner cases, moving beyond traditional adversarial examples. He emphasizes the paper's key insight: using neuron coverage (tracking activated neurons) and differential testing (comparing multiple models) to expose unexpected behaviors in state-of-the-art deep neural networks (DNNs). The blog praises DeepXplore's efficiency, demonstrating its ability to find thousands of erroneous corner cases—such as self-driving cars failing or malware evasion—in under a second on a laptop. Colyer underscores the importance of this work for safety- and security-critical DL systems, arguing that such testing is as essential as in traditional software. The method combines gradient ascent with a joint optimization problem to maximize neuron coverage and differential behavior, effectively probing decision boundaries between models.
paper_title: DeepXplore: Automated Whitebox Testing of Deep Learning Systems
paper_abstract: CCS CONCEPTS Deep learning (DL) systems are increasingly deployed in safety- and security-critical domains including self-driving cars and malware detection, where the correctness and predictability of a system’s behavior for corner case inputs are of great importance. Existing DL testing depends heavily on manually labeled data and therefore often fails to expose erroneous behaviors for rare inputs. We design, implement, and evaluate DeepXplore, the first whitebox framework for systematically testing real-world DL systems. First, we introduce neuron coverage for systematically measuring the parts of a DL system exercised by test inputs. Next, we leverage multiple DL systems with similar functionality as cross-referencing oracles to avoid manual checking. Finally, we demonstrate how finding inputs for DL systems that both trigger many differential behaviors and achieve high neuron coverage can be represented as a joint optimization problem and solved efficiently using gradientbased search techniques. DeepXplore efficiently finds thousands of incorrect corner case behaviors (e.g., self-driving cars crashing into guard rails and malware masquerading as benign software) in stateof-the-art DL models with thousands of neurons trained on five popular datasets including ImageNet and Udacity selfdriving challenge data. For all tested DL models, on average, DeepXplore generated one test input demonstrating incorrect behavior within one second while running only on a commodity laptop. We further show that the test inputs generated by DeepXplore can also be used to retrain the corresponding DL model to improve the model’s accuracy by up to 3%. • Computing methodologies → Neural networks; • Computer systems organization → Neural networks; Reliability; • Software and its engineering → Software testing and debugging; Permission to make digital or hard copies of all or part of this work for personal or classroom use is granted without fee provided that copies are not made or distr...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the paper's investigation into achieving VM-like isolation with container-like efficiency using Xen-based virtualization. The authors identify and eliminate bottlenecks in launching lightweight VMs (including unikernels and minimal Linux VMs), resulting in the LightVM system. With minimal unikernel images, LightVM can boot a VM in just 4ms, outperforming Docker containers (150ms) and even process creation (1ms). The paper introduces TinyX, an automated build system for creating minimalistic Linux VM images optimized for single applications. The authors demonstrate that Xen's scalability is limited by VM image size and XenStore overhead, which grows superlinearly. LightVM addresses these issues by redesigning the Xen control plane with a lean driver (noxs) that replaces XenStore and uses pre-prepared VM shells to reduce initialization overhead. The system achieves near-process-level boot times and supports use cases like personalized firewalls, just-in-time service instantiation, TLS termination, and lightweight compute services (e.g., AWS Lambda). The key insight is that lightweight virtualization can simultaneously provide strong isolation and performance comparable to or better than containers.
paper_title: LightVM: Lightweight Virtual Machines with Fast Boot and Deployment
paper_abstract: Containers are in great demand because they are lightweight when compared to virtual machines. On the downside, containers o�er weaker isolation than VMs, to the point where people run containers in virtual machines to achieve proper isolation. In this paper, we examine whether there is indeed a strict tradeo� between isolation (VMs) and e�ciency (containers). We �nd that VMs can be as nimble as containers, as long as they are small and the toolstack is fast enough. We achieve lightweight VMs by using unikernels for specialized applications and with Tinyx, a tool that enables creating tailor-made, trimmed-down Linux virtual machines. By themselves, lightweight virtual machines are not enough to ensure good performance since the virtualization control plane (the toolstack) becomes the performance bottleneck. We present LightVM, a new virtualization solution based on Xen that is optimized to o�er fast boot-times regardless of the number of active VMs. LightVM features a complete redesign of Xen’s control plane, transforming its centralized operation to a distributed one where interactions with the hypervisor are reduced to a minimum. LightVM can boot a VM in 2.3ms, comparable to fork/exec on Linux (1ms), and two orders of magnitude faster than Docker. LightVM can pack thousands of LightVM guests on modest hardware with memory and CPU usage comparable to that of processes. blog_summary: The blog post discusses a paper that tackles the challenge of optimally placing logging statements in software systems to balance information utility and performance overhead. Adrian Colyer highlights that current logging practices are often retrospective and manually adjusted, leading to inefficiencies. The paper introduces Log20, an automated tool that uses an entropy-based model to determine the most informative log placements under a specified overhead constraint. Log20 samples execution paths in production systems and selects log statement locations that minimize uncertainty (entropy) while staying within performance budgets. The algorithm employs a greedy approximation to efficiently solve this NP-hard problem. The paper also explores extensions like logging variable values to further reduce entropy. Evaluation on systems like HDFS and HBase shows significant entropy reduction with minimal overhead, outperforming manual logging approaches.
paper_title: Log20: Fully Automated Optimal Placement of Log Printing Statements under Specified Overhead Threshold
paper_abstract: When systems fail in production environments, log data is often the only information available to programmers for postmortem debugging. Consequently, programmers’ decision on where to place a log printing statement is of crucial importance, as it directly affects how effective and efficient postmortem debugging can be. This paper presents Log20, a tool that determines a near optimal placement of log printing statements under the constraint of adding less than a specified amount of performance overhead. Log20 does this in an automated way without any human involvement. Guided by information theory, the core of our algorithm measures how effective each log printing statement is in disambiguating code paths. To do so, it uses the frequencies of different execution paths that are collected from a production environment by a low-overhead tracing library. We evaluated Log20 on HDFS, HBase, Cassandra, and ZooKeeper, and observed that Log20 is substantially more efficient in code path disambiguation compared to the developers’ manually placed log printing statements. Log20 can also output a curve showing the trade-off between the informativeness of the logs and the performance slowdown, so that a developer can choose the right balance.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the critical importance of statistically rigorous methods in performance evaluation, using Georges et al.'s OOPSLA'07 paper as a foundation. The blog emphasizes that without proper experimental design and statistical analysis, performance evaluations can lead to misleading or incorrect conclusions, potentially steering research and development in unproductive directions. Colyer underscores the prevalence of non-rigorous methodologies in Java performance papers at the time, such as reporting only the best run out of many, which can distort results. The paper advocates for using confidence intervals and statistical tests (like Student's t-distribution and ANOVA) to distinguish meaningful performance differences from random fluctuations. Colyer particularly praises Section 3 of the paper, which serves as a mini-tutorial on statistical methods for benchmarking, making it accessible and practical for researchers.
paper_title: Statistically rigorous Java performance evaluation
paper_abstract: Java performance is far from being trivial to benchmark because it is affected by various factors such as the Java application, its input, the virtual machine, the garbage collector, the heap size, etc. In addition, non-determinism at run-time causes the execution time of a Java program to differ from run to run. There are a number of sources of non-determinism such as Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation and optimization in the virtual machine (VM) driven by timerbased method sampling, thread scheduling, garbage collection, and various system effects. There exist a wide variety of Java performance evaluation methodologies used by researchers and benchmarkers. These methodologies differ from each other in a number of ways. Some report average performance over a number of runs of the same experiment; others report the best or second best performance observed; yet others report the worst. Some iterate the benchmark multiple times within a single VM invocation; others consider multiple VM invocations and iterate a single benchmark execution; yet others consider multiple VM invocations and iterate the benchmark multiple times. This paper shows that prevalent methodologies can be misleading, and can even lead to incorrect conclusions. The reason is that the data analysis is not statistically rigorous. In this paper, we present a survey of existing Java performance evaluation methodologies and discuss the importance of statistically rigorous data analysis for dealing with non-determinism. We advocate approaches to quantify startup as well as steady-state performance, and, in addition, we provide the JavaStats software to automatically obtain performance numbers in a rigorous manner. Although this paper focuses on Java performance evaluation, many of the issues addressed in this paper also apply to other programming languages and systems that build on a managed runtime system.

figures.title: Comparison of execution times with prevalent 'best' method
figures.caption: Figure 1 compares the execution time for running Jikes RVM with five garbage collectors (CopyMS, GenCopy, GenMS, MarkSweep and SemiSpace) for the SPECjvm98 db benchmark with a 120MB heap size. The graph compares the prevalent 'best' method which reports the best performance observed across multiple runs.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a critical issue in VM benchmarking: many studies assume benchmarks reach a steady state of peak performance after a few iterations, but Barrett et al.'s paper reveals this assumption is often false. The authors conduct an exhaustive, three-year study across multiple languages (Java, JavaScript, Python, Lua, PHP, Ruby) and VMs, using controlled experiments to analyze warmup behavior. They employ changepoint analysis to detect when (or if) a VM reaches a steady state and whether that state represents peak performance. The results are alarming: only 37% of (VM, benchmark) pairs show consistent 'good' warmup behavior (flat or classic warmup), while nearly half exhibit 'bad inconsistent' behavior (slowdown or no steady state). This unpredictability undermines the reliability of VM optimizations based on microbenchmarks, as ineffective or harmful optimizations may be incorrectly adopted.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes Facebook's Flow, a fast and precise static type checker for JavaScript used at scale (13M LoC at Facebook). The paper details Flow's design, focusing on its constraint-based analysis with type refinements to handle JavaScript idioms like `x = x || 0` and refine types based on runtime tests (e.g., `f != null`). Flow prioritizes soundness over convenience, unlike TypeScript, and achieves scalability through modular, parallel analysis with module-level signatures. The blog highlights Flow's ability to catch common bugs with low false positives while maintaining fast response times, even on massive codebases. The core insight is modeling runtime tests to refine types dynamically, enabling precise bug detection without sacrificing performance.
paper_title: Fast and precise type checking for JavaScript

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the challenges of maintaining TypeScript declaration files for JavaScript libraries, which are manually written and prone to errors. The paper introduces TSTest, a tool that uses feedback-directed random testing to automatically generate type test scripts for JavaScript libraries and their corresponding TypeScript declarations. These scripts dynamically exercise the library code and perform runtime type checking to detect mismatches between declarations and implementations. The approach is shown to find more errors with fewer false positives than prior static analysis tools. Colyer notes the clever adaptation of Randoop's feedback-directed testing to TypeScript, along with the novel design choices required to handle structural types, function contracts, and recursion. The evaluation on 54 real-world libraries finds type mismatches in 49 of them, demonstrating the tool's practical utility despite theoretical limitations in soundness and completeness.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this OOPSLA'17 paper as an important step toward taming the complex semantics of JavaScript Promises. The core contribution is the introduction of a formal calculus (a promise calculus) that precisely models the behavior of promises, including their states (Pending, Fulfilled, Rejected) and operations (resolve, reject, then). This formalism enables the construction of promise graphs, which visually represent control- and dataflow in promise-based programs. The blog post emphasizes how these graphs can detect a wide range of common bugs in promise code, such as dead promises, missing resolve/reject reactions, double resolves, and broken chains. Colyer particularly enjoys the promise graph visualization, which provides both forward and backward reasoning about promise flows. The paper also demonstrates practical utility by analyzing real StackOverflow questions, showing how promise graphs could have helped diagnose issues faster.

As a result, the effects of errors may not manifest themselves until much later during a program’s execution, making the debugging of event-based code extremely challenging. Furthermore, several types of errors may occur that are specific to the event-driven programming model, such as lost events (situations where an event is emitted before a handler is registered) and dead listeners (situations where an event handler is never executed because the handler was registered too late or on the wrong object) [Madsen et al. 2015], and event race errors, i.e., situations where program behavior fails non-deterministically depending on the order in which event handlers are scheduled for execution [Adamsen et al. 2017; Hong et al. 2014; Jensen et al. 2015; Mutlu et al. 2015; Petrov et al. 2012; Raychev et al. 2013; Zhang and Wang 2017; Zheng et al. 2011]. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer introduces the concept of 'capsules' in neural networks, highlighting their potential to address exponential inefficiencies in traditional models like HMMs and CNNs. The key insight is that capsules encode viewpoint-invariant knowledge using transformation matrices, allowing for better generalization to novel viewpoints. The blog post explains that capsules represent entities and their properties (e.g., pose, deformation) as vectors, with the vector length indicating the existence of the entity and orientation encoding its properties. A dynamic routing mechanism ensures that capsules in lower layers send their outputs to appropriate parent capsules in higher layers based on agreement, improving upon the crude max-pooling approach in CNNs. The paper demonstrates these ideas on the MNIST dataset, showing how capsules can learn meaningful representations of digit variations.
paper_title: Dynamic Routing Between Capsules
paper_abstract: A capsule is a group of neurons whose activity vector represents the instantiation parameters of a specific type of entity such as an object or an object part. We use the length of the activity vector to represent the probability that the entity exists and its orientation to represent the instantiation parameters. Active capsules at one level make predictions, via transformation matrices, for the instantiation parameters of higher-level capsules. When multiple predictions agree, a higher level capsule becomes active. We show that a discrimininatively trained, multi-layer capsule system achieves state-of-the-art performance on MNIST and is considerably better than a convolutional net at recognizing highly overlapping digits. To achieve these results we use an iterative routing-by-agreement mechanism: A lower-level capsule prefers to send its output to higher level capsules whose activity vectors have a big scalar product with the prediction coming from the lower-level capsule.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer discusses a new capsule network architecture (CapsNetEM) that builds upon Hinton's capsule theory, introducing an EM-based routing procedure to improve performance and robustness. The paper highlights CapsNetEM's state-of-the-art results on the smallNORB dataset, achieving a 1.4% test error rate (compared to 2.7% for the original CapsNet and 2.56% for prior work), and demonstrates increased robustness to adversarial attacks, particularly in white-box scenarios where its accuracy never drops below chance. The key insight is the use of Expectation Maximization (EM) for routing-by-agreement, which addresses limitations of the original CapsNet's vector-length-based approach by modeling votes as Gaussian clusters and optimizing a free energy function. The blog post also recaps the core capsules concept and contrasts the EM routing mechanism with the original dynamic routing method.
paper_title: Matrix capsules with EM routing
paper_abstract: In this study, we explore capsule networks with dynamic routing for text classification. We propose three strategies to stabilize the dynamic routing process to alleviate the disturbance of some noise capsules which may contain “background” information or have not been successfully trained. A series of experiments are conducted with capsule networks on six text classification benchmarks. Capsule networks achieve competitive results over the compared baseline methods on 4 out of 6 datasets, which shows the effectiveness of capsule networks for text classification. We additionally show that capsule networks exhibit significant improvement when transfer single-label to multi-label text classification over the competitors. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that capsule networks have been empirically investigated for text modeling1 .

figures.title: Architecture of the proposed capsule network for text classification
figures.caption: Figure 1: The architecture of our capsule network for text classification. The proposed model consists of four layers: n-gram convolutional layer, primary capsule layer, convolutional capsule layer, and fully connected capsule layer.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this paper as groundbreaking, offering a novel theoretical framework to understand deep neural networks (DNNs) by applying information theory to analyze their internal workings. The paper introduces an information-theoretic lens to study DNN training, revealing insights into how representations evolve during learning and how noise (e.g., via sigmoid activations) enables meaningful analysis. The key insight is the use of mutual information and the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle to quantify the trade-off between compression and prediction accuracy, providing a way to visualize and compare network architectures. The author notes the paper's accessibility despite its theoretical depth and emphasizes its potential to improve DNN efficiency, even suggesting alternatives to SGD in later training phases. The blog post sets the stage for Part II, which will explore empirical applications of the theory to real DNNs.
paper_title: Opening the Black Box of Deep Neural Networks via Information
paper_abstract: Despite their great success, there is still no comprehensive theoretical understanding of learning with Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) or their inner organization. Previous work [Tishby and Zaslavsky (2015)] proposed to analyze DNNs in the Information Plane; i.e., the plane of the Mutual Information values that each layer preserves on the input and output variables. They suggested that the goal of the network is to optimize the Information Bottleneck (IB) tradeoff between compression and prediction, successively, for each layer. In this work we follow up on this idea and demonstrate the effectiveness of the InformationPlane visualization of DNNs. Our main results are: (i) most of the training epochs in standard DL are spent on compression of the input to efficient representation and not on fitting the training labels. (ii) The representation compression phase begins when the training errors becomes small and the Stochastic Gradient Decent (SGD) epochs change from a fast drift to smaller training error into a stochastic relaxation, or random diffusion, constrained by the training error value. (iii) The converged layers lie on or very close to the Information Bottleneck (IB) theoretical bound, and the maps from the input to any hidden layer and from this hidden layer to the output satisfy the IB self-consistent equations. This generalization through noise mechanism is unique to Deep Neural Networks and absent in one layer networks. (iv) The training time is dramatically reduced when adding more hidden layers. Thus the main advantage of the hidden layers is computational. This can be explained by the reduced relaxation time, as this it scales super-linearly (exponentially for simple diffusion) with the information compression from the previous layer. (v) As we expect critical slowing down of the stochastic relaxation near phase transitions on the IB curve, we expect the hidden layers to converge to such critical points.1

figures.title: The DNN layers form a Markov chain of successive internal representations
figures.caption: The DNN layers form a Markov chain of successive internal representations of the input layer X. Any representation of the input, T , is defined through an encoder, P (T |X), and a decoder P (Ŷ |T ), and can be quantified by its information plane coordinates: IX = I(X; T ) and IY = I(T ; Y ). The Information Bottleneck bound characterizes the optimal representations, which maximally compress the input X, for a given mutual information on the desired output Y . After training, the network receives an input X, and successively processes it through the layers, which form a Markov chain, to the predicted output Ŷ . I(Y ; Ŷ )/I(X; Y ) quantifies how much of the relevant information is captured by the network.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes a paper that applies information theory to analyze the inner workings of deep neural networks (DNNs). The authors train a 7-layer DNN and track mutual information between hidden layers and inputs/outputs across training epochs. They observe two distinct phases: an initial 'Empirical Error Minimization (ERM)' phase where layers rapidly increase mutual information with outputs while preserving input information, followed by a longer 'representation compression' phase where layers discard irrelevant input information. The compression phase behaves like a diffusion process, maximizing entropy under training constraints. The paper also shows that deeper networks converge faster and that training sample size significantly impacts the information bottleneck behavior. The key insight is that DNNs naturally follow an information bottleneck principle, discarding irrelevant information during training.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights AlphaGo Zero as a groundbreaking achievement in AI, demonstrating superhuman performance in Go without any human knowledge or guidance. Unlike its predecessors, AlphaGo Zero learns solely through self-play reinforcement learning, starting from random moves, and achieves superior results in a fraction of the time and computational resources. The paper showcases how AlphaGo Zero rediscovers fundamental Go strategies (like joseki) and even develops novel tactics beyond traditional human knowledge. The key insight is the feasibility of pure reinforcement learning in complex domains, eliminating the need for human data or heuristics. The blog emphasizes the remarkable efficiency of AlphaGo Zero, outperforming AlphaGo Lee in just 36 hours using a single machine with 4 TPUs, compared to AlphaGo Lee's months-long training and distributed setup with 48 TPUs.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the paper 'DéjàVu: A map of code duplicates on GitHub' from OOPSLA '17, which analyzes duplication in 4.5 million GitHub projects. The authors found that 82% of files have duplicates elsewhere in GitHub, though this is largely due to trivial files and dependency management practices. The study defines three levels of duplication: exact file hashes, token hashes (minor changes), and near-duplicates (80% token similarity via SourcererCC). JavaScript exhibits the highest duplication (94% file-level clones), primarily due to NPM dependencies being committed to repositories. The paper also explores project-level duplication and identifies auto-generated code and popular frameworks as major contributors to duplication. The authors propose their 'clone map' as a tool to help researchers curate non-duplicate samples for studies.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Algorand as a groundbreaking cryptocurrency system designed to address Bitcoin's scalability and performance limitations. The paper introduces BA★, a novel Byzantine agreement protocol that enables Algorand to confirm transactions in about a minute (vs. Bitcoin's hour) with negligible forking probability and 125x higher throughput. The core innovation lies in Algorand's proof-of-stake mechanism combined with cryptographic sortition, which randomly selects participants in a decentralized way to propose and vote on blocks. This approach eliminates the need for miners and ensures security even if an adversary controls the network for bounded periods. The BA★ protocol achieves both safety and liveness guarantees through a two-phase process, with tentative consensus serving as an intermediate step that can be finalized quickly under normal conditions. Colyer emphasizes the elegance of sortition's decentralized randomness and its resistance to adversarial manipulation.
paper_title: Algorand: Scaling Byzantine Agreements for Cryptocurrencies
paper_abstract: confirmed in Bitcoin requires about an hour long wait [7]. On the other hand, applications that require low latency cannot be certain that their transaction will be confirmed, and must trust the payer to not double-spend [46]. Algorand is a new cryptocurrency that confirms transactions with latency on the order of a minute while scaling to many users. Algorand ensures that users never have divergent views of confirmed transactions, even if some of the users are malicious and the network is temporarily partitioned. In contrast, existing cryptocurrencies allow for temporary forks and therefore require a long time, on the order of an hour, to confirm transactions with high confidence. Algorand uses a new Byzantine Agreement (BA) protocol to reach consensus among users on the next set of transactions. To scale the consensus to many users, Algorand uses a novel mechanism based on Verifiable Random Functions that allows users to privately check whether they are selected to participate in the BA to agree on the next set of transactions, and to include a proof of their selection in their network messages. In Algorand’s BA protocol, users do not keep any private state except for their private keys, which allows Algorand to replace participants immediately after they send a message. This mitigates targeted attacks on chosen participants after their identity is revealed. We implement Algorand and evaluate its performance on 1,000 EC2 virtual machines, simulating up to 500,000 users. Experimental results show that Algorand confirms transactions in under a minute, achieves 125× Bitcoin’s throughput, and incurs almost no penalty for scaling to more users. 1 Double-spending is the core problem faced by any cryptocurrency, where an adversary holding $1 gives his $1 to two different users. Cryptocurrencies prevent double-spending by reaching consensus on an ordered log (“blockchain”) of transactions. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Canopy as a significant evolution over Facebook's earlier 'Mystery Machine' system for end-to-end performance tracing. Canopy addresses three key challenges in heterogeneous, large-scale systems: the diversity of performance data, the need for high-level aggregated analysis despite fine-grained data, and information overload from shared tracing infrastructure. The paper emphasizes flexibility at all levels, decoupling instrumentation from the underlying trace model to accommodate Facebook's fast-moving environment. Canopy's pipeline includes trace propagation, event aggregation, a flexible trace model, and user-defined feature extraction, enabling rapid hypothesis testing for performance diagnostics. The system has been in production for two years, handling 1.3 billion traces daily, and demonstrates scalability and adaptability across diverse execution models and third-party integrations.
paper_title: Canopy: End-to-End Performance Tracing and Analysis at Scale
paper_abstract: This paper presents Canopy, Facebook’s end-to-end performance tracing infrastructure. Canopy records causally related performance data across the end-to-end execution path of requests, including from browsers, mobile applications, and backend services. Canopy processes traces in near real-time, derives user-specified features, and outputs to performance datasets that aggregate across billions of requests. Using Canopy, Facebook engineers can query and analyze performance data in real-time. Canopy addresses three challenges we have encountered in scaling performance analysis: supporting the range of execution and performance models used by different components of the Facebook stack; supporting interactive ad-hoc analysis of performance data; and enabling deep customization by users, from sampling traces to extracting and visualizing features. Canopy currently records and processes over 1 billion traces per day. We discuss how Canopy has evolved to apply to a wide range of scenarios, and present case studies of its use in solving various performance challenges.

blog_summary: The blog post highlights KV-Direct, an in-memory key-value store that achieves unprecedented performance by leveraging programmable NICs with FPGAs. Using 10 programmable NICs in a commodity server, the system delivers 1.22 billion KV operations per second—nearly an order of magnitude faster than existing systems—while also being 3x more power efficient and the first to reach 1 million KV operations per watt. KV-Direct bypasses the remote CPU by implementing key-value primitives directly on the FPGA-equipped NIC, extending RDMA operations to include GET, PUT, DELETE, and atomic operations, as well as vector-based primitives like UPDATE, REDUCE, and FILTER. This approach reduces network traffic and offloads computation to the NIC, enabling efficient handling of workloads like machine learning, graph computing, and distributed synchronization. The paper also addresses design challenges, including PCIe bandwidth saturation, load balancing between NIC DRAM and host memory, and minimizing memory access overhead through techniques like inline storage for small KV pairs and dynamic scheduling via a reservation station.
paper_title: KV-Direct: High-performance in-memory key-value store with programmable NIC
paper_abstract: CCS CONCEPTS Performance of in-memory key-value store (KVS) continues to be of great importance as modern KVS goes beyond the traditional object-caching workload and becomes a key infrastructure to support distributed main-memory computation in data centers. Recent years have witnessed a rapid increase of network bandwidth in data centers, shifting the bottleneck of most KVS from the network to the CPU. RDMA-capable NIC partly alleviates the problem, but the primitives provided by RDMA abstraction are rather limited. Meanwhile, programmable NICs become available in data centers, enabling in-network processing. In this paper, we present KV-Direct, a high performance KVS that leverages programmable NIC to extend RDMA primitives and enable remote direct key-value access to the main host memory. We develop several novel techniques to maximize the throughput and hide the latency of the PCIe connection between the NIC and the host memory, which becomes the new bottleneck. Combined, these mechanisms allow a single NIC KV-Direct to achieve up to 180 M key-value operations per second, equivalent to the throughput of tens of CPU cores. Compared with CPU based KVS implementation, KV-Direct improves power efficiency by 3x, while keeping tail latency below 10 µs. Moreover, KV-Direct can achieve near linear scalability with multiple NICs. With 10 programmable NIC cards in a commodity server, we achieve 1.22 billion KV operations per second, which is almost an order-of-magnitude improvement over existing systems, setting a new milestone for a general-purpose in-memory key-value store. •Information systems → Key-value stores; •Hardware → Hardware-software codesign; Permission to make digital or hard copies of all or part of this work for personal or classroom use is granted without fee provided that copies are not made or distributed for profit or commercial advantage and that copies bear this notice and the full citation on the first page. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes a critical analysis paper that challenges the Information Bottleneck (IB) theory of deep learning proposed by Schwartz-Viz & Tishby. The authors replicate the original findings but demonstrate that key results do not generalize across different network architectures, particularly when replacing tanh activations with ReLU. They show that the observed two-phase training dynamics (compression and fitting) depend heavily on the choice of activation function, with ReLU networks failing to exhibit compression. The paper further investigates the relationship between compression and generalization, finding no causal connection, and shows that compression is not dependent on randomness from SGD. The authors also explore task-irrelevant information compression, noting that while irrelevant information may compress, this does not necessarily correlate with generalization performance. Overall, the paper highlights limitations in applying information-theoretic analyses to deep learning systems, particularly regarding noise assumptions and activation function choices.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the SVE (Streaming Video Engine) paper from Facebook, highlighting its production-scale distributed video processing system. He emphasizes the stark contrast between simple cloud-based video pipelines (like AWS Elastic Transcoder) and Facebook's scale (tens of millions of uploads/day), arguing that custom solutions become necessary at such massive scale. The blog post explores Facebook's shift from a monolithic batch-processing system (MES) to SVE, which processes videos in a streaming fashion with parallel chunking (GOPs) and overlapping upload/processing/storage. Colyer notes the 2.3x-9.3x latency reduction in time-to-share as a key achievement, driven by parallelism, dynamic DAG generation, and priority-based scheduling. He also praises the paper's discussion of why existing frameworks (MapReduce, Spark, Storm) were unsuitable, and the system's fault tolerance and overload handling mechanisms.
paper_title: SVE: Distributed Video Processing at Facebook Scale
paper_abstract: Videos are an increasingly utilized part of the experience of the billions of people that use Facebook. These videos must be uploaded and processed before they can be shared and downloaded. Uploading and processing videos at our scale, and across our many applications, brings three key requirements: low latency to support interactive applications; a �exible programming model for application developers that is simple to program, enables e�cient processing, and improves reliability; and robustness to faults and overload. This paper describes the evolution from our initial monolithic encoding script (MES) system to our current Streaming Video Engine (SVE) that overcomes each of the challenges. SVE has been in production since the fall of 2015, provides lower latency than MES, supports many diverse video applications, and has proven to be reliable despite faults and overload.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses a paper from USENIX ATC'17 that tackles the challenge of predicting the popularity of videos on Facebook to optimize streaming quality and resource allocation. Adrian Colyer highlights the paper's key insight: Facebook's video popularity follows a power law, meaning a small fraction of videos (e.g., top 1%) account for the majority of watch time. This allows targeted optimization efforts, such as using the QuickFire engine to re-encode popular videos at higher quality with less storage overhead. The authors propose CHESS, a scalable and near-real-time popularity prediction algorithm that combines exponential decay kernels with a simple neural network to balance accuracy and computational efficiency. CHESS outperforms existing heuristics by improving watch time coverage by 8%-30% while reducing CPU overhead, and it operates in minutes rather than days, enabling timely decisions. The approach is generalizable beyond videos to other popularity prediction scenarios.
paper_title: Popularity prediction of Facebook videos for higher quality streaming
paper_abstract: Streaming video algorithms dynamically select between different versions of a video to deliver the highest quality version that can be viewed without buffering over the client’s connection. To improve the quality for viewers, the backing video service can generate more and/or better versions, but at a significant computational overhead. Processing all videos uploaded to Facebook in the most intensive way would require a prohibitively large cluster. Facebook’s video popularity distribution is highly skewed, however, with analysis on sampled videos showing 1% of them accounting for 83% of the total watch time by users. Thus, if we can predict the future popularity of videos, we can focus the intensive processing on those videos that improve the quality of the most watch time. To address this challenge, we designed Chess, the first popularity prediction algorithm that is both scalable and accurate. Chess is scalable because, unlike the state-ofthe-art approaches, it requires only constant space per video, enabling it to handle Facebook’s video workload. Chess is accurate because it delivers superior predictions using a combination of historical access patterns with social signals in a unified online learning framework. We have built a video prediction service, ChessVPS, using our new algorithm that can handle Facebook’s workload with only four machines. We find that re-encoding popular videos predicted by ChessVPS enables a higher percentage of total user watch time to benefit from intensive encoding, with less overhead than a recent production heuristic, e.g., 80% of watch time with one-third as much overhead.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the paper 'Concrete problems in AI safety' which examines potential accidents in machine learning systems and mechanisms to prevent them. The paper defines accidents as unintended harmful behavior arising from incorrect objective functions or learning processes, with a focus on reinforcement learning (RL) where agents interact with complex environments. The authors explore five key failure modes: negative side effects (unintended environmental disruptions), reward hacking (gaming the reward function), insufficient oversight (difficulty in evaluating complex objectives), unsafe exploration (harmful exploratory actions), and fragility under distributional shift (mismatch between training and real-world environments). The blog highlights the paper's pragmatic and grounded approach, emphasizing the growing importance of AI safety as systems become more autonomous and societally impactful. Colyer notes the paper's structured exploration of these problems and potential countermeasures, including impact regularizers, empowerment measures, trip wires, and adversarial reward functions.
paper_title: Concrete Problems in AI Safety
paper_abstract: Rapid progress in machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) has brought increasing attention to the potential impacts of AI technologies on society. In this paper we discuss one such potential impact: the problem of accidents in machine learning systems, defined as unintended and harmful behavior that may emerge from poor design of real-world AI systems. We present a list of five practical research problems related to accident risk, categorized according to whether the problem originates from having the wrong objective function (“avoiding side effects” and “avoiding reward hacking”), an objective function that is too expensive to evaluate frequently (“scalable supervision”), or undesirable behavior during the learning process (“safe exploration” and “distributional shift”). We review previous work in these areas as well as suggesting research directions with a focus on relevance to cutting-edge AI systems. Finally, we consider the high-level question of how to think most productively about the safety of forward-looking applications of AI.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a 2004 paper by Nancy Leveson that analyzes five major spacecraft accidents (1996-2000) to extract systemic lessons applicable to modern systems like autonomous vehicles. The paper reveals striking similarities across accidents in three areas: safety culture (complacency, overconfidence, and resource prioritization), management/organizational flaws (diffusion of responsibility, poor communication), and technical deficiencies (inadequate engineering practices). Leveson argues that safety cannot be retrofitted via QA alone and requires dedicated system engineering focus. The author notes parallels to machine learning systems and emphasizes the need for better modeling tools to handle increasing system complexity. Key insights include the prevalence of design errors over implementation bugs and the critical role of documenting design rationale.
paper_title: The role of software in spacecraft accidents
paper_venue: AIAA Journal of Spacecraft and Rockets

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a 1993 paper by Nancy G. Lutz that analyzes 209 safety-critical software errors from the Voyager and Galileo spacecraft projects. The paper uses a '3 whys' methodology to trace errors from program faults back to human factors and process flaws. Lutz categorizes safety-related program faults into behavioral, operating, conditional, and interface faults, with behavioral faults being the most common. The root causes often stem from communication gaps between teams (especially between software and systems engineers) and inadequate requirements specification. The paper concludes with six guidelines to reduce such errors, emphasizing early hazard identification, formal specification techniques, improved cross-team communication, and defensive design practices to account for worst-case scenarios.
paper_title: Analyzing software requirements errors in safety-critical embedded systems

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the paper 'ffwd: delegation is (much) faster than you think' by Roghanchi et al., presented at SOSP'17. The paper explores delegation as an alternative to traditional locking mechanisms for managing shared data structures across multi-core systems. Unlike fine-grained locking, which often fails to outperform single-threaded execution due to overheads, delegation dedicates a hardware thread to manage a shared data structure, forwarding all accesses through this thread. Surprisingly, this simple approach can outperform locking by an order of magnitude for data structures that perform best on a single thread, thanks to improved cache locality and reduced contention. The key insight is that delegation leverages the single-threaded performance ceiling while avoiding the scalability bottlenecks of locking. The paper also provides a comprehensive review of existing approaches to shared data management, including spinlocks, queue-based locks, lock-free structures, RCU, and STM, before diving into the design and evaluation of ffwd.
paper_title: ffwd: delegation is (much) faster than you think
paper_abstract: We revisit the question of delegation vs. synchronized access to shared memory, and show through analysis and demonstration that delegation can be much faster than locking under a range of common circumstances. Starting from first principles, we propose fast, fly-weight delegation (ffwd). The highly optimized design of ffwd allows it to significantly outperform prior work on delegation, while retaining the scalability advantage. In experiments with 6 benchmark applications, and 6 shared data structures, running on four different multi-socket systems with up to 128 hardware threads, we compare ffwd to a selection of lock, combining, lock-free, software transactional memory and delegation designs. Overall, we find that ffwd often offers a simple and highly competitive alternative to existing work. By definition, the performance of a fully delegated data structure is limited by the single-thread throughput of said data structure. However, due to cache effects, many data structures offer their best performance when confined to a single thread. With an efficient delegation mechanism, we approach this single-threaded performance in a multi-threaded setting. In application-level benchmarks, we see improvements up to 100% over the next best solution tested (RCL), and multiple micro-benchmarks show improvements in the 5–10× range.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a concerning trend in mobile browser security, noting that 98.6% of analyzed Android browsers are vulnerable to at least one attack, with an average of twelve vulnerabilities per browser. Contrary to expectations, vulnerabilities have been increasing over time, particularly in popular browsers like Chrome, Opera, and Dolphin. The paper introduces Hindsight, a tool developed to automate the analysis of 2,324 browser versions across 128 families, using techniques like OCR to identify UI elements like address bars. The study reveals that even top browsers remain highly vulnerable, with Firefox being the only exception, showing a steady decline in vulnerabilities since 2013. The authors categorize vulnerabilities into 27 'attack building blocks' (ABBs) across five groups, including event routing, URL display, address bar manipulation, security indicators, and content handling. The findings underscore the urgent need for greater attention to mobile browser security.
paper_title: Hindsight: Understanding the Evolution of UI Vulnerabilities in Mobile Browsers

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a decade of evolution in Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) attacks and defenses, noting that modern code-reuse attacks face significant challenges under state-of-the-art protections. The paper introduces Newton, a dynamic gadget-discovery framework that uses constraint-driven dynamic taint analysis to identify exploitable callsites and callees in protected programs. Unlike static approaches, Newton observes runtime execution to model attacker-controlled memory dependencies and uncover gadgets even in the presence of defenses like Control Flow Integrity (CFI), ASLR, or pointer encryption. The key insight is that Newton's dynamic analysis can systematically model and compare diverse defenses by adjusting write and target constraints, revealing equivalence classes among superficially different protections.
paper_title: The Dynamics of Innocent Flesh on the Bone: Code Reuse Ten Years Later
paper_abstract: In 2007, Shacham published a seminal paper on Return-Oriented Programming (ROP), the first systematic formulation of code reuse. The paper has been highly influential, profoundly shaping the way we still think about code reuse today: an attacker analyzes the “geometry” of victim binary code to locate gadgets and chains these to craft an exploit. This model has spurred much research, with a rapid progression of increasingly sophisticated code reuse attacks and defenses over time. After ten years, the common perception is that state-of-the-art code reuse defenses are effective in significantly raising the bar and making attacks exceedingly hard. In this paper, we challenge this perception and show that an attacker going beyond “geometry” (static analysis) and considering the “dynamics” (dynamic analysis) of a victim program can easily find function call gadgets even in the presence of state-of-the-art code-reuse defenses. To support our claims, we present Newton, a run-time gadget-discovery framework based on constraint-driven dynamic taint analysis. Newton can model a broad range of defenses by mapping their properties into simple, stackable, reusable constraints, and automatically generate gadgets that comply with these constraints. Using Newton, we systematically map and compare state-of-the-art defenses, demonstrating that even simple interactions with popular server programs are adequate for finding gadgets for all state-of-the-art code-reuse defenses. We conclude with an nginx case study, which shows that a Newton-enabled attacker can craft attacks which comply with the restrictions of advanced defenses, such as CPI and context-sensitive CFI.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a new attack vector on Bitcoin mining pools called Fork-After-Withholding (FAW), which combines elements of selfish mining and block withholding attacks. The FAW attack is more lucrative than traditional block withholding attacks (56% higher reward for the attacker) and lacks a viable defense. Unlike previous attacks, the Miner's Dilemma does not hold under FAW—when two pools attack each other, the larger pool gains at the expense of the smaller one, potentially leading to a duopoly in the Bitcoin mining ecosystem. The attack involves splitting computational power between honest mining and infiltrating a target pool, then strategically releasing or withholding full proofs-of-work (FPoW) to create forks or deny rewards. The paper demonstrates that FAW attacks are always more profitable than honest mining and that the attack can be scaled to target multiple pools simultaneously.
paper_title: Be selfish and avoid dilemmas: fork-after-withholding (FAW) attacks on Bitcoin
paper_abstract: 1 In the Bitcoin system, participants are rewarded for solving cryptographic puzzles. In order to receive more consistent rewards over time, some participants organize mining pools and split the rewards from the pool in proportion to each participant’s contribution. However, several attacks threaten the ability to participate in pools. The block withholding (BWH) attack makes the pool reward system unfair by letting malicious participants receive unearned wages while only pretending to contribute work. When two pools launch BWH attacks against each other, they encounter the miner’s dilemma: in a Nash equilibrium, the revenue of both pools is diminished. In another attack called selfish mining, an attacker can unfairly earn extra rewards by deliberately generating forks. In this paper, we propose a novel attack called a fork after withholding (FAW) attack. FAW is not just another attack. The reward for an FAW attacker is always equal to or greater than that for a BWH attacker, and it is usable up to four times more often per pool than in BWH attack. When considering multiple pools — the current state of the Bitcoin network – the extra reward for an FAW attack is about 56% more than that for a BWH attack. Furthermore, when two pools execute FAW attacks on each other, the miner’s dilemma may not hold: under certain circumstances, the larger pool can consistently win. More importantly, an FAW attack, while using intentional forks, does not suffer from practicality issues, unlike selfish mining. We also discuss partial countermeasures against the FAW attack, but finding a cheap and efficient countermeasure remains an open problem. As a result, we expect to see FAW attacks among mining pools. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes a study that infiltrated a prominent Russian cybercrime market ('RuMarket') to analyze the trade of software vulnerabilities and exploits from 2010 to 2017. The paper highlights the lifecycle of exploits, showing how standalone exploits often serve as innovation drivers before being repackaged into malware or exploit kits (EKITs) for broader deployment. The author notes that exploit vendors are becoming faster at releasing exploits for newly disclosed vulnerabilities, with a 30% annual increase in speed. The study also examines pricing dynamics, target preferences (Microsoft, Adobe, Oracle), and the correlation between market activity and real-world exploit usage. Notably, exploit kits reduce development costs and democratize access to exploits, while bug bounty programs often pay less than the cybercrime market, incentivizing vendors to sell exploits multiple times in underground markets rather than responsibly disclose them.
paper_title: Economic factors of vulnerability trade and exploitation
paper_abstract: Cybercrime markets support the development and diffusion of new attack technologies, vulnerability exploits, and malware. Whereas the revenue streams of cyber attackers have been studied multiple times in the literature, no quantitative account currently exists on the economics of attack acquisition and deployment. Yet, this understanding is critical to characterize the production of (traded) exploits, the economy that drives it, and its effects on the overall attack scenario. In this paper we provide an empirical investigation of the economics of vulnerability exploitation, and the effects of market factors on likelihood of exploit. Our data is collected first-handedly from a prominent Russian cybercrime market where the trading of the most active attack tools reported by the security industry happens. Our findings reveal that exploits in the underground are priced similarly or above vulnerabilities in legitimate bug-hunting programs, and that the refresh cycle of exploits is slower than currently often assumed. On the other hand, cybercriminals are becoming faster at introducing selected vulnerabilities, and the market is in clear expansion both in terms of players, traded exploits, and exploit pricing. We then evaluate the effects of these market variables on likelihood of attack realization, and find strong evidence of the correlation between market activity and exploit deployment. We discuss implications on vulnerability metrics, economics, and exploit measurement.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a novel and stealthy DDoS attack on n-tier web applications called 'Tail Attacks'. The attack cleverly exploits 'millibottlenecks'—brief resource contention periods lasting milliseconds—by sending timed pulses of attack traffic during 'ON' bursts, followed by 'OFF' periods to avoid detection. This causes queue overflows across distributed tiers, leading to dropped requests and significantly increased tail latencies (4x-8x at the 95th percentile) in real cloud environments like EC2, Azure, and NSF CloudLab. The paper models these attacks using queueing networks and introduces a sophisticated feedback control mechanism using a Kalman filter to dynamically adjust attack parameters, maintaining optimal stealth and effectiveness. Colyer notes the attack's cleverness in evading traditional IDS/IPS tools by mimicking normal traffic patterns while causing disproportionate damage.
paper_title: Tail Attacks on Web Applications
paper_abstract: 1 As the extension of Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks to application layer in recent years, researchers pay much interest in these new variants due to a low-volume and intermittent pattern with a higher level of stealthiness, invaliding the state-of-the-art DDoS detection/defense mechanisms. We describe a new type of low-volume application layer DDoS attack–Tail Attacks on Web Applications. Such attack exploits a newly identified system vulnerability of n-tier web applications (millibottlenecks with sub-second duration and resource contention with strong dependencies among distributed nodes) with the goal of causing the long-tail latency problem of the target web application (e.g., 95th percentile response time > 1 second) and damaging the long-term business of the service provider, while all the system resources are far from saturation, making it difficult to trace the cause of performance degradation. We present a modified queueing network model to analyze the impact of our attacks in n-tier architecture systems, and numerically solve the optimal attack parameters. We adopt a feedback control-theoretic (e.g., Kalman filter) framework that allows attackers to fit the dynamics of background requests or system state by dynamically adjusting attack parameters. To evaluate the practicality of such attacks, we conduct extensive validation through not only analytical, numerical, and simulation results but also real cloud production setting experiments via a representative benchmark website equipped with state-of-the-art DDoS defense tools. We further proposed a solution to detect and defense the proposed attacks, involving three stages: fine-grained monitoring, identifying bursts, and blocking bots. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Solidus as an innovative solution for confidential distributed ledger transactions in bank-intermediated systems, addressing the challenge of transaction-graph confidentiality where even pseudonyms can reveal sensitive information. The paper introduces a novel protocol leveraging publicly-verifiable oblivious RAM (PVORM) to conceal transaction values and sender-receiver relationships, ensuring only banks know their customers' identities while maintaining public verifiability for auditors. Colyer praises the system's ability to enable near-instantaneous asset settlement, reducing systemic risk in financial sectors, though notes potential limitations in supporting anti-money laundering obligations. The design closely mirrors real-world financial structures, with banks managing user accounts and asset notaries injecting new assets, while PVORM ensures confidentiality and correctness of ledger updates through zero-knowledge proofs.
paper_title: Solidus: confidential distributed ledger transactions via publicly verifiable ORAM
paper_abstract: and financial institutions are exploring ledger-based systems for instantaneous financial settlement. For many of these companies, confidentiality is a major concern and Bitcoin-type systems are markedly insufficient. Those systems expose transaction values and the pseudonyms of transacting entities, often permitting deanonymization [45]. Concerns over this leakage are driving many financial institutions to restrict on-chain storage to transaction digests, placing details elsewhere [12, 36, 60]. Such architectures discard the key benefits of blockchains as centralized authoritative ledgers and reduce them to little more than a timestamping service. The overall structure of current blockchains additionally misaligns with that of the modern financial system. The direct peer-topeer transactions in Bitcoin and similar systems interfere with the customer-service role and know-your-customer regulatory requirements of financial institutions. Instead, the financial industry is exploring a model that we call bank-intermediated systems [36, 60]. In such systems a small number of entities—which we call banks— manage transactions of on-chain assets on behalf of a large number of users. For example, a handful of retail banks could use a bankintermediated ledger to authoritatively record stock purchases by millions of customers. By design, bank-intermediated systems faithfully replicate asset flows within modern financial institutions. While a number of bank-intermediated blockchain systems have been proposed, e.g., [1, 26, 62], these systems either do not provide inherently strong confidentiality or do so by sequestering data off-chain, preventing on-chain settlement. Coin mixes, e.g., [30, 41, 54, 61], and cryptocurrencies such as Monero [3] and Zcash [7] do improve confidentiality, but with notable limitations.
