blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Bolt as a privacy-enhancing solution for payment channels in decentralized currencies like Bitcoin. While payment channels address scalability issues by moving transactions off-chain, they introduce privacy vulnerabilities where identities and balances can be exposed. Bolt aims to mitigate these weaknesses by providing strong anonymity guarantees: merchants cannot learn customer identities, customers can remain unaware of merchant identities, intermediaries cannot identify transacting parties or payment amounts, and multi-hop channels hide payment values from intermediaries. The paper builds on the concept of payment channels (e.g., Lightning Network) but focuses specifically on privacy rather than scalability. Colyer notes that while Bolt’s approach is promising, it doesn’t solve fundamental issues like escrow liquidity or regulatory challenges like KYC/AML compliance.
paper_title: Bolt: Anonymous Payment Channels for Decentralized Currencies
paper_abstract: It is well known that pseudonymity in blockchains such as Bitcoin or Ethereum does not really hide the identity of the author of a payment. A number of attacks have been documented in the literature to deanonymize blockchain transactions. This is also the case of fully anonymous blockchains such as Monero and ZCash for which traffic analysis methods can be used. The goal of this paper is to outline a solution to the above problem in the most general (and difficult) case, namely that of pseudonymous blockchains. We restrict to the case of blockchains supporting smart contracts, with specific reference to Ethereum. Borrowing an approach used in the context of anonymous communication networks, we design a solution supporting 𝑘-anonymous payments against every eavesdropper, including the network adversary. Roughly, the idea is to organize users in rings of cover transactions, through which users indistinguishably exchange actual data or random noise and the initiator is hidden within the ring. Importantly, no off-chain communication is required.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the Bolt paper, which introduces Blind Off-chain Lightweight Transactions (Bolt) for constructing privacy-preserving payment channels in decentralized currencies. The paper addresses the challenge of enabling secure, anonymous payments off-chain while minimizing information leakage to merchants or the network. Bolt achieves this through a combination of compact e-cash schemes, zero-knowledge proofs, and cryptographic techniques like encryption chains and blind signatures. The author highlights Bolt's ability to support unidirectional, bidirectional, and third-party payments while preserving privacy—merchants learn only the existence and value of payments, and intermediaries in third-party transactions remain oblivious to identities or amounts. The key insight is the use of cryptographic primitives to enforce fairness and prevent double-spending without relying on trusted intermediaries.
paper_title: Bolt: Anonymous Payment Channels for Decentralized Currencies

In cases where no direct payment channel exists between two parties, these proposals also allow participants to route transactions via intermediate peers [45]. The main benefit of the payment channel paradigm is that it dramatically reduces the transaction volume arriving at the blockchain, without adding new trusted and centralized parties. While payment channels offer a solution to the scaling problem, they inherit many of the well-known privacy weaknesses of Bitcoin [40, 46]. Although payments are conducted off chain, any party may learn the pseudonymous identities and initial (resp. final) channel balances of the participants. More critically, payment channels provide few privacy protections against transaction counterparties. By establishing a channel to pay for e.g., Tor bandwidth or web content, a user implicitly links each payment on a given channel to all of her other payments on this channel. This is particularly problematic in the likely event that payments are routed via a common intermediate peer — such as a currency exchange — since the intermediary must now be trusted to keep private your full payment history. Some proposals, such as the Lightning Network, have proposed to work around this problem by routing the payment via multiple intermediary nodes; however (as we discuss in §6) this approach substantially increases the complexity of establishing payment channels, and reveals payment information in the event that even a subset of the intermediaries collude. Several academic works have recently proposed solutions that address the privacy problems of Bitcoin-type currencies [29, 41, 42, 47]. blog_summary: The blog post marks the end of the year for 'The Morning Paper' and reflects on Adrian Colyer's three-year journey of reading and summarizing a computer science research paper every weekday. He highlights the unexpected value of exploring a broad range of topics, noting that the most useful papers were often those he couldn't predict in advance. The post also emphasizes the joy of sharing research that aids others in their work. Additionally, it includes a curated list of ten notable papers from the term, spanning diverse areas such as programming languages, security, machine learning, systems, and AI, showcasing the breadth of topics covered throughout the year.

Adrian Colyer highlights this paper as a groundbreaking exploration of integrating machine learning into core database systems, specifically through 'learned index structures.' The authors propose replacing traditional hand-engineered data structures like B-Trees with machine-learned models, demonstrating potential speed improvements of up to 70% and memory savings by an order of magnitude. Colyer emphasizes the broader implications of this approach, framing it as a shift toward 'workload personalization' in systems software, where models are tailored to specific workloads (akin to how modern web services personalize content for users). He notes that this idea could revolutionize systems design, particularly as neural networks become more efficient on GPUs and TPUs. The paper focuses on read-only in-memory analytical workloads, showing how learned models can approximate cumulative distribution functions to predict key positions, transforming O(log n) lookups into constant-time operations. Colyer also underscores the importance of preserving guarantees (e.g., error bounds) in such models, drawing parallels to probabilistic data structures like Bloom filters.
paper_title: The Case for Learned Index Structures
paper_abstract: Indexes are models: a B-Tree-Index can be seen as a model to map a key to the position of a record within a sorted array, a Hash-Index as a model to map a key to a position of a record within an unsorted array, and a BitMap-Index as a model to indicate if a data record exists or not. In this exploratory research paper, we start from this premise and posit that all existing index structures can be replaced with other types of models, including deep-learning models, which we term learned indexes. The key idea is that a model can learn the sort order or structure of lookup keys and use this signal to effectively predict the position or existence of records. We theoretically analyze under which conditions learned indexes outperform traditional index structures and describe the main challenges in designing learned index structures. Our initial results show, that by using neural nets we are able to outperform cache-optimized B-Trees by up to 70% in speed while saving an order-of-magnitude in memory over several real-world data sets. More importantly though, we believe that the idea of replacing core components of a data management system through learned models has far reaching implications for future systems designs and that this work just provides a glimpse of what might be possible.

figures.caption: Comparison between B-Tree Index and Learned Index. The B-Tree Index uses a tree structure to map keys to positions, while the Learned Index uses a model (e.g., neural network) to predict positions directly.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the impressive performance gains of using learned models to replace traditional index structures like B-Trees in systems software. The paper introduces Recursive Model Indexes (RMI), which use a hierarchy of models to predict the position of keys, achieving up to 3x speed improvements and an order-of-magnitude space reduction compared to B-Trees. The key insight is that learned models can better capture data distribution nuances, especially when layered recursively. The blog also explores learned point indexes (hash maps) and existence indexes (Bloom filters), demonstrating that learned models can optimize memory usage and performance, particularly in scenarios with skewed or complex data distributions. The paper evaluates these approaches on real-world datasets, showing consistent advantages over traditional methods.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights AlphaZero's remarkable achievement in generalizing the AlphaGo Zero approach to chess, shogi, and Go, demonstrating the power of a generic reinforcement learning algorithm. He emphasizes AlphaZero's ability to learn from self-play with only the rules of the game, achieving superhuman performance in hours rather than decades of handcrafted development. The blog post particularly focuses on AlphaZero's 'human-like' style of play, its rediscovery of classic openings, and its efficient search strategy that leverages deep neural networks to focus on promising variations. Colyer also notes the technical adaptations required to extend the AlphaGo Zero architecture to chess and shogi, which lack the translation-invariant properties of Go.
paper_title: Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General Reinforcement Learning Algorithm
paper_abstract: The game of chess is the most widely-studied domain in the history of artificial intelligence. The strongest programs are based on a combination of sophisticated search techniques, domain-specific adaptations, and handcrafted evaluation functions that have been refined by human experts over several decades. In contrast, the AlphaGo Zero program recently achieved superhuman performance in the game of Go, by tabula rasa reinforcement learning from games of self-play. In this paper, we generalise this approach into a single AlphaZero algorithm that can achieve, tabula rasa, superhuman performance in many challenging domains. Starting from random play, and given no domain knowledge except the game rules, AlphaZero achieved within 24 hours a superhuman level of play in the games of chess and shogi (Japanese chess) as well as Go, and convincingly defeated a world-champion program in each case. The study of computer chess is as old as computer science itself. Babbage, Turing, Shannon, and von Neumann devised hardware, algorithms and theory to analyse and play the game of chess. Chess subsequently became the grand challenge task for a generation of artificial intelligence researchers, culminating in high-performance computer chess programs that perform at superhuman level (9, 13). However, these systems are highly tuned to their domain, and cannot be generalised to other problems without significant human effort. A long-standing ambition of artificial intelligence has been to create programs that can instead learn for themselves from first principles (26). Recently, the AlphaGo Zero algorithm achieved superhuman performance in the game of Go, by representing Go knowledge using deep convolutional neural networks (22, 28), trained solely by reinforcement learning from games of self-play (29). In this paper, we apply a similar but fully generic algorithm, which we 1 call AlphaZero, to the games of chess and shogi as well as Go, without any additional domain knowledge except th...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a fascinating paper from OpenAI that demonstrates how emergent complexity can arise from multi-agent competition in simulated 3D environments using reinforcement learning. The key insight is that agents trained via self-play in competitive scenarios develop sophisticated and human-like strategies without explicit programming—just through sparse rewards tied to game outcomes. For example, in 'You Shall Not Pass,' a blocking agent learns to raise its hand to block, while the opponent adapts by ducking underneath. The paper also explores the training techniques behind these discoveries, including the use of proximal policy optimization (PPO), distributed training, and techniques to encourage exploration and prevent overfitting. Notably, the emergent behaviors show some transferability to new tasks, such as an agent trained in Sumo maintaining balance under strong wind forces despite never encountering wind during training.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the paper's ambitious goal of creating a unified deep learning model capable of handling multiple domains and modalities (speech, text, images) simultaneously. The author praises the MultiModel architecture for its ability to support diverse input/output modalities, maintain a shared representation across tasks, and incorporate necessary computational blocks like attention and mixture-of-experts layers. The paper demonstrates that a single model trained on eight different tasks (e.g., speech recognition, image classification, translation) performs comparably to task-specific models, even outperforming them in low-data scenarios. Notably, the model shows transfer learning benefits between seemingly unrelated tasks, suggesting shared computational primitives. The architecture's design—modality-specific sub-networks feeding into a shared encoder/decoder—is praised for its efficiency and flexibility.
paper_title: One Model To Learn Them All
paper_abstract: Deep learning yields great results across many fields, from speech recognition, image classification, to translation. But for each problem, getting a deep model to work well involves research into the architecture and a long period of tuning. We present a single model that yields good results on a number of problems spanning multiple domains. In particular, this single model is trained concurrently on ImageNet, multiple translation tasks, image captioning (COCO dataset), a speech recognition corpus, and an English parsing task. Our model architecture incorporates building blocks from multiple domains. It contains convolutional layers, an attention mechanism, and sparsely-gated layers. Each of these computational blocks is crucial for a subset of the tasks we train on. Interestingly, even if a block is not crucial for a task, we observe that adding it never hurts performance and in most cases improves it on all tasks. We also show that tasks with less data benefit largely from joint training with other tasks, while performance on large tasks degrades only slightly if at all.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes the Meltdown paper, highlighting its groundbreaking discovery of a critical security vulnerability in modern CPUs. The blog emphasizes how Meltdown exploits out-of-order execution—a feature introduced in 1967 by Tomasulo—to bypass memory isolation protections, allowing unprivileged processes to read kernel memory. Colyer notes the paper's clear explanation of the attack's mechanics, including speculative execution, transient instructions, and the Flush+Reload cache side-channel technique. He also points out the paper's thorough evaluation across various hardware platforms and its revelation that the vulnerability has existed in Intel microarchitectures since 2010. The independent discovery of Meltdown by Google's Project Zero underscores the significance of the finding.
paper_title: Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space
paper_abstract: The security of computer systems fundamentally relies on memory isolation, e.g., kernel address ranges are marked as non-accessible and are protected from user access. In this paper, we present Meltdown. Meltdown exploits side effects of out-of-order execution on modern processors to read arbitrary kernel-memory locations including personal data and passwords. Out-of-order execution is an indispensable performance feature and present in a wide range of modern processors. The attack is independent of the operating system, and it does not rely on any software vulnerabilities. Meltdown breaks all security guarantees provided by address space isolation as well as paravirtualized environments and, thus, every security mechanism building upon this foundation. On affected systems, Meltdown enables an adversary to read memory of other processes or virtual machines in the cloud without any permissions or privileges, affecting millions of customers and virtually every user of a personal computer. We show that the KAISER defense mechanism for KASLR has the important (but inadvertent) side effect of impeding Meltdown. We stress that KAISER must be deployed immediately to prevent largescale exploitation of this severe information leakage.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Spectre as a terrifying yet technically fascinating attack that combines side-channel attacks, fault attacks, and return-oriented programming (ROP) to read arbitrary memory from a victim's process. Unlike Meltdown, Spectre works on AMD and ARM processors, making it a widespread threat across billions of devices. The attack exploits speculative execution in modern CPUs, particularly branch prediction mechanisms like the Branch Target Buffer (BTB), to trick the CPU into executing malicious instruction sequences. Colyer emphasizes the attack's practicality, noting it can be mounted with just a few lines of JavaScript delivered via trusted websites (e.g., ads) and can exfiltrate data through cache side channels. The paper's key insight is the exploitation of speculative execution and branch misprediction to bypass security boundaries, even in well-written software.
paper_title: Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution
paper_abstract: —Modern processors use branch prediction and speculative execution to maximize performance. For example, if the destination of a branch depends on a memory value that is in the process of being read, CPUs will try to guess the destination and attempt to execute ahead. When the memory value finally arrives, the CPU either discards or commits the speculative computation. Speculative logic is unfaithful in how it executes, can access the victim’s memory and registers, and can perform operations with measurable side effects. Spectre attacks involve inducing a victim to speculatively perform operations that would not occur during correct program execution and which leak the victim’s confidential information via a side channel to the adversary. This paper describes practical attacks that combine methodology from side channel attacks, fault attacks, and return-oriented programming that can read arbitrary memory from the victim’s process. More broadly, the paper shows that speculative execution implementations violate the security assumptions underpinning numerous software security mechanisms, including operating system process separation, containerization, just-in-time (JIT) compilation, and countermeasures to cache timing and side-channel attacks. These attacks represent a serious threat to actual systems since vulnerable speculative execution capabilities are found in microprocessors from Intel, AMD, and ARM that are used in billions of devices. While makeshift processor-specific countermeasures are possible in some cases, sound solutions will require fixes to processor designs as well as updates to instruction set architectures (ISAs) to give hardware architects and software developers a common understanding as to what computation state CPU implementations are (and are not) permitted to leak. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer discusses Daniel Bernstein's 2007 paper on the security principles behind qmail, a mail transfer agent designed to address the numerous vulnerabilities in sendmail. Bernstein argues that security should be prioritized over speed, emphasizing the need for invulnerable software systems. The paper outlines three key principles for achieving security: reducing bug rates, minimizing code volume, and reducing trusted code. Bernstein also critiques three common distractions in security engineering: reactive patching, least privilege, and premature optimization. The blog highlights qmail's remarkable security record—only four known bugs and no security issues over ten years—attributed to its design choices, such as explicit data flow, simplified integer semantics, and modular architecture. Colyer underscores the importance of meta-engineering programming environments to make incorrect software harder to write, rather than easier to write.
paper_title: Some thoughts on security after ten years of qmail 1.0
paper_abstract: The qmail software package is a widely used Internet-mail transfer agent that has been covered by a security guarantee since 1997. In this paper, the qmail author reviews the history and security-relevant architecture of qmail; articulates partitioning standards that qmail fails to meet; analyzes the engineering that has allowed qmail to survive this failure; and draws various conclusions regarding the future of secure programming. Here’s what I wrote in the qmail documentation in December 1995: Every few months CERT announces Yet Another Security Hole In Sendmail—something that lets local or even remote users take complete control of the machine. I’m sure there are many more holes waiting to be discovered; Sendmail’s design means that any minor bug in 41000 lines of code is a major security risk. Other popular mailers, such as Smail, and even mailing-list managers, such as Majordomo, seem just as bad.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the RustBelt paper as a significant step toward formally verifying the safety claims of the Rust programming language. While Rust is praised for its ownership-based type system that provides high-level safety and low-level control, the blog notes that Rust's safety guarantees have never been formally proven. The paper addresses this gap by providing a formal, machine-checked safety proof for a meaningful subset of Rust using the Iris separation logic framework. The authors verify many standard Rust libraries (e.g., Arc, Rc, Mutex) and introduce a framework to determine when unsafe library code can be considered a safe extension of the language. The blog emphasizes the paper's depth and complexity, noting that it is a POPL paper requiring significant effort to fully grasp, but its core results and implications for Rust are profound.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews JaVerT, a JavaScript Verification Toolchain designed to verify functional correctness properties of JavaScript programs through annotations like pre-/post-conditions and loop invariants. The tool addresses JavaScript's dynamic behaviors (e.g., extensible objects, dynamic property access) by first compiling JavaScript to an intermediate language (JSIL) via a logic-preserving compiler (JS-2-JSIL). JaVerT uses JS Logic, a separation logic with heap models and predicates for JavaScript-specific structures (e.g., prototype chains, closures), to write specifications that abstract heap details for developers. The verification process relies on JSIL Verify, a semi-automatic tool combining symbolic execution and an entailment engine (using Z3 SMT solver) to check Hoare triples. The authors also axiomatize JavaScript internal functions (e.g., GetValue, PutValue) to enable reasoning about core language behaviors. JaVerT targets critical JavaScript code like Node.js libraries, aiming to ensure correctness in complex dynamic scenarios.
paper_title: JaVerT: JavaScript Verification Toolchain
paper_abstract: Having high-quality and reliable software is an increasingly stringent requirement for most organisations. While traditional static program analysis techniques, such as symbolic execution and formal verification, can help produce error-free software, their successful application to large, rapidly-changing codebases has been limited. In response to this, recent years have seen the development of a number of tools that specifically target their analysis at real-world projects. At Facebook, the Infer tool has been successfully deployed to find lightweight bugs in codebases spanning millions of lines of code, by leveraging various continuous reasoning techniques. This project extends Gillian, a multi-language platform for symbolic analysis developed in the Verified Software group at Imperial, with continuous reasoning foundations that substantially advance its applicability to real-world projects. In particular, we have: extended its instantiations for C and JavaScript in order to allow them to analyse multi-file projects; and incorporated a mechanism for reusing previously-stored results in order to focus analysis on only the fragments of the source program that have changed. Finally, by analysing two real-world JavaScript and C projects, we have demonstrated the significant improvement in the usability of Gillian by a general developer, as well as the correctness of our implementation. Acknowledgements I would like thank my supervisor, Professor Philippa Gardner, for her enthusiastic support and encouragement throughout the project. I would also like to extend a huge thanks to Sacha Ayoun and Petar Maksimović for their patience and near 24/7 availability in responding to my numerous questions. Last, but not least, I would like thank my family and friends for their unfaltering support throughout my entire degree. Contents

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Disel, a framework for developing and verifying message-passing distributed systems, as a significant contribution to the field. The key strengths of Disel are its use of dependent types to ensure program correctness with respect to abstract protocols and its support for compositional verification, where modules can be independently verified and composed without re-verification. Disel combines ideas from dependent type theory, interactive theorem proving, separation-style program logics, and distributed protocol design to provide a DSL for protocol designers, a higher-order programming language for system implementors, and an expressive program logic for human verifiers. The framework is implemented in Coq and allows programs to be extracted to OCaml for execution, with a small trusted shim ensuring type safety in distributed settings. The blog post emphasizes Disel's ability to separate concerns through protocols, its support for inductive invariants, and its capability to combine multiple protocols, making it a powerful tool for reasoning about distributed systems.

Following this trend, we identify the following challenges in designing a verification tool to support compositional proofs of distributed systems. (1) Protocol-program modularity. One should be able to define an abstract model of a distributed protocol (typically represented by a form of a state-transition system) without tying it to a specific implementation. Any purported implementation should then be proven to follow the protocol’s abstract model. This separation of concerns supports reuse of existing techniques for reasoning about the high-level behavior of a system, while allowing for optimized implementations, without redefining the high-level interaction protocol. (2) Modular program verification. Once proven to implement an abstract protocol, a program should be given a sufficiently expressive declarative specification, so that clients of the code never need to be examine the implementation itself. Furthermore, it should be possible to specify and verify programs made up of parts belonging to different protocols (horizontal compositionality). blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the surprising effectiveness of random testing in uncovering partition tolerance bugs in distributed systems, as demonstrated by tools like Jepsen. While academic wisdom often dismisses random testing as ineffective for such complex fault scenarios, the paper provides a theoretical foundation explaining why random testing works in practice. The author emphasizes the paper's contribution to defining coverage criteria (k-splitting, (k,l)-separation, minority isolation) that capture a large class of partition tolerance bugs and shows how random tests can probabilistically cover these criteria with high likelihood. The key insight is the application of the probabilistic method to prove the existence of small covering families of tests that can expose bugs with high probability, even without deterministic guarantees. The paper also extends these results to other domains like multi-threaded programs and VLSI circuits.
paper_title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Random Testing for Partition Tolerance Bugs
paper_abstract: Random testing has proven to be an effective way to catch bugs in concurrent and distributed systems. This is surprising, as the space of executions is enormous and conventional formal methods intuition would suggest that bad behaviors would only be found by extremely unlikely coincidences. Empirically, many bugs in distributed systems can be explained by interactions among only a small number of features. Thus, one can attempt to explain the effectiveness of random testing under various “small depth” hypotheses. In particular, it may be possible to test all interactions of k features for a small constant k by executing a family of tests that is exponentially or even doublyexponentially smaller than the family of all tests. Moreover, under certain conditions, a randomly chosen small set of tests is sufficient to cover all k-wise interactions with high probability. I will describe two concrete scenarios. First, I will describe bugs in distributed systems caused by network partition faults. In many practical instances, these bugs occur due to two or three key nodes, such as leaders or replicas, not being able to communicate, or because the leading node finds itself in a block of the partition without quorum. In this case, I will show using the probabilistic method that a small set of randomly chosen tests will cover all “small partition” scenarios with high probability. Second, I will consider bugs that arise due to unexpected schedules (interleavings) of concurrent events. Again, many bugs depend only on the relative ordering of a small number of events (the “bug depth” of the bug). In this case, I will show a testing algorithm that prioritizes low depth interleavings and a randomized testing algorithm that bounds the probability of sampling any behavior of bug depth k for a fixed k. The testing algorithm is based on combinatorial insights from the theory of partial orders, such as the notion of dimension and its generalization to d-hitting families as well as result...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer introduces 'Linear Haskell,' a paper from POPL 2018 that extends Haskell with linear types in a non-invasive way, ensuring existing programs remain compatible. The blog highlights the practical benefits of linear types, particularly in encoding resource usage protocols (e.g., file handling or socket APIs) to eliminate bugs and in enabling safe in-place updates for efficiency. The author praises the paper's readability and clarity, noting how linear types can statically enforce protocols and reduce unnecessary copying. The key insight is that linear types can bridge the gap between type safety and performance, making previously infeasible optimizations practical.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a static verification framework called 'Godel Checker' for message-passing concurrency in Go, addressing a notable gap in Go's ecosystem where existing tools offer minimal support for verifying correctness in concurrent programs. The paper leverages process calculi-based reasoning, translating Go source code into behavioral types that can be model-checked for safety and liveness properties, including global deadlock freedom and partial deadlock detection. The framework uses an SSA intermediate representation to infer behavioral types, which are then analyzed using the mCRL2 model checker and the KiTTeL termination analyzer. The approach is practical, completing analysis in seconds to minutes even for larger codebases, and abstracts away formal complexities from the user. Key insights include the translation of Go's channel-based concurrency into executable behavioral types and the application of formal verification techniques to a mainstream language like Go.
paper_title: A static verification framework for message passing in Go using behavioural types
paper_abstract: The Go programming language has been heavily adopted in industry as a language that efficiently combines systems programming with concurrency. Go’s concurrency primitives, inspired by process calculi such as CCS and CSP, feature channel-based communication and lightweight threads, providing a distinct means of structuring concurrent software. Despite its popularity, the Go programming ecosystem offers little to no support for guaranteeing the correctness of message-passing concurrent programs. This work proposes a practical verification framework for message passing concurrency in Go by developing a robust static analysis that infers an abstract model of a program’s communication behaviour in the form of a behavioural type, a powerful process calculi typing discipline. We make use of our analysis to deploy a model and termination checking based verification of the inferred behavioural type that is suitable for a range of safety and liveness properties of Go programs, providing several improvements over existing approaches. We evaluate our framework and its implementation on publicly available real-world Go code.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer provides a practitioner's guide to understanding programming languages papers, using Benjamin C. Pierce's 'Types and Programming Languages' as a reference. The post breaks down key concepts like syntax (terms, values), semantics (operational vs. denotational, small-step vs. big-step), and type systems. Colyer explains how to interpret mathematical notation, evaluation rules, and typing rules commonly found in such papers. The guide emphasizes the importance of understanding terms, values, and the difference between syntax and semantics, while also clarifying the role of type systems in ensuring program safety through progress and preservation theorems.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Robert Floyd's 1979 ACM Turing Award lecture, 'The paradigms of programming,' as a foundational discussion on how programming paradigms shape software design and engineering. Floyd argues that structured programming, while dominant, is not the sole paradigm, and emphasizes the importance of expanding one's repertoire of problem-solving strategies. The paper underscores how programming languages and environments either support or hinder these paradigms, and Floyd advocates for systematic self-improvement by revisiting and refining solutions to problems. He also critiques the incremental evolution of programming languages and stresses the need for languages to explicitly support major paradigms. The blog post particularly praises Floyd's insights on teaching programming methods explicitly rather than focusing solely on syntax or specific languages.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews Jon Bentley's 'Sample of Brilliance' column from 1987 in CACM, featuring contributions from Bob Floyd. The post highlights Floyd's improvements over Bentley's earlier sampling algorithm (Algorithm S), which was correct but inefficient for large N and M. Floyd's Algorithm F1 and its iterative variant F2 reduce the number of calls to the random number generator and improve performance significantly, especially for large inputs. The post also discusses Algorithm P for generating random permutations, which Floyd proved correct through a clever backward reasoning approach. The blog praises Floyd's mathematical insight and elegant solutions, demonstrating how a deeper understanding of the problem can lead to optimal algorithms.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer introduces Valiant's 1984 paper as a foundational work proposing a theory of learnability, analogous to computability but for what computers can learn rather than what they can compute. The paper seeks to define learnability in a general, algorithm-agnostic way, focusing on binary classification tasks where a learner must deduce a recognition algorithm from examples. Valiant formalizes this as 'probably approximately correct' (PAC) learning, where a learner must produce a hypothesis that approximates the target concept with high probability, using polynomial-time computations. Colyer highlights Valiant's abstract framework, which separates the learning protocol (e.g., querying examples or oracles) from the deduction procedure, and notes its relevance to both human learning and machine learning systems. The paper demonstrates learnability for classes like k-CNF and monotone DNF expressions, providing polynomial-time algorithms under specific conditions. Colyer underscores the paper's theoretical depth and its role in shaping modern machine learning theory.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer revisits Rumelhart et al.'s seminal 1986 paper on back-propagation, highlighting its role as a breakthrough algorithm for training neural networks with hidden layers. The blog post emphasizes how back-propagation enables hidden units to learn meaningful representations of input data by adjusting weights through gradient descent. Colyer walks through the paper's explanation of feed-forward computation, error calculation, and the chain rule-based derivation of weight updates, noting the elegance of the approach despite its simplicity. He also points out the paper's foundational contributions to modern deep learning, including the introduction of skip connections and momentum-based optimization techniques.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Shor's 1996 breakthrough paper as a 'Great moment in computing,' demonstrating that quantum computers can efficiently factor primes—a task with profound implications for cryptography. The blog post emphasizes the algorithm's significance, noting its first real-world execution in 2001 (factoring 15) and the challenge of understanding the paper's dense presentation. Colyer points to accessible explanations by Scott Aaronson and Kelsey Houston-Edward to clarify the algorithm's mechanics. Beyond the algorithm itself, the post explores the broader question of which problems quantum computers can solve efficiently, contrasting classical complexity classes (P, NP, NP-complete) with quantum complexity (BQP). It concludes that Shor's algorithm is a canonical example of a problem (factoring integers and discrete logarithms) where quantum computers outperform classical ones, leveraging superposition and interference to exploit global solution-space properties.
paper_title: Polynomial-time algorithms for prime factorization and discrete logarithms on a quantum computer
paper_abstract: A digital computer is generally believed to be an efficient universal computing device; that is, it is believed able to simulate any physical computing device with an increase in computation time by at most a polynomial factor. This may not be true when quantum mechanics is taken into consideration. This paper considers factoring integers and finding discrete logarithms, two problems which are generally thought to be hard on a classical computer and which have been used as the basis of several proposed cryptosystems. Efficient randomized algorithms are given for these two problems on a hypothetical quantum computer. These algorithms take a number of steps polynomial in the input size, e.g., the number of digits of the integer to be factored.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes John Preskill's keynote on the state of quantum computing, introducing the 'NISQ era' (Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum) which refers to quantum computers with 50-1000 qubits that are error-prone and limited in circuit depth. Preskill highlights the 'quantum chasm'—the gap between current NISQ devices and future fault-tolerant quantum computers requiring millions of qubits with error correction. The paper emphasizes quantum speedups in areas like optimization, deep learning, and simulation, while noting that quantum computers won't solve NP-hard problems efficiently. Preskill also distinguishes between circuit-based quantum computers and quantum annealers (like D-Wave), which are not yet theoretically proven to outperform classical methods.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews 'Quantum algorithms: an overview' by Montanaro, highlighting its broad survey of quantum algorithms and their applications rather than deep technical details. The post emphasizes key quantum algorithms like Grover's (quadratic speedup for unstructured search), amplitude amplification (quadratic speedup for heuristic search), and quantum walks (exponential speedups in hitting/mixing times). It also discusses adiabatic optimization and the limited number of exponential speedups in quantum computing due to query complexity bounds and reliance on hidden structures (e.g., Shor's algorithm exploiting the hidden subgroup problem). The paper introduces complexity classes like BPP and QMA and underscores the role of quantum Fourier transforms as a foundational building block.
paper_title: Quantum algorithms: an overview
paper_abstract: Quantum computers are designed to outperform standard computers by running quantum algorithms. Areas in which quantum algorithms can be applied include cryptography, search and optimisation, simulation of quantum systems, and solving large systems of linear equations. Here we briefly survey some known quantum algorithms, with an emphasis on a broad overview of their applications rather than their technical details. We include a discussion of recent developments and near-term applications of quantum algorithms.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the Blockstack paper, highlighting its exploration of building a naming and storage system on top of blockchain technology, starting with lessons learned from Namecoin. The paper critiques the challenges of using smaller blockchains like Namecoin for decentralized applications, emphasizing issues such as security vulnerabilities (e.g., 51% attacks), network reliability, selfish mining, and the failure of merged mining. The authors distill these challenges into five key lessons, concluding that decentralized systems should rely on the most secure and actively maintained blockchain, Bitcoin, in 2016. The paper then introduces Blockstack v2, which separates the control plane (handled by the blockchain) from the data plane (handled off-chain), using a 'virtualchain' layer to construct a state machine atop the blockchain. This design alleviates storage limitations and enables scalable naming and storage systems.
paper_title: Blockstack: a global naming and storage system secured by blockchains
paper_abstract: Blockchains like Bitcoin and Namecoin and their respective P2P networks have seen significant adoption in the past few years and show promise as naming systems with no trusted parties. Users can register human meaningful names and securely associate data with them, and only the owner of the particular private keys that registered them can write or update the name-value pair. In theory, many decentralized systems can be built using these blockchain networks, such as new, decentralized versions of DNS and PKI. As the technology is relatively new and evolving rapidly, however, little production data or experience is available to guide design tradeoffs. In this paper, we describe our experiences operating a large deployment of a decentralized PKI service built on top of the Namecoin blockchain. We present various challenges pertaining to network reliability, throughput, and security that we needed to overcome while registering and updating over 33,000 entries and 200,000 transactions on the Namecoin blockchain. Further, we discuss how our experience informed the design of a new blockchain-based naming and storage system called Blockstack. We detail why we switched from the Namecoin network to the Bitcoin network for the new system, and present operational lessons from this migration. Blockstack is released as open source software and currently powers a production PKI system for 55,000 users.

blog_summary: Chainspace is a decentralized application (DApp) platform built on smart contracts, designed to achieve higher scalability than Bitcoin or Ethereum. Adrian highlights its impressive performance, noting that a modest 60-core testbed achieves 350 transactions per second, far surpassing Bitcoin's 7 TPS and Ethereum's 4 TPS. The paper introduces a novel architecture where smart contracts are split into procedures (executed by a single party) and checkers (independent verifiers that validate correctness without executing the logic). This separation enables privacy-friendly contracts by design, as checkers can verify zero-knowledge proofs or SNARKs without exposing secret data. Adrian finds the concept intriguing but notes the challenge of practically writing checkers, comparing it to Hoare triples for pre- and post-condition verification. The paper also details Chainspace's sharded system design, which uses a Byzantine atomic commit protocol (S-BAC) combining PBFT and two-phase commit to ensure consistency across shards.
paper_title: Chainspace: A Sharded Smart Contracts Platform
paper_abstract: —Chainspace is a decentralized infrastructure, known as a distributed ledger, that supports user defined smart contracts and executes user-supplied transactions on their objects. The correct execution of smart contract transactions is verifiable by all. The system is scalable, by sharding state and the execution of transactions, and using S-BAC, a distributed commit protocol, to guarantee consistency. Chainspace is secure against subsets of nodes trying to compromise its integrity or availability properties through Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT), and extremely highauditability, non-repudiation and ‘blockchain’ techniques. Even when BFT fails, auditing mechanisms are in place to trace malicious participants. We present the design, rationale, and details of Chainspace; we argue through evaluating an implementation of the system about its scaling and other features; we illustrate a number of privacy-friendly smart contracts for smart metering, polling and banking and measure their performance. I. system, named CSCoin, as a system smart contract to allow for accounting between those parties. However, the security model of Chainspace, is different from traditional unpermissioned blockchains, that rely on proofof-work and global replication of state, such as Ethereum. In Chainspace smart contract authors designate the parts of the infrastructure that are trusted to maintain the integrity of their contract—and only depend on their correctness, as well as the correctness of contract sub-calls. This provides fine grained control of which part of the infrastructure need to be trusted on a per-contract basis, and also allows for horizontal scalability. This paper makes the following contributions: • It presents Chainspace, a system that can scale arbitrarily as the number of nodes increase, tolerates byzantine failures, and can be fully and publicly audited. • It presents a novel distributed atomic commit protocol, called S-BAC, for sharding generic smart contract transaction...

blog_summary: OmniLedger is presented as a groundbreaking decentralized ledger system that achieves Visa-level scalability while maintaining security and permissionless decentralization. Adrian Colyer highlights OmniLedger as a notable advancement in distributed systems and transaction processing, emphasizing its innovative combination of standard building blocks like sharding, Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT), and secure randomness generation. The paper introduces novel protocols such as Omnicon for intra-shard consensus and Atomix for secure cross-shard transactions, demonstrating how these components work together to enable linear scalability and low latency. The blog post also underscores the rapid progress in decentralized ledgers, positioning OmniLedger as a wake-up call for researchers in distributed systems who may have overlooked developments in this area. Key insights include the use of an identity blockchain, RandHound for secure randomness, and cryptographic sortition for leader election, all of which contribute to the system's robustness and security.
paper_title: OmniLedger: A secure, scale-out, decentralized ledger via sharding
paper_abstract: —Designing a secure permissionless distributed ledger (blockchain) that performs on par with centralized payment processors, such as Visa, is a challenging task. Most existing distributed ledgers are unable to scale-out, i.e., to grow their total processing capacity with the number of validators; and those that do, compromise security or decentralization. We present OmniLedger, a novel scale-out distributed ledger that preserves longterm security under permissionless operation. It ensures security and correctness by using a bias-resistant public-randomness protocol for choosing large, statistically representative shards that process transactions, and by introducing an efficient crossshard commit protocol that atomically handles transactions affecting multiple shards. OmniLedger also optimizes performance via parallel intra-shard transaction processing, ledger pruning via collectively-signed state blocks, and low-latency “trust-butverify” validation for low-value transactions. An evaluation of our experimental prototype shows that OmniLedger’s throughput scales linearly in the number of active validators, supporting Visa-level workloads and beyond, while confirming typical transactions in under two seconds. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the paper 'SoK: Consensus in the age of blockchains' by Bano et al., which provides a comprehensive systematization of knowledge (SoK) on blockchain consensus protocols. The blog highlights the complexity and rapid evolution of consensus mechanisms, emphasizing their foundational role in blockchain systems. Colyer notes that the paper categorizes consensus models into four main buckets: classical consensus (e.g., PBFT, XFT), permissionless decentralized networks (e.g., PoW, PoS), hybrid consensus (combining PoW with committee-based protocols like PBFT), and sharded systems (multiple committees with cross-shard agreement). The post delves into the trade-offs of probabilistic single-leader Proof-of-X systems (e.g., PoW, PoS) and hybrid consensus models, discussing their security guarantees, performance, and vulnerabilities. Key insights include the challenges of scaling PoW blockchains, the economic incentives in Nakamoto consensus, and the new attack vectors introduced by PoS systems.
paper_title: SoK: Consensus in the age of blockchains
paper_abstract: —The blockchain initially gained traction in 2008 as the technology underlying Bitcoin [105], but now has been employed in a diverse range of applications and created a global market worth over $150B as of 2017. What distinguishes blockchains from traditional distributed databases is the ability to operate in a decentralized setting without relying on a trusted third party. As such their core technical component is consensus: how to reach agreement among a group of nodes. This has been extensively studied already in the distributed systems community for closed systems, but its application to open blockchains has revitalized the field and led to a plethora of new designs. The inherent complexity of consensus protocols and their rapid and dramatic evolution makes it hard to contextualize the design landscape. We address this challenge by conducting a systematic and comprehensive study of blockchain consensus protocols. After first discussing key themes in classical consensus protocols, we describe: (i) protocols based on proof-of-work (PoW), (ii) proof-of-X (PoX) protocols that replace PoW with more energy-efficient alternatives, and (iii) hybrid protocols that are compositions or variations of classical consensus protocols. We develop a framework to evaluate their performance, security and design properties, and use it to systematize key themes in the protocol categories described above. This evaluation leads us to identify research gaps and challenges for the community to consider in future research endeavours. I. I NTRODUCTION Blockchains—the technology at the foundation of Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies—have been hailed as a major disruptive innovation with the potential to transform most industries. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 2015 paper as a foundational survey of Bitcoin and cryptocurrency technology, breaking down its core components into transactions and scripts, consensus and mining, and the peer-to-peer network. The blog emphasizes the paper's systematic analysis of Bitcoin's stability and practical workings, noting that while Bitcoin has functioned surprisingly well in practice, research is needed to understand *why* it works and whether it will continue to do so as conditions evolve. Colyer praises the paper's clarity in explaining Bitcoin's ad-hoc scripting language, the Nakamoto consensus mechanism, and the role of miners and transaction fees. He also underscores the paper's discussion of Bitcoin's governance challenges and the five key properties (eventual consensus, exponential convergence, liveness, correctness, and fairness) that underpin its stability.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the paper 'SoK: Research perspectives and challenges for Bitcoin and cryptocurrency' by Bonneau et al., focusing on modifications to Bitcoin, altcoins, and anonymity issues. The post highlights the three primary mechanisms for upgrading Bitcoin: hard forks, soft forks, and changes to relay policy, noting their trade-offs in terms of coordination and backward compatibility. Key parameters like block size, inter-block time, and monetary policy are discussed, with the authors emphasizing the controversial nature of increasing the 1 MB block size limit due to its impact on miner incentives. The paper also explores altcoins, their bootstrapping methods (e.g., forks, proof-of-burn, pegged sidechains), and mining strategies, including merged mining. Anonymity in Bitcoin is addressed, noting its limited unlinkability and the risks of transaction tracing and IP de-anonymization, with solutions like mixing protocols and systems like ZeroCash proposed for stronger privacy.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes a comprehensive survey by Conti et al. on security and privacy issues in Bitcoin, focusing on a catalog of major attacks and their defenses. The post highlights several double-spending attacks (Finney, Brute Force, Vector 76) and their mechanics, emphasizing that miners with disproportionate hashrate power can significantly increase the risk of such attacks. The key insight is that while waiting for multiple confirmations (e.g., 6 blocks) is the most effective defense, fast-payment scenarios require alternative detection mechanisms. The survey also discusses the catastrophic 51% attack (Goldfinger attack), selfish mining, block withholding, and other misbehavior attacks, concluding that no complete protection exists and that these remain open challenges for researchers.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a comprehensive measurement study on the decentralization of Bitcoin and Ethereum networks, conducted over 2016-2017. The paper challenges assumptions about decentralization by providing empirical data on mining power distribution, utilization, fairness, and network characteristics. Notably, the study finds that both networks rely heavily on a small number of mining entities, with Bitcoin's top four miners controlling over 53% of power and Ethereum's top three controlling 61%. The paper also reveals that proof-of-work mining is less decentralized than a Byzantine quorum system of size 20, and that miners may obfuscate their true power to appear more decentralized. Other findings include high mining power utilization (99% in Bitcoin, 90-97% in Ethereum) and evidence that top miners in both networks are more successful at appending blocks relative to their mining power, indicating potential centralization pressures.
paper_title: Decentralization in Bitcoin and Ethereum networks
paper_abstract: Blockchain-based cryptocurrencies have demonstrated how to securely implement traditionally centralized systems, such as currencies, in a decentralized fashion. However, there have been few measurement studies on the level of decentralization they achieve in practice. We present a measurement study on various decentralization metrics of two of the leading cryptocurrencies with the largest market capitalization and user base, Bitcoin and Ethereum. We investigate the extent of decentralization by measuring the network resources of nodes and the interconnection among them, the protocol requirements affecting the operation of nodes, and the robustness of the two systems against attacks. In particular, we adapted existing internet measurement techniques and used the Falcon Relay Network as a novel measurement tool to obtain our data. We discovered that neither Bitcoin nor Ethereum has strictly better properties than the other. We also provide concrete suggestions for improving both systems.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a novel approach to detecting fake news on social media by focusing on the propagation patterns ('footprints') of messages rather than their content. The key insight is that the way a message spreads through a network—its sequence of spreaders—provides strong signals about its authenticity. The authors' system, TraceMiner, achieves state-of-the-art classification accuracy even without analyzing message content, outperforming content-based methods in experiments. TraceMiner combines user embeddings (learned from social network structures) with sequence modeling using LSTM-RNNs to classify diffusion traces. The paper demonstrates that structural and temporal patterns in propagation are more reliable indicators of fake news than textual content alone.
paper_title: Tracing fake news footprints: characterizing social media messages by how they propagate
paper_abstract: Social media is becoming popular for news consumption due to its fast dissemination, easy access, and low cost. However, it also enables the wide propagation of fake news, i.e., news with intentionally false information. Detecting fake news is an important task, which not only ensures users receive authentic information but also helps maintain a trustworthy news ecosystem. The majority of existing detection algorithms focus on finding clues from news contents, which are generally not effective because fake news is often intentionally written to mislead users by mimicking true news. Therefore, we need to explore auxiliary information to improve detection. The social context during news dissemination process on social media forms the inherent tri-relationship, the relationship among publishers, news pieces, and users, which has potential to improve fake news detection. For example, partisan-biased publishers are more likely to publish fake news, and low-credible users are more likely to share fake news. In this paper, we study the novel problem of exploiting social context for fake news detection. We propose a tri-relationship embedding framework TriFN, which models publisher-news relations and user-news interactions simultaneously for fake news classification. We conduct experiments on two real-world datasets, which demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms other baseline methods for fake news detection.

figures.title: Tri-relationship among publishers, news pieces, and users
figures.caption: An illustration of tri-relationship among publishers, news pieces, and users, during the news dissemination process. For example, an edge (p → a) demonstrates that publisher p publishes news item a, an edge (a → u) represents news item a is spread by user u, and an edge (u 1 ↔ u 2 ) indicates the social relation between user u 1 and u 2 .

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a paper that applies computer science techniques to help ride-hailing drivers (e.g., Uber/Lyft) maximize their earnings. The key insight is that naive drivers following random schedules leave up to 50% of potential earnings on the table, while data-savvy drivers using dynamic programming algorithms can increase earnings by up to 70% (median) by strategically relocating or pausing work. The paper models the problem as a dynamic programming optimization with time-dependent transition, travel time, and reward matrices, and introduces robust strategies that handle uncertainty in data. The authors validate their approach using NYC taxi data enriched with Uber pricing data, showing significant earnings improvements over naive strategies.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a paper that addresses the problem of Simpson's paradox in social data analysis, where aggregated trends can mislead by hiding underlying subgroup patterns. The authors propose a method to systematically detect Simpson's paradoxes by examining trends in outcome variables (Y) as a function of independent variables (X), and checking if these trends reverse when data is disaggregated by conditioning on another variable (Z). The paper demonstrates this method using Stack Exchange data, revealing paradoxes such as the counterintuitive trend where later answers in a user's session appear more likely to be accepted as best, which reverses when disaggregated by session length due to survivorship bias. The authors argue that Simpson's paradox often indicates meaningful subgroup differences in social data, and their method can help researchers avoid incorrect inferences and uncover hidden insights.
paper_title: Can you trust the trend? Discovering Simpson’s paradoxes in social data
paper_abstract: arXiv:1801.04385v1 [cs.CY] 13 Jan 2018 Kristina Lerman We investigate how Simpson’s paradox affects analysis of trends in social data. According to the paradox, the trends observed in data that has been aggregated over an entire population may be different from, and even opposite to, those of the underlying subgroups. Failure to take this effect into account can lead analysis to wrong conclusions. We present a statistical method to automatically identify Simpson’s paradox in data by comparing statistical trends in the aggregate data to those in the disaggregated subgroups. We apply the approach to data from Stack Exchange, a popular question-answering platform, to analyze factors affecting answerer performance, specifically, the likelihood that an answer written by a user will be accepted by the asker as the best answer to his or her question. Our analysis confirms a known Simpson’s paradox and identifies several new instances. These paradoxes provide novel insights into user behavior on Stack Exchange. DOI: 10.1145/3159652.3159684 We describe a method to identify Simpson’s paradoxes in the analysis of trends in social data. Our statistical approach finds pairs of variables—that we call Simpson’s pairs—such that a trend in some outcome as a function of the first independent variable observed in the aggregate data disappears or reverses itself when the data is disaggregated into distinct subgroups on the second conditioning variable. We perform mathematical analysis, which identifies two necessary conditions for the paradox to occur: (1) the independent and conditioning variables are correlated and (2) the value of the outcome variable differs within conditioning subgroups. We apply the proposed approach to data collected from Stack Exchange, a popular question-answering platform. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a novel extension to word embeddings that tracks semantic changes of words over time, using data from The New York Times (1990-2016). The paper demonstrates how words like 'apple', 'amazon', and 'Trump' shift in meaning, reflecting real-world changes (e.g., from fruit to tech company). The key challenge addressed is the 'alignment problem'—ensuring embeddings from different time periods are comparable despite rotational invariance in training. The authors propose a joint optimization framework that learns temporal embeddings concurrently, eliminating the need for post-hoc alignment. The method improves interpretability, handles data sparsity, and enables robust time-series analysis of word trends. Colyer praises the approach for its elegance and practical applications, such as tracking brand evolution or political roles.
paper_title: Dynamic word embeddings for evolving semantic discovery
paper_abstract: Word evolution refers to the changing meanings and associations of words throughout time, as a byproduct of human language evolution. By studying word evolution, we can infer social trends and language constructs over different periods of human history. However, traditional techniques such as word representation learning do not adequately capture the evolving language structure and vocabulary. In this paper, we develop a dynamic statistical model to learn time-aware word vector representation. We propose a model that simultaneously learns time-aware embeddings and solves the resulting “alignment problem”. This model is trained on a crawled NYTimes dataset. Additionally, we develop multiple intuitive evaluation strategies of temporal word embeddings. Our qualitative and quantitative tests indicate that our method not only reliably captures this evolution over time, but also consistently outperforms state-of-the-art temporal embedding approaches on both semantic accuracy and alignment quality. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Vannevar Bush's 1945 Atlantic article as a foundational vision for modern computing and information systems. The post emphasizes Bush's prescient observations about the inadequacy of existing methods for organizing and accessing the rapidly growing body of scientific knowledge. Colyer particularly notes Bush's call for machines to augment human thinking by automating repetitive tasks and enabling new forms of information storage and retrieval. The most noteworthy aspect discussed is the concept of the 'memex'—a personal device for storing and associating information through hypertext-like trails, which Bush envisioned as a way to mimic the associative nature of human thought. Colyer underscores the lost emphasis on 'trails' as fundamental units of knowledge organization in today's digital landscape.

blog_summary: The blog post highlights a study on 'fail-slow' hardware incidents, where hardware components operate in a degraded mode but remain functional. Author Adrian Colyer notes that these incidents are under-studied and often go undetected for long periods, with detection times ranging from minutes to months. The paper catalogs various root causes, including internal hardware failures (e.g., device wear, firmware issues) and external factors (e.g., temperature, power, configuration errors). The author emphasizes the cascading effects of fail-slow hardware, which can trigger chains of events leading to broader system failures. The paper provides guidelines for hardware vendors, operators, and system designers to mitigate these issues, such as exposing fine-grained performance statistics, enabling online diagnosis, and converting fail-slow faults to fail-stop behaviors. The study underscores the need for systems to anticipate and handle this failure mode explicitly.
paper_title: Fail-slow at scale: evidence of hardware performance faults in large production systems
paper_abstract: Fail-slow hardware is an under-studied failure mode. We present a study of 101 reports of fail-slow hardware incidents, collected from large-scale cluster deployments in 12 institutions. We show that all hardware types such as disk, SSD, CPU, memory and network components can exhibit performance faults. We made several important observations such as faults convert from one form to another, the cascading root causes and impacts can be long, and fail-slow faults can have varying symptoms. From this study, we make suggestions to vendors, operators, and systems designers.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a critical oversight in the design of consensus-based storage systems like Raft and Paxos: they fail to account for storage faults and data corruptions, leading to data loss and unavailability. The paper demonstrates that most deployed systems lack protocol-aware recovery mechanisms, relying instead on naive strategies like crashing, truncating logs, or deleting data, which can exacerbate the problem. The authors propose CTRL (Corruption-Tolerant Replication), a protocol-aware recovery approach that extends the standard RSM fault model to include storage faults. CTRL ensures safety and high availability by reliably detecting faults locally (via CLStore) and recovering using redundant copies with RSM-specific knowledge. The solution addresses corruption in logs, snapshots, and metainfo, and introduces novel techniques like persistence records and chunked snapshots to disambiguate crashes from corruptions and enable granular recovery.
paper_title: Protocol-Aware Recovery for Consensus-Based Storage
paper_abstract: We introduce protocol-aware recovery (PAR), a new approach that exploits protocol-specific knowledge to correctly recover from storage faults in distributed systems. We demonstrate the efficacy of PAR through the design and implementation of corruption-tolerant replication (C TRL), a PAR mechanism specific to replicated state machine (RSM) systems. We experimentally show that the C TRL versions of two systems, LogCabin and ZooKeeper, safely recover from storage faults and provide high availability, while the unmodified versions can lose data or become unavailable. We also show that the C TRL versions have little performance overhead.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses a paper from FAST'18 that introduces a Barrier-enabled IO stack for flash storage, addressing the performance bottleneck caused by enforcing write ordering and durability. Adrian Colyer highlights that traditional transfer-and-flush mechanisms (waiting for data transfer and flush completion) severely degrade performance, reducing IOPS to just 1% of unordered writes in some cases. The paper proposes using barrier commands to control persist order without waiting for full transfers, enabling order-preserving dispatch with significant performance gains. The authors demonstrate headline improvements: SQLite performance increases by 270% (server) and 75% (smartphone), while BarrierFS boosts MySQL and SQLite performance by 43x and 73x respectively compared to EXT4. The key insight is leveraging barrier commands to separate control plane (dispatching writes) from data plane (persisting data) activities, enabling parallelism and reducing overhead. The paper also introduces Dual Mode Journaling in ext4, which further optimizes journal commit operations.
paper_title: Barrier-Enabled IO Stack for Flash Storage
paper_abstract: This work is dedicated to eliminating the overhead required for guaranteeing the storage order in the modern IO stack. The existing block device adopts a prohibitively expensive approach in ensuring the storage order among write requests: interleaving the write requests with Transfer-and-Flush. Exploiting the cache barrier command for Flash storage, we overhaul the IO scheduler, the dispatch module, and the filesystem so that these layers are orchestrated to preserve the ordering condition imposed by the application with which the associated data blocks are made durable. The key ingredients of Barrier-Enabled IO stack are Epoch-based IO scheduling, Order-Preserving Dispatch, and Dual-Mode Journaling. Barrier-enabled IO stack can control the storage order without Transfer-and-Flush overhead. We implement the barrier-enabled IO stack in server as well as in mobile platforms. SQLite performance increases by 270% and 75%, in server and in smartphone, respectively. In a server storage, BarrierFS brings as much as by 43× and by 73× performance gain in MySQL and SQLite, respectively, against EXT4 via relaxing the durability of a transaction.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the Clay codes paper as a significant advancement in erasure coding for storage systems. The blog emphasizes the problem of storage node failures and the need for efficient recovery mechanisms with minimal overhead. While MDS codes like Reed-Solomon reduce storage overhead compared to replication, their repair bandwidth is a major drawback. Clay codes, an extension of theoretical MSR codes by Ye and Barg, address this by offering optimal repair bandwidth, disk I/O, and sub-packetization levels, along with uniform repair performance for data and parity nodes. The paper demonstrates practical benefits through integration with Ceph, showing substantial reductions in repair network traffic, disk reads, and repair times (e.g., 2.9x, 3.4x, and 3x improvements respectively with 1.25x storage overhead). The key insight is the 'coupled-layer' design of Clay codes, which enables efficient repairs while maintaining MDS properties.
paper_title: Clay codes: moulding MDS codes to yield an MSR code
paper_abstract: With increase in scale, the number of node failures in a data center increases sharply. To ensure availability of data, failure-tolerance schemes such as ReedSolomon (RS) or more generally, Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) erasure codes are used. However, while MDS codes offer minimum storage overhead for a given amount of failure tolerance, they do not meet other practical needs of today’s data centers. Although modern codes such as Minimum Storage Regenerating (MSR) codes are designed to meet these practical needs, they are available only in highly-constrained theoretical constructions, that are not sufficiently mature enough for practical implementation. We present Clay codes that extract the best from both worlds. Clay (short for CoupledLayer) codes are MSR codes that offer a simplified construction for decoding/repair by using pairwise coupling across multiple stacked layers of any single MDS code. In addition, Clay codes provide the first practical implementation of an MSR code that offers (a) low storage overhead, (b) simultaneous optimality in terms of three key parameters: repair bandwidth, sub-packetization level and disk I/O, (c) uniform repair performance of data and parity nodes and (d) support for both single and multiple-node repairs, while permitting faster and more efficient repair. While all MSR codes are vector codes, none of the distributed storage systems support vector codes. We have modified Ceph to support any vector code, and our contribution is now a part of Ceph’s master codebase. We have implemented Clay codes, and integrated it as a plugin to Ceph. Six example Clay codes were evaluated on a cluster of Amazon EC2 instances and code parameters were carefully chosen to match known erasure-code deployments in practice. A particular example code, with storage overhead 1.25x, is shown to reduce repair network traffic by a factor of 2.9 in comparison with RS codes and similar reductions are obtained for both repair time and disk read.
