blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a detailed case study from Allspaw's 2015 master thesis, which analyzes the cognitive strategies and heuristics used by engineers at Etsy to resolve a critical outage during the holiday shopping season. The study employs process tracing to reconstruct the incident, including IRC transcripts, logs, and interviews, revealing how the team coordinated, diagnosed, and managed the outage. Key insights include the identification of five heuristics guiding the team's actions, such as correlating issues with recent changes, pattern matching symptoms to past events, and prioritizing peer consensus over automated tests. The analysis emphasizes the role of abductive reasoning in incident management, where engineers iteratively form and test hypotheses to stabilize the system. Colyer underscores the broader implication that human adaptability and cognitive processes, rather than automation alone, are critical to the success of complex systems.
paper_title: Trade-offs under pressure: heuristics and observations of teams resolving internet service outages
paper_abstract: The increasing complexity of software applications and architectures in Internet services challenge the reasoning of operators tasked with diagnosing and resolving outages and degradations as they arise. Although a growing body of literature focuses on how failures can be prevented through more robust and fault-tolerant design of these systems, a dearth of research explores the cognitive challenges engineers face when those preventative designs fail and they are left to think and react to scenarios that hadn’t been imagined. This study explores what heuristics or rules-of-thumb engineers employ when faced with an outage or degradation scenario in a business-critical Internet service. A case study approach was used, focusing on an actual outage of functionality during a high period of buying activity on a popular online marketplace. Heuristics and other tacit knowledge were identified, and provide a promising avenue for both training and future interface design opportunities. Three diagnostic heuristics were identified as being in use: a) initially look for correlation between the behaviour and any recent changes made in the software, b) upon finding no correlation with a software change, widen the search to any potential contributors imagined, and c) when choosing a diagnostic direction, reduce it by focusing on the one that most easily comes to mind, either because symptoms match those of a difficult-to-diagnose event in the past, or those of any recent events. A fourth heuristic is coordinative in nature: when making changes to software in an effort to mitigate the untoward effects or to resolve the issue completely, rely on peer review of the changes more than automated testing (if at all.) 3 ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS This research and thesis is the result of numerous people providing support and guidance and encouragement to me. I am indebted to all of them. I must first thank Dr. Richard Cook, whose infectious curiosity has continually propelled me forward to make conne...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Reverb as an award-winning record-and-replay debugging framework for JavaScript web applications that introduces speculative debugging—allowing developers to test candidate bug-fixes during replay. The paper addresses the notoriously difficult task of debugging pervasive asynchronous and event-driven JavaScript applications by tracking precise value provenance and enabling in-situ hypothesis testing. Key innovations include handling speculative edits during replay by managing nondeterministic inputs (e.g., Math.random(), Date()) and network events, as well as supporting wide-area debugging for distributed event-driven systems. The approach leverages vector clocks for causality tracking and demonstrates feasibility with minimal performance overhead and log sizes, even on complex real-world web applications.
paper_title: Reverb: speculative debugging for web applications
paper_abstract: Web pages today commonly include large amounts of JavaScript code in order to offer users a dynamic experience. These scripts often make pages slow to load, partly due to a fundamental inefficiency in how browsers process JavaScript content: browsers make it easy for web developers to reason about page state by serially executing all scripts on any frame in a page, but as a result, fail to leverage the multiple CPU cores that are readily available even on low-end phones. In this paper, we show how to address this inefficiency without requiring pages to be rewritten or browsers to be modified. The key to our solution, Horcrux, is to account for the non-determinism intrinsic to web page loads and the constraints placed by the browser’s API for parallelism. Horcrux-compliant web servers perform offline analysis of all the JavaScript code on any frame they serve to conservatively identify, for every JavaScript function, the union of the page state that the function could access across all loads of that page. Horcrux’s JavaScript scheduler then uses this information to judiciously parallelize JavaScript execution on the client-side so that the end-state is identical to that of a serial execution, while minimizing coordination and offloading overheads. Across a wide range of pages, phones, and mobile networks covering web workloads in both developed and emerging regions, Horcrux reduces median browser computation delays by 31-44% and page load times by 18-37%.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights 'Narrowing the gap between serverless and its state with storage functions' as a runner-up for the SoCC'19 best paper award. The paper introduces Shredder, a novel key-value store that enables function shipping—an old idea revisited—where computation is performed directly within storage nodes. This approach avoids moving large data over the network and reduces remote calls, improving efficiency. Shredder leverages V8 isolates for lightweight, isolated execution of JavaScript or WebAssembly functions, achieving low-latency and high-throughput with minimal overhead (196 ns for V8 context transitions). The paper addresses function isolation challenges but leaves resource isolation and side-channel concerns partially unresolved. The evaluation demonstrates Shredder's scalability (4M invocations/sec) and performance gains (up to 3.5x throughput with CSA), showcasing its potential to bridge the gap between stateless serverless compute and stateful storage by enabling computation near data.
paper_title: Narrowing the gap between serverless and its state with storage functions
paper_abstract: 1 Serverless computing has gained attention due to its fine-grained provisioning, large-scale multi-tenancy, and on-demand scaling. However, it also forces applications to externalize state in remote storage, adding substantial overheads. To fix this “data shipping problem” we built Shredder, a low-latency multi-tenant cloud store that allows small units of computation to be performed directly within storage nodes. Storage tenants provide Shredder with JavaScript functions (or WebAssembly programs), which can interact directly with data without moving them over the network. The key challenge in Shredder is safely isolating thousands of tenant storage functions while minimizing data interaction costs. Shredder uses a unique approach where its data store and networking paths are implemented in native code to ensure performance, while isolated tenant functions interact with data using a V8-specific intermediate representation that avoids expensive cross-protectiondomain calls and data copying. As a result, Shredder can execute 4 million remotely-invoked tenant functions per second spread over thousands of tenants with median and 99th -percentile response latencies of less than 50 µs and 500 µs, respectively. Our evaluation shows that Shredder achieves a 14% to 78% speedup against conventional remote storage when fetching items with just one to three data dependencies between them. We also demonstrate Shredder’s effectiveness in accelerating data-intensive applications, including a k-hop query on social graphs that shows orders of magnitude gain. Recent trends in cloud applications are improving resource utilization at the expense of efficiency; today, there is a growing gap between cloud applications and their data. This has gap has been widened by serverless computing, which cloud providers and their customers are increasingly embracing. Customers provide short functions to a cloud provider, who takes care of invoking and scaling instances in response to customer even...

blog_summary: The blog post highlights a novel approach to live migration of web workers in mobile applications, enabling seamless offloading of computation from mobile devices to edge clouds. Adrian Colyer emphasizes the elegance of leveraging the HTML5 Web Worker interface for this purpose, as workers are designed for separate-thread execution via message passing, making them ideal for migration. The paper addresses the challenge of snapshotting complex worker states, including JavaScript objects, WebAssembly functions, and native objects, while ensuring compatibility across different hardware architectures (e.g., ARM to x86). The Mobile Web Worker (MWW) System dynamically selects the optimal execution location (local device, edge, or cloud) based on predicted latency and connectivity, using regression models to estimate processing time. The system also handles disconnections by migrating workers to fallback servers or back to the client. The prototype, implemented in Chrome and Node.js, demonstrates significant performance improvements for applications like physics simulations, face detection, and image filtering, with edge offloading yielding up to 2.6x speedups. However, migration times vary widely depending on state size, with larger states (e.g., OpenCV) taking several seconds to migrate.
paper_title: Seamless offloading of web app computations from mobile device to edge clouds via HTML5 web worker migration

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the paper 'The measure and mismeasure of fairness: a critical review of fair machine learning' by Corbett-Davies and Goel, which critically examines popular models of fairness in machine learning. The blog highlights the flawed premise that fairness can be measured solely from within a model or its training data, arguing that external information (akin to a Trusted Information Base) is necessary to demonstrate fairness. The paper critiques three dominant fairness models—anti-classification, classification parity, and calibration—showing they all have significant limitations. For instance, anti-classification can harm protected groups by excluding predictive but correlated attributes, while classification parity and calibration fail to align with legal or economic notions of fairness. The authors propose threshold policies as a more equitable alternative, which evaluates individuals uniformly based on risk scores and aligns better with real-world fairness goals.
paper_title: The measure and mismeasure of fairness: a critical review of fair machine learning
paper_abstract: The field of fair machine learning aims to ensure that decisions guided by algorithms are equitable. Over the last decade, several formal, mathematical definitions of fairness have gained prominence. Here we first assemble and categorize these definitions into two broad families: (1) those that constrain the effects of decisions on disparities; and (2) those that constrain the effects of legally protected characteristics, like race and gender, on decisions. We then show, analytically and empirically, that both families of definitions typically result in strongly Pareto dominated decision policies. For example, in the case of college admissions, adhering to popular formal conceptions of fairness would simultaneously result in lower student-body diversity and a less academically prepared class, relative to what one could achieve by explicitly tailoring admissions policies to achieve desired outcomes. In this sense, requiring that these fairness definitions hold can, perversely, harm the very groups they were designed to protect. In contrast to axiomatic notions of fairness, we argue that the equitable design of algorithms requires grappling with their context-specific consequences, akin to the equitable design of policy. We conclude by listing several open challenges in fair machine learning and offering strategies to ensure algorithms are better aligned with policy goals.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses the paper 'POTS: Protective optimization technologies' by Kulynych, Overdorf, and others, which critiques the narrow focus of fairness frameworks in machine learning systems. Adrian Colyer highlights that such frameworks often ignore broader negative externalities imposed on non-users or the environment, such as how Waze or Airbnb can harm local communities despite being 'fair' within their own ecosystems. The paper argues for a wider perspective on system impacts, considering domain assumptions, requirements, specifications, and implementations. It introduces Protective Optimization Technologies (POTs) as tools for disadvantaged groups to counteract harmful optimization systems by manipulating inputs, thereby reshaping the system's impact on the environment. The post emphasizes the need to address systemic harms beyond algorithmic fairness, advocating for collective action to mitigate negative externalities caused by optimization-driven services.
paper_title: POTS: Protective optimization technologies
paper_abstract: Algorithmic fairness aims to address the economic, moral, social, and political impact that digital systems have on populations through solutions that can be applied by service providers. Fairness frameworks do so, in part, by mapping these problems to a narrow definition and assuming the service providers can be trusted to deploy countermeasures. Not surprisingly, these decisions limit fairness frameworks’ ability to capture a variety of harms caused by systems. We characterize fairness limitations using concepts from requirements engineering and from social sciences. We show that the focus on algorithms’ inputs and outputs misses harms that arise from systems interacting with the world; that the focus on bias and discrimination omits broader harms on populations and their environments; and that relying on service providers excludes scenarios where they are not cooperative or intentionally adversarial. We propose Protective Optimization Technologies (POTs). POTs, provide means for affected parties to address the negative impacts of systems in the environment, expanding avenues for political contestation. POTs intervene from outside the system, do not require service providers to cooperate, and can serve to correct, shift, or expose harms that systems impose on populations and their environments. We illustrate the potential and limitations of POTs in two case studies: countering road congestion caused by traffic-beating applications, and recalibrating credit scoring for loan applicants.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses 'Cloudburst: stateful functions-as-a-service' from the RISELab at Berkeley, addressing limitations in current serverless computing platforms that lack efficient state management. Adrian Colyer highlights Cloudburst's approach of using a highly-scalable key-value store (Anna) for persistent state, local caches co-located with function execution environments, and cache-consistency protocols to maintain data consistency while preserving the autoscaling and operational benefits of FaaS. The paper introduces the concept of 'logical disaggregation with physical colocation' (LDPC), where storage and compute are disaggregated but physically colocated to optimize data locality. The design includes a scheduler to place functions near cached data, enabling low-latency access and cross-function communication at wire speed. The programming model is Python-based, with support for function composition into DAGs and transparent state resolution via KVS references. The paper also explores consistency models, including causal consistency and repeatable reads, by wrapping Python state in lattice types to integrate with Anna's coordination-free consistency mechanisms.
paper_title: Cloudburst: stateful functions-as-a-service
paper_abstract: PVLDB Reference Format: Vikram Sreekanti, Chenggang Wu, Xiayue Charles Lin, Johann SchleierSmith, Jose M. Faleiro, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Joseph M. Hellerstein, Alexey Tumanov. Cloudburst: Stateful Functions-as-a-Service. PVLDB, 13(11): 2438-2452, 2020. DOI: https://doi.org/10.14778/3407790.3407836

blog_summary: The blog post highlights a study revealing extensive privacy and tracking issues in Over-The-Top (OTT) TV streaming devices, specifically Roku and Amazon Fire TV. The authors built a custom crawling engine to analyze the top 1000 channels on each platform, intercepting network traffic to quantify tracking behaviors. The findings are alarming: trackers are ubiquitous, with Google's DoubleClick and Amazon's ad system dominating on Roku and Fire TV, respectively. The study also found that video titles are often leaked to trackers in cleartext, and device identifiers are frequently exposed. Privacy settings offered by the platforms are largely ineffective, as they only address specific identifiers while leaving others exposed. Even using a Pi-hole to block trackers misses a significant portion of leaks, underscoring the pervasive nature of tracking in this ecosystem.
paper_title: Watching you watch: the tracking ecosystem of over-the-top TV streaming devices

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the remarkable success of Let's Encrypt as the world's largest HTTPS Certificate Authority (CA), accounting for more valid certificates than all other browser-trusted CAs combined. He emphasizes two key achievements: first, Let's Encrypt made the web more secure by prioritizing ease-of-use, breaking the typical trade-off between security and usability. Second, it established a sustainable funding model for an open-source project and free online service, avoiding the burnout of small benefactor-maintained initiatives. The blog post details Let's Encrypt's rapid growth since its launch in 2015, its fully automated end-to-end service, and its integration with hosting and CDN providers. Colyer also notes the significant impact of Let's Encrypt's shorter certificate lifetimes (90 days) in reducing expired certificate incidents. The paper delves into the technical and organizational challenges overcome to achieve this success, including the development of the ACME protocol and the Boulder CA software stack.
paper_title: Let's Encrypt: An automated certificate authority to encrypt the entire web
paper_abstract: 1 Let’s Encrypt is a free, open, and automated HTTPS certificate authority (CA) created to advance HTTPS adoption to the entire Web. Since its launch in late 2015, Let’s Encrypt has grown to become the world’s largest HTTPS CA, accounting for more currently valid certificates than all other browser-trusted CAs combined. By January 2019, it had issued over 538 million certificates for 223 million domain names. We describe how we built Let’s Encrypt, including the architecture of the CA software system (Boulder) and the structure of the organization that operates it (ISRG), and we discuss lessons learned from the experience. We also describe the design of ACME, the IETF-standard protocol we created to automate CA–server interactions and certificate issuance, and survey the diverse ecosystem of ACME clients, including Certbot, a software agent we created to automate HTTPS deployment. Finally, we measure Let’s Encrypt’s impact on the Web and the CA ecosystem. We hope that the success of Let’s Encrypt can provide a model for further enhancements to the Web PKI and for future Internet security infrastructure. HTTPS [78] is the cryptographic foundation of the Web, providing an encrypted and authenticated form of HTTP over the TLS transport [79]. When HTTPS was introduced by Netscape twenty-five years ago [51], the primary use cases were protecting financial transactions and login credentials, but users today face a growing range of threats from hostile networks—including mass surveillance and censorship by governments [99, 106], consumer profiling and ad injection by ISPs [30, 95], and insertion of malicious code by network devices [68]—which make HTTPS important for practically every Web request. Many cryptographic flaws in TLS have been discovered and mitigated (e.g., [11, 13, 17, 23, 37, 69]), but low adoption of HTTPS posed an even starker risk: as recently as 2015, 55–70% of browser page loads used plaintext HTTP [47]. A major barrier to wider HTTPS adoption was that ...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 1980 paper by Lehman as a foundational work that reframes software development as an ongoing evolutionary process rather than a one-time creation. The blog emphasizes Lehman's key insight that change is intrinsic to software systems, especially those interacting with the real world, and that maintenance costs dominate the software lifecycle. Colyer notes how the paper's observations remain strikingly relevant today, suggesting that software evolution problems may persist for decades. The post praises Lehman's classification of programs into S-programs (formally specifiable), P-programs (real-world problem solutions), and E-programs (embedded societal activities), and underscores the limitations of formal methods for the latter two classes where correctness depends on real-world outcomes rather than formal specifications.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses a case study from Google where a privacy-safe information extraction system was migrated from a traditional 'Software 1.0' design (hand-written rules) to a 'Software 2.0' design (machine-learned components). The author highlights the challenges of maintaining a complex rule-based system, which had become brittle and hard to improve, and how replacing it with a neural network-based approach simplified the codebase (deleting 45K lines of code) and improved performance. The key insight is the shift in effort from writing code to curating training data, especially in a privacy-sensitive context where real data cannot be inspected. The post also details Google's system 'Juicer,' which uses machine learning for information extraction from emails, and the innovative methods developed to manage training data in a privacy-safe manner, including synthetic data generation and counter metrics for quality control.
paper_title: Migrating a privacy-safe information extraction system to a software 2.0 design
paper_abstract: ing over a billion users worldwide from a traditional rulebased architecture to a machine-learned Software 2.0 architecture. This extraction system [27] is responsible for extracting structured objects from emails in different verticals – e.g. bill reminders, shipping confirmations for online purchases, hotel reservations, etc. Each vertical defines a set of fields to extract. In the case of hotel confirmations, this includes the check-in and check-out dates as well as the hotel name and address. These extractions enable experiences like allowing a smart assistant to answer personal queries such as “when is my electric bill due?” and “where is my Macy’s package?”. A legacy rule-based extraction system using hand-crafted rules has been in production since 2013. We leveraged extractions from the existing rule-based system as well as previously hand-written parsers as the source for training data. The biggest challenges we encountered during this migration were in generating and managing training data. Training data for field-classifiers (described in Section 2.2) requires writing a high-recall candidate generator and a highquality labeler. Detecting low quality training data from low-precision rules and improving data quality over time is critical. Developing these in the context of a privacy-safe system where no one can visually inspect the underlying data is particularly challenging. We tackled these problems by building several traditional “Software 1.0” components. We designed two abstractions called CandidateGenerators and CandidateLabelers that allowed us to generate training data for all fields across different verticals. We also built tools to evaluate CandidateGenerators and CandidateLabelers on synthetic emails that are generated using the boilerplate from real templatic emails. The same tool is used to acquire additional ground truth data, improve data quality over time, and evaluate the performance of new models The new architecture has delivered benefits ...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this vision paper from Microsoft researchers that predicts a major shift in machine learning (ML) from consumer-scale applications to enterprise-grade ML (EGML) systems. The paper argues that EGML applications will require stricter data handling, model fairness, privacy, and debuggability compared to current ML systems. The authors emphasize that ML models are software artifacts derived from data, combining software engineering needs (like CI/CD) with data lineage requirements. They predict that in the next decade, millions of ML-infused applications will be built by smaller teams, necessitating robust platforms for training, inference, and governance. The paper identifies three key areas for EGML systems: model development/training, model scoring (inference), and model management/governance, with a bold prediction that ML inference will become deeply integrated into DBMS as a foundational extension of relational algebra. The blog post also introduces Microsoft's Flock reference architecture, which treats ML models as software artifacts and explores in-DBMS inference for performance gains.
paper_title: Cloudy with a high chance of DBMS: a 10-year prediction for enterprise-grade ML
paper_abstract: Machine learning (ML) has proven itself in high-value web applications such as search ranking and is emerging as a powerful tool in a much broader range of enterprise scenarios including voice recognition and conversational understanding for customer support, autotuning for videoconferencing, intelligent feedback loops in large-scale sysops, manufacturing and autonomous vehicle management, complex financial predictions, just to name a few. Meanwhile, as the value of data is increasingly recognized and monetized, concerns about securing valuable data and risks to individual privacy have been growing. Consequently, rigorous data management has emerged as a key requirement in enterprise settings. How will these trends (ML growing popularity, and stricter data governance) intersect? What are the unmet requirements for applying ML in enterprise settings? What are the technical challenges for the DB community to solve? In this paper, we present our vision of how ML and database systems are likely to come together, and early steps we take towards making this vision a reality.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Microsoft's Raven system, which deeply integrates machine learning inference into a relational database management system (RDBMS) to leverage enterprise features like transactions, security, and high availability. The key insight is that while inference performance is not necessarily better inside the database, the database is the ideal place to manage and serve ML models as data, ensuring they meet the same scrutiny and performance requirements as other critical enterprise data. Raven treats model pipelines as first-class citizens in the database, stored and invoked via SQL, and optimizes them alongside relational queries through static analysis, cross-optimization, and runtime code generation. The system demonstrates significant performance improvements over external ML inference, especially for batch predictions, by leveraging SQL Server's parallelization and caching capabilities. The paper also explores advanced optimizations like predicate-based model pruning, model-projection pushdown, and neural network translation to further enhance efficiency.
paper_title: Extending relational query processing with ML inference
paper_abstract: The broadening adoption of machine learning in the enterprise is increasing the pressure for strict governance and cost-effective performance, in particular for the common and consequential steps of model storage and inference. The RDBMS provides a natural starting point, given its mature infrastructure for fast data access and processing, along with support for enterprise features, such as encryption, auditing, and high-availability. To take advantage of all of the above, we need to address a key concern: Can in-RDBMS scoring of ML models match (outperform?) the performance of dedicated frameworks? We answer the above positively by building Raven, a system that leverages native integration of ML runtimes (such as ONNX Runtime) deep within SQL Server and a unified intermediate representation (IR) to enable advanced crossoptimizations between ML and database operators. In this optimization space, we discover the most exciting research opportunities that combine DB/compiler/ML thinking. Our initial evaluation on real data demonstrates performance gains of up to 5.5× from the native integration of ML in SQL Server and up to 24× from cross-optimizations. An early preview of the ONNX Runtime integration is currently available with Azure’s SQL Database Edge.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights AnyLog as an ambitious attempt to create a decentralized web-like infrastructure for structured (relational) data, contrasting it with the Semantic Web and other efforts. The paper's key insight is the integration of a micropayment system to incentivize data contribution, integration, and querying in a decentralized setting, where advertising is not a viable revenue model. Colyer notes that while the paper frames this as an IoT use case, the technical solution is broadly applicable to any structured data scenario. He also observes that the micropayment mechanism could potentially extend to unstructured data (e.g., the traditional web), though this is not the paper's primary focus. The blog post emphasizes the system's architectural vision, including roles like coordinators (search engines), contractors (data hosts), and publishers (data producers), all coordinated via a blockchain for trust and micropayments. The paper's novelty lies in combining SQL interfaces, economic incentives, and decentralized infrastructure into a unified system.
paper_title: AnyLog: a grand unification of the Internet of Things
paper_abstract: AnyLog is a decentralized platform for data publishing, sharing, and querying IoT (Internet of Things) data that enables an unlimited number of independent participants to publish and access the contents of IoT datasets stored across the participants. AnyLog provides decentralized publishing and querying functionality over structured data in an analogous fashion to how the world wide web (WWW) enables decentralized publishing and accessing of unstructured data. However, AnyLog differs from the traditional WWW in the way that it provides incentives and financial reward for performing tasks that are critical to the well-being of the system as a whole, including contribution, integration, storing, and processing of data, as well as protecting the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of that data. Another difference is how Anylog enforces good behavior by the participants through a collection of methods, including blockchain, secure enclaves, and state channels. 1. owen@soe.ucsc.edu

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this NSDI'20 paper as a well-written exploration of Google G Suite's quest for a meaningful availability metric that reflects real user experience. The paper critiques traditional time-based and count-based metrics (e.g., 'nines' availability, success ratios) for failing to meet three key criteria: meaningfulness (capturing user experience), proportionality (reflecting severity of unavailability), and actionability (guiding fixes). The authors propose 'windowed user-uptime,' a metric that measures downtime from individual users' perspectives, combining time-based and count-based approaches. It accounts for real user request patterns, avoids arbitrary thresholds, and uses a sliding window technique (MCR) to identify problematic outages of varying durations. Google has deployed this metric across G Suite for a year, enabling engineers to pinpoint and address root causes of unavailability effectively.
paper_title: Meaningful Availability
paper_abstract: High availability is a critical requirement for cloud applications: if a sytem does not have high availability, users cannot count on it for their critical work. Having a metric that meaningfully captures availability is useful for both users and system developers. It informs users what they should expect of the availability of the application. It informs developers what they should focus on to improve user-experienced availability. This paper presents and evaluates, in the context of Google’s G Suite, a novel availability metric: windowed user-uptime. This metric has two main components. First, it directly models user-perceived availability and avoids the bias in commonly used availability metrics. Second, by simultaneously calculating the availability metric over many windows it can readily distinguish between many short periods of unavailability and fewer but longer periods of unavailability.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Gandalf, an intelligent analytics service deployed at Microsoft Azure for safe software rollouts. Gandalf processes over 20TB of data daily to monitor deployments, detecting issues by analyzing platform events, API calls, and fault types. It operates on a lambda architecture with fast and slow paths to identify immediate and latent problems, respectively. Gandalf's transparency and interactive evidence access have built trust among development teams, reducing deployment times by half. The paper emphasizes the challenges of spotting bad rollouts in large-scale, ever-changing systems, including ambient faults, delayed issues, and complex causal relationships. Gandalf's three-phase pipeline—anomaly detection, correlation analysis, and decision engine—addresses these challenges, using techniques like Holt-Winters forecasting and ensemble voting with vetoes to pinpoint faulty components.
paper_title: Gandalf: An Intelligent, End-to-End Analytics Service for Safe Deployment in Cloud-Scale Infrastructure
paper_abstract: Modern cloud systems have a vast number of components that continuously undergo updates. Deploying these frequent updates quickly without breaking the system is challenging. In this paper, we present Gandalf, an end-to-end analytics service for safe deployment in a large-scale system infrastructure. Gandalf enables rapid and robust impact assessment of software rollouts to catch bad rollouts before they cause widespread outages. Gandalf monitors and analyzes various fault signals. It will correlate each signal against all the ongoing rollouts using a spatial and temporal correlation algorithm. The core decision logic of Gandalf includes an ensemble ranking algorithm that determines which rollout may have caused the fault signals, and a binary classifier that assesses the impact of the fault signals. The analysis result will decide whether a rollout is safe to proceed or should be stopped. By using a lambda architecture, Gandalf provides both realtime and long-term deployment monitoring with automated decisions and notifications. Gandalf has been running in production in Microsoft Azure for more than 18 months, serving both data-plane and control-plane components. It achieves 92.4% precision and 100% recall (no high-impact service outages in Azure Compute were caused by bad rollouts) for dataplane rollouts. For control-plane rollouts, Gandalf achieves 94.9% precision and 99.8% recall.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Amazon's Firecracker as a groundbreaking virtual machine monitor (VMM) designed to meet the stringent requirements of serverless applications like AWS Lambda and Fargate. The paper addresses the traditional trade-off between virtualization's strong security and containers' minimal overhead, proposing a solution that combines the isolation benefits of virtualization with near-native performance and low overhead. Firecracker achieves this by leveraging KVM and targeting a specific workload (serverless/containers), resulting in a significantly smaller codebase (~50k lines of Rust) compared to traditional hypervisors like KVM+QEMU. The design simplifies the VMM by limiting supported devices and using host OS capabilities where possible, while ensuring strong isolation through hardware-supported boundaries. The paper also details Firecracker's integration into AWS's production environment, where it handles trillions of events monthly with minimal overhead and fast startup times (~100ms).
paper_title: Firecracker: Lightweight Virtualization for Serverless Applications
paper_abstract: Serverless containers and functions are widely used for deploying and managing software in the cloud. Their popularity is due to reduced cost of operations, improved utilization of hardware, and faster scaling than traditional deployment methods. The economics and scale of serverless applications demand that workloads from multiple customers run on the same hardware with minimal overhead, while preserving strong security and performance isolation. The traditional view is that there is a choice between virtualization with strong security and high overhead, and container technologies with weaker security and minimal overhead. This tradeoff is unacceptable to public infrastructure providers, who need both strong security and minimal overhead. To meet this need, we developed Firecracker, a new open source Virtual Machine Monitor (VMM) specialized for serverless workloads, but generally useful for containers, functions and other compute workloads within a reasonable set of constraints. We have deployed Firecracker in two publically-available serverless compute services at Amazon Web Services (Lambda and Fargate), where it supports millions of production workloads, and trillions of requests per month. We describe how specializing for serverless informed the design of Firecracker, and what we learned from seamlessly migrating Lambda customers to Firecracker.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the engineering and design principles behind Physalia, AWS's configuration database for Elastic Block Storage (EBS). The paper stands out for its focus on practical deployment and software engineering practices rather than just the core consensus algorithms (e.g., chain-replication, Paxos). The guiding principle is 'minimise the blast radius,' reflecting AWS's philosophy of reducing the impact of failures by limiting their scope. The paper details how Physalia is structured as 'millions of tiny databases' (cells) to isolate failures, with careful placement and reconfiguration strategies to ensure high availability and strong consistency, even under network partitions. The blog emphasizes the system's latency-critical nature, its handling of large-scale failures, and the innovative 'whack-a-mole' teaching mode for log gaps.
paper_title: Millions of tiny databases
paper_abstract: Starting in 2013, we set out to build a new database to act as the configuration store for a high-performance cloud block storage system (Amazon EBS).This database needs to be not only highly available, durable, and scalable but also strongly consistent. We quickly realized that the constraints on availability imposed by the CAP theorem, and the realities of operating distributed systems, meant that we didn’t want one database. We wanted millions. Physalia is a transactional keyvalue store, optimized for use in large-scale cloud control planes, which takes advantage of knowledge of transaction patterns and infrastructure design to offer both high availability and strong consistency to millions of clients. Physalia uses its knowledge of datacenter topology to place data where it is most likely to be available. Instead of being highly available for all keys to all clients, Physalia focuses on being extremely available for only the keys it knows each client needs, from the perspective of that client. This paper describes Physalia in context of Amazon EBS, and some other uses within Amazon Web Services. We believe that the same patterns, and approach to design, are widely applicable to distributed systems problems like control planes, configuration management, and service discovery.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews the Snowflake cloud-based data warehouse, highlighting its design as a disaggregated system where compute and storage are decoupled, enabling independent scaling and elasticity. He notes that while Snowflake excels in high-level cloud-native principles like disaggregation and isolation, challenges remain in fine-grained resource allocation and prediction of intermediate data volumes during query processing. The paper emphasizes how modern cloud infrastructure changes traditional assumptions in data warehouse design, particularly the need for elastic, fine-grained resource management. Colyer also points out Snowflake's three-tier ephemeral storage system for intermediate data, which is not fully disaggregated, and discusses the trade-offs in caching and elasticity, including the potential for future improvements like auto-scaling and serverless platforms.
paper_title: Building an elastic query engine on disaggregated storage
paper_abstract: We present operational experience running Snowflake, a cloudbased data warehousing system with SQL support similar to state-of-the-art databases. Snowflake design is motivated by three goals: (1) compute and storage elasticity; (2) support for multi-tenancy; and, (3) high performance. Over the last few years, Snowflake has grown to serve thousands of customers executing millions of queries on petabytes of data every day. This paper presents Snowflake design and implementation, along with a discussion on how recent changes in cloud infrastructure (emerging hardware, fine-grained billing, etc.) have altered the many assumptions that guided the design and optimization of Snowflake system. Using data collected from various components of our system during execution of 70 million queries over a 14 day period, our study both deepens the understanding of existing problems and highlights new research challenges along a multitude of dimensions including design of storage systems and high-performance query execution engines.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights that Facebook's analysis of three real-world RocksDB workloads reveals significant differences between actual production workloads and those generated by the popular YCSB benchmark. The paper demonstrates that YCSB fails to account for key-range distribution of hot keys, which is critical for accurate benchmarking, especially when RocksDB reads data in multi-key blocks. The authors propose a key-range based modeling approach and develop a new benchmark to generate more realistic synthetic workloads. The tools and benchmark are now part of the open-source RocksDB release. The key insight is that ignoring key-space locality leads to misleading performance evaluations, as shown by the 7.7x higher read amplification in YCSB-generated workloads compared to real ZippyDB workloads.
paper_title: Characterizing, modeling, and benchmarking RocksDB key-value workloads at Facebook
paper_abstract: Persistent key-value stores are widely used as building blocks in today’s IT infrastructure for managing and storing large amounts of data. However, studies of characterizing real-world workloads for key-value stores are limited due to the lack of tracing/analyzing tools and the difficulty of collecting traces in operational environments. In this paper, we first present a detailed characterization of workloads from three typical RocksDB production use cases at Facebook: UDB (a MySQL storage layer for social graph data), ZippyDB (a distributed key-value store), and UP2X (a distributed key-value store for AI/ML services). These characterizations reveal several interesting findings: first, that the distribution of key and value sizes are highly related to the use cases/applications; second, that the accesses to key-value pairs have a good locality and follow certain special patterns; and third, that the collected performance metrics show a strong diurnal pattern in the UDB, but not the other two. We further discover that although the widely used key-value benchmark YCSB provides various workload configurations and key-value pair access distribution models, the YCSBtriggered workloads for underlying storage systems are still not close enough to the workloads we collected due to ignorance of key-space localities. To address this issue, we propose a key-range based modeling and develop a benchmark that can better emulate the workloads of real-world key-value stores. This benchmark can synthetically generate more precise key-value queries that represent the reads and writes of key-value stores to the underlying storage system.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer presents two papers from NSDI'20 that tackle system reliability through correlation analysis. The first, Rex, is a tool deployed at Microsoft that prevents bugs and misconfigurations by identifying correlated changes developers often miss. By mining commit logs and using association mining (FP-Growth algorithm), Rex generates change rules that warn developers about files frequently changed together but not updated in tandem. Over 14 months, it caught 4,926 potential issues, including severe service disruptions, by flagging correlated changes in pull requests. The second paper, CloudCanary, focuses on detecting and removing harmful correlations that cause correlated failures. It introduces fault graphs—layered DAGs modeling component dependencies—and uses incremental auditing (SnapAudit) with MinCostSAT solvers to identify minimal risk groups (sets of components whose failure would disrupt the service). DepBooster then generates improvement plans to meet reliability goals. CloudCanary's evaluation on a real-world update trace from a major service provider found numerous risk groups, many of which were confirmed to cause or have caused correlated failures, demonstrating its potential to enhance system resilience.
paper_title: Rex: preventing bugs and misconfiguration in large services using correlated change analysis
paper_abstract: Large services experience extremely frequent changes to code and configuration. In many cases, these changes are correlated across files. For example, an engineer introduces a new feature following which they also change a configuration file to enable the feature only on a small number of experimental machines. This example captures only one of numerous types of correlations that emerge organically in large services. Unfortunately, in almost all such cases, no documentation or specification guides engineers on how to make correlated changes and they often miss making them. Such misses can be vastly disruptive to the service. We have designed and deployed Rex, a tool that, using a combination of machine learning and program analysis, learns change-rules that capture such correlations. When an engineer changes only a subset of files in a change-rule, Rex suggests additional changes to the engineer based on the change-rule. Rex has been deployed for 14 months on 360 repositories within Microsoft that hold code and configuration for services such as Office 365 and Azure. Rex has so far positively affected 4926 changes without which, at the very least, codequality would have degraded and, in some cases, the service would have been severely disrupted.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the significant challenge of partial failures (gray failures) in large system software, where some functionalities break while others appear normal. Traditional failure detectors often miss these issues due to their superficial nature. The paper, awarded Best Paper at NSDI'20, presents a study of partial failure causes across five major systems (ZooKeeper, Cassandra, HDFS, Apache, Mesos) and introduces OmegaGen, a novel approach to detect such failures using auto-generated, system-specific watchdogs. The study reveals that partial failures are common, severe, and often sticky, with a median diagnosis time of 6 days and 5 hours. OmegaGen addresses the limitations of existing health checks by creating intrinsic watchdogs that replicate vulnerable operations from long-running methods, capturing runtime context to detect failures with high accuracy and low overhead. The approach outperforms baseline detectors, detecting 20 out of 22 real-world partial failures with a median detection time of 4.2 seconds and pinpointing error sources in 18 cases.
paper_title: Understanding, Detecting and Localizing Partial Failures in Large System Software
paper_abstract: Partial failures occur frequently in cloud systems and can cause serious damage including inconsistency and data loss. Unfortunately, these failures are not well understood. Nor can they be effectively detected. In this paper, we first study 100 real-world partial failures from five mature systems to understand their characteristics. We find that these failures are caused by a variety of defects that require the unique conditions of the production environment to be triggered. Manually writing effective detectors to systematically detect such failures is both time-consuming and error-prone. We thus propose OmegaGen, a static analysis tool that automatically generates customized watchdogs for a given program by using a novel program reduction technique. We have successfully applied OmegaGen to six large distributed systems. In evaluating 22 real-world partial failure cases in these systems, the generated watchdogs can detect 20 cases with a median detection time of 4.2 seconds, and pinpoint the failure scope for 18 cases. The generated watchdogs also expose an unknown, confirmed partial failure bug in the latest version of ZooKeeper.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights that this paper provides the first real-world evaluation of Intel's Optane DIMM, a commercially available non-volatile memory (NVDIMM). The study reveals that many assumptions made in prior research about NVDIMM behavior—particularly the notion that Optane DIMMs behave like slower, persistent DRAM—are incorrect. The paper conducts an extensive empirical analysis, collecting around ten thousand data points, to uncover nuanced performance characteristics of Optane DIMMs. Key findings include Optane's higher read latency (2-3x DRAM), significant performance gaps between random and sequential access patterns (80% vs. 20% for DRAM), non-monotonic bandwidth scaling with thread count, and severe performance penalties under NUMA configurations. The authors derive four practical guidelines to optimize system design for Optane DIMMs, emphasizing the importance of access patterns, thread concurrency, and NUMA locality. The paper also introduces the Effective Write Ratio (EWR) metric to quantify write amplification and guide optimization strategies.
paper_title: An empirical guide to the behavior and use of scalable persistent memory
paper_abstract: After nearly a decade of anticipation, scalable nonvolatile memory DIMMs are finally commercially available with the release of Intel’s Optane DIMM. This new nonvolatile DIMM supports byte-granularity accesses with access times on the order of DRAM, while also providing data storage that survives power outages. Researchers have not idly waited for real nonvolatile DIMMs (NVDIMMs) to arrive. Over the past decade, they have written a slew of papers proposing new programming models, file systems, libraries, and applications built to exploit the performance and flexibility that NVDIMMs promised to deliver. Those papers drew conclusions and made design decisions without detailed knowledge of how real NVDIMMs would behave or how industry would integrate them into computer architectures. Now that Optane NVDIMMs are actually here, we can provide detailed performance numbers, concrete guidance for programmers on these systems, reevaluate prior art for performance, and reoptimize persistent memory software for the real Optane DIMM. In this paper, we explore the performance properties and characteristics of Intel’s new Optane DIMM at the micro and macro level. First, we investigate the basic characteristics of the device, taking special note of the particular ways in which its performance is peculiar relative to traditional DRAM or other past methods used to emulate NVM. From these observations, we recommend a set of best practices to maximize the performance of the device. With our improved understanding, we then explore and reoptimize the performance of prior art in application-level software for persistent memory.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses a paper analyzing serverless workloads on Microsoft Azure, highlighting a win-win scenario where both cloud providers and users benefit from improved performance and reduced costs. The key insight is a hybrid policy that combines pre-warming and keep-alive strategies to minimize cold starts (where functions take longer to execute due to initialization delays) while optimizing resource usage. The paper characterizes real-world serverless workloads, revealing that most functions are infrequently invoked with short execution times, making cold starts a critical performance bottleneck. The proposed policy uses a histogram-based approach to dynamically adjust pre-warming and keep-alive windows based on observed invocation patterns, outperforming the state-of-the-practice fixed keep-alive strategy.
paper_title: Serverless in the wild: characterizing and optimising the serverless workload at a large cloud provider
paper_abstract: Function as a Service (FaaS) has been gaining popularity as a way to deploy computations to serverless backends in the cloud. This paradigm shifts the complexity of allocating and provisioning resources to the cloud provider, which has to provide the illusion of always-available resources (i.e., fast function invocations without cold starts) at the lowest possible resource cost. Doing so requires the provider to deeply understand the characteristics of the FaaS workload. Unfortunately, there has been little to no public information on these characteristics. Thus, in this paper, we first characterize the entire production FaaS workload of Azure Functions. We show for example that most functions are invoked very infrequently, but there is an 8-order-of-magnitude range of invocation frequencies. Using observations from our characterization, we then propose a practical resource management policy that significantly reduces the number of function cold starts, while spending fewer resources than state-of-the-practice policies.

blog_summary: The blog post is a personal note from Adrian Colyer announcing a temporary pause of 'The Morning Paper' due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the closure of schools. He expresses concern for the safety of his family, friends, and neighbors, and shares his intention to prioritize helping others during this time. The post also mentions a potential shift to more sporadic or increased posting frequency in the future, depending on the circumstances. Additionally, it includes a brief section highlighting a few notable blog posts from the term so far.

Adrian Colyer discusses the migration of his blog, The Morning Paper, from WordPress to a statically rendered site using Strattic. He highlights the benefits of this transition, including significantly faster page loads, reduced attack surface for attackers (as only static pages are publicly accessible), and improved accessibility for screen-reading devices. The move also allows him to regain control over math rendering in posts. While he loses built-in analytics from WordPress.com, he prefers not to track visitors. Colyer expresses gratitude to the Strattic team for their assistance and recommends Strattic to others using WordPress for their websites or blogs.

Adrian Colyer highlights this paper as an insightful exploration of how superhuman AI aligns with human behavior, using chess as a model system. The blog emphasizes the importance of human-machine collaboration, noting that AI models often approach tasks differently from humans, making them less interpretable or learnable for humans. The paper's key focus is on comparing human and AI learning trajectories, particularly in chess, where the authors investigate whether AI can predict human moves (move matching) and identify human mistakes (blunder prediction) at different skill levels. The study introduces Maia, a neural network-based chess engine trained on human games, which outperforms traditional engines like Stockfish and AlphaZero/Leela in predicting human moves, especially when trained on specific skill levels. The blog underscores the potential for such models to serve as AI coaches, helping humans improve by identifying areas where their play diverges from stronger players.
paper_title: Aligning superhuman AI with human behavior: chess as a model system
paper_abstract: CCS CONCEPTS As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly intelligent—in some cases, achieving superhuman performance—there is growing potential for humans to learn from and collaborate with algorithms. However, the ways in which AI systems approach problems are often different from the ways people do, and thus may be uninterpretable and hard to learn from. A crucial step in bridging this gap between human and artificial intelligence is modeling the granular actions that constitute human behavior, rather than simply matching aggregate human performance. We pursue this goal in a model system with a long history in artificial intelligence: chess. The aggregate performance of a chess player unfolds as they make decisions over the course of a game. The hundreds of millions of games played online by players at every skill level form a rich source of data in which these decisions, and their exact context, are recorded in minute detail. Applying existing chess engines to this data, including an open-source implementation of AlphaZero, we find that they do not predict human moves well. We develop and introduce Maia, a customized version of AlphaZero trained on human chess games, that predicts human moves at a much higher accuracy than existing engines, and can achieve maximum accuracy when predicting decisions made by players at a specific skill level in a tuneable way. For a dual task of predicting whether a human will make a large mistake on the next move, we develop a deep neural network that significantly outperforms competitive baselines. Taken together, our results suggest that there is substantial promise in designing artificial intelligence systems with human collaboration in mind by first accurately modeling granular human decision-making. • Human-centered computing → Empirical studies in collaborative and social computing. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the significant problem of dependency conflicts in the Python ecosystem, particularly due to the prevalence of range constraints in version specifications (92.2% of top Python projects vs. 0.03% in Java). He notes that conflicts often arise from transitive dependencies and pip's eager dependency resolution strategy, which can lead to unexpected version changes. The paper studies 235 real-world dependency conflict issues, categorizing their causes (e.g., overly specific constraints, upper-bound violations) and common developer fixes (e.g., adjusting constraints, coordinating with upstream developers). The authors then introduce Watchman, a tool that builds a full dependency graph for PyPI packages to detect existing conflicts and predict future ones by analyzing version constraints and installation rules. Colyer praises Watchman's effectiveness, noting it detected all conflicts in backtesting and accurately predicted 143 of 156 potential conflicts, with real-world deployment identifying 63 confirmed issues.
paper_title: Watchman: monitoring dependency conflicts for Python library ecosystem
paper_abstract: CCS CONCEPTS The PyPI ecosystem has indexed millions of Python libraries to allow developers to automatically download and install dependencies of their projects based on the specified version constraints. Despite the convenience brought by automation, version constraints in Python projects can easily conflict, resulting in build failures. We refer to such conflicts as Dependency Conflict (DC) issues. Although DC issues are common in Python projects, developers lack tool support to gain a comprehensive knowledge for diagnosing the root causes of these issues. In this paper, we conducted an empirical study on 235 real-world DC issues. We studied the manifestation patterns and fixing strategies of these issues and found several key factors that can lead to DC issues and their regressions. Based on our findings, we designed and implemented Watchman, a technique to continuously monitor dependency conflicts for the PyPI ecosystem. In our evaluation, Watchman analyzed PyPI snapshots between 11 Jul 2019 and 16 Aug 2019, and found 117 potential DC issues. We reported these issues to the developers of the corresponding projects. So far, 63 issues have been confirmed, 38 of which have been quickly fixed by applying our suggested patches. • Software and its engineering → Software libraries and repositories; ∗ Ming Wen and Yepang Liu are the corresponding authors of this paper. blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the challenges of applying static analysis to Java enterprise applications, noting that popular tools like Soot, WALA, or Doop often fail to achieve acceptable results due to the complexity of enterprise frameworks. Key issues include heavy use of inversion of control, dependency injection, configuration-driven components, and meta-programming, which complicate static analysis. The paper introduces JackEE, a static analyzer that addresses these challenges by layering a framework-independent abstraction over a foundational analysis framework (Doop) and providing per-framework mappings. The authors also tackle scalability issues with a 'sound-modulo-analysis' technique, replacing inefficient library implementations (e.g., HashMap) to improve performance and precision. JackEE demonstrates significant speedups and better precision on large enterprise applications, offering a promising foundation for future research in this domain.
paper_title: Static Analysis of Java Enterprise Applications: Frameworks and Caches, the Elephants in the Room
paper_abstract: CCS Concepts: · Software and its engineering → Compilers; General programming languages; · Theory of computation → Program analysis. Enterprise applications are a major success domain of Java, and Java is the default setting for much modern static analysis research. It would stand to reason that high-quality static analysis of Java enterprise applications would be commonplace, but this is far from true. Major analysis frameworks feature virtually no support for enterprise applications and offer analyses that are woefully incomplete and vastly imprecise, when at all scalable. In this work, we present two techniques for drastically enhancing the completeness and precision of static analysis for Java enterprise applications. The first technique identifies domain-specific concepts underlying all enterprise application frameworks, captures them in an extensible, declarative form, and achieves modeling of components and entry points in a largely framework-independent way. The second technique offers precision and scalability via a sound-moduloanalysis modeling of standard data structures. In realistic enterprise applications (an order of magnitude larger than prior benchmarks in the literature) our techniques achieve high degrees of completeness (on average more than 4x higher than conventional techniques) and speedups of about 6x compared to the most precise conventional analysis, with higher precision on multiple metrics. The result is JackEE, an enterprise analysis framework that can offer precise, high-completeness static modeling of realistic enterprise applications.

blog_summary: The blog post discusses a paper from HPDC'20 that highlights the often-overlooked pitfalls of floating-point arithmetic in scientific computing applications. Adrian Colyer notes that despite the critical role of floating-point operations in these applications, developers frequently neglect the quirks of IEEE 754 representations, such as inaccuracies in representing numbers like 0.1 or 1/3. The paper introduces FPSpy, a tool designed to monitor floating-point operations in unmodified scientific applications by leveraging hardware features to detect exceptional events. The tool operates with minimal overhead and reveals widespread issues like NaNs and division by zero in real-world applications. The authors also demonstrate that rounding errors are pervasive and suggest that targeting a small subset of instructions could mitigate precision loss, potentially improving computational accuracy without modifying the original binaries.
paper_title: Spying on the floating point behavior of existing, unmodified scientific applications
paper_abstract: Scientific (and other) applications are critically dependent on calculations done using IEEE floating point arithmetic. A number of concerns have been raised about correctness in such applications given the numerous gotchas the IEEE standard presents for developers, as well as the complexity of its implementation at the hardware and compiler levels. The standard and its implementations do provide mechanisms for analyzing floating point arithmetic as it executes, making it possible to find and track problematic operations. However, this capability is seldom used in practice. In response, we have developed FPSpy, a tool that provides this capability when operating underneath existing, unmodified x64 application binaries on Linux, including those using thread- and process-level parallelism. FPSpy can observe application behavior without any cooperation from the application or developer, and can potentially be deployed as part of a job launch process. We present the design, implementation, and performance evaluation of FPSpy. FPSpy operates conservatively, getting out of the way if the application itself begins to use any of the OS or hardware features that FPSpy depends on. Its overhead can be throttled, allowing a tradeoff between which and how many unusual events are to be captured, and the slowdown incurred by the application, with the low point providing virtually zero slowdown. We evaluated FPSpy by using it to methodically study seven widely-used applications/frameworks from a range of domains (five of which are in the NSF XSEDE top-20), as well as the NAS and PARSEC benchmark suites. All told, these comprise about 7.5 million lines of source code in a wide range of languages, and parallelism models (including OpenMP and MPI). FPSpy was able to produce trace information for all of them. The traces show that problematic floating point events occur in both the applications and the benchmarks. Analysis of the rounding behavior captured in our traces also suggests th...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a practical problem with floating-point arithmetic in user-facing applications like calculators and spreadsheets, where approximations lead to user complaints and bug reports. The paper introduces a novel real number type that adheres to mathematical expectations, such as exact comparisons and finite decimal displays, addressing issues like non-associative addition and unexpected rounding. The author, Hans-J. Boehm, implements this in the Android calculator app, which saw a significant reduction in user complaints after adoption. The key insight is the use of recursive real arithmetic, which represents numbers as computable functions with error tolerances, enabling exact comparisons in most common cases. The paper also discusses the decidability of equality for recursive reals computed from integer constants using basic arithmetic and transcendental functions, leveraging Richardson and Fitch's work.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this SIGCOMM'20 paper as a critical first measurement study assessing whether real-world 5G deployments live up to their hype. The study, conducted on a commercial 5G network (Non-Standalone Architecture) on a university campus, reveals significant gaps between promised and actual performance. Key findings include poor coverage with 8.07% coverage holes (vs. 3.84% for 4G), severe throughput degradation during handovers (80% drop), and inefficient TCP performance due to mismatched buffer sizes in wireline networks. While 5G achieves lower latency (21.8ms vs. 32% higher on 4G), it still falls short of the 10ms target for real-time applications like VR. The paper emphasizes that 5G's potential requires co-evolution of wireline paths, protocols, and hardware architectures, particularly for indoor coverage and energy efficiency.
paper_title: Understanding operational 5G: a first measurement study on its coverage, performance and energy consumption
paper_abstract: 1 5G, as a monumental shift in cellular communication technology, holds tremendous potential for spurring innovations across many vertical industries, with its promised multi-Gbps speed, sub-10 ms low latency, and massive connectivity. On the other hand, as 5G has been deployed for only a few months, it is unclear how well and whether 5G can eventually meet its prospects. In this paper, we demystify operational 5G networks through a first-of-its-kind crosslayer measurement study. Our measurement focuses on four major perspectives: (i) Physical layer signal quality, coverage and hand-off performance; (ii) End-to-end throughput and latency; (iii) Quality of experience of 5G’s niche applications (e.g., 4K/5.7K panoramic video telephony); (iv) Energy consumption on smartphones. The results reveal that the 5G link itself can approach Gbps throughput, but legacy TCP leads to surprisingly low capacity utilization (< 32%), latency remains too high to support tactile applications and power consumption escalates to 2 − 3× over 4G. Our analysis suggests that the wireline paths, upper-layer protocols, computing and radio hardware architecture need to co-evolve with 5G to form an ecosystem, in order to fully unleash its potential. We are standing on the eve of the 5G era. Major US cellular operators such as Verizon and AT&T already rolled out their first 5G deployment in 2019. Meanwhile, China’s three major mobile service providers officially launched commercial 5G services, and have deployed more than 150 thousand 5G base stations by the end of 2019 [77]. 13.7 million of 5G-enabled smartphones have been sold within less than a year [94]. It is widely reported that 5G represents a giant leap beyond 4G. It is expected to attain multi-Gbps wireless bit-rate for bandwidth-hungry applications like 4K/8K UHD video/VR transmission, ultra reliable and low latency communication (uRLLC) for auto-driving or telesurgery [92] and also the massive machine to machine communication for IoT [66...

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the paper's exploration of 'Orbital Edge Computing' (OEC), a novel approach to satellite systems where clusters of autonomous nanosatellites perform distributed edge computing in space. The author emphasizes the shift from traditional monolithic satellites to nanosatellite constellations, which face severe physical constraints like limited power (7W), bandwidth, and volume. Colyer notes the inefficiency of the 'bent-pipe' architecture, where satellites store data until near a ground station, causing delays up to 5.5 hours. The key insight is that OEC enables onboard processing and intelligent data discard, reducing raw data (e.g., 15GB to 0.75GB) to optimize downlink bandwidth. This allows constellations to scale efficiently, servicing hundreds of satellites per revolution instead of just nine. The paper also introduces 'cote,' a full-system model for OEC, including formation-flying techniques and autonomous control libraries.
paper_title: Orbital Edge Computing: nanosatellite constellations as a new class of computer system
paper_abstract: Advances in nanosatellite technology and a declining cost of access to space have fostered an emergence of large constellations of sensor-equipped satellites in low-Earth orbit. Many of these satellite systems operate under a “bent-pipe” architecture, in which ground stations send commands to orbit and satellites reply with raw data. In this work, we observe that a bent-pipe architecture for Earth-observing satellites breaks down as constellation population increases. Communication is limited by the physical configuration and constraints of the system over time, such as ground station location, nanosatellite antenna size, and energy harvested on orbit. We show quantitatively that nanosatellite constellation capabilities are determined by physical system constraints. We propose an Orbital Edge Computing (OEC) architecture to address the limitations of a bent-pipe architecture. OEC supports edge computing at each camera-equipped nanosatellite so that sensed data may be processed locally when downlinking is not possible. In order to address edge processing latencies, OEC systems organize satellite constellations into computational pipelines. These pipelines parallelize both data collection and data processing based on geographic location and without the need for cross-link coordination. OEC satellites explicitly model constraints of the physical environment via a runtime service. This service uses orbit parameters, physical models, and ground station positions to trigger data collection, predict energy availability, and prepare for communication. We show that an OEC architecture can reduce ground infrastructure over 24× compared to a bent-pipe architecture, and we show that pipelines can reduce system edge processing latency over 617×. blog_summary: The blog post discusses a paper titled 'The case for a learned sorting algorithm' from SIGMOD'20, which introduces Learned Sort, a machine learning-based approach to sorting. The key insight is to use a model to predict the position of elements in a sorted array, reducing the need for traditional sorting algorithms. The author highlights that Learned Sort outperforms RadixSort by 1.49x on a 1 billion item dataset, even when including the model training time. The paper builds on prior work like SageDB and 'The case for learned index structures,' using a Recursive Model Index (RMI) architecture with linear spline fitting for efficient model training and inference. The blog also explores optimizations like cascading bucket sort to improve cache efficiency and reduce random memory accesses, which initially hindered performance. The evaluation demonstrates that Learned Sort is particularly effective when the number of elements is much smaller than the key domain size.
paper_title: The case for a learned sorting algorithm
paper_abstract: 1 Sorting is one of the most fundamental algorithms in Computer Science and a common operation in databases not just for sorting query results but also as part of joins (i.e., sortmerge-join) or indexing. In this work, we introduce a new type of distribution sort that leverages a learned model of the empirical CDF of the data. Our algorithm uses a model to efficiently get an approximation of the scaled empirical CDF for each record key and map it to the corresponding position in the output array. We then apply a deterministic sorting algorithm that works well on nearly-sorted arrays (e.g., Insertion Sort) to establish a totally sorted order. We compared this algorithm against common sorting approaches and measured its performance for up to 1 billion normally-distributed double-precision keys. The results show that our approach yields an average 3.38× performance improvement over C++ STL sort, which is an optimized Quicksort hybrid, 1.49× improvement over sequential Radix Sort, and 5.54× improvement over a C++ implementation of Timsort, which is the default sorting function for Java and Python. Sorting is one of the most fundamental and well-studied problems in Computer Science. Counting-based sorting algorithms, such as Radix Sort, have a complexity of O(wN ) with N being the number of keys and w being the key length and are often the fastest algorithms for small keys. However, for larger key domains comparison-based sorting algorithms are often faster, such as Quicksort or Mergesort, which have a time complexity of O(N log N ), or hybrid algorithms, which combine various comparative and distributive sorting techniques. Those are also the default sorting algorithms used in most standard libraries (i.e., C++ STL sort). In this paper, we introduce a ML-enhanced sorting algorithm by building on our previous work [28]. The core idea of the algorithm is simple: we train a CDF model F over a small sample of keys A and then use the model to predict the position of each key...
