blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Helios as a groundbreaking reference architecture for next-generation distributed big-data processing systems at Microsoft, capturing around a quadrillion events and indexing 16 trillion search keys daily. The paper argues for a shift from traditional cloud-centric architectures to a federated model that 'embraces the edge,' integrating end devices, edge computing, and cloud into a unified data processing platform. Colyer emphasizes the need for this architecture due to growing data volume, velocity, and privacy concerns, as well as latency limitations of centralized systems. The key insight is the concept of 'function spreading' and 'data spreading,' where computation and data are distributed across layers to minimize data movement and improve efficiency. The architecture also aims to unify batch and online processing, reducing the need for duplicated logic and enabling real-time analytics.
paper_title: Helios: Hyperscale Indexing for the Cloud & Edge
paper_abstract: Helios is a distributed, highly-scalable system used at Microsoft for flexible ingestion, indexing, and aggregation of large streams of real-time data that is designed to plug into relational engines. The system collects close to a quadrillion events indexing approximately 16 trillion search keys per day from hundreds of thousands of machines across tens of data centers around the world. Helios use cases within Microsoft include debugging/diagnostics in both public and government clouds, workload characterization, cluster health monitoring, deriving business insights and performing impact analysis of incidents in other large-scale systems such as Azure Data Lake and Cosmos. Helios also serves as a reference blueprint for other large-scale systems within Microsoft. We present the simple data model behind Helios, which offers great flexibility and control over costs, and enables the system to asynchronously index massive streams of data. We also present our experiences in building and operating Helios over the last five years at Microsoft. PVLDB Reference Format: Rahul Potharaju, Terry Kim, Wentao Wu, Vidip Acharya, Steve Suh, Andrew Fogarty, Apoorve Dave, Sinduja Ramanujam, Tomas Talius, Lev Novik, Raghu Ramakrishnan. Helios: Hyperscale Indexing for the Cloud & Edge. PVLDB, 13(12): 3231-3244, 2020. DOI: https://doi.org/10.14778/3415478.3415547

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Helios as a groundbreaking distributed system from Microsoft designed for hyperscale indexing in cloud and edge environments. The paper introduces a novel bottoms-up index construction algorithm that separates ingestion and indexing, enabling efficient handling of massive data streams (up to 16 trillion search keys daily). Key innovations include asynchronous index management for eventual consistency, a multi-level tree-based index structure built bottom-up, and federated indexing that distributes computation between edge agents and central ingestion servers. The system's ability to move computation to the edge while maintaining strong consistency for queries is particularly noteworthy. Colyer also emphasizes Helios' practical impact, with production deployments processing tens of petabytes daily while maintaining low resource overhead on edge machines (15-65% CPU and 1.6GB memory). The paper demonstrates how learned index concepts can be adapted to traditional indexing structures.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Delos, a system developed by Facebook to address the challenge of rapidly deploying a consensus-based table store for core control plane services while ensuring durability, consistency, and availability. The key insight is the introduction of a virtual shared log (VirtualLog) abstraction, which acts as an indirection layer over existing consensus implementations (Loglets). This allows Facebook to initially deploy with a ZooKeeper-backed Loglet and later hot-swap it with a custom-built NativeLoglet, achieving a 10x improvement in end-to-end latency without disrupting operations. The VirtualLog chains multiple Loglets into a single logical log, enabling seamless upgrades and reconfiguration. Colyer emphasizes the elegance of separating reconfiguration complexity into the VirtualLog control plane, simplifying Loglet implementations to focus solely on the data plane. The system's ability to seal Loglets and reconfigure via a MetaStore is noted as a powerful and practical solution.
paper_title: Virtual Consensus in Delos
paper_abstract: Consensus-based replicated systems are complex, monolithic, and difficult to upgrade once deployed. As a result, deployed systems do not benefit from innovative research, and new consensus protocols rarely reach production. We propose virtualizing consensus by virtualizing the shared log API, allowing services to change consensus protocols without downtime. Virtualization splits the logic of consensus into the VirtualLog, a generic and reusable reconfiguration layer; and pluggable ordering protocols called Loglets. Loglets are simple, since they do not need to support reconfiguration or leader election; diverse, consisting of different protocols, codebases, and even deployment modes; and composable, via RAID-like stacking and striping. We describe a production database called Delos1 which leverages virtual consensus for rapid, incremental development and deployment. Delos reached production within 8 months, and 4 months later upgraded its consensus protocol without downtime for a 10X latency improvement. Delos can dynamically change its performance properties by changing consensus protocols: we can scale throughput by up to 10X by switching to a disaggregated Loglet, and double the failure threshold of an instance without sacrificing throughput via a striped Loglet.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Pigasus as a groundbreaking example of pushing the limits of single-server performance, particularly in the domain of Intrusion Detection/Prevention Systems (IDS/IPS). The paper demonstrates how an FPGA-first design can achieve 100 Gbps throughput on a single server, inverting the traditional CPU-centric approach where accelerators are subordinate. The key insight is that FPGAs, when placed in charge of the primary compute pipeline, can handle stateful packet processing tasks like reassembly and multi-string pattern matching (MSPM) far more efficiently than traditional CPU-based systems. The paper also reveals the trade-offs and design decisions, such as offloading regular expression matching to the CPU to conserve FPGA memory (BRAM) and using a hybrid fast/slow path for reassembly to handle out-of-order packets within tight memory constraints. The architecture leverages a DMA engine to coordinate between the FPGA and CPU, ensuring low latency and high throughput.
paper_title: Achieving 100 Gbps Intrusion Prevention on a Single Server
paper_abstract: Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDS/IPS) are among the most demanding stateful network functions. Today’s network operators are faced with securing 100Gbps networks with 100K+ concurrent connections by deploying IDS/IPSes to search for 10K+ rules concurrently. In this paper we set an ambitious goal: Can we do all of the above in a single server? Through the Pigasus IDS/IPS, we show that this goal is achievable, perhaps for the first time, by building on recent advances in FPGA-capable SmartNICs. Pigasus’ design takes an FPGA-first approach, where the majority of processing, and all state and control flow are managed on the FPGA. However, doing so requires careful design of algorithms and data structures to ensure fast common-case performance while densely utilizing system memory resources. Our experiments with a variety of traces show that Pigasus can support 100Gbps using an average of 5 cores and 1 FPGA, using 38× less power than a CPU-only approach.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Elle, a new checker in the Jepsen family, designed to detect isolation anomalies in databases with unprecedented efficiency. Unlike its predecessor Knossos, which struggles with histories of hundreds of transactions due to NP-completeness, Elle can handle hundreds of thousands of transactions in tens of seconds. The paper introduces Elle's methodology, which infers Direct Serialization Graphs (DSGs) from observable transaction operations (reads, writes, commits) by leveraging recoverability and traceability properties. Elle uses these inferred DSGs to detect cycles, representing anomalies, and provides minimal reproducible bug reports. The evaluation demonstrates Elle's effectiveness by uncovering unexpected anomalies in multiple databases (TiDB, YugaByteDB, Fauna, Dgraph). The key insight is that by controlling the transaction process and using recoverable/traceable datatypes, Elle can reconstruct dependency edges and efficiently check for isolation violations.
paper_title: Elle: Inferring Isolation Anomalies from Experimental Observations
paper_abstract: Users who care about their data store it in databases, which (at least in principle) guarantee some form of transactional isolation. However, experience shows that many databases do not provide the isolation guarantees they claim. With the recent proliferation of new distributed databases, demand has grown for checkers that can, by generating client workloads and injecting faults, produce anomalies that witness a violation of a stated guarantee. An ideal checker would be sound (no false positives), efficient (polynomial in history length and concurrency), effective (finding violations in real databases), general (analyzing many patterns of transactions), and informative (justifying the presence of an anomaly with understandable counterexamples). Sadly, we are aware of no checkers that satisfy these goals. We present Elle: a novel checker which infers an Adya-style dependency graph between client-observed transactions. It does so by carefully selecting database objects and operations when generating histories, so as to ensure that the results of database reads reveal information about their version history. Elle can detect every anomaly in Adya et al’s formalism (except for predicates), discriminate between them, and provide concise explanations of each. This paper makes the following contributions: we present Elle, demonstrate its soundness over specific datatypes, measure its efficiency against the current state of the art, and give evidence of its effectiveness via a case study of four real databases. PVLDB Reference Format: Kyle Kingsbury and Peter Alvaro. Elle: Inferring Isolation Anomalies from Experimental Observations. PVLDB, 14(3): 268 - 280, 2021. doi:10.14778/3430915.3430918 PVLDB Artifact Availability: The source code, data, and/or other artifacts have been made available at https://github.com/jepsen-io/jepsen.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights 'Seeing is believing' as a groundbreaking paper that redefines database isolation levels from a client-centric perspective. Instead of defining isolation based on internal database mechanisms (e.g., serialization graphs), Crooks et al. propose a state-based formalization that focuses on externally observable states and read operations. This approach aligns isolation guarantees with what applications actually see, making it easier for developers to understand and reason about database behavior. The paper introduces a novel framework where isolation levels are specified in terms of admissible states and parent states, offering implementors greater flexibility while clarifying the guarantees for users. Colyer emphasizes the elegance of this idea, noting that prior definitions (including Adya's) were overly constrained by implementation concerns. The paper also reveals performance optimization opportunities by decoupling external guarantees from internal implementations.
paper_title: Seeing is believing: a client-centric specification of database isolation
paper_abstract: This paper introduces the first state-based formalization of isolation guarantees. Our approach is premised on a simple observation: applications view storage systems as black-boxes that transition through a series of states, a subset of which are observed by applications. Defining isolation guarantees in terms of these states frees definitions from implementation-specific assumptions. It makes immediately clear what anomalies, if any, applications can expect to observe, thus bridging the gap that exists today between how isolation guarantees are defined and how they are perceived. The clarity that results from definitions based on client-observable states brings forth several benefits. First, it allows us to easily compare the guarantees of distinct, but semantically close, isolation guarantees. We find that several well-known guarantees, previously thought to be distinct, are in fact equivalent, and that many previously incomparable flavors of snapshot isolation can be organized in a clean hierarchy. Second, freeing definitions from implementation-specific artefacts can suggest more efficient implementations of the same isolation guarantee. We show how a client-centric implementation of parallel snapshot isolation can be more resilient to slowdown cascades, a common phenomenon in large-scale datacenters. ACM Reference format: Natacha Crooks, Youer Pu, Lorenzo Alvisi, and Allen Clement. 2017. Seeing is Believing: A Client-Centric Specification of Database Isolation. In Proceedings of PODC ’17, Washington, DC, USA, July 25-27, 2017, 30 pages. http://dx.doi.org/10.1145/3087801.3087802

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a study that examines bias in word embeddings and its propagation into downstream machine learning models. The paper demonstrates that word embeddings trained on corpora like Wikipedia or social media embed societal biases, which are then perpetuated in models using these embeddings. The authors show that bias can be measured (e.g., via cosine distance between gendered word pairs) and is particularly insidious because embeddings strip words of their original context, freezing bias into static representations. The study also explores mitigation strategies, finding that debiasing at the classifier level is more effective than at the embedding level, as the latter may leave uncorrected biases intact. Additionally, the paper shows that biased embeddings can be repurposed to detect bias in new text samples, achieving high accuracy in classifying sexist comments when trained on similarly biased embeddings.
paper_title: Bias in word embeddings
paper_abstract: Social bias in language — towards genders, ethnicities, ages, and other social groups — poses a problem with ethical impact for many NLP applications. Recent research has shown that machine learning models trained on respective data may not only adopt, but even amplify the bias. So far, however, little attention has been paid to bias in computational argumentation. In this paper, we study the existence of social biases in large English debate portals. In particular, we train word embedding models on portal-specific corpora and systematically evaluate their bias using W EAT, an existing metric to measure bias in word embeddings. In a word co-occurrence analysis, we then investigate causes of bias. The results suggest that all tested debate corpora contain unbalanced and biased data, mostly in favor of male people with European-American names. Our empirical insights contribute towards an understanding of bias in argumentative data sources.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this ACM Computing Surveys paper as an excellent overview of entity resolution (ER), also known as record linking, a critical component in modern data workflows. The blog post emphasizes the complexity of scaling ER, which inherently requires quadratic comparisons, and breaks down the ER pipeline into key stages: blocking, block processing, matching, and clustering. Colyer notes the survey's thorough exploration of schema-aware vs. schema-less approaches, traditional batch processing vs. incremental methods, and the trade-offs between different techniques like token blocking and canopy clustering. He also appreciates the survey's classification of ER solutions along three dimensions and its detailed discussion of collective-based matching and advanced clustering methods like Markov Clustering. The key insight is the importance of redundancy in blocking to reduce computational overhead and the iterative nature of collective ER to uncover indirect matches.

blog_summary: Adrian Colyer announces the end of 'The Morning Paper' blog after six and a half years, reflecting on how the COVID-19 lockdowns disrupted his routines and expanded his intellectual interests beyond computer science. He highlights a fascinating analogy from a BBC podcast about ant pheromone trails and how disruption can lead to new solutions, drawing parallels to societal changes post-lockdown. Colyer expresses uncertainty about returning to a computer science-exclusive focus in the future. Before concluding, he points readers to an exciting research project from Berkeley's RISELab, led by Joe Hellerstein, which explores programmable cloud systems as the next evolution beyond serverless computing. The project, including the 'PACT' paper, represents a new chapter in cloud programming research.
paper_title: New Directions in Cloud Programming
paper_abstract: The declarative nature of the relational model and database engines shields users from system implementation complexity, system evolution, data representation details, and enables optimizations across workloads and use cases. However, recent trends in data management introduce significant challenges to declarative interfaces. For instance, these days, the engine might not own the data (e.g., data lakes), might have to deal with different data representations (e.g., CSV, Arrow, Parquet, Iceberg), and needs to support operations beyond relational SQL (e.g., vector databases, machine learning). To complicate matters, in the cloud, many layers of infrastructure — virtual machines (VMs), container schedulers, general-purpose OSes — stand between the engine and the compute/storage/network fabric. Today’s cloud infrastructure exposes only low-level, VMcentric knobs and treats analytics workloads as opaque binaries, leaving the engine with little visibility into data placement, hardware availability, and network congestion. We propose to extend the declarative approach to data management end-to-end. We start from a composite database engine and extend its declarative interfaces (SQL and query plans) down to the cloud execution layer. The database engine exposes each query as a dataflow graph, composed of functions (operators) that each declare their inputs, outputs, and available parallelism to the cloud platform. The cloud platform takes this graph as input and provides a declarative execution substrate responsible for resource scaling, data and operator placement, caching, and isolation mechanism implementation decisions. Our early prototype shows how rethinking the interface between the engine and the cloud platform enables elastic data-dependent parallel execution over data lakes, automatic caching, and opens new research directions for cloud analytics.

figures.title: Evolution of data analytics engine architecture
figures.caption: Figure 1: Evolution of data analytics engine architecture from (a) a monolithic engine that owns data on local storage and manages a buffer cache to (b) a composite engine running on cloud VMs that ingests data from disaggregated storage to (c) our proposal of co-designing the engine with declarative cloud infrastructure, enabling data-dependent parallel execution and ingestion from data lakes, elastic caching, and more.
